docs.title: CF-08: Garden Container Runtime and Network Namespaces
docs.text: Track: CF-B — CF Internals and Container Networking Duration: ~45 min (Deep Dive) / ~10 min (Quick Read) Prerequisites: CF-01 through CF-07, Linux namespace fundamentals

docs.title: Quick Read (10 min)
docs.text:
What Garden is: - Garden is the container runtime for Cloud Foundry, analogous to containerd in Kubernetes - It runs on every Diego Cell and is managed by the garden-runc process - Each CF app instance = one Garden container = one set of Linux namespaces

Network namespace basics in CF: - Garden creates a dedicated network namespace per container at startup - Silk CNI plugin wires the namespace into the VXLAN overlay (10.255.0.0/16) - Each Diego Cell gets a /24 subnet; up to ~254 containers per Cell - Container gets: one eth0 (overlay), one lo, default route via Cell's vtep

Key isolation layers: - Mount namespace: private rootfs (GrootFS layered image) - PID namespace: container sees only its own processes - Network namespace: private stack, routes, iptables chains - User namespace: optional, maps container root → unprivileged host UID - UTS namespace: independent hostname

iptables roles in CF: - ASG (Application Security Group) rules → netout-* chains, enforced per container - C2C policy rules → cni-forward chain, managed by VXLAN Policy Agent - SNAT rule → outbound traffic masquerades as Diego Cell IP

graph TD
    A[App Instance] -->|eth0 10.255.x.y| B[veth pair]
    B --> C[silk-vtep bridge on Diego Cell]
    C -->|VXLAN UDP 4789| D[Underlay Network]
    D --> E[Other Diego Cell silk-vtep]
    E --> F[Target Container eth0]
    C -->|SNAT to Cell IP| G[Gorouter / External]

What you need to know fast: - Garden containers use runc under the hood — same OCI runtime as K8s pods - Network setup is done by the CNI plugin at container create time, not at startup - Silk CNI writes routes and iptables rules; Garden itself is CNI-agnostic - bosh ssh to a Diego Cell, then runc list or ip netns list to inspect containers - MTU = underlay MTU - 50 (VXLAN overhead); misconfigured MTU is the #1 silent networking bug

K8s Engineer's Translation: Garden is to CF what containerd + kubelet are to Kubernetes. Garden creates containers; a CNI plugin (Silk) handles all networking. The "Garden container" maps directly to a K8s pod with one container. Linux namespaces are identical at the kernel level.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
You need two terminals for this lesson.

Terminal 1 — BOSH SSH (Diego Cell kernel inspection)

# Target your BOSH environment
bosh -e my-env -d cf-deployment ssh diego-cell/0

# Once inside the Diego Cell:
sudo -i
runc list                          # list all running containers (Garden handles)
ip netns list                      # list network namespaces
ls /var/vcap/data/garden/depot/    # Garden container directories

Terminal 2 — CF CLI (app-level operations)

# Target your CF environment
cf api https://api.sys.example.com
cf login

# Push a test app for inspection
cf push nettest -o cloudfoundry/test-app --no-start
cf set-env nettest GOPACKAGENAME main
cf start nettest

# Get the app GUID — needed to correlate with Garden container ID
cf app nettest --guid

docs.title: 1. Garden Container Runtime Architecture
docs.text:
Garden is the Cloud Foundry container runtime daemon. It runs as a BOSH-deployed process on every Diego Cell and exposes the Garden API over a Unix socket. Diego's executor component calls Garden to create, manage, and destroy containers for every app instance and task.

graph TB
    subgraph "Diego Cell"
        CELL_REP[Diego Cell Rep] -->|Garden API calls| GARDEN[Garden Server\n/var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock]
        GARDEN -->|fork+exec| RUNC[runc OCI runtime]
        GARDEN -->|rootfs layers| GROOTFS[GrootFS\noverlay filesystem]
        GARDEN -->|CNI plugin exec| SILK_CNI[silk-cni binary]
        RUNC -->|create namespace set| NS[Linux Namespaces\nmnt/pid/net/uts/ipc]
        SILK_CNI -->|configure network| NETNS[Container netns\neth0 + iptables]
        GROOTFS -->|layer cache| BTRFS[Btrfs or Overlay2\n/var/vcap/data/grootfs]
    end
    subgraph "BBS / Auctioneer"
        AUCTIONEER -->|LRP scheduling| CELL_REP
    end

Garden server process: /var/vcap/jobs/garden/bin/garden_ctl

The Garden server listens on a Unix socket (/var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock) and exposes a garden-api (a simple HTTP+JSON API). Diego's executor calls endpoints like POST /containers to create a container, PUT /containers/:handle/run to execute processes, and DELETE /containers/:handle to destroy.

Container handles: Garden identifies each container by a UUID handle. This handle maps one-to-one to the Diego LRP instance GUID and is also used as the container directory name under /var/vcap/data/garden/depot/.

# On Diego Cell: list running containers with their handles
curl --unix-socket /var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock \
     http://localhost/containers | python3 -m json.tool

# Or use the gaol CLI (Garden API Object List)
# gaol is the Garden equivalent of crictl/ctr
gaol -t unix:///var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock list
gaol -t unix:///var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock properties <handle>

K8s Engineer's Translation: Garden is functionally equivalent to containerd's CRI endpoint. The Garden API socket (garden.sock) is the analog of the containerd socket (containerd.sock). gaol list is equivalent to crictl ps. The Diego Cell Rep is the analog of kubelet — it talks to the local container runtime to manage instance lifecycle.

GrootFS — layered image filesystem:

GrootFS manages the OCI image layers that form each container's rootfs. It uses either overlay2 or btrfs as the backend. When a container is created, GrootFS:

  1. Downloads the application droplet (the compiled app artifact) and stack image layers
  2. Stacks them using an overlay mount
  3. Creates a unique read-write layer for the container
# Inspect GrootFS stores on a Diego Cell
ls /var/vcap/data/grootfs/store/unprivileged/images/
ls /var/vcap/data/grootfs/store/unprivileged/volumes/

# Get disk usage per container image
/var/vcap/packages/grootfs/bin/grootfs \
  --config /var/vcap/jobs/garden/config/grootfs_config.yml \
  stats <image-id>

docs.title: 2. Linux Namespace Creation and Network Namespace Wiring
docs.text:
When Garden creates a container, it invokes runc to set up the full namespace set. The network namespace is initially empty — it has only the loopback interface. Garden then calls the configured CNI plugin (Silk CNI in standard CF deployments) to wire in networking.

Namespace creation sequence:

1. runc create <handle>
   - new mnt namespace  (private rootfs via GrootFS overlay)
   - new pid namespace  (container PID 1 = app process)
   - new net namespace  (empty: only lo)
   - new uts namespace  (hostname = container handle)
   - new ipc namespace

2. CNI plugin exec: silk-cni ADD
   - create veth pair (eth0 in container, cni-<id> on host)
   - assign IP from /24 Cell subnet (e.g. 10.255.42.3/24)
   - set default route: 10.255.42.1 via eth0
   - create/join silk-vtep bridge on host side
   - program VXLAN FDB entries
   - install iptables rules: netout (ASG), netin, SNAT

3. runc start <handle>
   - process begins executing inside all namespaces

Inspecting network namespaces from the Diego Cell:

# List all network namespaces (each Garden container has one)
ip netns list

# Garden container net namespaces are in /proc/<pid>/ns/net
# Find the PID of a container process given a handle
HANDLE="<garden-container-handle>"
CONTAINER_PID=$(cat /var/vcap/data/garden/depot/${HANDLE}/state.json \
                | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d['pid'])")

# Enter the container's network namespace
nsenter --net=/proc/${CONTAINER_PID}/ns/net ip addr show
nsenter --net=/proc/${CONTAINER_PID}/ns/net ip route show
nsenter --net=/proc/${CONTAINER_PID}/ns/net iptables -L -n -v

# View the container's iptables rules (ASG enforcement chains)
nsenter --net=/proc/${CONTAINER_PID}/ns/net iptables -L netout-<handle-short> -n -v

What you will see inside the container's netns:

# ip addr show inside container netns
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 ...
    inet 127.0.0.1/8
2: eth0@if47: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1450 ...
    inet 10.255.42.3/24

# ip route show inside container netns
default via 169.254.0.1 dev eth0
10.255.0.0/16 via 169.254.0.1 dev eth0

Note the gateway 169.254.0.1 — this is a link-local address assigned to the host-side veth. Silk uses this trick to avoid consuming overlay IP space for the gateway.

K8s Engineer's Translation: In Kubernetes, the kubelet calls the CNI plugin to wire a pod's network namespace in exactly the same sequence: create netns, exec CNI ADD, then start containers. The veth pair + bridge model is identical to Flannel or Calico with VXLAN. The main difference is that CF uses 169.254.0.1 as a fake gateway on the host-side veth, while most K8s CNIs assign a real IP to the bridge interface.

MTU considerations:

The MTU inside every CF container is set to: underlay_mtu - 50

VXLAN encapsulation adds an outer UDP header (8 bytes), outer IP header (20 bytes), VXLAN header (8 bytes), and outer Ethernet header (14 bytes) = 50 bytes total overhead.

# Verify MTU on the container's eth0
nsenter --net=/proc/${CONTAINER_PID}/ns/net ip link show eth0
# Should show: mtu 1450 if underlay MTU is 1500

# Verify MTU on the host-side vtep
ip link show silk-vtep
# Should also show mtu 1450

# Check Garden/Silk configuration for MTU
cat /var/vcap/jobs/silk-cni/config/cni.conf | python3 -m json.tool
# Look for "mtu": 1450

Mismatched MTU is the most common silent performance bug: TCP sessions work but throughput is degraded because IP fragmentation occurs silently on the underlay.

docs.title: 3. Silk CNI Internals and VXLAN Policy Agent
docs.text:
Silk CNI plugin layout:

Silk is CF's purpose-built CNI plugin. It consists of several cooperating processes:

Process Role silk-controller Central IP address management (runs on control plane VMs) silk-daemon Per-Cell agent; leases /24 subnet from controller; programs VXLAN FDB silk-cni CNI plugin binary; called by Garden at container create/destroy vxlan-policy-agent Per-Cell agent; polls Policy Server; pushes C2C iptables rules 
# On Diego Cell: check silk-daemon health
monit summary | grep silk
curl http://127.0.0.1:23954/state | python3 -m json.tool
# Shows: overlay subnet assigned to this Cell, VTEP IP, lease expiry

# Check which subnet this Cell owns
cat /var/vcap/data/silk/client-state.json
# Example: {"subnet":"10.255.42.0/24","vtep_ip":"10.0.1.5","overlay_ip":"10.255.42.1"}

# Inspect VXLAN FDB (forwarding database) — where other Cells' VTEPs are
bridge fdb show dev silk-vtep
# Each line: <mac> dst <cell-underlay-ip> self permanent

VXLAN Policy Agent and C2C rules:

The VXLAN Policy Agent runs on each Diego Cell and is responsible for C2C (container-to-container) network policy enforcement. It polls the CF Policy Server every 5 seconds and translates network policies into iptables rules inside each container's network namespace.

# Check Policy Agent health
curl http://127.0.0.1:4007/stats | python3 -m json.tool

# View current C2C iptables rules installed by Policy Agent
# These are in the FORWARD chain on the host, keyed by overlay IP
iptables -L FORWARD -n -v | grep cni
iptables -L cni-forward -n -v

# Policy Agent log — shows policy polling and rule updates
tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/vxlan-policy-agent/vxlan-policy-agent.stdout.log

How a C2C policy becomes a packet filter:

CF API: cf add-network-policy frontend --destination-app backend --port 8080 --protocol tcp

Policy Server stores:
  source_app_id:      <frontend-guid>
  destination_app_id: <backend-guid>
  protocol:           tcp
  port:               8080

VXLAN Policy Agent on each Cell polls Policy Server →
  resolves app GUID → overlay IPs of running instances →
  generates iptables rule per container netns:

iptables -A cni-forward -s 10.255.11.3 -d 10.255.42.7 -p tcp --dport 8080 -j ACCEPT

K8s Engineer's Translation: The CF Policy Server + VXLAN Policy Agent is the analog of a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy controller (e.g., Calico Felix or Cilium agent). The policy is stored centrally, translated to kernel-level iptables/eBPF rules per node, and enforced in-kernel. The key CF difference: policies are defined by app GUID (not IP), so they survive app redeploys and IP changes automatically. K8s NetworkPolicy uses pod label selectors instead.

Overlay vs underlay routing:

# On Diego Cell: show the routing table
ip route show

# Key routes:
# 10.255.0.0/16 dev silk-vtep  — all overlay traffic goes to VTEP
# 10.255.42.0/24 dev silk-cni-eth0  — local Cell containers (no VXLAN needed)

# Packet path for cross-Cell C2C:
# container eth0 → veth → silk-vtep → VXLAN encap → underlay → remote silk-vtep → remote container eth0

# Packet path for same-Cell C2C:
# container eth0 → veth → bridge → remote container veth → remote eth0
# No VXLAN — hairpin bridging within the Cell

docs.title: Common Failure Modes
docs.text:
Failure 1: Container fails to start with network error

Symptom: cf logs myapp --recent shows "Failed to create container" or timeout.

# On Diego Cell: check Garden logs
tail -100 /var/vcap/sys/log/garden/garden.stdout.log | grep -i error

# Check CNI plugin logs
tail -100 /var/vcap/sys/log/silk-cni/silk-cni.stdout.log

# Check if silk-daemon has a valid subnet lease
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:23954/state | python3 -m json.tool
# If "subnet" is empty, silk-daemon cannot reach silk-controller

# Check silk-controller reachability from the Cell
curl -s https://<silk-controller-ip>:4103/leases/renew

Failure 2: Containers can reach external IPs but not each other (C2C broken)

Symptom: cf add-network-policy is set, but curl between apps times out.

# Step 1: verify the policy is registered
cf network-policies

# Step 2: check Policy Agent is running and polling
monit summary | grep vxlan
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4007/stats

# Step 3: check that rules exist in iptables for the container
# Get overlay IPs of both containers
nsenter --net=/proc/${SRC_PID}/ns/net ip addr show eth0
nsenter --net=/proc/${DST_PID}/ns/net ip addr show eth0

# Step 4: look for the specific rule
iptables -L cni-forward -n -v | grep <dst-overlay-ip>
# If missing: Policy Agent did not translate the policy to this Cell

# Step 5: check Policy Server reachability
curl -sk https://<policy-server-ip>:4003/networking/v1/internal/policies

Failure 3: MTU mismatch — high packet loss or TCP stalls

Symptom: HTTP requests succeed for small payloads, fail or stall for large responses (file downloads, large JSON).

# Verify MTU inside container matches expected value
nsenter --net=/proc/${CONTAINER_PID}/ns/net ip link show eth0
# Expected: mtu 1450 (for 1500 underlay)

# Check actual underlay MTU on the Cell's NIC
ip link show eth0  # or ens4, enp1s0 — the Cell's physical/VM NIC
# If this shows 9000 (jumbo frames), container MTU should be 8950

# Test with explicit MTU: ping with large packet from inside container
nsenter --net=/proc/${CONTAINER_PID}/ns/net \
  ping -M do -s 1422 10.255.0.1
# -M do: don't fragment; -s 1422 = 1422 bytes payload + 28 IP/ICMP header = 1450 total

# Fix: update silk-cni config and recreate containers
# /var/vcap/jobs/silk-cni/config/cni.conf: "mtu": <correct value>
# Then bosh restart diego-cell (rolling)

Failure 4: Container IP address exhaustion on a Cell

Symptom: New containers fail to start on a specific Cell with "no available IP" errors.

# Check how many containers are running on the Cell
runc list | wc -l
# Silk /24 gives 254 usable IPs; if you're near that, you need more Cells

# Check the allocated IPs
# VTEP's ARP table shows all container IPs on this Cell
arp -n | grep 10.255.<cell-subnet>

# If you are using the full /24, the Cell is at capacity
# Resolution: scale Diego Cells (bosh deploy with higher instance count)
# or investigate stuck containers that failed to be cleaned up

# Find zombie/stuck containers
runc list | grep stopped
# Destroy a stuck container
runc delete <handle>

Failure 5: ASG rules not taking effect

Symptom: App cannot reach an external endpoint that an ASG should allow.

# Step 1: verify ASG is bound correctly
cf security-groups
cf security-group <sg-name>
cf running-security-groups

# Step 2: check ASG rules are in iptables inside container
nsenter --net=/proc/${CONTAINER_PID}/ns/net \
  iptables -L netout-<handle-prefix> -n -v
# Should show ACCEPT rules matching the ASG JSON spec

# Step 3: test connectivity from inside container
# Using cf ssh
cf ssh myapp -c "curl -v https://target-host:443"

# Step 4: check if the destination is blocked by default ASG
# Default ASGs: dns (allow port 53), public_networks (block RFC1918)
# If your target is RFC1918, you need a custom Running ASG

# Step 5: check dynamic ASG update (cf-deployment v20.0.0+)
# ASG changes apply without restart — verify with:
cf update-security-group <sg-name> updated-rules.json
# Wait up to 60s, then re-test without restarting the app

Diagnostic command quick reference:

# Garden container state
gaol -t unix:///var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock list
gaol -t unix:///var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock info <handle>

# Network namespace for a specific container
runc state <handle>  # gives PID
nsenter --net=/proc/<pid>/ns/net ip addr
nsenter --net=/proc/<pid>/ns/net ip route
nsenter --net=/proc/<pid>/ns/net iptables -L -n -v

# Silk overlay state
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:23954/state | python3 -m json.tool
bridge fdb show dev silk-vtep
ip -d link show silk-vtep  # show VXLAN config (VNI, port, group)

# VXLAN Policy Agent
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4007/stats
iptables -L cni-forward -n -v

# ASG rules inside container
nsenter --net=/proc/<pid>/ns/net iptables -L netout-<short-handle> -n -v

# Packet capture on VTEP (see all VXLAN traffic)
tcpdump -i silk-vtep -n -s0 -w /tmp/silk-vtep.pcap
# Capture on underlay to see encapsulated frames
tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 -w /tmp/vxlan-raw.pcap

K8s Engineer's Translation: CF troubleshooting follows exactly the same pattern as K8s CNI debugging: get the PID of the container process, enter its network namespace with nsenter, then use standard Linux tools (ip, iptables, ss, ping). The difference is how you find the container PID: in K8s you use crictl inspect <container-id> | jq .info.pid; in CF you use runc state <garden-handle> or read the Garden depot state file.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm MTU is set correctly on all Diego Cells: container MTU = underlay MTU - 50
  • Verify silk-daemon has a valid subnet lease on every Cell: curl http://127.0.0.1:23954/state
  • Confirm VXLAN Policy Agent is running and showing recent poll timestamps on every Cell
  • Review Cell capacity: each Cell is limited to ~254 containers (/24 overlay subnet)
  • Ensure default Running ASGs cover required egress (DNS on 53 at minimum)
  • Confirm dynamic ASG updates are enabled (cf-deployment v20.0.0+) to avoid app restarts for policy changes
  • Add custom Running ASG if apps need to reach RFC1918 addresses (blocked by default public_networks ASG)
  • Verify Garden disk quota is configured appropriately to prevent one app consuming all GrootFS volume
  • Test C2C connectivity end-to-end after any Diego Cell rolling restart
  • Monitor cni-forward iptables chain size on heavily-loaded Cells — large policy sets can slow iptables traversal
  • Confirm Garden ephemeral disk cleanup is not falling behind: check /var/vcap/data/grootfs/store/ disk usage
  • Validate that cross-Cell VXLAN traffic is not blocked by underlay firewall rules (UDP 4789 must be open between all Cells)
  • Check Garden process file descriptor limits on cells hosting many containers: ulimit -n should be 65536+

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command List all Garden containers on a Cell gaol -t unix:///var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock list Get container details (IPs, state) gaol -t unix:///var/vcap/sys/run/garden/garden.sock info <handle> Find container PID from handle runc state <handle> \| python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d['pid'])" Enter container network namespace nsenter --net=/proc/<pid>/ns/net <command> Show container IP address nsenter --net=/proc/<pid>/ns/net ip addr show eth0 Show container routes nsenter --net=/proc/<pid>/ns/net ip route Show container ASG iptables rules nsenter --net=/proc/<pid>/ns/net iptables -L netout-<handle> -n -v Show C2C policy iptables rules iptables -L cni-forward -n -v Check silk-daemon subnet lease curl -s http://127.0.0.1:23954/state \| python3 -m json.tool Show VXLAN FDB (Cell-to-Cell mapping) bridge fdb show dev silk-vtep Check VXLAN Policy Agent stats curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4007/stats Capture VXLAN overlay traffic tcpdump -i silk-vtep -n -s0 Capture raw VXLAN encapsulated traffic tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 List CF network policies cf network-policies Add C2C network policy cf add-network-policy <src-app> --destination-app <dst-app> --port <port> --protocol tcp Check running security groups cf running-security-groups Get app GUID cf app <name> --guid Check Garden logs tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/garden/garden.stdout.log Check Silk CNI logs tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/silk-cni/silk-cni.stdout.log Check Policy Agent logs tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/vxlan-policy-agent/vxlan-policy-agent.stdout.log List GrootFS images ls /var/vcap/data/grootfs/store/unprivileged/images/ Get GrootFS disk stats for image /var/vcap/packages/grootfs/bin/grootfs --config /var/vcap/jobs/garden/config/grootfs_config.yml stats <id>

docs.title: CF-09 — Gorouter: HTTP Routing Architecture
docs.text: Track: CF-C — Ingress and Routing Prerequisite: CF-02 (Garden Container Networking), CF-04 (Silk CNI) or equivalent Companion K8s lessons: Lesson 15 — Ingress Controllers, Lesson 16 — Gateway API, Lesson 19 — Service Mesh TLS

docs.title: Quick Read (10 min)
docs.text:
What Gorouter is: CF's built-in HTTP/WebSocket L7 reverse proxy. Every inbound request to any cf push-deployed app flows through one or more Gorouter instances sitting behind a load balancer. No Nginx, no Envoy, no Ingress YAML required — Gorouter is the platform's answer to all of those.

Key mental model:

  • Gorouter holds an in-memory routing table: hostname → [{ cell_ip:port, instance_id }, ...]
  • Routes are registered via NATS (pub/sub message bus), not etcd or a K8s API — there is no persistent route store
  • Route Emitter (on each Diego Cell) publishes router.register NATS messages every 20 seconds; Gorouter sets TTL of 2 minutes per route entry
  • If a Route Emitter stops, routes expire from the table within 2 minutes — traffic drops silently
  • Gorouter uses round-robin across all healthy app instances for a given route; sticky sessions via JSESSIONID cookie are supported
  • TLS modes: edge termination (default), passthrough, or full re-encrypt to containers
  • WebSocket upgrade is supported — the Upgrade: websocket header triggers a connection hijack

Gorouter in one diagram:

flowchart LR
    client["External Client\nHTTPS :443"]
    lb["Load Balancer\n(IaaS L4)"]
    gr1["Gorouter 1\n(in-memory route table)"]
    gr2["Gorouter 2\n(in-memory route table)"]
    nats["NATS Message Bus\n(route registration)"]
    re1["Route Emitter\n(Diego Cell 1)"]
    re2["Route Emitter\n(Diego Cell 2)"]
    app1["App Instance 0\nCell1 IP:61001"]
    app2["App Instance 1\nCell2 IP:61002"]

    client -->|"TLS SNI"| lb
    lb -->|"round-robin"| gr1 & gr2
    gr1 & gr2 <-->|"NATS sub router.register"| nats
    re1 & re2 -->|"NATS pub router.register\nevery 20s"| nats
    re1 --- app1
    re2 --- app2
    gr1 -->|"HTTP X-CF-InstanceID"| app1
    gr1 -->|"HTTP X-CF-InstanceID"| app2

CF vs K8s translation (Quick Read):

CF Concept K8s Equivalent Gorouter Ingress Controller (nginx/Envoy/Contour) NATS route registration Ingress resource + controller reconcile loop Route Emitter Endpoints controller cf map-route kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml Sticky session via JSESSIONID nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity: cookie TCP Router Service type=NodePort / LoadBalancer (non-HTTP)

What you will learn in the Deep Dive: how Gorouter's routing table is built and maintained, the full NATS registration flow, TLS termination modes, sticky sessions, WebSocket handling, TCP Router for non-HTTP traffic, and how to diagnose route registration failures.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
You need two terminals for every exercise in this lesson.

Terminal 1 — cf CLI (your laptop or jumpbox)

cf api https://api.cf.example.com --skip-ssl-validation
cf login -u admin
cf target -o myorg -s myspace

# Confirm Gorouter is reachable
curl -sk https://api.cf.example.com/v2/info | jq '.routing_endpoint'

Terminal 2 — BOSH SSH into the Gorouter VM

# List deployments
bosh -e my-env deployments

# Find Gorouter VMs
bosh -e my-env -d cf vms | grep router

# SSH into the first Gorouter
bosh -e my-env -d cf ssh router/0

# Once inside — Gorouter runs as a BOSH job
sudo -i
monit status | grep gorouter
ls /var/vcap/jobs/gorouter/
ls /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/

K8s Engineer's Translation: There is no kubectl exec into Gorouter — CF uses BOSH SSH to access platform VMs. monit is BOSH's process supervisor, analogous to systemd for K8s node daemons like kubelet or kube-proxy.

docs.title: 1. Gorouter Architecture and the Routing Table
docs.text:
Gorouter is a single Go binary (gorouter) running as a BOSH job on one or more router VMs. It maintains a purely in-memory routing table: a map from (hostname, path-prefix) to a list of backends, where each backend is a cell_ip:ephemeral_port pair plus a unique instance_id GUID.

flowchart TB
    subgraph "Gorouter Process"
        rt["Routing Table\n(in-memory map)\nhostname → []Backend"]
        proxy["HTTP Reverse Proxy\n(net/http RoundTripper)"]
        nats_sub["NATS Subscriber\nrouter.register\nrouter.unregister"]
        health["Health Endpoint\n:8080/health"]
        metrics["StatsD / Prometheus\nrouter.requests_total\nrouter.latency"]
    end

    nats["NATS Message Bus"]
    re["Route Emitter\n(per Diego Cell)"]
    client["Inbound HTTP/S"]
    backend["App Container\ncell_ip:ephemeral_port"]

    re -->|"router.register {host, uris, port, tags}"| nats
    nats -->|"push to subscriber"| nats_sub
    nats_sub -->|"upsert with TTL=2min"| rt
    client --> proxy
    proxy -->|"lookup hostname"| rt
    rt -->|"selected backend"| proxy
    proxy -->|"HTTP + X-CF headers"| backend
    proxy --> health
    proxy --> metrics

docs.title: Routing Table Entry Structure
docs.text:
Each entry in the table corresponds to one app instance registration message received over NATS. The Route Emitter on each Diego Cell publishes the following JSON payload to the router.register subject every 20 seconds:

{
  "host": "10.0.1.42",
  "port": 61001,
  "uris": ["myapp.cf.example.com", "myapp-custom.example.com"],
  "app": "6fa7c8a3-beef-4c0d-9abc-123456789abc",
  "instance_id": "0f1e2d3c-4b5a-6978-8796-aabbccddeeff",
  "private_instance_index": "0",
  "server_cert_domain_san": "0f1e2d3c-4b5a-6978-8796-aabbccddeeff",
  "tags": {
    "component": "route-emitter",
    "index": "0"
  }
}

Key fields: - host — Diego Cell underlay IP (not the container's Silk IP) - port — ephemeral port opened by the host-side iptables DNAT rule that forwards to container port 8080 - uris — one or more hostnames; a single container can serve multiple routes - instance_id — used for sticky session affinity and the X-CF-InstanceID header - server_cert_domain_san — SAN in the container's mutual-TLS certificate, used for route integrity verification

K8s Engineer's Translation: The NATS router.register message is equivalent to an Endpoints object update in Kubernetes — it tells the proxy where to send traffic for a given hostname. In K8s, the Endpoints controller watches Pod IP changes and writes to the API server. In CF, Route Emitter watches the BBS (Bulletin Board System) for actual LRP state and publishes directly to NATS. No persistent store for routes — everything is rebuilt from live NATS messages.

docs.title: Route TTL and Expiry
docs.text:
Gorouter sets a 2-minute TTL on each route entry when it receives a registration. If the Route Emitter stops sending router.register heartbeats (cell crash, BBS connectivity loss, process restart), entries expire and traffic to those instances drops with a 502 Bad Gateway. This is by design — stale routes pointing at dead containers are worse than fast expiry.

# Terminal 2 — watch Gorouter logs for route registration/expiry
tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log | grep -E "register|unregister|expire"

# Check the current route table via Gorouter's debug port (requires localhost access)
curl http://localhost:8082/routes | jq 'to_entries | .[0:5]'

# Count total registered routes
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | jq 'keys | length'

docs.title: 2. Route Registration Flow
docs.text:
The end-to-end flow from cf push to a live route involves four components: CC (Cloud Controller), Diego, Route Emitter, and Gorouter. Understanding this chain is essential for diagnosing "route not found" failures.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant CC as Cloud Controller
    participant BBS as Diego BBS
    participant RE as Route Emitter (Cell)
    participant NATS as NATS Bus
    participant GR as Gorouter

    Dev->>CC: cf push myapp --route myapp.cf.example.com
    CC->>BBS: DesiredLRP with routes[] annotation
    BBS->>RE: ActualLRP started (instance 0 on Cell 1)
    Note over RE: RE watches BBS state
    RE->>NATS: router.register {host:cell_ip, port:61001, uris:[myapp.cf.example.com]}
    NATS->>GR: deliver registration message
    GR->>GR: upsert routing table entry (TTL=2min)
    Note over RE,GR: RE re-publishes every 20s
    Dev->>GR: GET https://myapp.cf.example.com/
    GR->>GR: lookup myapp.cf.example.com → cell_ip:61001
    GR->>RE: HTTP forward to cell_ip:61001
    Note over RE: iptables DNAT → container:8080

docs.title: Mapping and Unmapping Routes
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — route operations

# List all routes in a space
cf routes

# Map an additional hostname to an existing app
cf map-route myapp cf.example.com --hostname myapp-v2

# Map a path-based route (Gorouter supports prefix matching)
cf map-route myapp cf.example.com --hostname myapp --path /api

# Unmap a route (triggers router.unregister NATS message)
cf unmap-route myapp cf.example.com --hostname myapp-v2

# Delete a route entirely
cf delete-route cf.example.com --hostname myapp-v2 -f

# Check which app owns a route
cf routes | grep myapp

docs.title: Blue-Green Deployments via Route Mapping
docs.text:
Gorouter's round-robin model makes blue-green deployments a pure route-mapping operation:

# Push new version as blue (no route yet)
cf push myapp-blue --no-route

# Map production route to blue — Gorouter now splits traffic 50/50
cf map-route myapp-blue cf.example.com --hostname myapp

# Verify both apps get traffic, then unmap green
cf unmap-route myapp cf.example.com --hostname myapp

# Clean up
cf delete myapp -f
cf rename myapp-blue myapp

K8s Engineer's Translation: This is equivalent to editing an Ingress backend to point to a new Service, or using a Gateway API HTTPRoute with weighted backends. The key difference: CF Gorouter can split traffic between multiple apps on the same route simultaneously (while both have the route mapped), whereas K8s Ingress typically sends all traffic to one Service. For weighted traffic splitting in K8s you need Gateway API backendRefs with weight fields — CF gets this for free.

docs.title: 3. TLS, Sticky Sessions, and Advanced Routing
TLS Termination Modes
docs.text:
Gorouter supports three TLS modes, configured in gorouter.yml (the BOSH job property router.tls_port and router.backends.enable_tls):

Mode Client → Gorouter Gorouter → Container Use Case Edge termination TLS Plain HTTP Default; simplest TLS passthrough TLS (SNI routing only) TLS (unchanged) End-to-end encryption, mTLS apps Full re-encrypt TLS TLS (new cert) Compliance, route integrity verification

Route Integrity Verification (full re-encrypt mode): Gorouter presents a certificate to the container whose SAN matches the instance_id from the routing table. The container's sidecar TLS agent validates this. If the SAN does not match, Gorouter rejects the backend — this prevents routing to a stale iptables DNAT pointing at the wrong container after a rapid reschedule.

# Terminal 2 — check TLS config on the running Gorouter
cat /var/vcap/jobs/gorouter/config/gorouter.yml | grep -A5 "tls\|backends"

# Verify which port handles HTTPS termination
ss -tlnp | grep gorouter

# Check container-side TLS cert SAN (from inside a cf ssh session)
# Terminal 1
cf ssh myapp -i 0
# Inside container:
openssl x509 -in /etc/cf-instance-credentials/instance.crt -noout -text | grep -A3 "Subject Alternative Name"

docs.title: X-Forwarded Headers
docs.text:
Gorouter injects standard proxy headers and CF-specific headers:

X-Forwarded-For: <client-ip>
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
X-Request-Start: 1700000000.000
X-CF-InstanceID: 0f1e2d3c-4b5a-6978-8796-aabbccddeeff
X-CF-ApplicationID: 6fa7c8a3-beef-4c0d-9abc-123456789abc
X-CF-InstanceIndex: 0

Apps can read X-CF-InstanceID to identify which instance is serving a request — useful for debugging uneven load distribution or sticky-session issues.

docs.title: Sticky Sessions
docs.text:
Gorouter implements sticky sessions via the JSESSIONID cookie (or any cookie named in the sticky_session_cookie_names Gorouter configuration). When a response sets a JSESSIONID cookie, Gorouter wraps it in a __VCAP_ID__ cookie containing the encoded instance_id. On subsequent requests carrying __VCAP_ID__, Gorouter routes to the specific instance rather than round-robining.

# Terminal 1 — observe sticky session behavior
# First request: no cookie → round-robin assignment
curl -c /tmp/cookies.txt -v https://myapp.cf.example.com/ 2>&1 | grep -E "Set-Cookie|X-CF-InstanceID"

# Second request: __VCAP_ID__ cookie present → pinned to same instance
curl -b /tmp/cookies.txt -v https://myapp.cf.example.com/ 2>&1 | grep "X-CF-InstanceID"

# Verify __VCAP_ID__ decodes to a known instance ID
cf app myapp --guid

K8s Engineer's Translation: Sticky sessions in K8s require nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity: "cookie" and nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/session-cookie-name: "INGRESSCOOKIE" annotations. CF Gorouter does this automatically for apps that set JSESSIONID — zero config from the app developer, and the cookie is managed by the router, not the app.

docs.title: WebSocket Routing
docs.text:
Gorouter detects Upgrade: websocket / Connection: Upgrade headers and hijacks the connection for bidirectional TCP streaming. No special route configuration is needed — any CF route works for WebSocket as long as the app handles the upgrade.

# Terminal 1 — test WebSocket upgrade path
curl -v \
  -H "Upgrade: websocket" \
  -H "Connection: Upgrade" \
  -H "Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==" \
  -H "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13" \
  https://myapp.cf.example.com/ws

# Terminal 2 — confirm Gorouter is forwarding the upgrade
tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log | grep -i websocket

docs.title: TCP Router (Non-HTTP Traffic)
docs.text:
For TCP apps that do not speak HTTP (databases, MQTT brokers, raw socket servers), CF provides a separate TCP Router component. TCP routes use port numbers from the reservable_ports range instead of hostnames.

flowchart LR
    client["TCP Client\ntcp.cf.example.com:1024"]
    tclb["L4 Load Balancer"]
    tcpr["TCP Router\n(port-based routing)"]
    cell["Diego Cell\niptables DNAT"]
    cont["App Container\n:8080"]

    client --> tclb
    tclb -->|"round-robin per connection"| tcpr
    tcpr -->|"random Cell IP:ephemeral_port\ntranslates to container:8080"| cell
    cell -->|"iptables DNAT"| cont
# Terminal 1 — create a TCP route
# First, find the TCP router domain
cf router-groups
# Output: default-tcp   tcp

# Create TCP route (CF assigns a random port from reservable_ports)
cf create-route tcp.cf.example.com --random-port

# Map to your app
cf map-route myapp tcp.cf.example.com --port 1025

# List TCP routes
cf routes | grep tcp

# Test
nc -zv tcp.cf.example.com 1025

K8s Engineer's Translation: TCP Router is equivalent to Service type=LoadBalancer with a specific nodePort — it exposes a fixed external port that routes to containers. The key difference is that CF's TCP routing is on-demand and self-service (developers reserve ports), whereas K8s NodePort/LoadBalancer services are typically operator-managed. In K8s, the platform does not give developers a self-service way to open arbitrary L4 ports by default.

docs.title: Failure Mode 1: 502 Bad Gateway After Deploy
docs.text:
Symptom: App returns 502 for 30-120 seconds after cf push or after a Diego Cell restart.

Root cause: Route Emitter has not yet published router.register, or the registration message has not been processed by all Gorouter instances.

Diagnosis:

# Terminal 1 — check app instance state
cf app myapp
# Look for: instances 1/1 (running)

# Check route emitter logs on the cell running your app
# First, find the cell
cf curl /v2/apps/$(cf app myapp --guid)/stats | jq '."0".stats.host'
CELL_IP="10.0.1.42"  # from above

# Terminal 2 — BOSH SSH to the cell
bosh -e my-env -d cf ssh diego_cell/0  # find index from 'bosh vms | grep $CELL_IP'
sudo tail -100 /var/vcap/sys/log/route_emitter/route_emitter.stdout.log | grep -E "register|error|failed"

# Check NATS connectivity from the cell
sudo /var/vcap/packages/nats/bin/nats-sub -s nats://nats:$NATS_PASSWORD@10.0.0.6:4222 "router.register" &
# Wait 20s — should see registration messages

docs.title: Failure Mode 2: Routes Not Appearing (502 Persistent)
docs.text:
Symptom: 502 persists even after the app is confirmed running. No router.register messages seen on NATS.

Diagnosis:

# Terminal 2 — on the router VM
# Check Gorouter is healthy
monit status | grep gorouter
curl -s http://localhost:8080/health

# Check NATS connection in Gorouter logs
grep -i "nats\|connect\|disconnect" /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log | tail -20

# Check routing table for the hostname
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | jq '.["myapp.cf.example.com"]'
# If null: route not registered. If present: Gorouter has it but something else is wrong.

# Verify Gorouter is listening on expected ports
ss -tlnp | grep gorouter
# Should show: :80, :443 (or 8080/8443), :8082 (debug)

docs.title: Failure Mode 3: Sticky Sessions Not Working
docs.text:
Symptom: Requests with __VCAP_ID__ cookie are still round-robined to different instances.

Diagnosis:

# Terminal 1 — verify the instance the app was pinned to is still running
cf app myapp
# If instances show < desired, the pinned instance died and Gorouter fell back to round-robin

# Check if __VCAP_ID__ decodes to a live instance
# The cookie value is base64-encoded instance_id
echo "BASE64_VALUE_FROM_COOKIE" | base64 -d

# Compare with running instance GUIDs
cf curl /v2/apps/$(cf app myapp --guid)/stats | jq '.[].stats.instance_guid'

docs.title: Failure Mode 4: TLS Certificate Errors (Route Integrity)
docs.text:
Symptom: Gorouter returns 526 (SSL Handshake Failed) or logs tls: bad certificate.

Diagnosis:

# Terminal 2 — on router VM
grep -i "tls\|certificate\|handshake" /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log | tail -30

# Check if the container cert SAN matches the instance_id in the routing table
# Terminal 1 — get instance ID from routing table
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | jq '.["myapp.cf.example.com"][0].instance_id'

# cf ssh into the app and inspect cert
cf ssh myapp -i 0
openssl x509 -in /etc/cf-instance-credentials/instance.crt -noout -text | grep -A5 "Subject Alternative"
# SAN should contain the instance_id GUID

docs.title: Failure Mode 5: High Latency / Uneven Instance Load
docs.text:
Symptom: Some app instances are overloaded; Gorouter's round-robin is not distributing evenly.

Diagnosis:

# Terminal 2 — Gorouter metrics (if StatsD/Prometheus is configured)
curl -s http://localhost:8080/metrics | grep -E "router_requests|router_latency|router_responses"

# Check per-instance request counts via app metrics
# Terminal 1
cf ssh myapp -i 0 -- ps aux | grep "ruby\|java\|node\|python"

# Check if sticky sessions are causing the skew
curl -b /tmp/cookies.txt -v https://myapp.cf.example.com/ 2>&1 | grep "X-CF-InstanceIndex"
# If always 0: sticky session is pinning all sessions to instance 0

# Verify Gorouter sees all instances
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | jq '.["myapp.cf.example.com"] | length'
# Should equal: cf app myapp | grep instances

K8s Engineer's Translation: Uneven load in K8s is a common problem with iptables-mode kube-proxy (random, not least-connections) and with Ingress NGINX (also round-robin by default). CF Gorouter has the same limitation. The fix in both ecosystems is an application-level load balancing strategy (consistent hashing, least-connections) which requires a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd in K8s, or CF's forthcoming Envoy sidecar integration).

docs.title: Quick Diagnostic Checklist
docs.text:
# 1. Is the app running?
cf app myapp | grep -E "instances|state"

# 2. Are routes mapped?
cf routes | grep myapp

# 3. Is Gorouter healthy?
# (From router VM via BOSH SSH)
curl -s http://localhost:8080/health && echo "OK"

# 4. Is the route in the routing table?
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | jq 'keys | map(select(test("myapp")))'

# 5. Are NATS registration messages flowing?
# (From any CF VM with NATS access)
/var/vcap/packages/nats/bin/nats-sub -s nats://... "router.register" | head -5

# 6. Is the Diego Cell healthy?
bosh -e my-env -d cf vms --vitals | grep diego_cell

# 7. Is Route Emitter running on the cell?
# (From target cell via BOSH SSH)
monit status | grep route_emitter

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Deploy at least 2 Gorouter instances behind an IaaS L4 load balancer — single Gorouter is a hard SPOF for all HTTP traffic
  • Set Gorouter max_backends_per_app to match your expected max instance count per app
  • Enable route integrity verification (full re-encrypt TLS to containers) for PCI/HIPAA workloads
  • Configure sticky_session_cookie_names to include all session cookie names used by apps (not just JSESSIONID)
  • Set router.drain_timeout to match your app's graceful shutdown time — prevents in-flight requests being dropped during rolling deploys
  • Monitor router.total_routes gauge — sudden drops indicate Route Emitter/NATS connectivity issues
  • Monitor router.responses.5xx rate — spikes indicate backend failures or misrouted requests
  • Monitor router.latency p99 — spikes often indicate Diego Cell resource pressure, not Gorouter itself
  • Size reservable_ports range on TCP Router before go-live — expanding the range requires Gorouter restart
  • Confirm TLS cipher suites in gorouter.yml meet your compliance baseline; default set includes TLS 1.2+
  • Set router.forwarded_client_cert to sanitize_set in production to prevent header injection by clients claiming to be internal services
  • Test WebSocket routes explicitly after Gorouter upgrades — connection hijack behavior has changed between versions
  • Validate blue-green route mapping automation in staging before using in production — partial route-mapping windows can cause mixed-version traffic

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command List routes in a space cf routes Map route to app cf map-route APP DOMAIN --hostname HOST Map path-based route cf map-route APP DOMAIN --hostname HOST --path /api Unmap route cf unmap-route APP DOMAIN --hostname HOST Delete a route cf delete-route DOMAIN --hostname HOST -f Create TCP route (random port) cf create-route tcp.DOMAIN --random-port List router groups cf router-groups Check app instance health cf app APP Get app GUID cf app APP --guid Get app instance stats cf curl /v2/apps/GUID/stats SSH into app instance cf ssh APP -i INDEX Check Gorouter health curl http://localhost:8080/health (from router VM) Dump full routing table curl http://localhost:8082/routes (from router VM) Count registered routes curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes \| jq 'keys \| length' Watch Gorouter access log tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/access.log Watch Gorouter error log tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log Check Route Emitter monit status \| grep route_emitter (from Diego Cell) NATS sub to route events /var/vcap/packages/nats/bin/nats-sub -s nats://HOST "router.register" Check BOSH job config cat /var/vcap/jobs/gorouter/config/gorouter.yml

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
K8s lessons in this course:

  • Lesson 15 — Ingress Controllers: Nginx and HAProxy ingress controllers implement the same L7 routing model as Gorouter, but require explicit Ingress resource YAML and a controller deployment. Compare Gorouter's NATS-driven auto-registration with the Ingress controller's watch loop over Ingress resources.
  • Lesson 16 — Gateway API: The successor to Ingress in K8s. HTTPRoute resources provide path-matching, header manipulation, and weighted traffic splitting — features that CF Gorouter provides automatically via route mapping. Korifi (CF on K8s, 2026) replaces Gorouter with Contour, which implements Gateway API.
  • Lesson 19 — Service Mesh TLS: Covers mTLS between services, certificate rotation, and SPIFFE/SPIRE identity — the K8s equivalents of CF route integrity verification and the CredHub-issued container certificates used in full re-encrypt mode.
  • Lesson 11 — iptables and kube-proxy: The DNAT rules that CF's TCP Router and host-port forwarding use on Diego Cells are identical in mechanism to kube-proxy iptables rules for NodePort services. Reading this lesson will make the CF iptables chain easier to understand.

docs.title: Online Resources
docs.text:
• Gorouter architecture (CF docs) — official overview of routing components, NATS message bus, and route registration flow
  • CF Routing Release on GitHub — source for Gorouter, TCP Router, and Route Registrar BOSH jobs; config/gorouter.yml.erb shows all tunable properties
  • Route Services in CF — covers binding service brokers into the routing path (rate limiting, auth, logging) — CF's answer to K8s admission webhooks on ingress traffic
  • CF Routing Acceptance Tests — the upstream integration test suite; reading the test cases is the most reliable way to understand edge-case routing behavior
  • Korifi Routing (Contour) — 2026 CF-on-K8s project; CFRoute CRD is translated to Contour HTTPProxy resources, replacing Gorouter with a Gateway API-compatible Envoy proxy

docs.title: CF-10 — TCP Router: Non-HTTP Traffic Routing
docs.text: Track: CF-C — Advanced Routing Prerequisite: CF-09 (Gorouter TLS and Route Integrity) or equivalent Companion K8s lessons: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers Deep Dive, Lesson 18 — Gateway API and L4 Routing, Lesson 19 — MetalLB and LoadBalancer Services

docs.title: Quick Read (10 min)
docs.text:
What TCP Router is: CF's dedicated Layer 4 router for non-HTTP workloads. While Gorouter handles HTTP/HTTPS at Layer 7 (with headers, sticky sessions, and route integrity), TCP Router forwards raw TCP connections by mapping an external port to a backend application instance. No HTTP parsing, no header injection, no TLS termination by default — just bytes in, bytes out.

Key mental model:

  • TCP Router = a port-reservation system + reverse proxy for TCP, not HTTP
  • Operators define reservable_ports (e.g., 1024-1123) in the routing API; apps claim one port per TCP route
  • Each TCP route is <tcp-router-hostname>:<reserved-port> → one or more app instances (round-robin per connection)
  • The Diego Cell uses iptables DNAT to rewrite the destination from cell-IP:ephemeral-port to container-IP:8080 (or the app's declared port)
  • No Route Emitter NATS heartbeats for TCP routes — the Routing API persists TCP route mappings in a database
  • TLS: app can do its own TLS; TCP Router passes bytes through unchanged unless configured for TLS termination

Who uses TCP Router:

  • Databases (MySQL replication, Redis, Postgres)
  • gRPC services (HTTP/2 binary protocol, incompatible with Gorouter HTTP/1.1 routing table)
  • WebSocket-only apps that want a dedicated port instead of Gorouter WebSocket upgrade
  • IoT/MQTT brokers
  • Custom TCP protocols (game servers, financial FIX protocol, etc.)

Quick architecture diagram:

flowchart LR
    client["External Client\nTCP :1024"]
    lb["IaaS Load Balancer\n(TCP passthrough)"]
    tcpr["TCP Router VM\n:1024 listener"]
    cell["Diego Cell\niptables DNAT"]
    ctr["Container\n10.255.x.y:8080"]

    client -->|"TCP SYN → :1024"| lb
    lb -->|"TCP passthrough"| tcpr
    tcpr -->|"route lookup\nRouting API DB"| tcpr
    tcpr -->|"forward to\ncell-IP:ephemeral-port"| cell
    cell -->|"DNAT → 10.255.x.y:8080"| ctr
    ctr -->|"TCP data\nreverse DNAT"| cell
    cell --> tcpr --> lb --> client

Core facts — bullet form:

  • reservable_ports: operator-configured range in Cloud Controller / Routing API (e.g., 1024-1123, max 100 ports per router group by default)
  • One TCP route = one port number on the TCP Router's public hostname
  • Multiple app instances behind one TCP route = round-robin, one backend chosen per new connection (not per request like HTTP)
  • Backend selection is stateless — no sticky sessions for TCP routes
  • TCP Router discovers backends from the Routing API (REST + Postgres), not from NATS
  • If all backends are unhealthy, TCP Router drops new connections (no circuit breaker built in)
  • cf map-route for TCP requires --port <N> flag; cf create-route requires domain with router group type tcp
  • Diego Cell port mapping: Gorouter uses a random high port + iptables DNAT; TCP Router uses the same DNAT mechanism

K8s Engineer's Translation: TCP Router is equivalent to a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer with protocol: TCP combined with a bare-metal ingress controller for L4. The reservable_ports concept maps to NodePort ranges in K8s (--service-node-port-range). The routing table in Routing API DB maps to kube-proxy iptables rules or IPVS entries. The key difference: in K8s you create a Service per app; in CF all TCP apps share a pool of reserved ports on the same set of TCP Router VMs.

What you will learn in the Deep Dive: how the TCP Router component stack is wired together, how to create and manage TCP routes with the cf CLI, how the iptables DNAT chain works on a Diego Cell for TCP backends, how to configure router groups and port ranges as an operator, and how to diagnose TCP routing failures end to end.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
You need two terminals for every exercise in this lesson.

Terminal 1 — cf CLI (your laptop or jumpbox)

cf api https://api.cf.example.com --skip-ssl-validation
cf login -u admin
cf target -o myorg -s myspace

# Verify the routing API is reachable
cf curl /routing/v1/router_groups
cf curl /routing/v1/tcp_routes

Terminal 2 — BOSH SSH into a Diego Cell

# List VMs in the CF deployment
bosh -e my-env -d cf vms | grep -E 'diego_cell|tcp_router'

# SSH into a TCP Router VM (not a Diego Cell) for router-side inspection
bosh -e my-env -d cf ssh tcp_router/0

# Or SSH into a Diego Cell for DNAT chain inspection
bosh -e my-env -d cf ssh diego_cell/0
sudo su -

Both terminals are needed: Terminal 1 to push apps and manipulate routes, Terminal 2 to observe raw iptables rules, TCP Router process state, and Routing API database entries.

docs.title: Component Stack
docs.text:
TCP Router is a separate BOSH job (tcp_router) that runs alongside Gorouter but handles only Layer 4 TCP forwarding. The two routers share the Routing API as their source of truth but use different registration mechanisms.

flowchart TB
    subgraph "Control Plane"
        cc["Cloud Controller\n(CF API)"]
        ra["Routing API\n(REST service)"]
        db["Routing DB\n(Postgres / MySQL)"]
        re["Route Emitter\n(Diego Cell agent)"]
        cc -->|"TCP route CRUD\nvia CF API"| ra
        ra <-->|"persist routes"| db
        re -->|"POST /routing/v1/tcp_routes/create\nRefresh every 20s"| ra
    end

    subgraph "Data Plane"
        lb["IaaS LB\n(TCP passthrough)"]
        subgraph "TCP Router VM"
            tcproc["tcp_router process\n(Go, based on gorouter)"]
            poller["Routing API Poller\n(subscribes SSE /events)"]
            mem["In-memory route table\nport → [cell:port, ...]"]
        end
        subgraph "Diego Cell"
            ipt["iptables\nDNAT chain"]
            ctr["App Container\n10.255.x.y:8080"]
        end
        lb -->|"TCP :reserved-port"| tcproc
        poller -->|"GET /routing/v1/tcp_routes\nSSE stream"| ra
        poller --> mem
        tcproc -->|"round-robin backend\nfrom in-memory table"| lb
        tcproc -->|"forward TCP → cell:random-port"| ipt
        ipt -->|"DNAT"| ctr
    end

Key architectural points:

  • TCP Router subscribes to the Routing API via Server-Sent Events (SSE) for real-time updates — no NATS
  • The in-memory route table maps external-port → []backend{cell-IP, host-port} entries
  • Each backend host-port is a random ephemeral port allocated by Diego when the app instance starts
  • iptables DNAT on the Diego Cell translates cell-IP:host-port → container-IP:8080
  • Round-robin is per-connection (TCP SYN), not per-request — a long-lived TCP connection always stays on one backend

K8s Engineer's Translation: The Routing API + SSE subscription is analogous to how kube-proxy watches the Kubernetes API server for Endpoints changes. The TCP Router's in-memory route table plays the role of kube-proxy's iptables/IPVS rules, but lives in a user-space Go process rather than kernel-space. The Diego Cell iptables DNAT is the same mechanism as kube-proxy's per-node service DNAT rules.

docs.title: Router Groups and Port Ranges
docs.text:
TCP routes are assigned from operator-defined router groups. A router group defines:

  • A unique name (e.g., default-tcp)
  • Type: tcp (not http)
  • reservable_ports: a comma-separated list of port ranges (e.g., 1024-1123,2000-2099)
# List all router groups (requires admin or routing.router_groups.read scope)
cf curl /routing/v1/router_groups

# Example response
[
  {
    "guid": "abc12345-...",
    "name": "default-tcp",
    "type": "tcp",
    "reservable_ports": "1024-1123"
  }
]

# Check how many TCP ports are currently in use
cf curl /routing/v1/tcp_routes | python3 -c "import json,sys; r=json.load(sys.stdin); print(len(r), 'TCP routes registered')"

Port reservation rules:

  • Each TCP route occupies exactly one port from the router group's reservable_ports range
  • Ports cannot be shared between TCP routes (unlike HTTP routes sharing port 443 via SNI/Host)
  • When a space requests a TCP route, Cloud Controller picks the next available port from the range
  • If the range is exhausted, cf create-route returns HTTP 507 (Insufficient Storage)
  • Maximum recommended range: 100 ports per router group per TCP Router instance (operational limit, not hard limit)

docs.title: Operator Steps (one-time setup)
docs.text:
Before developers can create TCP routes, an operator must:

  1. Create a shared domain with the TCP router group
  2. Ensure the domain's DNS resolves to the TCP Router VMs (or the IaaS LB in front of them)
# Step 1: Identify the router group GUID
cf curl /routing/v1/router_groups | python3 -m json.tool

# Step 2: Create a shared domain for TCP routing
cf create-shared-domain tcp.cf.example.com --router-group default-tcp

# Verify the domain shows router group type
cf domains
# NAME                    STATUS   TYPE   DETAILS
# apps.cf.example.com     shared
# tcp.cf.example.com      shared   tcp    router-group: default-tcp

# Step 3: Confirm TCP Router VMs are healthy
bosh -e my-env -d cf vms | grep tcp_router
# tcp_router/0   running   z1   10.0.1.20   ...
# tcp_router/1   running   z2   10.0.1.21   ...

docs.title: Developer Steps — Pushing a TCP App
docs.text:
# Push an app that listens on TCP (e.g., a Redis clone on port 6379)
# The app must listen on the PORT env var (CF injects it)
cf push myapp --no-route

# Create a TCP route — CF picks an available port from the range
cf create-route tcp.cf.example.com --random-port
# Route tcp.cf.example.com:1055 has been created

# Or request a specific port (must be in reservable_ports range)
cf create-route tcp.cf.example.com --port 1080

# Map the route to the app
cf map-route myapp tcp.cf.example.com --port 1055

# Verify
cf routes
# space    host   domain               port   path   type   apps
# myspace        tcp.cf.example.com   1055          tcp    myapp

docs.title: Testing a TCP Route
docs.text:
# Simple TCP connectivity test (using netcat)
nc -vz tcp.cf.example.com 1055

# Or use curl for a plain TCP echo service
curl tcp://tcp.cf.example.com:1055

# For a Redis app
redis-cli -h tcp.cf.example.com -p 1055 ping
# PONG

# Check which instances are mapped
cf curl "/v3/apps/$(cf app myapp --guid)/routes"

# Scale up and verify round-robin (each nc connection goes to a different instance)
cf scale myapp -i 3
# Connect three times; watch cf logs to see which instance handles each
cf logs myapp --recent &
nc -vz tcp.cf.example.com 1055
nc -vz tcp.cf.example.com 1055
nc -vz tcp.cf.example.com 1055

K8s Engineer's Translation: cf create-route tcp.cf.example.com --random-port is equivalent to creating a Service of type NodePort with an auto-assigned port. cf map-route myapp tcp.cf.example.com --port 1055 is equivalent to updating the selector on that Service to point to your Deployment's pods. The difference: in CF you explicitly bind routes to apps; in K8s the Service selector links to pods automatically via labels.

docs.title: Route Lifecycle — What Happens Under the Hood
docs.text:
# 1. cf map-route calls Cloud Controller POST /v3/routes/<guid>/destinations
# 2. Cloud Controller writes the mapping to the CCDB
# 3. Route Emitter on the Diego Cell polls CC every 20s
# 4. Route Emitter POSTs to Routing API: POST /routing/v1/tcp_routes/create
#    Body: [{"router_group_guid":"...","port":1055,"backend_ip":"10.0.1.5","backend_port":61002,"ttl":120}]
# 5. TCP Router SSE subscriber receives the event
# 6. TCP Router updates its in-memory table: 1055 → [10.0.1.5:61002, ...]
# 7. New connections to :1055 are forwarded to 10.0.1.5:61002
# 8. iptables DNAT on the Diego Cell (10.0.1.5) rewrites 10.0.1.5:61002 → 10.255.3.4:8080

# Inspect the Routing API directly for a specific port
cf curl "/routing/v1/tcp_routes?port=1055"

docs.title: 3. Diego Cell Port Mapping and iptables DNAT
How Diego Allocates Backend Ports
docs.text:
When a container starts on a Diego Cell, Diego allocates a random ephemeral port on the host (the cell VM) for each application port the container declares. This host port is what the TCP Router (and Gorouter) use as the backend destination.

# On the Diego Cell VM (Terminal 2)
# List all DNAT rules in the nat table
iptables -t nat -L -n -v | grep -A2 "DNAT"

# Show the specific chain CF uses for container port mapping
# CF names this chain "netin--<container-handle>"
iptables -t nat -L -n -v | grep netin

# Example output:
# Chain netin--abc123 (1 references)
#  pkts bytes target   prot opt in  out  source      destination
#  1234  789K DNAT     tcp  --  *   *    0.0.0.0/0  10.0.1.5     tcp dpt:61002 to:10.255.3.4:8080

# Find which container handle owns a given host port
cat /var/vcap/data/garden/properties/*.json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "
import json, sys, glob
for f in glob.glob('/var/vcap/data/garden/properties/*.json'):
    with open(f) as fh:
        props = json.load(fh)
    if 'mapped_ports' in str(props):
        print(f, props.get('mapped_ports',''))
"

# Or use the garden CLI tool (if available)
gaol list
gaol properties <container-handle> | grep port

docs.title: Tracing a Single TCP Connection
docs.text:
This is the most valuable skill for debugging TCP routing issues. Use it to verify the full path from TCP Router to container.

# From Terminal 1: start a long-lived connection
nc tcp.cf.example.com 1055 &
NC_PID=$!

# From Terminal 2 (Diego Cell): find the connection in conntrack
conntrack -L -p tcp --dport 61002 2>/dev/null
# tcp 6 86300 ESTABLISHED src=10.0.1.20 dst=10.0.1.5 sport=54321 dport=61002 \
#   src=10.255.3.4 dst=10.0.1.20 sport=8080 dport=54321 [ASSURED]

# Verify the iptables DNAT rule is hit (packet counter increments)
watch -n1 'iptables -t nat -L netin--abc123 -n -v'

# From Terminal 1: kill the nc and check the counter stopped
kill $NC_PID

docs.title: Port Ranges and Conflicts
docs.text:
# On the Diego Cell: see all currently allocated host ports
ss -tlnp | grep -E '6[0-9]{4}'

# Or via Diego BBS (if you have bbs-cli)
bbs-lrp-client actual-lrp-groups | grep -A5 "port_mapping"

# Check for port exhaustion on a cell (should be well below 60K)
ss -tlnp | wc -l

# View the host port range reserved for containers (set in Diego manifest)
cat /var/vcap/jobs/rep/config/rep.json | python3 -c "
import json, sys
c = json.load(sys.stdin)
print('Port range:', c.get('listen_addr_host_port_start'), '-', c.get('listen_addr_host_port_end'))
"

K8s Engineer's Translation: The Diego Cell's iptables DNAT mechanism is identical to what kube-proxy does for NodePort and ClusterIP services. In K8s, kube-proxy writes DNAT rules to KUBE-SVC-* and KUBE-SEP-* chains. In CF, the rep agent (Diego Cell component) writes netin--<handle> chains. The underlying Linux netfilter kernel code is the same in both cases.

docs.title: Common Failure Modes
docs.text:
Failure 1: Connection refused on TCP Router port

# Symptom: nc -vz tcp.cf.example.com 1055 → Connection refused

# Check 1: Is the port actually in the reservable range?
cf curl /routing/v1/router_groups | python3 -c "
import json, sys
for rg in json.load(sys.stdin):
    print(rg['name'], '→', rg['reservable_ports'])
"

# Check 2: Is the route registered in the Routing API?
cf curl /routing/v1/tcp_routes | python3 -c "
import json, sys
for r in json.load(sys.stdin):
    if r.get('port') == 1055:
        print(r)
"
# If empty: Route Emitter has not registered it yet, or the app is not running

# Check 3: Is the TCP Router process listening on the port?
# On TCP Router VM (Terminal 2):
ss -tlnp | grep 1055
# If nothing: TCP Router has not received the route from Routing API

# Check 4: TCP Router logs
tail -100 /var/vcap/sys/log/tcp_router/tcp_router.stdout.log | grep -i "1055\|error\|fail"

Failure 2: Connection accepted but immediately reset (TCP RST)

# Symptom: nc connects but gets RST immediately

# Check 1: Is the app instance actually running?
cf app myapp
# Look for "running" state on all instances

# Check 2: Is the backend registered in Routing API with a valid cell IP?
cf curl "/routing/v1/tcp_routes?port=1055" | python3 -m json.tool
# Check backend_ip and backend_port fields

# Check 3: Can the TCP Router reach the Diego Cell?
# On TCP Router VM:
nc -vz <cell-ip> <backend-port>
# If refused: iptables DNAT rule is missing on the cell

# Check 4: Is the DNAT rule present on the correct Diego Cell?
bosh -e my-env -d cf ssh diego_cell/0 -c \
  "sudo iptables -t nat -L -n -v | grep ':1055\|dpt:61002'"

Failure 3: Route Emitter not registering TCP routes

# Symptom: app is running but tcp_routes API shows no entry for port 1055

# Check Route Emitter logs on the Diego Cell
tail -200 /var/vcap/sys/log/route_emitter/route_emitter.stdout.log | \
  grep -i "tcp\|error\|routing_api"

# Check Route Emitter config — is routing_api_url set?
cat /var/vcap/jobs/route_emitter/config/route_emitter.json | \
  python3 -c "import json,sys; c=json.load(sys.stdin); print(c.get('routing_api_url','NOT SET'))"

# Manually trigger a route refresh (by restarting the app)
cf restart myapp --strategy rolling

Failure 4: Port range exhausted

# Symptom: cf create-route returns HTTP 507 or "no ports available"

# Check current TCP route count vs reservable range
TOTAL_ROUTES=$(cf curl /routing/v1/tcp_routes | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(len(json.load(sys.stdin)))")
echo "TCP routes in use: $TOTAL_ROUTES"

# Check the range size
cf curl /routing/v1/router_groups | python3 -c "
import json, sys, re
for rg in json.load(sys.stdin):
    total = 0
    for part in rg['reservable_ports'].split(','):
        if '-' in part:
            lo, hi = part.split('-')
            total += int(hi) - int(lo) + 1
        else:
            total += 1
    print(rg['name'], '→', rg['reservable_ports'], '→ total ports:', total)
"

# Fix: expand the range (operator action via BOSH manifest or CF API)
# BOSH manifest path: routing_api.router_groups[name=default-tcp].reservable_ports
# Or update via API (requires routing.router_groups.write scope):
cf curl -X PUT /routing/v1/router_groups/<guid> \
  -d '{"reservable_ports":"1024-1223"}'

Failure 5: Long-lived TCP connections dropping after idle timeout

# Symptom: persistent connections (DB, Redis, MQTT) are silently dropped after ~10 minutes

# Root cause: IaaS load balancer idle timeout (commonly 10 minutes for AWS NLB)
# TCP Router itself has no idle timeout by default

# Check TCP Router config for keep-alive settings
cat /var/vcap/jobs/tcp_router/config/tcp_router.yml | grep -i "idle\|keepalive\|timeout"

# Fix options:
# 1. Configure TCP keepalive on the application (recommended for databases)
#    For Redis: set tcp-keepalive 60 in redis.conf
# 2. Set IaaS LB idle timeout higher (AWS NLB: set to 350s or 0 for no timeout)
# 3. If using HAProxy as TCP Router fronting: set timeout tunnel 1h

# Verify conntrack timeout on Diego Cell
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established
# Default: 432000 (5 days) — not the culprit; look at IaaS LB

# Monitor conntrack table for dropped connections
conntrack -E -p tcp 2>&1 | grep "DESTROY.*dport=61002"

docs.title: Diagnostic Command Summary
docs.text:
# Quick health check for a specific TCP port end to end
PORT=1055
echo "=== Routing API ===" && \
  cf curl "/routing/v1/tcp_routes?port=$PORT" | python3 -m json.tool

echo "=== CF Route ===" && \
  cf routes | grep "$PORT"

echo "=== CF App State ===" && \
  cf apps

echo "=== TCP Router listener ===" && \
  bosh -e my-env -d cf ssh tcp_router/0 -c "ss -tlnp | grep $PORT"

echo "=== TCP connect test ===" && \
  nc -vz tcp.cf.example.com $PORT && echo "OK" || echo "FAILED"

K8s Engineer's Translation: These TCP routing failure modes map closely to K8s LoadBalancer / NodePort debugging. "No backend registered" = K8s pod not matching Service selector or Endpoints object empty. "Port range exhausted" = K8s NodePort range full or port conflict. "DNAT rule missing" = kube-proxy failed to write iptables rules (check kube-proxy logs, iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SVC-*). The same conntrack and iptables tools work in both environments.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Router group port range sized correctly: calculate expected peak TCP route count + 20% buffer; expand reservable_ports before hitting 507 errors
  • IaaS LB configured for TCP passthrough: no SSL termination, no HTTP health checks; use TCP or HTTP health check on the TCP Router health port (default: 8080)
  • IaaS LB idle timeout set appropriately: for database workloads, set to 350 seconds (AWS NLB) or 0 (no timeout); shorter timeouts cause silent connection drops
  • TCP Router VMs behind IaaS LB: minimum 2 TCP Router VMs across availability zones for HA; IaaS LB distributes at L4 before TCP Router does app-level round-robin
  • DNS for TCP domain: tcp.cf.example.com must resolve to IaaS LB VIP or directly to TCP Router VM IPs; wildcard DNS not needed (no host-based routing for TCP)
  • App declares correct port: app must listen on the $PORT env var injected by Diego, not a hardcoded port; CF's container-to-host DNAT always maps to the declared port
  • Health check configured: use a process or TCP health check on the app (cf set-health-check myapp tcp --endpoint :8080); unhealthy instances are removed from the Routing API backend list
  • Monitor Routing API DB: TCP route registrations are persisted; a Routing API DB failure means Route Emitter re-registration on restart; monitor Postgres/MySQL availability
  • Route TTL awareness: TCP route TTL is 120 seconds (same as HTTP); if Route Emitter on a cell stops refreshing (e.g., BOSH network issue), backends expire after 2 minutes and new connections are dropped
  • TLS design decision documented: decide upfront whether the app terminates TLS (passthrough mode — recommended for mTLS databases) or if the platform terminates TLS at the IaaS LB before TCP Router; document which ports are plaintext vs TLS

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command List TCP router groups cf curl /routing/v1/router_groups List all TCP routes cf curl /routing/v1/tcp_routes List TCP routes for a port cf curl "/routing/v1/tcp_routes?port=1055" List all CF domains with type cf domains Create TCP shared domain (admin) cf create-shared-domain tcp.cf.example.com --router-group default-tcp Create TCP route (random port) cf create-route tcp.cf.example.com --random-port Create TCP route (specific port) cf create-route tcp.cf.example.com --port 1080 Map TCP route to app cf map-route myapp tcp.cf.example.com --port 1055 Unmap TCP route cf unmap-route myapp tcp.cf.example.com --port 1055 Delete TCP route cf delete-route tcp.cf.example.com --port 1055 List app routes cf routes Check app health cf app myapp Set TCP health check cf set-health-check myapp tcp Test TCP connectivity nc -vz tcp.cf.example.com 1055 View TCP Router logs (BOSH SSH) tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/tcp_router/tcp_router.stdout.log View Route Emitter logs (BOSH SSH) tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/route_emitter/route_emitter.stdout.log List DNAT rules on Diego Cell iptables -t nat -L -n -v \| grep netin Show conntrack TCP entries conntrack -L -p tcp Update router group port range (admin) cf curl -X PUT /routing/v1/router_groups/<guid> -d '{"reservable_ports":"1024-1223"}' Get router group GUID cf curl /routing/v1/router_groups \| python3 -c "import json,sys; [print(r['guid'],r['name']) for r in json.load(sys.stdin)]"
