docs.title: CF-11: Routes, Domains, and Route Services
docs.text: Track: CF-C — Cloud Foundry Application Networking Prerequisites: CF-09 (Gorouter Internals), CF-10 (TCP Routing)

docs.title: Quick Read (10 min)
docs.text:
Core mental model: In CF, a route is a DNS name + optional path that maps to one or more app instances. Domains are the namespace from which routes are carved. Route services intercept traffic before it reaches the app.

Essential facts:

  • A shared domain is org-agnostic; a private domain belongs to a single org.
  • Routes are <hostname>.<domain>[/<path>] — path-based routing is first-match, longest-prefix wins.
  • One route can map to multiple apps (blue/green, canary); one app can have multiple routes.
  • Gorouter holds routes in an in-memory table, populated via NATS. Route Emitter refreshes every 20 seconds; TTL is 2 minutes.
  • Route services are CF-managed request proxies — user-provided or broker-provisioned — that sit in front of your app to handle auth, rate-limiting, or logging.
  • Route drain: unmap a route before cf stop to drain in-flight requests gracefully.

What breaks most often:

  1. 404 — route unmapped or Gorouter table stale (wait up to 2 min or push again).
  2. 502 — backend app crashed; route still registered for 2 min after crash.
  3. Route conflict — another org/space owns the same hostname on a shared domain.

Mermaid — Route Resolution Path:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Gorouter
    participant RouteService as Route Service (optional)
    participant App as App Container

    Client->>Gorouter: GET app.example.com/api
    Gorouter->>Gorouter: Lookup route table (in-memory)
    alt Route service bound
        Gorouter->>RouteService: Forward with X-CF-Forwarded-Url header
        RouteService->>Gorouter: Re-submit to original URL
        Gorouter->>App: Proxy to Diego Cell IP:port
    else No route service
        Gorouter->>App: Proxy to Diego Cell IP:port
    end
    App->>Gorouter: Response
    Gorouter->>Client: Response

K8s Engineer's Translation: Routes + domains = Ingress rules + IngressClass. Route services = admission webhooks or external auth proxies (OAuth2-proxy) inserted before the backend Service.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
Open two terminals before working through this lesson.

Terminal 1 — cf CLI (Mac/local):

cf api https://api.sys.example.com
cf login -u admin
cf target -o my-org -s my-space

Terminal 2 — Gorouter BOSH SSH:

# From BOSH director
bosh -e my-env -d cf ssh router/0

# Inside the Gorouter VM
cd /var/vcap/jobs/gorouter/config
cat gorouter.yml | grep -A5 "routing_api"

# Live route table (requires gorouter debug port)
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | python3 -m json.tool | head -60

docs.title: 1. Domains and the Route Namespace
docs.text:
A domain in CF is the DNS suffix from which routes are created. CF has two domain types:

  • Shared domains — available to all orgs in the foundation. Typically apps.example.com or cfapps.io. Created by platform admins.
  • Private domains — scoped to one org (and optionally shared with specific sub-orgs). Useful for vanity domains owned by a team.
# List all domains visible to your org
cf domains

# Admin: create a shared domain
cf create-shared-domain apps.example.com

# Admin: create a shared domain backed by the TCP router
cf create-shared-domain tcp.example.com --router-group default-tcp

# Org manager: create a private domain for the org
cf create-private-domain my-org internal.my-org.com

# Share a private domain with another org
cf share-private-domain other-org internal.my-org.com

# Delete (must unmap all routes first)
cf delete-shared-domain apps.example.com
cf delete-private-domain internal.my-org.com

K8s Engineer's Translation: Shared domains resemble a cluster-wide IngressClass with a wildcard DNS entry (*.apps.example.com). Private domains are namespace-scoped Ingress controllers or dedicated IngressClasses tied to a team's namespace group.

DNS wildcard requirement:

The platform operator must create a wildcard DNS record pointing to the Gorouter VIP (or load balancer in front of Gorouter):

*.apps.example.com  →  10.0.0.5  (Gorouter HA-proxy or external LB)
*.sys.example.com   →  10.0.0.5
*.tcp.example.com   →  10.0.0.6  (TCP Router)

Without the wildcard, every new route requires a manual DNS entry — not how CF is meant to work.

graph LR
    subgraph DNS
        WILD["*.apps.example.com → 10.0.0.5"]
    end

    subgraph CF Foundation
        LB["External LB / HAProxy\n10.0.0.5:443"]
        GR["Gorouter cluster\n(active-active)"]
        RT["Route Table\n(in-memory NATS)"]
        APP1["app1.apps.example.com\n→ 10.255.1.3:8080"]
        APP2["app2.apps.example.com\n→ 10.255.2.7:8080"]
    end

    Client -->|HTTPS| LB
    LB --> GR
    GR --> RT
    RT --> APP1
    RT --> APP2

docs.title: 2. Routes — Creation, Mapping, and Lifecycle
docs.text: A route is a fully qualified hostname (and optional path) bound to zero or more app instances. Routes exist independently of apps — you can create a route, reserve the name, then map it later.

docs.title: Route anatomy
docs.text:
<hostname>.<domain>[/<path>]

Examples: - myapp.apps.example.com — simple hostname route - myapp.apps.example.com/v2 — path route (Gorouter does longest-prefix match) - *.apps.example.com — wildcard route (matches any unregistered subdomain)

docs.title: CRUD commands
docs.text:
# Create a route (does not map it yet)
cf create-route my-space apps.example.com --hostname myapp

# Create a path route
cf create-route my-space apps.example.com --hostname myapp --path /v2

# Map to an app (the app starts receiving traffic)
cf map-route myapp apps.example.com --hostname myapp

# Map with path
cf map-route myapp apps.example.com --hostname myapp --path /v2

# Map multiple apps to same route (blue/green, canary)
cf map-route myapp-green apps.example.com --hostname myapp
cf map-route myapp-blue  apps.example.com --hostname myapp

# Unmap (removes from Gorouter table within ~2 min)
cf unmap-route myapp-blue apps.example.com --hostname myapp

# Delete the route object entirely
cf delete-route apps.example.com --hostname myapp

# Clean up unmapped routes in a space
cf delete-orphaned-routes

docs.title: Push with custom route
docs.text:
cf push myapp -f manifest.yml

# manifest.yml excerpt:
# routes:
#   - route: myapp.apps.example.com
#   - route: myapp.apps.example.com/api

docs.title: Gorouter route table inspection
docs.text:
# On Gorouter VM — full table as JSON
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | python3 -m json.tool

# Filter for a specific hostname
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); \
  [print(k,v) for k,v in d.items() if 'myapp' in k]"

# Check NATS subscriptions
curl -s http://localhost:8082/varz | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A3 "nats"

K8s Engineer's Translation: cf map-route is equivalent to adding an Ingress rule (spec.rules[].host or spec.rules[].http.paths[]). Orphaned routes are equivalent to Ingress objects with no backend Service — they consume the hostname reservation but send nothing anywhere useful.

docs.title: Sticky sessions
docs.text:
Gorouter supports sticky sessions via the JSESSIONID cookie (or any VCAP_ID cookie). When a client's first request hits a backend instance, Gorouter sets __VCAP_ID__ on the response. Subsequent requests with that cookie are pinned to the same instance.

# Verify sticky session header is present
curl -v https://myapp.apps.example.com/ 2>&1 | grep -i vcap_id

docs.title: WebSocket support
docs.text:
Gorouter upgrades HTTP/1.1 connections to WebSocket automatically. No special configuration needed on the route. The app must handle the Upgrade: websocket header.

# Test WebSocket upgrade
wscat -c wss://myapp.apps.example.com/ws

docs.title: 3. Route Services
docs.text:
A route service is a network component that intercepts all requests bound to a route before they reach the app. Use cases: authentication, rate limiting, WAF, audit logging.

CF supports two kinds of route services:

Type Description Fully-brokered Provisioned via a service broker; broker manages the route service instance lifecycle User-provided Operator supplies the route service URL directly

docs.title: How the interception works
docs.text:
When a route has a route service bound, Gorouter adds an X-CF-Forwarded-Url header containing the original destination URL, then forwards the request to the route service endpoint. The route service processes the request and re-submits it to the URL in X-CF-Forwarded-Url. Gorouter validates that re-submitted requests carry a valid X-CF-Proxy-Signature header (HMAC-signed, 1-hour TTL) to prevent bypass.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant LB as Load Balancer
    participant GR as Gorouter
    participant RS as Route Service
    participant App as App Instance

    Client->>LB: GET https://myapp.apps.example.com/
    LB->>GR: Forward
    GR->>GR: Route table lookup\nRoute service bound → rs.example.com
    GR->>RS: POST https://rs.example.com/\nX-CF-Forwarded-Url: https://myapp.apps.example.com/\nX-CF-Proxy-Metadata: <base64>\nX-CF-Proxy-Signature: <hmac>
    RS->>RS: Auth check / rate-limit / log
    RS->>GR: GET https://myapp.apps.example.com/\nX-CF-Proxy-Signature: <valid-hmac>
    GR->>App: Proxy to 10.255.x.x:8080
    App->>GR: 200 OK
    GR->>Client: 200 OK

docs.title: User-provided route service
docs.text:
# Create a user-provided route service pointing to your proxy
cf create-user-provided-service my-rate-limiter \
  -r https://rate-limiter.internal.example.com

# Bind the route service to a route
cf bind-route-service apps.example.com my-rate-limiter --hostname myapp

# Verify binding
cf service my-rate-limiter

# Unbind
cf unbind-route-service apps.example.com my-rate-limiter --hostname myapp

docs.title: Brokered route service
docs.text:
# Marketplace must expose a route-service-capable plan
cf marketplace -s my-waf-service

# Provision an instance
cf create-service my-waf-service standard waf-instance

# Bind to route (broker provisions interception endpoint)
cf bind-route-service apps.example.com waf-instance --hostname myapp

# Inspect binding parameters if needed
cf service waf-instance --guid

docs.title: Route service log inspection on Gorouter
docs.text:
# On Gorouter VM
tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log | \
  grep -i "route-service"

# Look for 403 Forbidden — means proxy signature validation failed
grep "signature" /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log | tail -20

K8s Engineer's Translation: CF route services are analogous to Kubernetes admission webhooks or service mesh policies (Istio EnvoyFilter / AuthorizationPolicy) that intercept traffic before it reaches the backend pod. The X-CF-Proxy-Signature HMAC is CF's equivalent of a Kubernetes webhook caBundle — it prevents policy bypass.

docs.title: Route service configuration in BOSH manifest
docs.text:
# cloud_controller.yml property relevant to route services
cc:
  route_services_enabled: true
  route_services_timeout: 60      # seconds before Gorouter gives up waiting for RS
  route_services_secret: <secret> # used to sign X-CF-Proxy-Signature
  route_services_secret_decrypt_only: <old-secret>  # for rotation

# On Gorouter VM — verify route service secret is set
grep -i route_service /var/vcap/jobs/gorouter/config/gorouter.yml

docs.title: Failure mode matrix
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic 404 Not Found from Gorouter Route not mapped, or Gorouter table stale cf routes, check Gorouter /routes endpoint 502 Bad Gateway App crashed; route still alive (up to 2 min TTL) cf app myapp, cf logs myapp --recent 503 Service Unavailable No healthy backends; all instances down cf app myapp, check Diego Cell health Route already exists Another space/org holds the route on a shared domain cf routes --orgs (admin), contact platform team Route service 403 HMAC signature expired or mismatched secret Check route_services_secret in manifest Route service 504 Route service taking > route_services_timeout Tune timeout or investigate RS latency WebSocket drops Gorouter idle timeout (default 900s) shorter than WS keepalive Adjust request_timeout_in_seconds in gorouter.yml Wildcard route hijacking all traffic Wildcard route bound before specific routes resolve List routes, ensure specific routes are registered

docs.title: Route table stale — step-by-step
docs.text:
# Step 1: check the route is mapped
cf routes | grep myapp

# Step 2: check the app is running and has instances
cf app myapp

# Step 3: check Gorouter table on the VM
# (requires BOSH SSH access)
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | \
  python3 -m json.tool | grep -A5 "myapp"

# Step 4: if route missing from table, check Route Emitter logs on Diego Cell
bosh -e my-env -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
grep "route_emitter" /var/vcap/sys/log/route_emitter/route_emitter.stdout.log | \
  grep -i "myapp" | tail -20

# Step 5: force route refresh by restarting the app
cf restart myapp

docs.title: 502 after crash — verify TTL drain
docs.text:
# Crash the app deliberately for testing
cf stop myapp

# Immediately poll — expect 502 for up to 2 minutes
for i in $(seq 1 15); do
  STATUS=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://myapp.apps.example.com/)
  echo "$(date +%T)  HTTP $STATUS"
  sleep 10
done

docs.title: Route conflict debugging
docs.text:
# As admin — find which org/space owns a route
cf curl /v3/routes?hosts=myapp | python3 -m json.tool

# Output includes space_guid and organization relationship
# Cross-reference:
cf curl /v3/spaces/<space-guid> | python3 -m json.tool

docs.title: Route service bypass attempt detection
docs.text:
# On Gorouter VM — look for requests with forged/missing signatures
grep "signature_validation" \
  /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log | \
  grep -i "failed" | tail -30

# Check route service binding is active
cf curl /v3/service_route_bindings | python3 -m json.tool

docs.title: Path routing order debugging
docs.text:
# CF uses longest-prefix match — verify which route wins
cf curl "/v3/routes?hosts=myapp&paths=/v2" | python3 -m json.tool
cf curl "/v3/routes?hosts=myapp&paths=/" | python3 -m json.tool

# On Gorouter — routes with paths appear as "myapp.apps.example.com/v2"
curl -s http://localhost:8082/routes | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); \
  [print(k) for k in d.keys() if 'myapp' in k]"

K8s Engineer's Translation: CF route TTL and stale-route behavior maps to Kubernetes Endpoint propagation delay. When a pod crashes, the Endpoint is removed, but in-flight connections and DNS caches may keep routing to the dead pod for seconds to tens of seconds. CF's 2-minute TTL is longer — plan for it in health checks and load balancer drain settings.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Wildcard DNS entry exists for all shared domains pointing to the Gorouter VIP or external LB.
  • Private domains for each production org are created and owned by the correct org manager.
  • All app routes are defined in manifest.yml under routes: — no manual cf map-route in production pipelines (prevents drift).
  • Blue/green or canary routes are unmapped from the old version before the old app is stopped, to avoid 502 during TTL drain.
  • cf delete-orphaned-routes runs as part of cleanup pipelines to avoid hostname reservation leaks.
  • Route services have their route_services_timeout tuned to match the actual SLA of the upstream proxy.
  • Route service secrets (route_services_secret) are rotated via route_services_secret_decrypt_only without downtime.
  • WebSocket apps have Gorouter request_timeout_in_seconds set higher than the WebSocket keepalive interval.
  • Sticky session behavior is explicitly tested and documented per app — do not rely on it for stateless apps.
  • Path-routed apps are tested with longest-prefix ordering validated against the Gorouter route table.
  • Platform team has documented the shared domain ownership and DNS TTL for planned maintenance windows.
  • Gorouter /routes debug endpoint is firewalled — only accessible from BOSH management network.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command List all domains cf domains Create shared domain cf create-shared-domain example.com Create TCP shared domain cf create-shared-domain tcp.example.com --router-group default-tcp Create private domain cf create-private-domain my-org example.com Share private domain cf share-private-domain other-org example.com List routes in space cf routes Create a route cf create-route my-space apps.example.com --hostname myapp Create path route cf create-route my-space apps.example.com --hostname myapp --path /v2 Map route to app cf map-route myapp apps.example.com --hostname myapp Unmap route from app cf unmap-route myapp apps.example.com --hostname myapp Delete route cf delete-route apps.example.com --hostname myapp Delete orphaned routes cf delete-orphaned-routes Create user-provided RS cf create-user-provided-service my-rs -r https://rs.example.com Bind route service cf bind-route-service apps.example.com my-rs --hostname myapp Unbind route service cf unbind-route-service apps.example.com my-rs --hostname myapp Inspect Gorouter table curl http://localhost:8082/routes (on Gorouter VM) Find route owner (admin) cf curl /v3/routes?hosts=myapp Check route service bindings cf curl /v3/service_route_bindings View Gorouter logs tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/gorouter.stdout.log

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
Related CF lessons:

  • CF-09: Gorouter Internals — route table population via NATS, Route Emitter, TTL behavior
  • CF-10: TCP Routing — reservable_ports, TCP Router, non-HTTP route domains
  • CF-12: TLS in CF — edge termination, passthrough, full re-encrypt, route integrity
  • CF-07: App Security Groups — egress rules that apply alongside inbound route policies

Kubernetes equivalent lessons:

  • Lesson 18 — Ingress Controllers and IngressClass: Direct equivalent of Gorouter + shared domains. Covers wildcard DNS, path-based routing, and backend Service selection — the same mental model as cf map-route with paths.
  • Lesson 19 — Gateway API: The successor to Ingress, analogous to CF V3 route model and Korifi's use of Contour as the Gorouter replacement. HTTPRoute resources map closely to CF route objects.
  • Lesson 22 — Service Mesh (Istio): Covers VirtualService and DestinationRule — the K8s equivalent of route services for traffic shaping, auth policy, and canary rollout.
  • Lesson 15 — Network Policies: Default-deny and allow rules; compare to CF C2C policies which also use a default-deny model but are enforced at the Silk/VXLAN layer rather than iptables directly.

docs.title: Online Resources
docs.text:
• CF Docs — Managing Routes and Domains — official reference for all route and domain CLI commands, including path routing and wildcard routes.
  • CF Docs — Route Services — covers fully-brokered and user-provided route services, the proxy signature protocol, and binding lifecycle.
  • Gorouter GitHub Repository — source code, configuration reference (gorouter.yml schema), and issue tracker for Gorouter bugs including TTL and sticky session behavior.
  • CF V3 API — Routes Resource — machine-readable route management via cf curl /v3/routes; useful for scripting and pipeline automation.
  • Korifi Routing Design (2026) — documents how Korifi replaces Gorouter with Contour and maps CF route concepts to HTTPRoute CRDs; relevant for foundations evaluating the K8s-native CF runtime.

docs.title: Appendix: Route Weights and Canary Rollout
docs.text:
CF V3 API supports route weights — a numeric weight (1–128) assigned per route binding that controls the fraction of traffic sent to each app. This is the native CF mechanism for canary and blue/green deployments without external load balancers.

# Map both old and new app versions to the same route with weights
# 90% to stable, 10% to canary
cf map-route myapp-stable apps.example.com --hostname myapp
cf map-route myapp-canary apps.example.com --hostname myapp

# Set weights via V3 API (cf CLI does not expose weights directly)
# Step 1: get route destination GUIDs
cf curl "/v3/routes?hosts=myapp" | python3 -m json.tool

# Step 2: patch weights on route destinations
# (replace <route-guid> and <dest-guid-stable>, <dest-guid-canary>)
cf curl -X PATCH /v3/routes/<route-guid>/destinations \
  -d '{
    "destinations": [
      { "guid": "<dest-guid-stable>", "weight": 90 },
      { "guid": "<dest-guid-canary>", "weight": 10 }
    ]
  }'

# Gradually shift: 50/50
cf curl -X PATCH /v3/routes/<route-guid>/destinations \
  -d '{
    "destinations": [
      { "guid": "<dest-guid-stable>", "weight": 50 },
      { "guid": "<dest-guid-canary>", "weight": 50 }
    ]
  }'

# Full cutover: 0/100 — then unmap stable
cf curl -X PATCH /v3/routes/<route-guid>/destinations \
  -d '{
    "destinations": [
      { "guid": "<dest-guid-stable>", "weight": 0 },
      { "guid": "<dest-guid-canary>", "weight": 100 }
    ]
  }'
cf unmap-route myapp-stable apps.example.com --hostname myapp

K8s Engineer's Translation: Route weights are the CF equivalent of Argo Rollouts canarySteps with setWeight, or Istio VirtualService with traffic split across two Kubernetes Services. The difference: in CF the split lives in the Gorouter route table; in K8s it lives either in the mesh control plane or the rollout controller.

Gorouter weight distribution: Gorouter uses a weighted random algorithm. With weights 90/10, approximately 1 in 10 requests (randomly selected) will go to the canary. This is not round-robin with skipping — traffic distribution converges toward the weight ratio over many requests, not every 10th request exactly.

docs.title: CF-12: Service Discovery Deep Dive
docs.text: Track: CF-C — Application Networking Prerequisites: CF-09 (Gorouter Internals), CF-10 (C2C Policies), CF-11 (BOSH DNS)

docs.title: Quick Read (10 min)
docs.text:
The essential mental model for CF service discovery:

  • CF has two discovery planes: HTTP (Gorouter) and C2C (Silk overlay)
  • Gorouter builds its routing table from NATS router.register messages — no etcd, no Kubernetes Service objects
  • Route Emitter (on each Diego Cell) publishes registrations every 20 s; TTL is 2 min — a silent app still stays routable
  • BOSH DNS (apps.internal) handles C2C discovery by app name + instance index; it is health-aware at the DNS layer — unhealthy instances are removed from DNS before the app restarts
  • C2C discovery requires both a Network Policy and an apps.internal route — policy alone is not enough to reach the app by name
  • There is no kube-proxy, no ClusterIP, no Endpoints object — CF discovery is fully NATS + DNS + iptables
  • CF containers get ndots:0 (no search chain); K8s pods get ndots:5 (5-step search chain) — CF DNS queries are always absolute

Key addresses: - App reachable externally: https://myapp.cfapps.example.com via Gorouter → Diego Cell SNAT - App reachable internally: myapp.apps.internal → BOSH DNS → overlay IP directly (no SNAT, no Gorouter) - Specific instance: 0.myapp.apps.internal → instance 0 overlay IP only

graph LR
    subgraph "HTTP Discovery — Gorouter"
        A[App starts] -->|NATS router.register| B[Route Emitter]
        B --> C[Gorouter in-memory table]
        C --> D[Incoming request routed]
    end
    subgraph "C2C Discovery — BOSH DNS"
        E[Source app] -->|DNS query myapp.apps.internal| F[BOSH DNS\nhealth-aware]
        F -->|overlay IP 10.255.x.x\nunhealthy IPs excluded| E
        E -->|direct VXLAN — no Gorouter| G[Dest app]
    end

Critical differences from Kubernetes:

K8s concept CF equivalent kube-dns / CoreDNS + ndots:5 BOSH DNS + ndots:0 (no search chain) Service (ClusterIP) Gorouter route OR apps.internal DNS name Headless Service (all pod IPs in DNS) apps.internal returns only healthy instance IPs Endpoints / EndpointSlices Route table in Gorouter memory (NATS-updated) kube-proxy iptables rules VXLAN Policy Agent iptables + Diego Cell NAT StatefulSet pod DNS (pod-0.svc.ns.svc.cluster.local) Per-instance: 0.myapp.apps.internal Service mesh sidecar No sidecar — Gorouter does TLS/LB at edge

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
You need two terminals for every exercise in this lesson.

Terminal 1 — cf CLI (local Mac)

cf login -a https://api.sys.example.com --skip-ssl-validation
cf target -o myorg -s myspace
cf apps   # confirm apps are running

Terminal 2 — BOSH SSH into a Diego Cell

# list deployments
bosh deployments

# ssh into Diego Cell 0 of cf deployment
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0

# once inside the VM
sudo -i
# confirm Silk network interface
ip addr show silk-vtep
# confirm BOSH DNS is listening on link-local
dig @169.254.0.2 myapp.apps.internal
# confirm iptables NAT rules exist
iptables -t nat -L -n --line-numbers | head -40

K8s Engineer's Translation: Terminal 1 is equivalent to your kubectl terminal against the API server. Terminal 2 is equivalent to kubectl debug node/<nodename> or directly SSH-ing into a worker node — something you rarely do in K8s but do regularly in CF/BOSH to inspect the data plane.

docs.title: 1. The Two Discovery Planes
docs.text:
CF service discovery splits cleanly into two planes that never overlap:

  • North-South (external) discovery: HTTP/HTTPS traffic entering through Gorouter. Apps are discovered by DNS name resolving to a load balancer VIP that fronts multiple Gorouter instances.
  • East-West (C2C) discovery: Container-to-container traffic on the Silk VXLAN overlay. Apps are discovered via BOSH DNS name <app-name>.apps.internal resolving directly to overlay IPs.

Understanding which plane you are on determines every diagnostic step.

graph TD
    Internet -->|HTTPS :443| LB[Load Balancer]
    LB --> GR1[Gorouter instance 1]
    LB --> GR2[Gorouter instance 2]
    GR1 -->|HTTP to Diego Cell IP:port + SNAT| Cell1[Diego Cell 1\n10.0.1.10]
    GR2 -->|HTTP to Diego Cell IP:port + SNAT| Cell2[Diego Cell 2\n10.0.1.11]

    subgraph "Silk Overlay 10.255.0.0/16"
        Cell1 --- ContA[Container A\n10.255.1.5]
        Cell2 --- ContB[Container B\n10.255.2.7]
        ContA -->|VXLAN direct — no Gorouter| ContB
    end

    BOSHDNS[BOSH DNS\napps.internal] -.->|resolves myapp.apps.internal\nto healthy overlay IPs only| ContA

Underlay vs overlay addressing:

# On Diego Cell: underlay IP (what Gorouter connects to)
ip addr show eth0
# inet 10.0.1.10/24

# Silk VTEP: overlay gateway for this cell's /24
ip addr show silk-vtep
# inet 10.255.1.1/16

# A running container's overlay IP
cat /var/vcap/data/silk/state.json | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A3 overlay

K8s Engineer's Translation: This is identical to the K8s node IP (eth0) vs pod IP (veth pair into the pod network CIDR). In K8s, kube-proxy handles east-west load balancing via ClusterIP. In CF, there is no ClusterIP — BOSH DNS returns individual overlay IPs, and clients connect directly.

docs.title: 2. Gorouter Registration: NATS-Based Discovery
docs.text:
Gorouter does not poll an API, watch a database, or use etcd. It listens on NATS for two message types:

  • router.register — add or refresh a route entry
  • router.unregister — remove a route entry

The Route Emitter component on each Diego Cell is responsible for publishing these messages on behalf of every app instance running on that cell.

docs.title: Registration lifecycle
docs.text:
# Watch NATS registration messages in real time (from NATS VM)
bosh -d cf ssh nats/0
/var/vcap/packages/nats/bin/nats-sub "router.*" \
  -s nats://nats:$(cat /var/vcap/jobs/nats/config/nats.conf \
    | grep password | awk '{print $2}' | tr -d '"')@127.0.0.1:4222

A router.register message payload looks like:

{
  "host": "10.0.1.10",
  "port": 61234,
  "uris": ["myapp.cfapps.example.com", "myapp-blue.cfapps.example.com"],
  "app": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-...",
  "private_instance_id": "uuid-of-this-instance",
  "tags": {"component": "route-emitter", "source_id": "a1b2c3d4-..."},
  "server_cert_domain_san": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-...",
  "stale_threshold_in_seconds": 120
}

Key fields: - host + port: Diego Cell underlay IP + mapped port (not container overlay IP) - uris: one entry per CF route bound to this app - stale_threshold_in_seconds: 120 — Gorouter marks an entry stale if no refresh within 2 minutes - server_cert_domain_san: used for route integrity verification (mTLS Diego Cell to app)

docs.title: Route Emitter refresh cycle
docs.text:
# Inspect Route Emitter config on a Diego Cell
cat /var/vcap/jobs/route_emitter/config/route_emitter.json \
  | python3 -m json.tool | grep -i sync

# Key fields:
# "sync_interval": "20s"   -- full table re-emit every 20 seconds
# "heartbeat_interval": "20s"

# Check Route Emitter logs for registration activity
tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/route_emitter/route_emitter.stdout.log \
  | grep -E "register|unregister|sync"

docs.title: Gorouter in-memory routing table
docs.text:
# Query Gorouter routing table via its debug endpoint (from Gorouter VM)
bosh -d cf ssh router/0
curl -s http://localhost:8080/routes | python3 -m json.tool | head -60

# Count routes
curl -s http://localhost:8080/routes | python3 -m json.tool | grep '"host"' | wc -l

# Filter for a specific app route
curl -s http://localhost:8080/routes \
  | python3 -m json.tool \
  | grep -A5 "myapp.cfapps.example.com"

docs.title: Sticky sessions
docs.text:
Gorouter supports session affinity via the JSESSIONID cookie. When a request arrives with a known JSESSIONID, Gorouter routes to the same backend that served the original request.

# Inspect sticky session header in a response
curl -v https://myapp.cfapps.example.com/ 2>&1 | grep -i set-cookie
# Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=abc123...; Path=/; HttpOnly

# Second request with same JSESSIONID goes to same instance
curl -v -b "JSESSIONID=abc123..." https://myapp.cfapps.example.com/

K8s Engineer's Translation: Gorouter is a combination of an Ingress controller and a software load balancer (comparable to NGINX Ingress or Envoy). The NATS-based registration is conceptually similar to how Endpoints/EndpointSlices are populated in K8s — except there is no central API server write; Route Emitters publish directly to the NATS bus. There is no equivalent of a ClusterIP in this path — every route maps to one or more {Diego Cell IP, port} pairs.

docs.title: 3. BOSH DNS Internals and C2C Service Discovery
docs.text: For container-to-container communication, CF uses BOSH DNS with the apps.internal domain. This path bypasses Gorouter entirely — traffic flows directly on the Silk VXLAN overlay.

docs.title: BOSH DNS architecture
docs.text:
BOSH DNS runs as an agent on every Diego Cell VM at the link-local address 169.254.0.2. Every container's /etc/resolv.conf points to this address. BOSH DNS does three things:

  1. Answers *.apps.internal queries by consulting the CF Networking API (CAPI) for the current set of healthy overlay IPs for an app.
  2. Performs health-aware client-side load balancing — it only returns IPs for instances that Diego reports as running and healthy.
  3. Forwards all other queries to the upstream resolvers configured in the BOSH manifest (typically the IaaS DNS).
sequenceDiagram
    participant Cont as Container
    participant BDNS as BOSH DNS\n169.254.0.2
    participant CAPI as CF Networking API\n(Policy Server)
    participant Diego as Diego BBS
    participant Upstream as Upstream DNS\n(IaaS)

    Cont->>BDNS: DNS query: mybackend.apps.internal A?
    BDNS->>CAPI: GET /v1/internal/routes?hostname=mybackend.apps.internal
    CAPI->>Diego: check instance health for app GUID
    Diego-->>CAPI: instance 0: running, instance 1: crashed, instance 2: running
    CAPI-->>BDNS: [10.255.1.5, 10.255.3.9]  (instance 1 excluded)
    BDNS-->>Cont: A 10.255.1.5\nA 10.255.3.9

    Note over Cont,BDNS: Next query may rotate order (round-robin)\nor drop IPs if health changes

    Cont->>BDNS: DNS query: google.com A?
    BDNS->>Upstream: forward query
    Upstream-->>BDNS: A 142.250.x.x
    BDNS-->>Cont: A 142.250.x.x

docs.title: ndots:0 — no search chain
docs.text:
CF containers are configured with ndots:0 in /etc/resolv.conf. This means every DNS query is treated as a fully qualified domain name immediately, with no search path expansion.

# From inside a running container (via cf ssh)
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'cat /etc/resolv.conf'
# nameserver 169.254.0.2
# options ndots:0

Compare this directly to Kubernetes:

# From inside a K8s pod
kubectl exec -it mypod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 10.96.0.10
# search myns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
# options ndots:5

The K8s ndots:5 rule means that any name with fewer than 5 dots triggers up to 4 search-path expansions before the absolute query. For example, resolving mybackend from a pod in myns:

1. mybackend.myns.svc.cluster.local   -> NXDOMAIN
2. mybackend.svc.cluster.local        -> NXDOMAIN
3. mybackend.cluster.local            -> NXDOMAIN
4. mybackend.                         -> NXDOMAIN or answer

In CF, mybackend.apps.internal has 2 dots (fewer than 5) but ndots:0 means no expansion occurs — the query is sent as-is immediately. This eliminates the latency overhead of multiple failed DNS lookups that K8s pods experience for every short service name resolution.

K8s Engineer's Translation: The CF ndots:0 approach is equivalent to always using the fully qualified mybackend.myns.svc.cluster.local form in K8s. CF enforces this globally; K8s engineers must opt into it per pod with dnsConfig.options: [{name: ndots, value: "1"}].

docs.title: BOSH DNS health awareness vs K8s headless Services
docs.text:
This is a critical architectural difference. In K8s, a headless Service (ClusterIP: None) returns all pod IPs regardless of pod readiness:

# K8s headless Service — returns ALL pod IPs, even unready ones
kubectl run -it --rm debug --image=busybox -- nslookup my-headless-svc.myns.svc.cluster.local
# Server:    10.96.0.10
# Address 1: 10.96.0.10
# Name: my-headless-svc.myns.svc.cluster.local
# Address 1: 10.0.0.5  (pod-0, Terminating but still returned)
# Address 2: 10.0.0.6  (pod-1, Running)
# Address 3: 10.0.0.7  (pod-2, Running)

Readiness filtering in K8s happens at the kube-proxy / Service / Endpoints level, not at the DNS level. A headless Service does not filter unready pods from DNS.

BOSH DNS works differently — health filtering happens inside the DNS response:

# CF: BOSH DNS only returns healthy instance IPs
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'dig +short mybackend.apps.internal'
# 10.255.2.7
# 10.255.3.4
# Instance 1 (10.255.1.9) is crashed — absent from DNS response

# Kill one instance and watch DNS change within seconds
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do \
  echo "Query $i:"; dig +short mybackend.apps.internal; sleep 2; done'

The result: a client using BOSH DNS for C2C discovery will naturally avoid connecting to crashed instances without any client-side retry logic, circuit breaker, or Endpoints watch.

docs.title: Per-instance addressing
docs.text:
BOSH DNS supports per-instance addressing with the syntax <index>.<hostname>.apps.internal:

# Always reach instance 0 specifically
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'curl http://0.mybackend.apps.internal:8080/'

# Always reach instance 2 specifically
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'curl http://2.mybackend.apps.internal:8080/'

# Useful for leader/follower topology or shard-based routing
# Instance 0 is the write primary; instances 1+ are read replicas
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'curl -X POST http://0.mydb.apps.internal:5432/ ...'
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'curl -X GET  http://1.mydb.apps.internal:5432/ ...'

The index corresponds to the CF instance index (CF_INSTANCE_INDEX environment variable inside the container). It is stable across restarts as long as the app is not scaled down below that index.

K8s Engineer's Translation: Per-instance addressing is equivalent to StatefulSet pod DNS (pod-0.my-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local). K8s only provides this stable per-instance DNS for StatefulSets, not Deployments. CF provides it for all apps regardless of how they are deployed — every app gets indexed instance DNS names automatically.

docs.title: Internal route registration
docs.text:
# Create an internal domain (operator, once per foundation)
cf create-shared-domain apps.internal --internal

# Map an internal route to an app
cf map-route mybackend apps.internal --hostname mybackend

# Verify
cf routes | grep apps.internal
# mybackend   apps.internal   mybackend

docs.title: Network Policy requirement
docs.text:
An internal route alone is not enough for C2C traffic to succeed. You must also create a network policy allowing the source app to reach the destination app on the specific port.

# Allow myapp to reach mybackend on port 8080 over TCP
cf add-network-policy myapp --destination-app mybackend \
  --protocol tcp --port 8080

# Verify policy exists
cf network-policies
# source      destination   protocol  ports
# myapp       mybackend     tcp       8080

# Test from inside myapp
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'curl -s http://mybackend.apps.internal:8080/health'

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as myapp container<br/>10.255.1.5
    participant BDNS as BOSH DNS<br/>169.254.0.2
    participant Policy as VXLAN Policy Agent
    participant IPT as iptables on Diego Cell
    participant Dest as mybackend container<br/>10.255.2.7

    App->>BDNS: DNS query: mybackend.apps.internal (ndots:0, no expansion)
    BDNS-->>App: 10.255.2.7  (unhealthy instances excluded)
    Note over Policy,IPT: Policy Server poll every 5s<br/>pushes allow rules to iptables
    App->>IPT: TCP SYN to 10.255.2.7:8080 via VXLAN
    IPT->>IPT: Check: src=myapp GUID, dst=mybackend GUID, port=8080 — ACCEPT
    IPT->>Dest: Packet forwarded on overlay
    Dest-->>App: TCP response (direct, no SNAT)

docs.title: Failure mode matrix
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause First command App returns 404 from Gorouter Route not bound or emitter down cf routes, check Route Emitter logs App returns 502 Bad Gateway Backend unhealthy or port mismatch cf app myapp, check Cell iptables DNAT mybackend.apps.internal NXDOMAIN No internal route mapped cf routes \| grep apps.internal C2C connection refused Missing network policy or app not listening cf network-policies C2C connection timeout iptables DROP — policy missing or wrong port iptables on Diego Cell, VXLAN Policy Agent logs Intermittent C2C errors BOSH DNS health drop + slow recovery BOSH DNS logs on Diego Cell DNS returns wrong number of IPs Instances crashing/recovering dig loop to watch health changes Sticky session broken Multiple Gorouter instances, table diverged Check NATS connectivity between Gorouters

docs.title: Diagnostic commands — Route Emitter and Gorouter
docs.text:
# Step 1: confirm app has routes
cf routes | grep myapp

# Step 2: check app is running and cell is healthy
cf app myapp
cf events myapp

# Step 3: on Diego Cell — check Route Emitter is publishing
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
grep -i "router.register" \
  /var/vcap/sys/log/route_emitter/route_emitter.stdout.log | tail -20

# Step 4: on Gorouter — confirm route is in table
bosh -d cf ssh router/0
curl -s http://localhost:8080/routes | python3 -m json.tool \
  | grep -B2 -A10 "myapp.cfapps.example.com"

# Step 5: check Gorouter can reach backend — look for 5xx error log entries
grep -E "HTTP [45][0-9][0-9]" /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/access.log | tail -20

# Step 6: check Gorouter access log for backend IP
grep "myapp.cfapps.example.com" /var/vcap/sys/log/gorouter/access.log \
  | tail -5
# Format: host backend_ip:port response_time status

docs.title: Diagnostic commands — BOSH DNS and C2C
docs.text:
# Step 1: verify internal route exists
cf routes | grep apps.internal

# Step 2: verify network policy exists
cf network-policies --source-app myapp

# Step 3: DNS resolution from source app
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'dig +short mybackend.apps.internal'
# Should return one or more 10.255.x.x IPs
# No IPs returned = internal route missing OR all instances unhealthy

# Step 4: test TCP reachability
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'nc -zv mybackend.apps.internal 8080'
# If timeout: policy iptables rules not applied yet
# If refused: app not listening on 8080

# Step 5: on Diego Cell — inspect iptables for C2C policy
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
# Find the source container's overlay IP
cat /var/vcap/data/silk/state.json | python3 -m json.tool

# Check iptables FORWARD chain for overlay traffic
iptables -L FORWARD -n | grep -E "10\.255\."

# Check the netout chain for the specific container
iptables -L netout--<container-handle> -n 2>/dev/null | head -20

docs.title: BOSH DNS diagnostic
docs.text:
# From inside any container on the foundation
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'cat /etc/resolv.conf'
# Should show 169.254.0.2 as nameserver and options ndots:0

# Check BOSH DNS is healthy on the Diego Cell
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
dig @169.254.0.2 mybackend.apps.internal
# If SERVFAIL: BOSH DNS agent unhealthy or CAPI unreachable
# If NXDOMAIN: no internal route mapped for this hostname

# Check BOSH DNS health server
curl -s http://169.254.0.2:8080/health | python3 -m json.tool

# View BOSH DNS logs
tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/bosh-dns/bosh_dns.stdout.log \
  | grep -i "apps.internal"

# Verify ndots:0 is in effect — confirm no search expansion
# This query should NOT expand to mybackend.svc.cluster.local etc.
cf ssh myapp -t -c 'dig mybackend.apps.internal +noall +answer +stats 2>&1 \
  | grep -E "ANSWER|Query"'

docs.title: VXLAN Policy Agent sync
docs.text:
# Policy Agent polls Policy Server every 5 seconds
# Check last successful sync time
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
grep -i "poll\|sync\|update" \
  /var/vcap/sys/log/vxlan-policy-agent/vxlan-policy-agent.stdout.log | tail -20

# Force immediate iptables rule dump
iptables-save | grep -E "ACCEPT|DROP" | grep "10\.255\." | head -30

K8s Engineer's Translation: CF's C2C troubleshooting path closely mirrors NetworkPolicy debugging in K8s: 1. Does the DNS name resolve? (dig for CF; nslookup in a debug pod for K8s) 2. Does the policy exist? (cf network-policies vs kubectl get networkpolicy) 3. Are the iptables rules actually in place? (same iptables -L command on the node)

Key difference: in K8s, NetworkPolicy is enforced by the CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium) and DNS health filtering does not happen — CoreDNS returns all Endpoints regardless of pod readiness for headless Services. In CF, enforcement is VXLAN Policy Agent + iptables and DNS health filtering is built into BOSH DNS. This means CF C2C is more self-healing by default.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Internal routes are mapped with cf map-route <app> apps.internal --hostname <name> for all apps that need C2C reachability
  • Network policies are created with least privilege: exact app GUID pairs, specific port, specific protocol
  • Route Emitter sync interval is validated (sync_interval: 20s) — increase only if NATS bus is under heavy load
  • Gorouter route table size is monitored: greater than 10,000 routes can cause memory pressure
  • BOSH DNS health check endpoint (port 8080 on 169.254.0.2) is included in Diego Cell health monitoring
  • ndots:0 in container resolv.conf is confirmed — prevents unnecessary DNS search chain queries; verify after platform upgrades
  • Per-instance addressing (0.myapp.apps.internal) is used for stateful leader/follower apps rather than relying on client-side logic
  • Sticky sessions (JSESSIONID) are only enabled when the application actually requires session affinity — stateless apps should disable it to get true round-robin
  • WebSocket apps have cf set-env <app> CF_DIAL_TIMEOUT <n> tuned for long-lived connections through Gorouter
  • TCP Router port ranges are pre-allocated and documented per space/app if non-HTTP TCP services are deployed
  • VXLAN Policy Agent poll interval is verified against Policy Server capacity — default 5 s is safe up to ~500 apps; consider 10 s for larger foundations
  • After cf delete-network-policy, confirm iptables rules are flushed on all relevant Diego Cells within one poll cycle
  • C2C policies use app GUIDs internally — confirm that cf network-policies output is audited after app renames or redeployments (GUIDs do not change on cf push)
  • BOSH DNS health awareness is tested during maintenance: scale down app instances and confirm DNS response drops corresponding IPs within 30 s

docs.title: CF Network Policies — C2C Security Model
docs.text: Track: CF-D | Lesson: 13 | Duration: 45 min (Deep Dive) / 10 min (Quick Read)

docs.title: Quick Read (10 min)
docs.text: What this lesson covers: How Cloud Foundry implements container-to-container (C2C) networking with a default-deny security model enforced by iptables and the VXLAN Policy Agent.

docs.title: Core Mental Model
docs.text:
• Default deny all C2C. No two app containers can reach each other unless a network policy explicitly allows it. This is true even if apps share a space or org.
  • Policy = source app GUID + dest app GUID + protocol + port. GUIDs survive redeploys; policy does not break when you push a new version.
  • Enforcement is local. The VXLAN Policy Agent (VPA) on each Diego Cell polls the central Policy Server every 5 seconds, then programs iptables directly on the host. No kube-proxy, no etcd fanout.
  • Overlay only. C2C traffic never leaves the VXLAN overlay (10.255.0.0/16). It never touches the Gorouter, never gets SNAT'd, and never exits to the external network.
  • Dynamic update. Adding or removing a policy takes effect within ~5 seconds. No container restart required.

docs.title: Key Numbers
docs.text: Parameter Value Overlay CIDR 10.255.0.0/16 Per-cell subnet /24 (~254 containers) Max cells (default) 250 VPA poll interval 5 seconds Policy Server endpoint internal BOSH DNS

docs.title: Quick Diagram
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Cell1["Diego Cell 1 (10.255.1.0/24)"]
        A["App A\n10.255.1.5"]
    end
    subgraph Cell2["Diego Cell 2 (10.255.2.0/24)"]
        B["App B\n10.255.2.7"]
    end
    PS["Policy Server"]
    VPA1["VPA"]
    VPA2["VPA"]

    PS -->|"poll every 5s"| VPA1
    PS -->|"poll every 5s"| VPA2
    VPA1 -->|"iptables rules"| A
    VPA2 -->|"iptables rules"| B
    A -->|"VXLAN C2C (allowed)"| B

docs.title: Essential Commands
docs.text:
# Allow app-a to reach app-b on port 8080/tcp
cf add-network-policy app-a --destination-app app-b --port 8080 --protocol tcp

# List all policies in space
cf network-policies

# Remove a policy
cf remove-network-policy app-a --destination-app app-b --port 8080 --protocol tcp

# Verify connectivity from app-a container
cf ssh app-a -c "curl -s http://app-b.apps.internal:8080/health"

K8s Engineer's Translation: C2C network policy is CF's equivalent of a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy with a default-deny podSelector: {} applied to every namespace. The Policy Server is roughly analogous to a network policy controller, and the VXLAN Policy Agent is analogous to the CNI plugin (e.g., Calico) that programs iptables/eBPF rules on each node.

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
You need two terminals for every exercise in this lesson.

Terminal 1 — cf CLI (Mac/local)

# Log in and target your space
cf login -a https://api.your-cf.example.com
cf target -o my-org -s my-space

# Confirm apps are running
cf apps

# Check existing network policies
cf network-policies

Terminal 2 — BOSH SSH into Diego Cell

# List deployments to find cf deployment name
bosh deployments

# SSH into a Diego Cell (adjust index as needed)
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0

# Once inside, switch to root to inspect iptables
sudo -i
iptables -L -n -v | grep -i silk

Tip: Keep Terminal 2 open throughout the lesson. You will watch iptables rules appear and disappear in real time as you create and remove network policies from Terminal 1.

docs.title: Why Default-Deny Matters
docs.text:
In a multi-tenant PaaS, the default networking posture must be deny-all between workloads. Without this, any compromised app container could freely reach all other containers on the overlay — including apps belonging to other orgs and spaces.

Cloud Foundry's C2C model enforces this at the iptables level on every Diego Cell. When an app container is created, Silk CNI assigns it an IP from the cell's /24 subnet (carved out of 10.255.0.0/16). The VXLAN Policy Agent then programs three iptables chains:

  • silk-input — governs inbound traffic to containers on this cell
  • silk-forward — governs traffic transiting this cell
  • silk-netout — governs egress from containers (enforces ASGs)

By default, the silk-input chain has a final DROP rule. Only explicitly allowed C2C policies generate ACCEPT rules above that DROP.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Diego Cell
        subgraph iptables
            IN["silk-input chain"]
            FW["silk-forward chain"]
            NO["silk-netout chain"]
            DROP["DROP (default)"]
        end
        C1["Container A\n10.255.1.5"]
        C2["Container B\n10.255.1.9"]
    end
    VXLAN["VXLAN overlay\n(vtep0)"]

    VXLAN -->|inbound pkt| IN
    IN -->|matched policy| C2
    IN -->|no policy| DROP
    C1 -->|outbound pkt| FW
    FW -->|routed to overlay| VXLAN
    C1 -->|egress to internet| NO

K8s Engineer's Translation: The silk-input chain enforces ingress policy, like a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy with policyTypes: [Ingress]. The silk-netout chain enforces egress policy, like policyTypes: [Egress]. Unlike K8s NetworkPolicy (which is namespace-scoped), CF network policies are org-scoped and reference apps by GUID.

docs.title: The Policy Tuple
docs.text:
A CF network policy is a 4-tuple:

Field Description Example source_app GUID of the calling app abc-123-def... destination_app GUID of the target app xyz-456-ghi... protocol tcp or udp tcp port (or range) destination port(s) 8080 or 8080-8090

Why GUIDs instead of app names?

App names can be reused or changed. GUIDs are immutable per app instance and persist across cf push redeploys. This means: if you deploy version 2 of app-b, the network policy allowing app-a to reach app-b continues to work without any policy update.

# Find the GUID for an app
cf app app-b --guid

# Policy Server stores the policy using these GUIDs
# The VPA resolves GUIDs -> overlay IPs at enforcement time

docs.title: Basic Policy Operations
docs.text:
# Allow tcp from app-a to app-b on port 8080
cf add-network-policy app-a \
  --destination-app app-b \
  --port 8080 \
  --protocol tcp

# Allow a port range
cf add-network-policy app-a \
  --destination-app app-b \
  --port 8080-8090 \
  --protocol tcp

# Allow UDP (e.g., for game servers, telemetry)
cf add-network-policy sensor-app \
  --destination-app collector-app \
  --port 9125 \
  --protocol udp

# List all policies in current space
cf network-policies

# List policies with source app filter
cf network-policies --source app-a

# Remove a specific policy
cf remove-network-policy app-a \
  --destination-app app-b \
  --port 8080 \
  --protocol tcp

docs.title: Cross-Space Policies
docs.text:
Apps in different spaces can communicate via C2C if a policy is created. The policy must reference apps in the same org; cross-org C2C is not supported.

# Target source space and get source app GUID
cf target -s space-frontend
SOURCE_GUID=$(cf app frontend-app --guid)

# Target destination space and get dest app GUID
cf target -s space-backend
DEST_GUID=$(cf app backend-api --guid)

# Create cross-space policy (must have SpaceDeveloper in both spaces)
# Note: cf CLI v7+ supports --source-space and --destination-space flags
cf add-network-policy frontend-app \
  --destination-app backend-api \
  --destination-space space-backend \
  --port 9090 \
  --protocol tcp

docs.title: BOSH DNS for C2C Service Discovery
docs.text:
Apps on the overlay communicate using BOSH DNS .apps.internal hostnames, not IP addresses. This decouples application code from the underlying IP allocation.

# From inside app-a container:
# Reach app-b (any instance, load-balanced)
curl http://app-b.apps.internal:8080/api/status

# Reach a specific instance of app-b (index 0)
curl http://0.app-b.apps.internal:8080/api/status
curl http://1.app-b.apps.internal:8080/api/status

# Verify DNS resolution from container
cf ssh app-a -c "nslookup app-b.apps.internal"
cf ssh app-a -c "dig app-b.apps.internal"

K8s Engineer's Translation: .apps.internal is CF's equivalent of a Kubernetes Service ClusterDNS entry (app-b.namespace.svc.cluster.local). BOSH DNS on Diego Cells provides health-aware client-side load balancing — similar to CoreDNS + kube-proxy readiness gate, but resolved on the client side rather than in a virtual IP.

docs.title: How the VPA Programs iptables
docs.text:
After you run cf add-network-policy, here is the propagation sequence:

sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as cf CLI
    participant PS as Policy Server
    participant VPA1 as VPA (Cell 1)
    participant VPA2 as VPA (Cell 2)
    participant IPT1 as iptables (Cell 1)
    participant IPT2 as iptables (Cell 2)

    CLI->>PS: POST /networking/v1/external/policies
    Note over PS: stores policy tuple in DB
    loop every 5 seconds
        VPA1->>PS: GET /networking/v1/internal/policies?id=cell1
        PS-->>VPA1: policy list for containers on cell1
        VPA1->>IPT1: update silk-input ACCEPT rules
        VPA2->>PS: GET /networking/v1/internal/policies?id=cell2
        PS-->>VPA2: policy list for containers on cell2
        VPA2->>IPT2: update silk-input ACCEPT rules
    end
    Note over IPT1,IPT2: Policy active within ~5s, no restart needed

docs.title: Inspecting iptables Rules on a Diego Cell
docs.text:
# SSH into Diego Cell
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
sudo -i

# View the silk-input chain (inbound C2C rules)
iptables -L silk-input -n -v --line-numbers

# View with numeric ports (faster)
iptables -nL silk-input

# View the silk-forward chain
iptables -nL silk-forward

# Count packets hitting each rule (useful for verification)
iptables -L silk-input -n -v -x

# Watch rules update in real time (run from Terminal 2 while adding policies in Terminal 1)
watch -n 2 "iptables -nL silk-input | wc -l"

Expected iptables output after a policy allowing 10.255.2.7:8080 to receive from 10.255.1.5:

Chain silk-input (1 references)
target     prot opt source               destination
ACCEPT     tcp  --  10.255.1.5           10.255.2.7           tcp dpt:8080
...
DROP       all  --  0.0.0.0/0            10.255.0.0/16

docs.title: Microservice Mesh Without a Service Mesh
docs.text:
For a 3-tier app (frontend → API → database), you need explicit policies at each hop:

# Frontend can reach API
cf add-network-policy frontend --destination-app api-service --port 8080 --protocol tcp

# API can reach database
cf add-network-policy api-service --destination-app postgres-proxy --port 5432 --protocol tcp

# Database cannot reach anything (no policies from db)
# Frontend cannot directly reach database (no policy)

This creates a topology equivalent to K8s NetworkPolicy with strict per-tier allow rules.

docs.title: Bulk Policy Management with cf CLI and jq
docs.text:
# Export all current policies to JSON
cf curl /networking/v1/external/policies | jq '.' > policies-backup.json

# Count total policies
cf curl /networking/v1/external/policies | jq '.total_policies'

# List policies for a specific destination app GUID
DEST_GUID=$(cf app backend --guid)
cf curl "/networking/v1/external/policies?id=${DEST_GUID}" | jq '.policies[]'

# Apply policies from a JSON file (using cf curl)
# policies.json format:
# {"policies": [{"source":{"id":"<src-guid>"},"destination":{"id":"<dst-guid>","protocol":"tcp","ports":{"start":8080,"end":8080}}}]}
cf curl -X POST /networking/v1/external/policies -d @policies.json

docs.title: Policy Quotas
docs.text:
Operators can cap the number of network policies per space to prevent misconfiguration sprawl:

# Check current quota (operator command)
cf space-quota my-space-quota

# Example quota manifest (operator sets via CF API or BOSH manifest)
# network_policies: 50  (default is unlimited)

docs.title: UDP C2C: Metrics and Telemetry
docs.text:
UDP policies are useful for high-frequency telemetry where dropped packets are acceptable:

# Allow Prometheus scraping over UDP (unusual but valid)
cf add-network-policy prometheus --destination-app app-metrics --port 9090 --protocol tcp

# Allow StatsD metrics (UDP is correct here)
cf add-network-policy app-a --destination-app statsd-sink --port 8125 --protocol udp

# Verify UDP connectivity from container
cf ssh app-a -c "echo 'test' | nc -u app-b.apps.internal 8125"

K8s Engineer's Translation: CF network policies support port ranges and both TCP/UDP — matching K8s NetworkPolicy ports: field. CF does not yet support ICMP policies at the C2C layer; CF does not support namespaceSelector or ipBlock within C2C policies (those functions are served by ASGs for egress and there is no equivalent ingress ipBlock concept).

docs.title: Korifi (2026) — C2C Policy Migration Note
docs.text:
In Korifi deployments (CF V3 on Kubernetes), the Silk CNI + VXLAN Policy Agent stack is replaced by standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects. CF network policies created via cf add-network-policy are translated into K8s NetworkPolicy resources by the Korifi controller:

# Korifi-generated K8s NetworkPolicy equivalent of:
# cf add-network-policy app-a --destination-app app-b --port 8080 --protocol tcp
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: cf-policy-app-a-to-app-b-8080-tcp
  namespace: cf-space-guid
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      korifi.cloudfoundry.org/app-guid: <app-b-guid>
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              korifi.cloudfoundry.org/space-guid: <source-space-guid>
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              korifi.cloudfoundry.org/app-guid: <app-a-guid>
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080

This means existing cf network-policies workflows remain unchanged in Korifi — the abstraction is preserved at the CF API layer.

docs.title: Failure Mode 1: Policy Created But Traffic Still Blocked
docs.text:
Symptoms: cf add-network-policy succeeds but curl from app-a to app-b times out.

Diagnostic steps:

# Step 1: Confirm policy exists in Policy Server
cf network-policies --source app-a

# Step 2: Confirm apps are running and get container IPs
cf ssh app-a -c "ip addr show eth0"
cf ssh app-b -c "ip addr show eth0"

# Step 3: Check VPA health on Diego Cell
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
sudo monit summary | grep vxlan-policy-agent
sudo tail -100 /var/vcap/sys/log/vxlan-policy-agent/vxlan-policy-agent.stdout.log | grep -i error

# Step 4: Verify iptables rule was programmed
# Replace IPs with actual container IPs from Step 2
sudo iptables -nL silk-input | grep 10.255.1.5

# Step 5: If rule is missing, force VPA to repoll
sudo monit restart vxlan-policy-agent

docs.title: Failure Mode 2: DNS Resolution Fails for .apps.internal
docs.text:
Symptoms: cf ssh app-a -c "curl http://app-b.apps.internal:8080" returns Could not resolve host.

# Check BOSH DNS is running on the Diego Cell
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
sudo monit summary | grep bosh-dns

# Check /etc/resolv.conf inside container
cf ssh app-a -c "cat /etc/resolv.conf"
# Expected: nameserver pointing to 169.254.0.2 (BOSH DNS)

# Test raw DNS resolution
cf ssh app-a -c "dig @169.254.0.2 app-b.apps.internal"

# If NXDOMAIN: app-b may not be registered with BOSH DNS
# Confirm app-b is running and has a process ID
cf app app-b

docs.title: Failure Mode 3: Cross-Space Policy Not Working
docs.text:
Symptoms: Cross-space cf add-network-policy fails with "insufficient scope" or policy is not enforced.

# Confirm you have SpaceDeveloper role in BOTH spaces
cf space-users my-org space-frontend
cf space-users my-org space-backend

# Confirm apps exist in their respective spaces
cf target -s space-frontend && cf app frontend-app --guid
cf target -s space-backend  && cf app backend-api --guid

# Re-run with explicit space flags
cf add-network-policy frontend-app \
  --destination-app backend-api \
  --destination-space space-backend \
  --destination-org my-org \
  --port 9090 \
  --protocol tcp

docs.title: Failure Mode 4: Policy Quota Exceeded
docs.text:
Symptoms: cf add-network-policy returns HTTP 422 with "policy quota exceeded".

# Check current policy count
cf network-policies | wc -l

# Check space quota
cf space my-space | grep -i quota

# Remove stale policies (apps that no longer exist)
cf network-policies | grep "app-not-found"

# Operator: raise quota
# bosh manifest edit or cf API PATCH /v3/spaces/<guid>

docs.title: Failure Mode 5: VPA Cannot Reach Policy Server
docs.text:
Symptoms: iptables rules not updating; VPA logs show connection refused or timeout to Policy Server.

# Check Policy Server health
bosh -d cf ssh policy-server/0
sudo monit summary

# Check Policy Server logs
sudo tail -50 /var/vcap/sys/log/policy-server/policy-server.stdout.log

# Check network connectivity from Diego Cell to Policy Server
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
curl -v https://policy-server.service.cf.internal:4003/networking/v1/internal/policies \
  --cacert /var/vcap/jobs/vxlan-policy-agent/config/certs/ca.crt \
  --cert   /var/vcap/jobs/vxlan-policy-agent/config/certs/client.crt \
  --key    /var/vcap/jobs/vxlan-policy-agent/config/certs/client.key

# Check mTLS cert expiry
openssl x509 -in /var/vcap/jobs/vxlan-policy-agent/config/certs/client.crt \
  -noout -enddate

docs.title: Packet-Level Debugging with tcpdump
docs.text:
# On Diego Cell: capture VXLAN traffic on underlay interface
bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 -w /tmp/vxlan.pcap

# On Diego Cell: capture decapsulated traffic on overlay interface
sudo tcpdump -i silk0 -n host 10.255.2.7 and port 8080

# Transfer pcap to local machine for Wireshark analysis
bosh -d cf scp diego-cell/0:/tmp/vxlan.pcap ./vxlan.pcap

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm all C2C policies are documented in a policy manifest file under version control.
  • Validate that no wildcard policies exist (avoid policy from app-X to app-X on port range 1-65535).
  • Confirm policy quotas are set per space to prevent unbounded growth.
  • Verify BOSH DNS .apps.internal resolution works from every app that uses C2C.
  • Test that removing a policy (simulated incident) blocks traffic within 10 seconds.
  • Confirm VPA logs are shipped to your log aggregation system (Splunk, ELK, etc.).
  • Audit cross-space and cross-org policies quarterly; remove stale ones.
  • Confirm Policy Server mTLS certificates are rotated per your cert lifecycle policy (CredHub rotate).
  • For Korifi deployments: verify that CF network policies are reflected as K8s NetworkPolicy objects in the correct namespaces.
  • Run iptables -nL silk-input | wc -l baseline before and after any large policy batch to detect rule table bloat.
  • Confirm apps use .apps.internal hostnames (not hardcoded overlay IPs) so policies survive container restarts.
  • Test UDP policies separately from TCP — VPA programs separate iptables rules for each protocol.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command Add TCP policy cf add-network-policy src --destination-app dst --port 8080 --protocol tcp Add UDP policy cf add-network-policy src --destination-app dst --port 9125 --protocol udp Add port range policy cf add-network-policy src --destination-app dst --port 8080-8090 --protocol tcp List all policies cf network-policies List by source app cf network-policies --source app-name Remove a policy cf remove-network-policy src --destination-app dst --port 8080 --protocol tcp Get app GUID cf app app-name --guid Curl via C2C cf ssh app-a -c "curl http://app-b.apps.internal:8080/path" Specific instance DNS cf ssh app-a -c "curl http://0.app-b.apps.internal:8080/" Inspect iptables rules sudo iptables -nL silk-input (on Diego Cell via bosh ssh) Count active rules sudo iptables -nL silk-input \| wc -l Watch rules live watch -n 2 "iptables -nL silk-input \| wc -l" Restart VPA sudo monit restart vxlan-policy-agent View VPA logs sudo tail -f /var/vcap/sys/log/vxlan-policy-agent/vxlan-policy-agent.stdout.log Export all policies cf curl /networking/v1/external/policies \| jq '.' Import policies from file cf curl -X POST /networking/v1/external/policies -d @policies.json DNS resolution test cf ssh app-a -c "dig app-b.apps.internal" Check resolv.conf cf ssh app-a -c "cat /etc/resolv.conf"

docs.text:
These Kubernetes lessons cover the same concepts at the K8s layer:

  • Kubernetes NetworkPolicy — lessons/14-network-policies.md — Default-deny podSelector, ingress/egress rules, namespaceSelector; direct equivalent of CF C2C policies.
  • Calico Network Policy — lessons/15-calico-network-policy.md — Extended K8s network policy with GlobalNetworkPolicy and HostEndpoint; comparable to CF ASGs + C2C combined.
  • Cilium and eBPF — lessons/16-cilium-ebpf.md — eBPF-based enforcement replacing iptables; Cilium NetworkPolicy; contrast with CF's iptables-based Silk enforcement.
  • DNS and Service Discovery — lessons/08-dns-service-discovery.md — CoreDNS, SRV records, headless Services; compare with BOSH DNS .apps.internal and per-instance addressing.
  • Pod Networking and CNI — lessons/06-pod-networking-cni.md — VXLAN overlay mechanics, CNI plugin interface; directly comparable to Silk CNI overlay architecture.

  • CF CLI Network Policies Reference — Full flag reference for cf add-network-policy, cf network-policies, cf remove-network-policy.
  • CF Networking Release on GitHub — Source for Silk CNI, VXLAN Policy Agent, and Policy Server; issues and release notes.
