docs.title: CF-21: Compliance Networking in Cloud Foundry
docs.text:
Track: CF-H — Security & Compliance Prerequisites: CF-07 — Application Security Groups, CF-13 — C2C Network Policies, CF-14 — TLS Certificates, CF-15 — Org/Space Isolation Time: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Map Cloud Foundry's native network controls — ASGs, C2C policies, TLS, org/space isolation — to specific audit requirements in HIPAA, PCI-DSS, IEC 62443, and GDPR. Produce the exact CF CLI commands and evidence artifacts that satisfy each control.

Jump to: Theory · HIPAA · PCI-DSS · IEC-62443 · GDPR · Audit Evidence Runbook · Production Checklist · Quick Reference

K8s parallel: This lesson is the CF equivalent of K8s Lesson 37 — Compliance Networking. The controls differ (ASGs vs NetworkPolicy, Gorouter TLS vs Cilium WireGuard) but the regulatory requirements are identical.

docs.title: 1. CF Network Controls vs Compliance Requirements
docs.text:
Cloud Foundry provides four network control primitives. Each maps to one or more compliance controls:

flowchart LR
    subgraph CF["CF Network Controls"]
        ASG["Application Security Groups\n(egress from container to external IP:port)"]
        C2C["C2C Network Policies\n(container-to-container, overlay network)"]
        TLS["TLS / CredHub certificates\n(mTLS between platform components)"]
        ISO["Org / Space isolation\n(multi-tenancy boundaries)"]
    end
    subgraph Frameworks["Compliance Controls"]
        H["HIPAA\n§164.312(a)(1) Access Control\n§164.312(b) Audit\n§164.312(e)(1) Transmission Security"]
        P["PCI-DSS v4.0\nReq 1.3 CDE segmentation\nReq 4.2.1 Encryption in transit\nReq 10.2 Audit logs"]
        I["IEC 62443\nSR 5.1 Zone/Conduit\nCR 2.1 Auth enforcement"]
        G["GDPR\nArt. 25 Privacy by Design\nArt. 32 Encryption\nArt. 44 Data residency"]
    end

    ASG --> H
    ASG --> P
    ASG --> I
    ASG --> G
    C2C --> H
    C2C --> P
    ISO --> I
    ISO --> G
    TLS --> H
    TLS --> P
    TLS --> G

docs.title: 2. The Default-Open Problem in CF
docs.text:
CF's default posture, like Kubernetes, is open. The default running ASG (public_networks) allows all outbound internet traffic from every container. Without operator intervention:

  • Any app can reach any IP on the internet (HIPAA/PCI violation)
  • Containers in different spaces can communicate freely via overlay if C2C policies are added without policy (less of an issue — C2C is default-deny)
  • No audit log of which container reached which IP

Before any compliance claim, verify the default ASG posture:

# Check what global running ASGs exist
cf running-security-groups
# If you see "public_networks" or "all_open" → audit-fail for PCI-DSS Req 1.3

# Show what public_networks allows
cf security-group public_networks
# Typically: destination 0.0.0.0/0, protocol all → allows EVERYTHING

# For regulated environments: unbind or replace with explicit allow-list ASGs
cf unbind-running-security-group public_networks

docs.title: §164.312(a)(1) — Access Control
docs.text:
Requirement: Only authorized persons or software may access ePHI.

CF control: Space-scoped ASGs limiting which containers can reach the ePHI datastore, combined with C2C policy limiting which apps can call the ePHI service internally.

// asg-phi-db-access.json
// Allow only the EHR application containers to reach the ePHI PostgreSQL database
[
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "10.0.5.20",
    "ports": "5432",
    "description": "HIPAA 164.312(a)(1): EHR app → ePHI PostgreSQL. Reviewed 2026-11-25.",
    "log": true
  }
]

# Create the ASG
cf create-security-group hipaa-phi-db-access asg-phi-db-access.json

# Bind only to the ePHI-handling space (NOT globally)
cf bind-security-group hipaa-phi-db-access phi-org phi-production --lifecycle running

# Verify no other space has access to this CIDR
cf curl /v3/security_groups?per_page=100 | \
  python3 -c "
import json,sys
data=json.load(sys.stdin)
for sg in data['resources']:
    for rule in sg.get('rules',[]):
        if '10.0.5.20' in rule.get('destination',''):
            print(sg['name'], rule)
"

Auditor evidence: Show cf security-group hipaa-phi-db-access output + demonstrate a container in a different space cannot reach 10.0.5.20:5432.

docs.title: §164.312(b) — Audit Controls
docs.text:
Requirement: Record and examine activity in systems containing ePHI.

CF control: "log": true on all ASG rules touching ePHI resources. This writes kernel-level connection logs to Diego Cell syslog, which forwards to your SIEM.

// asg-phi-audit.json — all rules touching ePHI resources have log:true
[
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "10.0.5.0/24",
    "ports": "5432,8080,8443",
    "description": "ePHI data tier — audit all access",
    "log": true
  }
]

# Verify logging is enabled on all ePHI-scoped ASGs
cf curl /v3/security_groups?per_page=100 | \
  python3 -c "
import json,sys
data=json.load(sys.stdin)
for sg in data['resources']:
    for rule in sg.get('rules',[]):
        if not rule.get('log') and '10.0.5' in rule.get('destination',''):
            print('AUDIT-FAIL: log:false on ePHI rule:', sg['name'], rule['destination'])
"

# On Diego Cell: verify iptables LOG rules are present (run via BOSH SSH)
# bosh -d cf ssh diego-cell/0 -c "sudo iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v | grep LOG"

# Check syslog forwarding is configured for Diego Cells to your SIEM
# cf-deployment: ops/use-external-syslog.yml or syslog-releases

Auditor evidence: iptables -L OUTPUT -n | grep LOG on a Diego Cell showing ASG log rules, plus a sample syslog entry showing connection timestamp, source container IP, destination IP:port.

docs.title: §164.312(e)(1) — Transmission Security
docs.text:
Requirement: Guard against unauthorized access to ePHI transmitted over electronic communications networks.

CF control: Gorouter enforces TLS termination (mTLS between Gorouter and apps via route integrity). CredHub-managed certificates rotate automatically.

# Verify route integrity (mTLS between Gorouter and Diego Cells) is enabled
cf curl /v2/info | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d.get('app_ssh_endpoint',''))"

# Check TLS certificate expiry on the CF API endpoint
echo | openssl s_client -connect api.cf.example.com:443 -servername api.cf.example.com 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -dates

# Verify CredHub has certificates for the deployment
# bosh -d cf ssh cloud_controller/0 -c "sudo /var/vcap/packages/cf-cli/bin/cf curl /v2/info"

# Check that apps are mapped to HTTPS routes only (no plain HTTP in regulated spaces)
cf routes | grep -v "https\|HTTPS" | grep -v "^Getting\|^org\|^space\|^url"
# Any plain HTTP routes in regulated spaces = audit finding

Auditor evidence: TLS certificate chain for the CF API domain + confirmation of route integrity enabled in cf-deployment manifest.

docs.title: Req 1.3 — CDE Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Requirement: Restrict inbound and outbound traffic to that which is necessary for the cardholder data environment.

CF mapping: The CDE = one dedicated CF Org + Space. ASGs for that space allow only traffic required by payment processing. All other spaces are isolated by default (C2C is deny-by-default across spaces).

// asg-cde-egress.json
// PCI-DSS Req 1.3.2: Restrict CDE outbound to payment network endpoints only
[
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "192.168.10.5",
    "ports": "8443",
    "description": "PCI Req 1.3.2: CDE → internal payment gateway only",
    "log": true
  },
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "10.0.1.53",
    "ports": "53",
    "description": "PCI Req 1.3.2: CDE → internal DNS only",
    "log": false
  }
]

# Create CDE-specific ASG (no global bind — space-scoped only)
cf create-security-group pci-cde-egress asg-cde-egress.json
cf bind-security-group pci-cde-egress payment-org cde-production --lifecycle running

# CRITICAL: Ensure public_networks is NOT bound to the CDE space
cf space-security-groups cde-production
# Must NOT show: public_networks, all_open, or any 0.0.0.0/0 rule

# Demonstrate segmentation: app in CDE space cannot reach arbitrary internet IP
cf target -o payment-org -s cde-production
cf ssh payment-processor -c "nc -zv 8.8.8.8 443"
# nc: connect to 8.8.8.8 port 443 (tcp) failed: Connection timed out  ← PASS

Auditor evidence: cf space-security-groups cde-production output (no wildcard rules) + failed nc to arbitrary IP from CDE container.

docs.title: Req 4.2.1 — Encryption of PAN in Transit
docs.text:
Requirement: Strong cryptography for PAN transmitted over open, public networks.

CF controls: 1. Gorouter TLS termination (all external traffic encrypted) 2. Route integrity / mTLS between Gorouter and application containers 3. CredHub-managed certificates with automatic rotation

# 1. Verify Gorouter TLS config (all HTTPS routes)
cf routes --orgs payment-org | grep "^payment"
# All routes should show port 443 / HTTPS

# 2. Verify route integrity is enabled in the deployment manifest
# grep -A5 "route_integrity" ~/cf-deployment/cf-deployment.yml
# Should show: mode: mtls-required

# 3. Check certificate expiry (must be valid, rotation < 1 year)
bosh -d cf ssh router/0 -c \
  "sudo cat /var/vcap/jobs/gorouter/config/gorouter.yml | grep -A3 'tls_pem'"

# 4. Verify no plain-HTTP routes exist for payment apps
cf curl "/v3/routes?organization_guids=$(cf org payment-org --guid)" | \
  python3 -c "
import json,sys
data=json.load(sys.stdin)
for r in data['resources']:
    if r['protocol'] == 'http':
        print('PLAIN HTTP ROUTE:', r['url'])
"

docs.title: Req 10.2 — Audit Log Access to CDE
docs.text:
# Enable ASG logging for all CDE-touching rules (verify log:true in ASG JSON)
cf security-group pci-cde-egress | grep -i log

# Configure Diego Cell syslog to forward to SIEM (12-month retention per PCI Req 10.5.1)
# In cf-deployment, use: cf-deployment/operations/experimental/enable-oci-phase-1.yml
# and syslog-release to configure forwarding

# Generate audit report: all CDE security group changes via CC audit events
cf curl "/v3/audit_events?types=audit.security_group.create,audit.security_group.update,audit.security_group.delete,audit.security_group.bind_space,audit.security_group.unbind_space&per_page=100" | \
  python3 -c "
import json,sys
data=json.load(sys.stdin)
for e in data['resources']:
    print(e['created_at'], e['type'], e.get('target',{}).get('name',''))
"

Auditor evidence: CC audit event log showing all changes to CDE security groups, with timestamps and actor (who made the change).

docs.title: SR 5.1 — Network Segmentation (Zone / Conduit Model)
docs.text:
CF mapping: CF Org = IEC 62443 Zone, CF Space = sub-zone, ASG = Conduit rules.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Zone3["IEC 62443 Zone 3 — SL2 (CF Org: operations)"]
        subgraph SpaceA["Space: scada-integration (SL2)"]
            APP1["SCADA data aggregator app"]
        end
        subgraph SpaceB["Space: historian (SL2)"]
            APP2["Historian API app"]
        end
    end
    subgraph Zone4["IEC 62443 Zone 4 — SL1 (CF Org: enterprise-it)"]
        subgraph SpaceC["Space: erp-reporting"]
            APP3["ERP reporting app"]
        end
    end
    C1["Conduit C1\nASG: allow historian:8443 from Zone 4\nC2C policy: scada→historian:8080"]

    Zone4 -->|"C1 (HTTPS :8443 only)"| Zone3
    APP1 -->|"C2C policy: :8080"| APP2
// asg-iec62443-conduit-c1.json
// IEC 62443 SR 5.1: Conduit C1 — Zone 4 (ERP) → Zone 3 (Historian)
// Only the historian app's external IP, only HTTPS
[
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "10.1.2.100",
    "ports": "8443",
    "description": "IEC62443 SR5.1 Conduit C1: ERP → Historian API. Zone 4→Zone 3.",
    "log": true
  }
]

# Map org/space → security level in CF annotations (CF v3 metadata)
cf curl -X PATCH /v3/organizations/$(cf org operations-zone --guid) \
  -d '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"iec62443/zone":"operations","iec62443/sl":"2"}}}'

cf curl -X PATCH /v3/organizations/$(cf org enterprise-it --guid) \
  -d '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"iec62443/zone":"enterprise","iec62443/sl":"1"}}}'

# Verify zone annotations
cf curl /v3/organizations?per_page=100 | \
  python3 -c "
import json,sys
data=json.load(sys.stdin)
for o in data['resources']:
    ann = o.get('metadata',{}).get('annotations',{})
    if 'iec62443/zone' in ann:
        print(o['name'], ann)
"

docs.title: CR 2.1 — Authorization Enforcement Between Zones
docs.text:
# Verify only authorized C2C policies exist between zone-mapped spaces
# C2C policies are the conduits between containers in the same overlay network

# List all C2C policies and audit against conduit register
cf curl /networking/v1/external/policies | \
  python3 -c "
import json,sys
data=json.load(sys.stdin)
for p in data['policies']:
    print(f\"SRC: {p['source']['id']}  →  DST: {p['destination']['id']} :{p['destination']['port']}/{p['destination']['protocol']}\")
" 

# Cross-reference with app GUIDs to identify which apps have cross-space access
# (C2C policies that cross space boundaries are cross-zone conduits per IEC 62443)

docs.title: Art. 25 — Privacy by Design (Default Deny)
docs.text:
# Verify no wildcard ASGs are globally bound (default-open violates Art. 25)
cf running-security-groups
# MUST NOT contain: public_networks (0.0.0.0/0), all_open, or similar

# Every space processing personal data must have explicit ASG instead of global open
# Check spaces in personal-data org have no wildcard bindings:
ORG_GUID=$(cf org personal-data-org --guid)
cf curl "/v3/security_groups?running_space_guids=$(cf space production --guid)" | \
  python3 -c "
import json,sys
data=json.load(sys.stdin)
for sg in data['resources']:
    for rule in sg.get('rules',[]):
        if rule.get('destination','') in ['0.0.0.0/0','0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255']:
            print('GDPR Art.25 VIOLATION: wildcard ASG:', sg['name'])
"

docs.title: Art. 44 — Cross-Border Data Transfer Restriction
docs.text:
CF control: ASGs can restrict egress to only EU-hosted IP ranges. Combined with CF's deployment geography (EU-only CF foundations), this ensures personal data doesn't leave the EU.

// asg-gdpr-eu-only.json
// GDPR Art. 44: Restrict personal data containers to EU datacenter IPs only
[
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "10.0.0.0/8",
    "ports": "443,5432,6379",
    "description": "GDPR Art.44: internal EU datacenter services only",
    "log": true
  },
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "52.28.0.0/14",
    "ports": "443",
    "description": "GDPR Art.44: AWS eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) HTTPS only",
    "log": true
  }
]

cf create-security-group gdpr-eu-only asg-gdpr-eu-only.json
cf bind-security-group gdpr-eu-only personal-data-org production --lifecycle running

# Test: container cannot reach US-only endpoint
cf target -o personal-data-org -s production
cf ssh user-service -c "nc -zv --max-time 5 54.239.28.85 443 || echo BLOCKED"
# BLOCKED ← PASS

docs.title: Art. 32 — Encryption of Personal Data in Transit
docs.text:
# Verify CF foundation is configured with TLS everywhere:
# 1. External: Gorouter TLS termination (all external routes HTTPS)
cf routes | awk '{print $4}' | sort -u
# Should only show 443, no 80

# 2. Internal: route integrity (mTLS Gorouter ↔ app containers)
# Check cf-deployment manifest or platform team confirmation

# 3. Personal data apps use internal C2C (overlay VXLAN) not external routes
#    to communicate — VXLAN traffic stays within Diego Cell network
cf network-policies --source user-service
# Should show internal service communication via C2C, not external ASG egress

docs.title: Audit Evidence Runbook
docs.text:
Run this sequence before any compliance audit. Save all output.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# cf-compliance-audit.sh
# Run as CF admin. Saves evidence to ./cf-audit-$(date +%Y%m%d)/

AUDIT_DIR="cf-audit-$(date +%Y%m%d)"
mkdir -p "$AUDIT_DIR"

# 1. All global ASGs (look for wildcard rules = compliance fail)
cf running-security-groups > "$AUDIT_DIR/01-global-running-asgs.txt"
cf staging-security-groups > "$AUDIT_DIR/02-global-staging-asgs.txt"

# 2. All ASG definitions (full rule JSON)
cf curl /v3/security_groups?per_page=100 \
  > "$AUDIT_DIR/03-all-security-groups.json"

# 3. All space-ASG bindings
cf curl "/v3/security_groups?per_page=100&running_space_guids=*" \
  > "$AUDIT_DIR/04-space-asg-bindings.json"

# 4. All C2C network policies (cross-space = cross-zone conduits)
cf curl /networking/v1/external/policies \
  > "$AUDIT_DIR/05-c2c-policies.json"

# 5. All routes (check for plain HTTP)
cf curl /v3/routes?per_page=200 \
  > "$AUDIT_DIR/06-routes.json"

# 6. CC audit events: ASG changes in last 90 days
cf curl "/v3/audit_events?types=audit.security_group.create,audit.security_group.update,audit.security_group.bind_space&per_page=200" \
  > "$AUDIT_DIR/07-asg-audit-events.json"

# 7. TLS certificate expiry check
echo | openssl s_client -connect "$(cf api | awk '{print $3}' | sed 's|https://||')" 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates \
  > "$AUDIT_DIR/08-tls-cert-expiry.txt"

# 8. Org metadata (IEC 62443 zone annotations)
cf curl /v3/organizations?per_page=100 \
  > "$AUDIT_DIR/09-org-metadata.json"

echo "Audit evidence saved to $AUDIT_DIR/"
ls -la "$AUDIT_DIR/"

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Default public_networks and all_open ASGs unbound from all regulated spaces
  • Every space processing regulated data has explicit allow-list ASGs (no 0.0.0.0/0)
  • All ASG rules touching regulated data destinations have "log": true
  • Diego Cell syslog forwarding configured to SIEM with 12-month retention (PCI Req 10.5.1)
  • All external routes use HTTPS (no plain HTTP routes for regulated apps)
  • Route integrity (mTLS) enabled in cf-deployment
  • CredHub certificate rotation configured (auto-rotate before expiry)
  • CC audit events retained and queryable (ASG create/update/bind events)
  • IEC 62443 zone/conduit model documented and CF org metadata annotated
  • C2C policies cross-referenced against conduit register (no undocumented cross-org flows)
  • GDPR: no wildcard ASG in spaces processing personal data
  • GDPR: egress-to-EU-only ASG applied to all personal data spaces
  • Quarterly audit: run cf-compliance-audit.sh and compare against baseline

docs.title: CF-22: SAP BTP Networking Deep Dive
docs.text:
Track: CF-H — Security & Compliance Prerequisites: CF-01 — Platform Architecture, CF-19 — CF-to-K8s Migration Time: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Understand how SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) handles network isolation, private connectivity to on-premise systems, and the boundary between the BTP CF environment and BTP Kyma (Kubernetes). This lesson is specifically for engineers working in SAP BTP — the most widely deployed CF platform in enterprise CH/DE/USA markets.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Production Checklist · Quick Reference

docs.title: 1. BTP Platform Overview for Network Engineers
docs.text:
SAP BTP is a multi-runtime platform-as-a-service. From a networking perspective it has three distinct environments with separate network planes:

flowchart TD
    subgraph BTP["SAP BTP Global Account (single XSUAA tenant)"]
        subgraph SA["BTP Subaccount (network isolation boundary)"]
            subgraph CFE["BTP CF Environment\n(Cloud Foundry runtime)"]
                APP1["CF App (Silk CNI overlay)\nGorouter ingress\nASG egress control"]
            end
            subgraph KYM["BTP Kyma Environment\n(Kubernetes — Gardener-managed)"]
                APP2["K8s workload\nIstio service mesh\nNetworkPolicy"]
            end
            subgraph NEO["BTP Neo (legacy Java EE)\n(deprecated, still in production use)"]
                APP3["Java EE app\n(proprietary networking)"]
            end
        end
        subgraph XSUAA["XSUAA / Authorization Service"]
            OA["OAuth 2.0 / OIDC\n(shared identity across all runtimes)"]
        end
    end
    subgraph OnPrem["On-Premise / Private Cloud"]
        SAP1["SAP S/4HANA"]
        SAP2["SAP ECC / legacy systems"]
        DB["On-prem databases"]
    end
    subgraph Hyperscaler["Hyperscaler VPC\n(AWS/Azure/GCP)"]
        CUST["Customer-managed\nservices / databases"]
    end

    CFE <-->|"Cross-runtime: HTTPS via public FQDNs only\n(no pod-to-pod, no VPC peering)"| KYM
    SA <-->|"BTP Connectivity Service\n(Cloud Connector tunnel)"| OnPrem
    SA <-->|"BTP Private Link Service\n(PrivateLink / Private Endpoint)"| Hyperscaler

    style CFE fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style KYM fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
    style OnPrem fill:#5a2d27,color:#fff

Critical networking insight: The BTP CF environment and Kyma environment are completely separate network planes. There is no VPC peering, no shared overlay, no pod-to-pod routing between them. All cross-runtime communication goes through public HTTPS endpoints (Gorouter FQDN → Kyma Istio Gateway FQDN). This simplifies firewall rules but means every cross-runtime call pays a full TLS handshake and external network round-trip.

docs.title: 2. BTP Subaccount as Network Isolation Boundary
docs.text:
The BTP subaccount is the primary isolation unit — not the org or space (CF) or namespace (Kyma):

flowchart LR
    subgraph GA["Global Account"]
        subgraph SA1["Subaccount: Production-EU\n(GDPR data residency: eu-central-1)"]
            CF1["CF Org: prod\nSpace: api, workers"]
            K1["Kyma Namespace: prod"]
        end
        subgraph SA2["Subaccount: Production-US\n(HIPAA workloads: us-east-1)"]
            CF2["CF Org: prod-us\nSpace: phi-api"]
            K2["Kyma Namespace: prod-us"]
        end
        subgraph SA3["Subaccount: Dev\n(non-regulated)"]
            CF3["CF Org: dev"]
        end
    end

    SA1 -->|"separate XSUAA tenant\nseparate network plane\nseparate ASG scope"| SA2

Each subaccount: - Has its own XSUAA service instance (OAuth tokens are scoped per subaccount) - Has its own CF environment with separate Gorouter, Diego Cells, and Silk CNI overlay - Has independent connectivity service entitlement (separate Cloud Connector) - Maps to a specific hyperscaler region for data residency compliance

For GDPR compliance: one subaccount per data residency region (eu-central-1 for EU personal data, never co-mingled with US).

docs.title: 3. BTP Private Link Service
docs.text:
Private Link Service enables CF apps and Kyma workloads to reach hyperscaler-managed services (AWS RDS, Azure SQL, etc.) without traffic traversing the public internet. Traffic stays within the hyperscaler backbone.

flowchart LR
    subgraph BTP_VPC["BTP-managed VPC\n(hyperscaler region)"]
        CFApp["CF App container\n(BTP CF environment)"]
        PLE["BTP Private Link\nEndpoint\n(ENI in BTP VPC)"]
    end
    subgraph CUST_VPC["Customer VPC\n(same hyperscaler region)"]
        NLB["Network Load Balancer\n(customer-managed)"]
        SVC["Customer service\n(RDS, Azure SQL,\nself-hosted DB)"]
    end
    subgraph Backbone["Hyperscaler Private Backbone\n(no public internet)"]
        PLS["AWS PrivateLink /\nAzure Private Link\nService"]
    end

    CFApp -->|"TCP to\nprivate hostname"| PLE
    PLE <-->|"PrivateLink connection\n(encrypted, private)"| Backbone
    Backbone <-->|"NLB forwards\nto target service"| NLB
    NLB --> SVC

    style Backbone fill:#5a4a1a,color:#fff

docs.title: Enabling Private Link in BTP CF
docs.text:
# 1. Create a Private Link service instance in BTP CF
# (requires Private Link entitlement in the subaccount)
cf create-service privatelink standard my-private-link \
  -c '{"resourceId": "/subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/.../providers/Microsoft.Sql/servers/my-sql-server"}'
  # For Azure: resourceId is the ARM resource ID of the target service
  # For AWS: serviceId is the VPC Endpoint Service name (com.amazonaws.vpce.us-east-1.xxx)

# 2. Check provisioning status
cf service my-private-link
# Status: create succeeded
# Shows: hostname: my-private-link.privatelink.prod.eu20.hana.ondemand.com

# 3. Bind to your CF app
cf bind-service my-cf-app my-private-link

# 4. The VCAP_SERVICES env var now contains the private hostname
cf env my-cf-app | grep -A10 "privatelink"
# "credentials": {
#   "hostname": "fd12:3456::1",    ← IPv6 address in BTP overlay
#   "port": 1433
# }

# 5. Add ASG to allow egress to the private link endpoint
# Private Link endpoints use IPv6 addresses in BTP's internal range
cat > asg-private-link.json << 'EOF'
[
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "fd12:3456::/32",
    "ports": "1433",
    "description": "BTP Private Link: Azure SQL via PrivateLink (no public internet)",
    "log": true
  }
]
EOF
cf create-security-group private-link-db asg-private-link.json
cf bind-security-group private-link-db my-org my-space --lifecycle running

Compliance note: Private Link satisfies PCI-DSS Req 4.2.1 (encryption in transit) and HIPAA §164.312(e)(1) for traffic to customer-managed databases, because traffic never traverses the public internet and uses hyperscaler-level encryption.

docs.title: 4. BTP Connectivity Service and Cloud Connector
docs.text:
For on-premise systems (SAP S/4HANA, legacy databases, OT systems), BTP uses the Connectivity Service paired with the Cloud Connector — a reverse proxy that creates an outbound-only TLS tunnel from on-premise to BTP.

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as CF App (BTP)
    participant CS as Connectivity Service (BTP)
    participant CC as Cloud Connector (on-premise)
    participant SAP as SAP S/4HANA (on-premise)

    Note over CC,SAP: Cloud Connector runs on-premise as a Java process
    CC->>CS: Outbound TLS tunnel to BTP\n(no inbound ports opened on firewall)
    Note over CS,CC: Persistent HTTPS tunnel (port 443 outbound only)

    App->>CS: HTTP request to virtual host\nsap-s4.on-premise.example:443
    CS->>CC: Forward via tunnel\n(virtual host → real host mapping)
    CC->>SAP: Forward to real RFC/HTTP endpoint
    SAP-->>CC: Response
    CC-->>CS: Response via tunnel
    CS-->>App: Response

Key networking properties: - Outbound-only tunnel — the on-premise firewall needs only port 443 outbound to BTP. No inbound rules. - Virtual host mapping — CF apps reference virtual hostnames (sap-s4.on-premise), never the real on-premise IPs. This prevents IP leakage into app config. - TLS mutual authentication — the Cloud Connector authenticates to BTP using a certificate issued from the BTP subaccount.

docs.title: Configuring Connectivity Service in CF
docs.text:
# 1. Create Connectivity Service instance
cf create-service connectivity lite my-connectivity

# 2. Bind to app
cf bind-service my-cf-app my-connectivity

# 3. VCAP_SERVICES provides the proxy endpoint
cf env my-cf-app | grep -A5 "connectivity"
# "onpremise_proxy_host": "connectivityproxy.internal.cf.eu10.hana.ondemand.com"
# "onpremise_proxy_port": "20003"
# "onpremise_proxy_ldap_port": "20001"

# 4. Add ASG to allow egress to the connectivity proxy
cat > asg-connectivity.json << 'EOF'
[
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "10.0.3.0/24",
    "ports": "20003,20004",
    "description": "BTP Connectivity Service proxy for on-premise access",
    "log": true
  }
]
EOF
cf create-security-group btp-connectivity asg-connectivity.json
cf bind-security-group btp-connectivity my-org my-space --lifecycle running

# In your CF app: use the connectivity proxy to reach on-premise S/4HANA via RFC
import os, json

vcap = json.loads(os.environ['VCAP_SERVICES'])
conn = vcap['connectivity'][0]['credentials']

proxy_host = conn['onpremise_proxy_host']
proxy_port = conn['onpremise_proxy_port']

# Set JVM proxy (for Java-based SAP apps)
# -Dhttp.proxyHost=$proxy_host -Dhttp.proxyPort=$proxy_port
# Or for Python requests:
proxies = {
    'http': f'http://{proxy_host}:{proxy_port}',
    'https': f'http://{proxy_host}:{proxy_port}'
}
# The virtual hostname is configured in Cloud Connector's mapping
response = requests.get('http://sap-s4.on-premise/sap/bc/rest/api', proxies=proxies)

docs.title: 5. BTP CF vs Kyma Network Boundary
docs.text:
Understanding the network boundary between CF and Kyma is critical for architects designing cross-runtime solutions.

flowchart TD
    subgraph CFRuntime["BTP CF Environment"]
        CFAPP["CF App\n(Silk overlay: 10.255.x.x)"]
        GR["Gorouter\nPublic FQDN:\nmy-app.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com\n(Anycast IP, SAP-managed)"]
    end
    subgraph KymaRuntime["BTP Kyma Environment"]
        KAPP["K8s Pod\n(Gardener CNI: 100.96.x.x)"]
        IG["Istio Ingress Gateway\nPublic FQDN:\nmy-svc.c-abc123.kyma.ondemand.com\n(LoadBalancer IP)"]
    end
    subgraph Network["Communication path"]
        INT["Public Internet\n(HTTPS only)\nNo VPC peering\nNo pod-to-pod"]
    end

    CFAPP -->|"HTTPS to Kyma FQDN"| INT
    INT -->|"443 → Istio Gateway TLS termination"| IG
    IG --> KAPP
    KAPP -->|"HTTPS to CF FQDN"| INT
    INT -->|"443 → Gorouter TLS termination"| GR
    GR --> CFAPP

    style INT fill:#c0392b,color:#fff

docs.title: Cross-runtime call from CF app to Kyma service
docs.text:
# In CF app: call a Kyma-hosted service
# No special networking needed — just HTTPS to the Kyma gateway FQDN
# The Kyma FQDN is available in BTP service binding credentials

# Example: CF app calling a Kyma API
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://my-svc.c-abc123.kyma.ondemand.com/api/v1/resource

# ASG needed: allow egress to *.kyma.ondemand.com on port 443
cat > asg-kyma-egress.json << 'EOF'
[
  {
    "protocol": "tcp",
    "destination": "0.0.0.0/0",
    "ports": "443",
    "description": "HTTPS egress for Kyma API calls (and other HTTPS traffic)",
    "log": false
  }
]
EOF
# Note: This is broader than ideal — Kyma gateway IPs can be pinned if static

docs.title: Cross-runtime call from Kyma pod to CF app
docs.text:
# In Kyma: standard Kubernetes egress — no special configuration needed
# CF Gorouter is a public HTTPS endpoint reachable from Kyma pods
# NetworkPolicy in Kyma: allow egress to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443 (usually default)

# If Kyma NetworkPolicy is restrictive:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-cf-egress
  namespace: my-namespace
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-service
  egress:
  - ports:
    - port: 443
      protocol: TCP
    # CF Gorouter IPs can be pinned here if BTP provides static ranges

docs.title: XSUAA token sharing between CF and Kyma
docs.text:
Both runtimes share the same XSUAA tenant, so OAuth tokens issued for CF apps are valid for Kyma services:

# CF app: get token from XSUAA
TOKEN=$(cf oauth-token)

# Use same token to call Kyma service
curl -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" \
  https://my-kyma-svc.c-abc123.kyma.ondemand.com/api

# Kyma service: validate token against XSUAA JWKS endpoint
# JWKS: https://<subaccount>.authentication.eu10.hana.ondemand.com/token_keys

docs.title: Lab 1 — Inspect BTP subaccount network topology
docs.text:
# Log in to BTP CF
cf login -a https://api.cf.eu10.hana.ondemand.com

# List all orgs and spaces (understand the isolation model)
cf orgs
cf spaces   # after targeting an org

# Check current global ASGs (default BTP posture)
cf running-security-groups
# BTP default: usually includes restricted set, but verify — some global accounts
# still have public_networks bound

# List all security groups and check for wildcards
cf curl /v3/security_groups?per_page=100 | \
  python3 -c "
import json,sys
data=json.load(sys.stdin)
for sg in data['resources']:
    for rule in sg.get('rules',[]):
        if rule.get('destination','') == '0.0.0.0/0':
            print('WILDCARD ASG:', sg['name'], '→', rule.get('ports','*'))
"

docs.title: Lab 2 — Configure Private Link (Azure SQL example)
docs.text:
# Prerequisites: Private Link entitlement in BTP subaccount
# and an Azure SQL server with PrivateLink service configured

# Create Private Link service instance
cf create-service privatelink standard sql-private-link \
  -c '{"resourceId": "/subscriptions/SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/RG/providers/Microsoft.Sql/servers/my-sql"}'

# Wait for provisioning (may take 2-5 minutes)
watch -n10 "cf service sql-private-link | grep -E 'status|message'"

# Bind to app and check credentials
cf bind-service my-app sql-private-link
cf restage my-app
cf env my-app | grep -A10 "privatelink"

# Add ASG for the private link IPv6 range
# (get actual range from cf env output)
cf ssh my-app -c "env | grep VCAP_SERVICES" | \
  python3 -c "import json,sys,os; v=json.loads(os.environ.get('VCAP_SERVICES','{}')); [print(s) for s in v.get('privatelink',[{}])[0].get('credentials',{}).items()]"

docs.title: Lab 3 — Cloud Connector and on-premise connectivity
docs.text:
# Verify Connectivity Service is entitled and available
cf marketplace | grep connectivity

# Create instance
cf create-service connectivity lite onprem-conn
cf bind-service my-app onprem-conn
cf restage my-app

# Test connectivity to on-premise virtual host
# (must be configured in Cloud Connector mapping first)
cf ssh my-app -c "curl -x \$VCAP_SERVICES_CONNECTIVITY_PROXY http://sap-erp.onpremise/ping"

# Check Cloud Connector status from BTP cockpit:
# BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Connectivity → Cloud Connectors
# Or via API:
cf curl /v2/service_instances?q=service_plan_guid:CONNECTIVITY_PLAN_GUID

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• One BTP subaccount per data residency region (EU personal data never in US subaccount)
  • Default public_networks ASG reviewed — replace with explicit allow-list ASGs for regulated spaces
  • Private Link used for all hyperscaler database connections (no public internet for data-tier)
  • Cloud Connector configured with certificate-based auth (not username/password)
  • Cloud Connector subaccount mapping uses virtual host names, never real on-premise IPs in app config
  • Cross-runtime (CF ↔ Kyma) calls use service-to-service OAuth (not user tokens)
  • XSUAA token expiry configured appropriately (default 12h may be too long for PCI)
  • GDPR: EU-only subaccounts annotated, US subaccounts have separate XSUAA tenant
  • Private Link ASG restricted to IPv6 range issued by BTP (not 0.0.0.0/0)
  • Cloud Connector audit log enabled and forwarded to SIEM
  • BTP Audit Log Service enabled on subaccount (captures all CF API and XSUAA events)

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
# BTP CF login
cf login -a https://api.cf.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

# List BTP CF environments
# BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Cloud Foundry → Environments

# Create Private Link instance (Azure)
cf create-service privatelink standard <name> \
  -c '{"resourceId": "<ARM_RESOURCE_ID>"}'

# Create Private Link instance (AWS)
cf create-service privatelink standard <name> \
  -c '{"serviceId": "com.amazonaws.vpce.<region>.<service>"}'

# Create Connectivity Service instance
cf create-service connectivity lite <name>

# Check BTP Audit Log
cf create-service auditlog-management default my-audit
cf bind-service my-app my-audit
# Then query: GET /auditlog/v2/auditlogrecords

# Get Kyma kubeconfig (from BTP Cockpit or btp CLI)
btp get accounts/environment-instance <INSTANCE_ID> --global-account <GA_GUID>

# BTP CLI: list subaccounts
btp list accounts/subaccount

# BTP CLI: list entitlements
btp list accounts/entitlement --subaccount <SA_GUID>

docs.title: Network Namespaces
docs.text:
• Isolated network stack: interfaces, routes, iptables rules, sockets
  • Each pod gets its own netns; default netns: /proc/1/ns/net
  • Pod netns path: /proc/<pid>/ns/net
  • Pods connect to the host via veth pairs bridged to the node bridge
graph LR
    A[pod netns A<br/>eth0 10.244.0.2] -->|vethXXX| B((cni0 bridge<br/>10.244.0.1))
    C[pod netns B<br/>eth0 10.244.0.3] -->|vethYYY| B
    B --> D[host netns<br/>eth0 node IP]

docs.title: ip netns Commands
docs.text: Task Command List namespaces ip netns list Create namespace ip netns add <name> Delete namespace ip netns del <name> Run command in ns ip netns exec <name> <cmd> Open shell in ns ip netns exec <name> bash Show interfaces in ns ip netns exec <name> ip link Move interface into ns ip link set <iface> netns <name>

docs.title: veth Pairs
docs.text:
• Virtual Ethernet cable — always created as a pair
  • Packet in one end exits the other end
  • One end stays in host netns; other end moves into pod netns
  • Deleting either end removes both: ip link del veth0
  • If one end goes down, the other shows NO-CARRIER
Task Command Create pair ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1 Move end to netns ip link set veth1 netns <name> Bring up ip link set veth0 up Assign address ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev veth0 Delete pair ip link del veth0

docs.title: Linux Bridge
docs.text:
• Layer-2 software switch — forwards by MAC address
  • K8s node bridges: cbr0 (kubenet), cni0 (Flannel/Calico)
  • veth host-ends attach as bridge ports
  • Bridge gets pod-subnet gateway IP (e.g., 10.244.0.1/24)
Task Command Create bridge ip link add br0 type bridge Bring up ip link set br0 up Attach port ip link set veth0 master br0 Detach port ip link set veth0 nomaster Show ports bridge link show Show MAC table bridge fdb show Assign gateway IP ip addr add 10.244.0.1/24 dev br0

docs.title: ip link / ip addr / ip route
docs.text: Task Command Show all interfaces ip link show Show addresses ip addr show Show routes ip route show Add static route ip route add 10.0.0.0/8 via 192.168.1.1 Delete route ip route del 10.0.0.0/8 Default gateway ip route show default Enable IP forwarding sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 Persist IP forwarding echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward=1' >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-k8s.conf

docs.title: iptables Basics
docs.text:
• Four built-in tables: filter, nat, mangle, raw
  • K8s uses nat (Service ClusterIP DNAT) and filter (pod policy)
  • Chain traversal order for incoming: PREROUTING → FORWARD → POSTROUTING
Chain Table Kubernetes use PREROUTING nat DNAT ClusterIP → PodIP INPUT filter Host-local traffic policy FORWARD filter Pod-to-pod routing OUTPUT nat Localhost ClusterIP rewrite POSTROUTING nat MASQUERADE for node egress Task Command List rules verbose iptables -t nat -nvL --line-numbers Append rule iptables -A FORWARD -i br0 -j ACCEPT Insert rule at top iptables -I FORWARD 1 -i br0 -j ACCEPT Delete rule by number iptables -D FORWARD 1 Flush chain iptables -F FORWARD Add MASQUERADE iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.244.0.0/16 -j MASQUERADE Trace a packet iptables -t raw -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j TRACE

docs.title: Pod Network Setup Sequence (CNI)
docs.text:
1. Runtime calls CNI plugin with pod netns path
  2. CNI creates veth pair (vethXXXX host-end, eth0 pod-end)
  3. CNI moves eth0 into pod netns
  4. CNI attaches vethXXXX to node bridge (cni0)
  5. CNI assigns PodIP via IPAM, sets routes inside pod netns
  6. Host IP forwarding already enabled by kubelet bootstrap

docs.title: Cheat Sheet 02 — VXLAN / Geneve / Silk Overlay Mechanics
Encapsulation Header Formats
docs.text: Field VXLAN Geneve Outer transport UDP UDP Default port 4789 (IANA); Flannel legacy: 8472 6081 Segment ID VNI — 24-bit (16M segments) VNI — 24-bit Fixed overhead 50 bytes 30 bytes minimum (variable TLV) Extensible options No Yes — TLV options field L2 or L3 carry L2 Ethernet frame L2 or L3 (protocol field) Used by Flannel, Calico VXLAN, Silk OVN-Kubernetes, Geneve mode Cilium

docs.title: VXLAN Packet Anatomy
docs.text: Layer Header Size Outer Ethernet src/dst node MAC 14 bytes Outer IP src: node IP, dst: remote node IP 20 bytes Outer UDP src: ephemeral, dst: 4789 8 bytes VXLAN flags + VNI (24-bit) 8 bytes Total overhead 50 bytes Inner Ethernet pod src MAC → dst pod MAC 14 bytes Inner IP pod src IP → pod dst IP 20 bytes Inner TCP/UDP payload application data variable

docs.title: MTU Math
docs.text:
• Rule: pod MTU = underlay NIC MTU − VXLAN overhead
  • VXLAN overhead = 50 bytes
  • Geneve overhead = 30 bytes (no TLV options)
Underlay MTU VXLAN pod MTU Geneve pod MTU Jumbo (9000) VXLAN 1500 1450 1470 — 9000 8950 8970 8950 1480 (some clouds) 1430 1450 —
  • Silent fragmentation risk: if pod MTU is too high, inner packets exceed outer MTU → drops, not errors
  • Verify: ip link show flannel.1 or ip link show cilium_vxlan and check MTU

docs.title: Silk VXLAN (CF) Key Numbers
docs.text: Parameter Value Overlay CIDR 10.255.0.0/16 (default) Subnet per Diego Cell /24 Max containers per Cell ~254 Max Cells 250 VXLAN port UDP 4789 MTU penalty 50 bytes (1500 → 1450) Lease TTL 24 h, renewed on boot

docs.title: Encap / Decap Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P1 as Pod A (node1)
    participant V1 as VTEP node1
    participant N as Underlay Network
    participant V2 as VTEP node2
    participant P2 as Pod B (node2)

    P1->>V1: inner frame (src pod IP, dst pod IP)
    V1->>V1: FDB lookup: dst pod MAC → remote VTEP IP
    V1->>N: outer UDP/IP (src: node1 IP, dst: node2 IP, VNI)
    N->>V2: routed outer packet
    V2->>V2: decap: strip outer headers, verify VNI
    V2->>P2: inner frame delivered

docs.title: FDB (Forwarding Database) — VXLAN Control Plane
docs.text:
• FDB maps inner pod MAC → remote VTEP IP
  • Populated by: CNI agent (Flannel, Calico node, Silk daemon) via kernel bridge fdb or netlink
  • Flannel: writes FDB entries on flannel.1; uses etcd/k8s annotations for peer discovery
  • Calico VXLAN: uses BGP to exchange VTEP/MAC info; FDB on vxlan.calico
  • Silk: Silk Controller pushes cell VTEP IPs; FDB on silk-vtep

docs.title: Quick-Select Decision Points
docs.text:
• Dev / learning cluster — Flannel: zero config, works immediately
  • Production K8s + rich policy — Calico: mature, broad cloud support, BGP peering to ToR
  • High-throughput / observability required — Cilium: eBPF data plane, Hubble for flow visibility
  • Cloud Foundry / SAP BTP — Silk: built into CF, not portable to K8s
  • Service mesh without sidecars — Cilium only (Envoy sidecar-free mode)
  • Air-gapped BGP fabric — Calico with BGP peering to leaf switches

docs.text:
.:53 {
    errors
    health
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
        pods insecure
        fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
    }
    forward . /etc/resolv.conf
    cache 30
    loop
    reload
    loadbalance
}

docs.title: Common Gotchas
docs.text:
• No Endpoints? Check: selector matches pod labels, pod is Running, readinessProbe passes

docs.title: CF Routing: Gorouter / TCP Router / Internal Routes
docs.text: CS-05 | Track CF-C — Ingress and Routing | Lessons: CF-09, CF-10, CF-11, CF-12

docs.title: Gorouter — Key Facts
docs.text:
• In-memory routing table: hostname → [{ cell_ip:port, instance_id }, ...]
  • Populated via NATS router.register messages — no persistent store, no etcd
  • Route Emitter (per Diego Cell) publishes every 20 s; Gorouter TTL = 2 min
  • Routes expire silently if Route Emitter stops — traffic drops after 2 min
  • Load balancing: round-robin across healthy instances
  • Sticky sessions: JSESSIONID cookie (opt-in)
  • WebSocket: Upgrade: websocket header triggers connection hijack
  • TLS modes: edge termination (default), passthrough, full re-encrypt to container

docs.title: NATS Registration Sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant RE as Route Emitter (20s)
    participant NA as NATS Bus
    participant GR as Gorouter
    participant AP as App Container
    RE->>NA: publish router.register {host, port, uris}
    NA->>GR: deliver message
    GR->>GR: upsert in-memory table (TTL=2m)
    Note over GR: Client request arrives
    GR->>AP: HTTP + X-CF-InstanceID header

docs.title: Gorouter vs TCP Router
docs.text: Attribute Gorouter TCP Router Layer L7 (HTTP/HTTPS/WS) L4 (raw TCP) Route registration NATS heartbeat Routing API DB (Postgres) TTL / expiry 2 min if emitter stops Persisted in DB Load balancing unit Per HTTP request Per TCP connection Sticky sessions Yes (JSESSIONID) No TLS termination Yes (edge / passthrough) Passthrough by default Port model Wildcard domain + path One reserved port per route Use cases Web apps, REST, WebSocket Databases, gRPC, MQTT, Redis K8s equivalent Ingress Controller Service type=LoadBalancer (TCP)

docs.title: TCP Router — Key Facts
docs.text:
• Port range set by operator: reservable_ports (e.g., 1024-1123)
  • One TCP route = one port on the TCP Router's public hostname
  • Multiple instances behind one port = round-robin per connection
  • No NATS — Routing API REST + Postgres persists TCP route mappings
  • Diego Cell uses iptables DNAT to reach container IP (10.255.x.y:8080)
  • No circuit breaker — if all backends unhealthy, connections are dropped
  • cf map-route requires --port <N>; domain must have router group type tcp

docs.title: Route Types and DNS
docs.text: Route Type Format Resolved By Traffic Path HTTP shared domain app.cfapps.example.com Public DNS → LB Client → LB → Gorouter → Cell HTTP private domain app.my-org.com Custom DNS → LB Same as above TCP route tcp.example.com:1025 Public DNS → TCP Router Client → LB → TCP Router → Cell Internal (C2C) app.apps.internal BOSH DNS (health-aware) Direct VXLAN overlay, no SNAT

docs.title: apps.internal — C2C Service Discovery
docs.text:
• Domain apps.internal served by BOSH DNS, not public DNS
  • Resolves to container overlay IP (10.255.x.y) — Gorouter not involved
  • Requires both: a Network Policy AND a mapped apps.internal route
  • Health-aware: BOSH DNS removes unhealthy instances from responses
  • No kube-proxy, no ClusterIP, no Endpoints — DNS + iptables only

  matchLabels: {app: backend}

- from:

flowchart TD

    Q1 -->|K8s| Q2{NetworkPolicy\nexists for pod?}
    Q1 -->|CF| Q3{C2C or\nexternal?}

docs.title: Key Distinctions
docs.text:
• K8s default is permissive — traffic flows freely until a NetworkPolicy is applied
  • CF default is restrictive — egress denied and C2C denied from day one
  • K8s uses label selectors; CF C2C uses app names/GUIDs; CF ASGs use CIDRs
  • CF ASGs are egress-only; K8s NetworkPolicy controls ingress and egress independently
  • CF C2C is symmetric — one policy rule enables bidirectional communication
  • K8s policies are namespace-scoped — podSelector cannot reach across namespaces without namespaceSelector
  • CF space = isolation boundary — different-space apps cannot reach each other without C2C policy
  • K8s requires CNI enforcement — without Calico/Cilium/etc., NetworkPolicy objects are ignored
  • CF enforces at hypervisor layer (Garden) — apps cannot bypass ASGs from inside the container
  • Both platforms support dynamic updates — no pod/app restart required when policies change

→ Full lessons: K8s 16 — Network Policies · CF-07 — Application Security Groups · CF-13 — C2C Network Policies

docs.title: Key Facts
docs.text:
• NGINX Ingress — annotations for everything; mature but config is non-portable
  • Gateway API — role-split (infra / app); portable across implementations (Cilium, Istio, Contour)
  • Gorouter — CF-native; routes auto-registered by Diego via NATS; no K8s CRDs
  • Weighted splits — first-class only in Gateway API; NGINX uses canary hack; Gorouter lacks it
  • Cross-namespace — Gateway API uses ReferenceGrant; NGINX requires same namespace or IngressClass trick
  • Sticky sessions — NGINX: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity: cookie; Gateway API: implementation-dependent
  • WebSocket — all three support it; no special config needed in Gateway API or Gorouter

docs.title: Traffic Management Patterns
docs.text:
• Canary: VirtualService splits weight 90/10 between two DestinationRule subsets
  • Retries: retries.attempts: 3, retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure
  • Timeouts: .spec.http[].timeout: 5s on VirtualService
  • Circuit breaker: DestinationRule.trafficPolicy.outlierDetection
  • Fault inject: fault.delay.percentage or fault.abort.httpStatus for chaos testing
  • Mirror: mirror + mirrorPercentage for shadow traffic (zero-impact canary)

docs.title: Observability (Golden Signals)
docs.text:
Signal Istio source Cilium source Latency Envoy istio_request_duration_ms Hubble flow.latency Traffic istio_requests_total Hubble HTTP flows Errors istio_requests_total{response_code=~"5.."} Hubble drop reasons Saturation envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_active cilium_drop_count_total
  • Kiali: topology graph, mTLS status, config validation
  • Jaeger/Zipkin: distributed tracing via x-b3-traceid headers (propagate in app)
  • Prometheus scrape: port 15020 (sidecar) or 15090 (Envoy admin)

docs.title: Cilium Mesh Specifics
docs.text:
• Enable: helm upgrade cilium --set meshConfig.enabled=true
  • WireGuard encryption: --set encryption.enabled=true --set encryption.type=wireguard
  • Mutual auth (mTLS): --set authentication.mutual.spire.enabled=true
  • Hubble UI: cilium hubble ui — real-time L3–L7 flow graph
  • CiliumNetworkPolicy can combine with AuthorizationPolicy (Cilium as CNI + mesh)

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Ambient requires kernel >= 5.15 for eBPF-based ztunnel redirect
  • PERMISSIVE mode leaks plaintext — set STRICT before going production
  • Waypoint proxies are namespace-scoped; one per namespace using L7 policy
  • DestinationRule host must match ServiceEntry host exactly (case-sensitive)
  • Init container istio-init needs NET_ADMIN — blocked by some PSA restricted policies
  • Sidecar injection requires pod restart; ambient does not

→ Full lessons: Lesson 21 — Service Mesh with Istio | Lesson 12 — Cilium CNI + eBPF | Lesson 16 — Network Policies | Lesson 13 — Kubernetes Services + kube-proxy

docs.title: CF Loggregator Architecture
docs.text:
graph LR
    App["CF App\n(Diego Cell)"] -->|dropsonde UDP| Metron
    Metron -->|mTLS| Doppler

docs.title: Loggregator Components
docs.text:
• Metron — sidecar agent on each Diego cell; collects app logs + metrics
  • Doppler — aggregates streams from Metron over mTLS
  • Traffic Controller — exposes Firehose WebSocket endpoint to consumers
  • Log Cache — time-series store for recent logs and metrics (PromQL API)
  • RLP Gateway — Reverse Log Proxy; feeds external nozzles (Prometheus, SIEM)

docs.title: CF Diagnostic Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose cf logs <app> Tail app stdout/stderr live cf logs <app> --recent Last ~200 log lines cf app <app> Instances, memory, CPU, routes cf events <app> Deployment / crash events cf network-policies List active C2C policies cf curl /v2/info Platform version and endpoints log-cache tail <app-guid> Log Cache CLI plugin tail log-cache query --metric cpu Query metric by name

docs.title: Diagnostic Workflows
docs.text:
Flow drop investigation (K8s): - hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --namespace <ns> — identify dropped flows - Check cilium_drop_count_total{reason="Policy denied"} in Prometheus - kubectl describe ciliumnetworkpolicy — verify policy selectors

DNS failure investigation (K8s): - hubble observe --protocol dns --verdict DROPPED - Watch coredns_dns_responses_total{rcode="NXDOMAIN"} spike - kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup <svc> — confirm DNS resolution path

CF app connectivity issue: - cf logs <app> --recent — look for connection refused / timeout - cf app <app> — confirm instances in running state - cf network-policies — verify C2C policy exists between source and target apps - cf curl /networking/v1/external/policies — list all active C2C policies

docs.title: K8s PodSecurity Admission — Levels
docs.text:
Level Privileged HostNetwork RunAsRoot seccompProfile Use Case privileged Yes Yes Yes None Node agents, CNI plugins baseline No No Yes RuntimeDefault optional General workloads restricted No No No (must set runAsNonRoot) RuntimeDefault required Hardened prod apps
  • Apply at namespace level via label: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
  • Audit mode: pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted — logs violations without blocking
  • Warn mode: pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted — returns admission warnings to kubectl

docs.title: K8s NetworkPolicy Hardening Checklist
docs.text: Control YAML Snippet Purpose Default-deny ingress podSelector: {} + policyTypes: [Ingress] (no rules) Block all inbound per namespace Default-deny egress podSelector: {} + policyTypes: [Egress] (no rules) Block all outbound per namespace Allow DNS only Egress to kube-system port 53 TCP+UDP Permit name resolution Block cloud metadata Egress ipBlock: cidr: 0.0.0.0/0 + except: 169.254.169.254/32 Prevent IMDS abuse Namespace isolation namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: <ns> Cross-ns traffic control

docs.title: K8s mTLS (Istio / Cilium)
docs.text:
• Istio PeerAuthentication — set mtls.mode: STRICT per namespace or mesh-wide
  • Istio AuthorizationPolicy — deny-all base + explicit allow rules per service
  • Cilium mTLS — enabled via CiliumNetworkPolicy with authentication.mode: required
  • Verify: istioctl x authz check <pod> or cilium monitor --type drop

docs.title: K8s RBAC Checklist
docs.text:
• Prefer RoleBinding over ClusterRoleBinding — scope to namespace
  • Avoid cluster-admin for user accounts; use dedicated service accounts
  • Audit with: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>
  • Remove default service account token automount: automountServiceAccountToken: false

docs.title: CF Application Security Group (ASG) Defaults
docs.text:
ASG Type Bound To Default Behavior Staging ASGs Staging lifecycle Allow outbound during app staging Running ASGs Running lifecycle Allow outbound during app runtime Space-scoped ASGs Specific org/space Override or extend platform defaults No ASG Any lifecycle Deny all outbound (implicit)
  • Platform defaults set by admin: cf bind-staging-security-group / cf bind-running-security-group
  • Restrict to minimal CIDRs + ports — avoid 0.0.0.0/0 with all protocol
  • Audit effective ASGs: cf security-groups + cf space-security-groups <org> <space>

docs.title: CF TLS Configuration
docs.text:
• Gorouter: TLS 1.2+ minimum; disable RC4, 3DES; enforce HSTS headers
  • C2C (Silk): Mutual TLS between containers enabled by default via policy agent
  • Internal routes: Use apps.internal domain + C2C policies instead of public routes
  • Service bindings: Verify credentials use TLS endpoints (jdbcUrl / uri with ssl=true)
  • Custom domains: Provide cert via cf create-shared-domain or cf update-domain --router-group

docs.title: CF CredHub — Secret Management
docs.text:
• CredHub stores service credentials, certs, and arbitrary secrets — not env vars in plaintext
  • Service bindings via CredHub: credential value is a CredHub reference, not the secret itself
  • Rotate secrets: credhub set -n /cf/broker/<guid>/<key> -t value -v <new-value>
  • List credentials bound to app: cf env <app> — look for credhub-ref entries
  • Never store secrets in cf set-env for production — use CredHub-backed service bindings

docs.title: CF Org / Space Isolation
docs.text:
Boundary What It Isolates Breaks With Org Quota, billing, admin scope Shared domains (cross-org reachable) Space App deployment, service bindings Explicit C2C policies across spaces Security group Egress from apps ASG bound to multiple spaces Network segment VXLAN overlay per cell Misconfigured Silk subnet overlaps
  • Separate orgs for prod/non-prod — quota and isolation boundary
  • Never bind broad running ASGs to prod spaces
  • Audit C2C policies: cf network-policies — remove stale cross-space rules

docs.text: Task K8s Command CF Command Check pod security level kubectl get ns <ns> --show-labels n/a List NetworkPolicies kubectl get netpol -A cf network-policies Enforce default-deny kubectl apply -f default-deny.yaml Ensure no over-permissive ASG Inspect mTLS status istioctl x authz check <pod> cf ssh <app> -- openssl s_client ... List ASGs n/a cf security-groups Bind ASG to space n/a cf bind-security-group <sg> <org> <space> Remove C2C policy n/a cf remove-network-policy <src> --destination-app <dst> Audit pod capabilities kubectl get pod -o json \| jq '.spec.containers[].securityContext' cf ssh <app> -- cat /proc/1/status RBAC audit kubectl auth can-i --list --as=... cf org-users <org>

docs.title: Hardening Decision Flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    START[New namespace / space] --> K8S{Platform?}
    K8S -->|K8s| PSA[Set PodSecurity label\nrestricted or baseline]
    K8S -->|CF| ASG[Audit running ASG\nminimize CIDR+port]

docs.title: VPC CNI — ENI per Pod Model
docs.text:
• aws-node DaemonSet manages ENIs and IP assignments on every node
  • Each pod gets a real VPC IP — no overlay; pods are first-class VPC citizens
  • Node gets a primary ENI + secondary ENIs; each secondary ENI holds multiple IPs
  • IP pool is pre-warmed via WARM_IP_TARGET / MINIMUM_IP_TARGET env vars
  • Max pods per node = (ENIs × IPs-per-ENI) − 1; instance type determines limits
  • Prefix delegation (ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true) multiplies IP capacity on Nitro
Instance Type Max ENIs IPs per ENI Max Pods t3.medium 3 6 17 m5.large 3 10 29 m5.xlarge 4 15 58 c5.4xlarge 8 30 234

docs.title: Security Groups for Pods
docs.text:
• Requires VPC CNI ≥ 1.7.7 and trunk ENI support (Nitro instances only)
  • Pod gets a dedicated branch ENI with its own SG — independent of the node SG
  • Configured via SecurityGroupPolicy CRD (vpcresources.k8s.aws/v1beta1)
graph LR
    N[Node - trunk ENI] --> P[Pod - branch ENI]
    P -->|SG allow 5432| R[RDS Postgres]
    P -->|SG deny| X[Other Resources]

SecurityGroupPolicy example:

apiVersion: vpcresources.k8s.aws/v1beta1
kind: SecurityGroupPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-rds
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  securityGroups:
    groupIds:
      - sg-0abc123def456

docs.text: Aspect OVN-Kubernetes (default) OpenShift SDN (legacy) Dataplane OVS + OVN logical flows OVS + iptables NetworkPolicy enforcement OVN ACLs iptables rules Multi-tenant isolation AdminNetworkPolicy Built-in multitenant plugin IPv6 / dual-stack Yes Limited EgressFirewall Yes EgressNetworkPolicy only Status (OCP 4.14+) Default Deprecated

docs.text:
Component Role ovn-northd Translates logical intent to physical flows ovn-controller Programs OVS on each node per southbound DB OVS (Open vSwitch) Kernel dataplane — enforces flows Northbound DB Logical state: pods, policies, routers Southbound DB Physical bindings: chassis, port locations

docs.title: Route vs Ingress
docs.text:
Feature OpenShift Route Kubernetes Ingress Controller HAProxy Router Any (nginx, traefik, etc.) TLS strategies Edge / Passthrough / Re-encrypt Edge only (standard) Wildcard host Native Annotation-based mTLS Re-encrypt strategy Controller-dependent Weight-based split alternateBackends Annotation-based Auto hostname <svc>.<ns>.<cluster-domain> Manual
  • Routes are OpenShift-native; Ingress is portable
  • OpenShift Router also processes networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress objects
  • Use Routes when TLS re-encrypt or weight splitting is needed

docs.title: NetworkPolicy + EgressFirewall
docs.text:
Resource Scope Purpose NetworkPolicy Namespace Ingress/egress pod-to-pod rules (upstream compatible) AdminNetworkPolicy Cluster Admin-override; highest precedence BaselineAdminNetworkPolicy Cluster Low-precedence baseline; namespace policies override EgressFirewall Namespace Allow/deny egress by CIDR or DNS (OVN-K) EgressIP Namespace Stable outbound SNAT IP bound to a node EgressRouter Pod Dedicated NAT pod for fixed external IP
  • EgressNetworkPolicy is the SDN-era name; OVN-K uses EgressFirewall
  • AdminNetworkPolicy requires OVN-K 1.0+ (OCP 4.14+)

docs.title: Service Mesh (OSSM / Istio)
docs.text:
• Operator: OpenShift Service Mesh (OSSM) — wraps Istio + Kiali + Jaeger + Prometheus
  • Control plane CR: ServiceMeshControlPlane in a dedicated namespace
  • Namespace opt-in: ServiceMeshMemberRoll
  • mTLS modes: STRICT (reject plaintext) or PERMISSIVE (allow both)
  • Traffic CRs: VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway — identical to upstream Istio
  • Sidecar injection: enabled per namespace label or per-pod annotation

docs.title: Migration Decision Checklist
docs.text:
• Routes — run cf routes; map each entry to Ingress (HTTP) or Gateway+TCPRoute (TCP)
  • C2C policies — export with cf network-policies; replace app GUIDs with pod label selectors
  • ASGs — list with cf security-groups; translate each CIDR/port to NetworkPolicy egress ipBlock
  • DNS — replace all *.apps.internal references with svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local
  • Service bindings — replace CredHub bindings with Secret+envFrom or External Secrets Operator
  • Org/Space RBAC — map CF roles to ClusterRole/Role + RoleBinding per Namespace
  • Isolation segments — label nodes; add nodeSelector + tolerations to workload manifests
  • TLS — install cert-manager; replace Gorouter wildcard with per-domain Certificate CRs
  • Health checks — add readinessProbe + livenessProbe to every container spec
  • Canary / blue-green — adopt HTTPRoute weights or Argo Rollouts before final cutover
  • Coexistence — add bidirectional NetworkPolicy rules: CF cell overlay CIDR ↔ K8s pod CIDR
  • DNS egress rule — add explicit port-53 egress rule to every namespace using default-deny

docs.title: XDP Return Codes
docs.text: Code Action XDP_PASS Forward packet up the stack XDP_DROP Drop silently (fastest path) XDP_TX Redirect out same interface XDP_REDIRECT Forward to another iface/CPU XDP_ABORTED Drop + trace event (debug)

docs.title: Cilium eBPF Features
docs.text:
• Kube-proxy replacement — Service LB via BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_HASH; no iptables
  • Host routing — packets bypass netfilter; routed entirely in BPF
  • Sockmap acceleration — same-node pod-to-pod via sk_msg; bypasses TCP stack
  • Network Policy — enforced per-pod at cgroup_skb hook
  • Hubble — flow metadata streamed via BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF / perf events
  • Bandwidth Manager — TC egress rate limiting per pod
  • XDP load balancer — optional XDP_TX for Direct Server Return (DSR)
  • Encryption — WireGuard or IPsec triggered by BPF policy lookup

docs.title: Cilium CLI — eBPF Inspection
docs.text: Command Description cilium status Health + BPF feature flags cilium bpf policy get <ep-id> BPF policy map for a pod cilium bpf ct list global Connection tracking table cilium bpf lb list Service entries (kube-proxy replacement) cilium bpf nat list SNAT/DNAT map cilium bpf endpoint list endpoint → IP mappings cilium monitor Live packet event stream hubble observe Flow-level visibility (requires relay)

docs.title: BCC vs libbpf
docs.text: Aspect BCC libbpf + CO-RE Language Python + C embedded strings C with BTF headers Portability Requires kernel headers at runtime Runs on any BTF-enabled kernel Compilation JIT at load time Ahead-of-time (portable ELF) Overhead High (LLVM at load) Low Use case Rapid prototyping / tracing Production / Cilium internals Tools bcc-tools, bpftrace Cilium, Katran, XDP-tools

docs.title: Kernel Version Requirements
docs.text:
• 4.1+ — eBPF base support
  • 4.19 / 5.1+ — Cilium minimum (5.10+ recommended)
  • 5.2+ — BTF + CO-RE portability
  • 5.8+ — BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF
  • 5.18+ — XDP multi-buffer support

→ Full lessons: Lesson 10 — eBPF & XDP · Lesson 12 — Cilium CNI & eBPF

docs.text: Config Item Setting Why PFC (Priority Flow Control) Enable on priority 3 Pause frames prevent buffer overflow / drops ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) Enable on ToR and NICs Early signal before drops, smoother backpressure MTU 9000 (jumbo frames) Reduce per-packet overhead for large transfers DCQCN Enable on ConnectX NICs RDMA-specific congestion control algorithm Buffer reservation ~20% headroom per port Absorb PFC pause bursts without tail drop QoS DSCP marking DSCP=26 (CS3) for RDMA Separate queues for RDMA vs. control traffic

docs.title: Rail-Optimized Topology (small diagram)
docs.text:
graph TD
    SP["Spine (400 GbE)"]
    SP --> R0["Rail-0 ToR"]
    SP --> R1["Rail-1 ToR"]
    R0 --> NIC0["GPU0 NIC0 (RoCE)"]
    R0 --> NIC0b["GPU0 NIC0 (server B)"]
    R1 --> NIC1["GPU1 NIC1 (RoCE)"]
    R1 --> NIC1b["GPU1 NIC1 (server B)"]
    NIC0 --- NVL["NVLink fabric (intra-node)"]

  • Each GPU has its own dedicated NIC on its own ToR (rail)
  • All-reduce between servers = one NIC per GPU, no bandwidth sharing
  • Intra-node GPU comms stay on NVSwitch fabric, never hit Ethernet

docs.title: Kubernetes: Multus + SR-IOV for RDMA
docs.text:
• Multus CNI attaches multiple network interfaces to a pod
  • SR-IOV Device Plugin exposes VFs (Virtual Functions) as K8s resources
  • RDMA resource (rdma/rdma_shared_device_a) allocated per pod via resource limits
  • NetworkAttachmentDefinition selects VF pool bound to RDMA-capable NIC
  • Pod requests: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 + rdma/rdma_shared_device_a: 1

docs.text: Command What It Shows ibstat IB/RoCE port state, GID, link speed ibv_devinfo RDMA device attributes perftest / ib_send_bw RDMA bandwidth test between two nodes rdma link Linux RDMA subsystem link state ethtool -S <nic> \| grep pause PFC pause frame counters mlnx_qos -i <nic> Show QoS / PFC / ETS config on Mellanox NIC nccl-tests allreduce End-to-end NCCL bandwidth / latency nvidia-smi nvlink -s NVLink bandwidth and error counters kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nvidia-smi topo -m GPU-NIC topology matrix nsenter -t <pid> -n ip addr Inspect pod network namespace

docs.title: Common Failure Modes
docs.text:
• Packet drop on RoCE — missing PFC or ECN config; check ethtool -S pause counters
  • NCCL timeout / hang — NCCL bootstrap TCP fails; check NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME and firewall
  • GPUDirect disabled — NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL not set; kernel module nv_peer_mem missing
  • NVLink errors — hardware fault; check nvidia-smi nvlink -e
  • SR-IOV VF not assigned — device plugin not running or VF pool exhausted
  • MTU mismatch — jumbo frames not enabled end-to-end; causes fragmentation/drops
  • DCQCN not active — NICs or switches not configured; causes head-of-line blocking

docs.title: Lesson 00 — Kubernetes Networking: Visual Overview
docs.text:
Track: Orientation · Prerequisites: None · Duration: ~30 minutes (read-only)

Goal: Build a complete mental picture of Kubernetes networking before touching a single command. Every diagram in this lesson maps directly to a later lesson — use it as a reference you return to throughout the course.

docs.title: How to Use This Lesson
docs.text:
Read this top-to-bottom once before starting Track A. The six diagrams progress from the inside out:

  1. Kubernetes control/data plane split
  2. Pod networking on a single node
  3. Pod-to-pod traffic across nodes
  4. CNI plugin comparison (Calico vs Cilium vs VPC CNI)
  5. Service types and traffic paths
  6. State-of-the-art 2026 dataplane (eBPF vs iptables)

Each diagram is self-contained. On a reMarkable or e-reader, zoom in on each one individually.

docs.title: 1. Kubernetes Architecture — Control Plane and Data Plane
docs.text:
Every Kubernetes cluster splits into two planes. The control plane decides what should happen; the data plane makes it happen.

flowchart TD
    subgraph CP["Control Plane (master nodes)"]
        API["kube-apiserver\nREST gateway\nAuthn/Authz/Admission"]
        ETCD["etcd\nDistributed KV store\nCluster state"]
        SCHED["kube-scheduler\nPod placement\nTopology / taints"]
        CM["kube-controller-manager\nNode / ReplicaSet /\nEndpoint controllers"]
        CCM["cloud-controller-manager\nCloud LB / Route\nprogramming"]
    end

    subgraph DP["Data Plane (worker nodes)"]
        KL["kubelet\nPod lifecycle\nCNI / CSI invocation"]
        KP["kube-proxy\niptables / IPVS\nService VIP → Pod IP"]
        CNI["CNI Plugin\nveth / bridge / eBPF\nIPAM"]
        POD1["Pod A\nnetns + veth0\n10.0.0.5"]
        POD2["Pod B\nnetns + veth1\n10.0.0.6"]
    end

    API <-->|watches / updates| ETCD
    SCHED -->|bind pod to node| API
    CM -->|reconcile desired state| API
    CCM -->|cloud API calls| API
    KL -->|node heartbeat + pod status| API
    KL -->|exec add/del| CNI
    KP -->|watch Services + Endpoints| API
    CNI --> POD1
    CNI --> POD2

    style CP fill:#1a2a4a,color:#fff
    style DP fill:#1a3a2a,color:#fff
    style API fill:#1565C0,color:#fff
    style ETCD fill:#0d47a1,color:#fff
    style SCHED fill:#1976D2,color:#fff
    style CM fill:#1976D2,color:#fff
    style CCM fill:#1976D2,color:#fff
    style KL fill:#2E7D32,color:#fff
    style KP fill:#2E7D32,color:#fff
    style CNI fill:#388E3C,color:#fff
    style POD1 fill:#43A047,color:#fff
    style POD2 fill:#43A047,color:#fff

Key insight: The control plane never touches packet forwarding. kubelet and kube-proxy on each worker node do all the dataplane work, driven by watch streams from the API server.

docs.title: 2. Pod Networking — Single Node
docs.text:
Every pod gets its own Linux network namespace connected to the node via a veth pair. The node side of each veth attaches to a bridge (or eBPF program), which forwards between pods and to the node's physical NIC.

flowchart LR
    subgraph NODE["Worker Node (Linux kernel)"]
        subgraph NS1["Pod A netns"]
            ETH0A["eth0\n10.0.0.5/24"]
        end
        subgraph NS2["Pod B netns"]
            ETH0B["eth0\n10.0.0.6/24"]
        end
        subgraph NS3["Pod C netns"]
            ETH0C["eth0\n10.0.0.7/24"]
        end
        VETHA["veth-a (host end)"]
        VETHB["veth-b (host end)"]
        VETHC["veth-c (host end)"]
        BR["cni0 bridge\n10.0.0.1/24"]
        ETH1["eth1 (physical NIC)\n192.168.1.10"]
    end

    ETH0A <-->|veth pair| VETHA
    ETH0B <-->|veth pair| VETHB
    ETH0C <-->|veth pair| VETHC
    VETHA --> BR
    VETHB --> BR
    VETHC --> BR
    BR --> ETH1

    style NS1 fill:#0d47a1,color:#fff
    style NS2 fill:#0d47a1,color:#fff
    style NS3 fill:#0d47a1,color:#fff
    style BR fill:#2E7D32,color:#fff
    style ETH1 fill:#4a4a4a,color:#fff

What CNI does: At pod start, kubelet calls the CNI plugin binary with ADD. CNI creates the veth pair, moves one end into the pod's netns, assigns an IP via IPAM, and programs a route on the bridge. At pod deletion it calls DEL to clean up.

docs.title: 3. Pod-to-Pod Traffic — Across Nodes
docs.text:
When Pod A on Node 1 sends a packet to Pod B on Node 2, the packet must cross the underlay network. CNI plugins solve this in two fundamentally different ways: overlay (encapsulate) or underlay routing (BGP).

flowchart LR
    subgraph N1["Node 1  192.168.1.10"]
        PA["Pod A\n10.0.0.5"]
        BR1["bridge / eBPF"]
        VTEP1["VTEP\n(VXLAN encap)\nor BGP route"]
        NIC1["eth1"]
    end

    subgraph UNDERLAY["Physical Network / VPC"]
        SW["L3 Switch / Router\nor AWS VPC route table"]
    end

    subgraph N2["Node 2  192.168.1.11"]
        NIC2["eth1"]
        VTEP2["VTEP\n(VXLAN decap)\nor BGP route"]
        BR2["bridge / eBPF"]
        PB["Pod B\n10.1.0.5"]
    end

    PA --> BR1
    BR1 --> VTEP1
    VTEP1 -->|"OVERLAY: UDP/4789 outer: 192.168.1.10→192.168.1.11\nUNDERLAY: BGP route 10.1.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.11"| SW
    SW --> NIC2
    NIC2 --> VTEP2
    VTEP2 --> BR2
    BR2 --> PB

    style N2 fill:#1a2a4a,color:#fff

The three dominant CNI families use fundamentally different dataplanes.

docs.title: 5. Kubernetes Service Types — Traffic Paths
docs.text:
A Service is a stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) backed by an Endpoints list. kube-proxy (or eBPF) translates the VIP to a real pod IP at the kernel level using DNAT.

flowchart LR
    subgraph EXTERNAL["External Traffic"]
        INET["Internet\nclient"]
        INTCLIENT["Internal\nclient (VM)"]
    end

    subgraph CLUSTER["Kubernetes Cluster"]
        subgraph SVC["Service Types"]
            CIP["ClusterIP\n10.96.x.x\ncluster-internal only"]
            NP["NodePort\n:30000-32767\nreachable via any node IP"]
            LB["LoadBalancer\nCloud LB IP\npublic or internal"]
            EXT["ExternalName\nCNAME alias\nno proxy"]
        end

        POD1["Pod replica 1\n10.0.0.5:8080"]
        POD2["Pod replica 2\n10.0.1.5:8080"]
        POD3["Pod replica 3\n10.0.2.5:8080"]

        CIP -->|"DNAT (iptables/eBPF)\nrandom / session-affinity"| POD1
        CIP --> POD2
        CIP --> POD3
        NP --> CIP
        LB --> NP
    end

    INET -->|"TCP :443"| LB
    INTCLIENT -->|"TCP :30080"| NP
    INTCLIENT -->|"TCP ClusterIP"| CIP

    style EXTERNAL fill:#3a2a1a,color:#fff
    style CLUSTER fill:#1a2a1a,color:#fff
    style CIP fill:#1565C0,color:#fff
    style NP fill:#2E7D32,color:#fff
    style LB fill:#E65100,color:#fff
    style EXT fill:#6a1a8a,color:#fff
    style POD1 fill:#0d47a1,color:#fff
    style POD2 fill:#0d47a1,color:#fff
    style POD3 fill:#0d47a1,color:#fff

How kube-proxy works: It watches the API server for Service/Endpoints changes and writes iptables DNAT rules (or IPVS entries, or loads eBPF programs in Cilium kube-proxy replacement mode). The kernel intercepts packets destined for the ClusterIP and rewrites the destination before routing.

docs.title: 6. State of the Art — 2026 Kubernetes Dataplane
docs.text:
Modern production clusters are moving from iptables to eBPF. Here is the full picture of where the industry stands.

        L2["CNI uses Linux bridge + iptables\nconntrack for every flow"]
        L3["No per-flow observability\nonly node-level metrics"]
        L1 --> L2 --> L3
    end

    subgraph MODERN["Modern Dataplane (2023+)"]
        M1["Cilium kube-proxy replacement\neBPF O(1) hash map — scales to 100k Services"]
        M2["XDP for DDoS / LB offload\npackets never enter kernel stack"]
        M3["Hubble / Tetragon\nper-flow L3-L7 visibility + security audit"]
        M4["WireGuard node-to-node encryption\nkernelspace — zero user-space overhead"]
        M1 --> M2
        M1 --> M3
        M1 --> M4
    end

    subgraph CLOUD["Cloud-Native Additions"]
        CL1["Gateway API replaces Ingress\nexpressive routing, multi-tenant"]
        CL2["SPIFFE/SPIRE + mTLS\nworkload identity without IP trust"]
        CL3["IPAM from cloud IPAM\n(AWS prefix delegation, Azure CNI overlay)"]
    end

    LEGACY -->|"Migration path: deploy Cilium\nin migration mode alongside kube-proxy"| MODERN

docs.title: Lesson 01 — Linux Networking Fundamentals
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud · Prereqs: Basic Linux command line familiarity · Time: ~2 hours

Goal: Wire two virtual pods together on a single Linux host using veth pairs, a bridge, and ip_forward — replicating exactly what every CNI plugin does on node startup.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. The Linux Network Stack
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Application sockets (HTTP/gRPC)"] --"syscall send/recv"--> B["Transport Layer (TCP/UDP :80/:443)"]
    B --"IP datagram"--> C["Network Layer (IPv4/IPv6)"]
    C --"Ethernet frame"--> D["Link Layer (eth/veth driver)"]
    D --"electrical/optical"--> E["Physical NIC (1G/10G/25G)"]
    C --"kernel virtual path"--> F["CNI Layer (veth/bridge/VXLAN)"]
    F --"kernel xmit"--> D

    style A fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style D fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style E fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style F fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff

Kubernetes adds virtual layers (veth pairs, bridges, tunnels) between the Link and Network layers. The kernel enforces namespace isolation at the network layer — each pod gets its own complete stack. CNI plugins operate at this virtual layer, never touching the physical NIC directly.

docs.title: 2. Network Namespaces
docs.text:
A network namespace gives a process its own isolated network stack: interfaces, routing table, iptables rules, and sockets.

# Create a namespace
ip netns add ns-blue

# List namespaces
ip netns list

# Run a command inside the namespace
ip netns exec ns-blue ip link list

# Delete
ip netns del ns-blue

Each Kubernetes pod runs in its own network namespace. The pause (infra) container holds the namespace; app containers join it via --network=container:<id>.

See also: Lesson 04 — Network Namespaces Deep Dive covers the full pod namespace lifecycle, CNI invocation sequence, and how to debug pod namespaces from the host using nsenter.

docs.title: 3. Virtual Ethernet Pairs (veth)
docs.text:
A veth pair is a bidirectional virtual wire connecting two network namespaces. Packets written into one end emerge from the other — zero buffering, kernel-internal path.

# Create a veth pair
ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1

# Move veth1 into ns-blue
ip link set veth1 netns ns-blue

# Configure veth0 on the host
ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev veth0
ip link set veth0 up

# Configure veth1 inside the namespace
ip netns exec ns-blue ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev veth1
ip netns exec ns-blue ip link set veth1 up
ip netns exec ns-blue ip link set lo up

# Test connectivity
ping -c3 10.0.0.2
ip netns exec ns-blue ping -c3 10.0.0.1

This is exactly what a CNI plugin does when it creates a pod: one veth end goes into the pod namespace (named eth0 by convention), the other stays on the host (named cali<hash>, veth<hash>, or similar).

docs.title: 4. Linux Bridge
docs.text:
A bridge (layer 2 switch in software) connects multiple veth endpoints so pods on the same node can communicate without routing.

# Create a bridge
ip link add br0 type bridge
ip link set br0 up
ip addr add 10.244.0.1/24 dev br0

# Attach veth0 (host side of pod veth pair) to the bridge
ip link set veth0 master br0

Flannel's cbr0, Docker's docker0, and Calico's cali*-to-bridge wiring all follow this pattern.

flowchart LR

    end

    PA <-->|"veth pair L2"| VA
    PB <-->|"veth pair L2"| VB
    VA --- BR
    VB --- BR
    BR --- ETH
    BR --- RT

    style poda fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
    style podb fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
    style host fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff

docs.title: Flow: Pod A to Pod B (same node)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PA as Pod A nginx :80
    participant VA as veth-a-br host-side
    participant ARP as ARP/FDB table
    participant BR as br0 bridge
    participant VB as veth-b-br host-side
    participant PB as Pod B redis :6379

    PA->>VA: Ethernet frame src=10.244.0.10 dst=10.244.0.11
    VA->>BR: Frame arrives at bridge port
    BR->>ARP: Lookup dst MAC for 10.244.0.11
    ARP-->>BR: MAC aa:bb:cc:00:01:02 on port veth-b-br
    BR->>VB: Frame forwarded to matched bridge port
    VB->>PB: Packet delivered TCP :6379
    PB-->>VB: TCP reply ACK
    VB-->>BR: Reply frame
    BR-->>VA: Forwarded via FDB lookup
    VA-->>PA: Reply delivered to Pod A

docs.title: 5. Routing Table
docs.text:
Linux uses routing rules to decide where to send packets.

# Show main routing table
ip route show

# Add a route: reach 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.10
ip route add 10.244.1.0/24 via 192.168.1.10 dev eth0

# Add a host route for a pod IP (Calico-style)
ip route add 10.244.0.5/32 dev veth_pod0

# Policy routing — multiple tables
ip rule list
ip route show table local

For cross-node pod routing, CNI plugins either: - Add static routes per remote pod CIDR (Calico BGP, Flannel host-gw) - Encapsulate packets in a tunnel and route the outer header (VXLAN, Geneve)

See also: Lesson 02 — IP Routing and Forwarding for longest-prefix match, ECMP, policy routing, and cloud provider differences.

docs.title: 6. ARP and Neighbor Table
docs.text:
ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses within a L2 segment. The kernel caches results in the neighbor table.

# Show ARP cache
ip neigh show

# Flush ARP for an interface
ip neigh flush dev eth0

# Static ARP entry (useful for VXLAN FDB population)
ip neigh add 10.244.0.5 lladdr aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff dev eth0

Calico uses proxy_arp on each veth so pods can reach any IP without an ARP for the gateway:

cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/cali1234abcd/proxy_arp
# → 1

docs.title: 7. Key Kernel Parameters for Kubernetes
docs.text:
# IP forwarding — required so the node can route between pod and external traffic
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1

# Allow iptables to see bridged traffic (needed by kube-proxy and many CNIs)
sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1
sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables=1

# Avoid conntrack table exhaustion
sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=1000000

These are set in /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes.conf by kubeadm.
