docs.title: Lesson 19 — Load Balancing on Bare Metal: MetalLB and kube-vip
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal Prerequisites: Lesson 06 — BGP Fundamentals, Lesson 13 — Kubernetes Services Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Configure MetalLB in L2 and BGP modes to provide LoadBalancer services on bare-metal clusters, compare with kube-vip for control-plane HA, and diagnose ARP and BGP announcement failures.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. The Bare Metal LB Problem
docs.text:
# Without a LB controller, LoadBalancer services hang:
kubectl get svc web
# NAME   TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)        AGE
# web    LoadBalancer   10.96.42.10   <pending>     80:30080/TCP   10m

The Cloud Controller Manager (CCM) provisions cloud LBs. On bare metal, you need to run your own LB controller.

flowchart LR
    subgraph cloud["Cloud Cluster (EKS / GKE / AKS)"]
        SVC1["Service type: LoadBalancer app: web"]
        CCM["Cloud Controller Manager aws-cloud-provider v1.28"]
        CLB["AWS NLB / GCP Passthrough NLB / Azure SLB external IP assigned"]
    end
    subgraph bare["Bare Metal Cluster (on-prem / BTP)"]
        SVC2["Service type: LoadBalancer app: web"]
        MLB["MetalLB v0.14 controller + speaker DaemonSet"]
        VIP["VIP 192.168.100.100 ARP reply (L2) or BGP /32 route"]
    end

    SVC1 --"EnsureLoadBalancer() call"--> CCM --"cloud API provision"--> CLB
    SVC2 --"EnsureLoadBalancer() call"--> MLB --"ARP or BGP announce :179"--> VIP

    style CLB fill:#cce,stroke:#66c
    style VIP fill:#cec,stroke:#6c6

docs.title: 2. MetalLB Overview
docs.text:
MetalLB implements LoadBalancer by either: - L2 mode: answers ARP/NDP for the VIP on the local subnet - BGP mode: advertises VIP routes to upstream routers

# Install MetalLB
helm repo add metallb https://metallb.github.io/metallb
helm install metallb metallb/metallb \
  --namespace metallb-system \
  --create-namespace

kubectl get pods -n metallb-system
# metallb-controller-xxx  (allocates IPs)
# metallb-speaker-xxx     (announces IPs — DaemonSet)

docs.title: 3. MetalLB L2 Mode
docs.text:
The speaker pod on the node holding the VIP responds to ARP requests for that IP.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Router as Upstream Router / ToR Switch
    participant Node1 as Node 1 worker-1 (elected speaker)
    participant Node2 as Node 2 worker-2
    participant Spk as MetalLB Speaker v0.14 (Node 1)
    participant Pod as Backend Pod app:web

    Note over Spk: Leader election: worker-1 wins VIP 192.168.100.100

    Router->>Node1: ARP request: who has 192.168.100.100?
    Spk-->>Router: ARP reply: 192.168.100.100 is at <worker-1-MAC> gratuitous ARP
    Router->>Node1: TCP :80 to 192.168.100.100
    Node1->>Pod: forward via kube-proxy DNAT (may cross to Node 2 pod)

    Note over Node1,Node2: On node failure: leader re-election
    Spk-->>Router: gratuitous ARP from Node 2 worker-2 (new leader)
    Note over Router: Router updates ARP cache within ~10 s
# Configure an IP address pool
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: production-pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 192.168.100.100-192.168.100.200
    - 192.168.200.0/24
---
# Enable L2 advertisement
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: L2Advertisement
metadata:
  name: l2-advert
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - production-pool
  nodeSelectors:               # optional: which nodes can announce
    - matchLabels:
        node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: ""

L2 mode limitations: - Single node holds the VIP at a time (failover on node failure, ~10s) - All traffic enters through one node (no true load balancing at the LB layer) - Works only within the same L2 broadcast domain

docs.title: 4. MetalLB BGP Mode
docs.text:
Announces VIPs via BGP to upstream routers. Multiple nodes can announce the same VIP via ECMP.

# BGP Peer (ToR switch)
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta2
kind: BGPPeer
metadata:
  name: tor-switch
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  myASN: 64512
  peerASN: 65000
  peerAddress: 192.168.1.1
  holdTime: 30s
  keepaliveTime: 10s
---
# Advertise pool via BGP
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BGPAdvertisement
metadata:
  name: bgp-advert
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - production-pool
  communities:
    - 64512:100       # tag with community for upstream policy
  aggregationLength: 32   # advertise host routes (/32)

BGP mode advantages: - ECMP: multiple nodes announce same VIP → load balancing at router level - Fast failover (BFD sub-second) - Works across L3 boundaries (across routers, not just L2)

docs.title: Key BGP/Pool Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change myASN — Local AS number for the BGP session Use private ASN (64512-65535); must match router config peerASN — Upstream router's AS number Match the ToR switch configuration holdTime 90s BGP session dead timer Reduce to 30s for faster failover detection aggregationLength 32 (IPv4) Prefix length for advertised routes Use 32 for per-VIP /32 host routes; aggregate with /24 to reduce BGP table size communities (none) BGP community strings appended to routes Signal upstream policy (e.g., no-export, local-pref) bfdProfile (none) Enables BFD for sub-second failure detection Production BGP — combine with fast BFD for <1s failover IPAddressPool.addresses — CIDR or range of allocatable IPs Must not overlap with node or pod subnets

docs.title: 5. Using the LoadBalancer Service
docs.text:
# Assign from a specific pool
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    metallb.io/address-pool: production-pool
    metallb.io/loadBalancerIPs: 192.168.100.105  # request specific IP
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

kubectl get svc web
# NAME   TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP       PORT(S)   AGE
# web    LoadBalancer   10.96.42.10   192.168.100.105   80/TCP    30s

docs.title: 6. kube-vip
docs.text:
kube-vip provides VIP management using VRRP (ARP-based HA) or BGP. Also handles HA for the Kubernetes control plane API server.

# Install kube-vip as a DaemonSet for LoadBalancer services
kubectl apply -f https://kube-vip.io/manifests/rbac.yaml

# Generate kube-vip DaemonSet manifest
docker run --network host --rm \
  ghcr.io/kube-vip/kube-vip:latest \
  manifest daemonset \
  --services \
  --arp \
  --leaderElection \
  | kubectl apply -f -

# kube-vip ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: kube-vip
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  range-global: "192.168.100.100-192.168.100.200"

kube-vip vs MetalLB:

Feature kube-vip MetalLB Control-plane VIP (HA API server) Yes No L2 / ARP mode Yes (VRRP) Yes BGP mode Yes Yes (more mature) IP pool management CRDs Basic (ConfigMap range) Full (IPAddressPool, L2Advertisement, BGPAdvertisement) Recommended for Control-plane HA + simple LB Production LoadBalancer services

docs.title: 7. Shared IPs Across Services
docs.text:
Both tools support multiple services sharing one IP (different ports).

# MetalLB shared IP
metadata:
  annotations:
    metallb.io/allow-shared-ip: "web-group"   # same key = shared IP
---
# Service 1: port 80
# Service 2: port 443
# Both get the same EXTERNAL-IP

docs.title: 8. Production Considerations
docs.text:
# Separate the LB VIP range from node IPs to avoid conflicts
# Node subnet:  192.168.1.0/24
# VIP pool:     192.168.100.0/24  (different subnet, routed via ToR)

# Use BGP mode for production — no single point of failure
# Use L2 mode for dev/lab — simpler, no BGP required

# MetalLB BGP with BFD for fast failover
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta2
kind: BGPPeer
spec:
  bfdProfile: fast-bfd
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BFDProfile
metadata:
  name: fast-bfd
spec:
  receiveInterval: 300    # 300ms
  transmitInterval: 300
  detectMultiplier: 3     # 3 × 300ms = 900ms failure detection

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get pods -n metallb-system 2>/dev/null || echo "MetalLB not installed"
kubectl get ipaddresspools,l2advertisements -n metallb-system 2>/dev/null
kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=LoadBalancer

# Terminal 2 — minikube Linux node (inspect ARP for L2 mode)
minikube ssh
arp -n | head -20
ip neigh show

Observation commands — run after installing MetalLB and creating a LoadBalancer service:

# Watch MetalLB speaker announcements in real time
kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=speaker -f &

# Create a test LoadBalancer service
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment web --type=LoadBalancer --port=80

# Watch the service get an EXTERNAL-IP assigned from the pool
kubectl get svc web -w
# Expect: EXTERNAL-IP changes from <pending> to 192.168.100.xxx

# From outside the cluster, verify ARP resolution (L2 mode)
# arping -I eth0 192.168.100.100   # should respond from the elected speaker node

# Check which node is currently serving the VIP
kubectl get events -n metallb-system | grep -i announcing

See also: Lesson 06 — BGP Fundamentals for BGP session setup and ECMP concepts used by MetalLB BGP mode.

docs.title: Hands-On Lab
docs.text:
Work through the Theory sections to build a fully functional bare-metal LoadBalancer setup:

  1. Install MetalLB via Helm (Section 2) and verify controller + speaker pods are Running
  2. Create an IPAddressPool and L2Advertisement (Section 3); expose a deployment and watch EXTERNAL-IP assigned
  3. Test ARP announcement: run arping -I eth0 <VIP> from outside the cluster and confirm speaker node responds
  4. Switch to BGP mode (Section 4): configure BGPPeer to point at your router (or a mock with gobgp) and verify session
  5. Add a BFDProfile (Section 8) and check sub-second failover by cordoning the elected speaker node
  6. Install kube-vip (Section 6) and compare VIP failover behavior to MetalLB L2 mode

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
Key parameter tables are embedded in the Theory sections above:

Section Table Section 4 — BGP Mode Key BGP/Pool Parameters: myASN, peerASN, holdTime, aggregationLength, bfdProfile Section 6 — kube-vip kube-vip vs MetalLB feature comparison table

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> after MetalLB install No IPAddressPool or L2Advertisement/BGPAdvertisement created kubectl get ipaddresspools,l2advertisements -n metallb-system Create IPAddressPool and the appropriate Advertisement CRD VIP assigned but unreachable from outside cluster VIP is in a different subnet than clients (L2 mode) or BGP session is not established arping -I eth0 <VIP> from outside; kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l component=speaker | grep bgp For L2: ensure VIP is in same broadcast domain; for BGP: check session with router ARP not responding for VIP Speaker not elected or port security on switch blocking gratuitous ARP kubectl get events -n metallb-system | grep announcing Check speaker pod logs; disable port-security / ARP inspection on the connected switch port BGP session not established Firewall blocking TCP 179 between node and router telnet <router-ip> 179 from node Open TCP 179 on host firewall and network ACLs IP pool exhausted — service stays pending All IPs in pool are allocated kubectl describe ipaddresspool production-pool -n metallb-system Expand pool address range or add a second IPAddressPool Traffic only reaches one pod (L2 mode) L2 mode is single-node ingress; kube-proxy distributes after the node kubectl get pods -o wide -l app=web — all traffic enters one node Accept this limitation for L2; switch to BGP mode with ECMP for true per-node distribution kube-vip leader not switching after node failure Leader lease stuck or ARP cache not refreshed on upstream router kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=kube-vip | grep -E 'leader|VIP' Increase ARP probe frequency in kube-vip config; check upstream router ARP cache timeout

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• VIP address pool configured in a separate subnet from node and pod CIDRs to prevent IP conflicts
  • BGP mode used for production workloads (L2 mode is for dev/lab only — single ingress node is a bottleneck)
  • BGP peer holdTime and keepaliveTime tuned; BFDProfile configured for sub-second failover
  • Switch port security and gratuitous ARP inspection disabled (or explicitly permitted) for nodes running MetalLB speakers
  • IP address pool size planned with headroom — allocating 100% causes new services to stay pending
  • kube-vip deployed for control-plane HA if running a multi-master bare-metal cluster
  • MetalLB speaker resource limits set (DaemonSet pods run on every node — size accordingly)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use L2 mode in production expecting high availability L2 mode is single-node: only one node holds the VIP at a time; failover takes ~10 s and traffic is not distributed across nodes Use BGP mode with ECMP in production for true multi-node load distribution and sub-second failover with BFD Put VIP pool in the same /24 as the node IPs The LB may assign an IP already used by a node or another static device on the subnet Always allocate the VIP pool from a dedicated subnet or range that is not shared with node addresses Forget to open TCP 179 (BGP) on node firewalls BGP sessions never establish; MetalLB speaker logs show repeated connection refused; VIPs stay unannounced Pre-open TCP 179 between all nodes and each BGP peer (ToR switch) in the host firewall before installing MetalLB Use MetalLB and kube-vip for LoadBalancer services simultaneously Both tools race to handle the same Service resources; one or both fail to announce correctly Pick one tool per cluster for LoadBalancer services; kube-vip for control-plane HA can coexist if LoadBalancer mode is disabled in one of them Request a specific IP with metallb.io/loadBalancerIPs without first checking pool availability Service stays pending with an event saying the requested IP is not in any pool Verify the IP is within a configured IPAddressPool range before annotating the Service

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List MetalLB pods kubectl get pods -n metallb-system List IP address pools kubectl get ipaddresspools -n metallb-system List all LoadBalancer services kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=LoadBalancer Watch speaker announcement logs kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=speaker -f Check events in metallb-system kubectl get events -n metallb-system --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' Check which node is speaker for a VIP kubectl get events -n metallb-system | grep announcing Test ARP response for VIP (from outside cluster) arping -I <iface> <VIP> Describe IP pool allocation kubectl describe ipaddresspool <name> -n metallb-system Check kube-vip leader election kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=kube-vip | grep -E 'leader\|VIP' Request specific IP for a service Add annotation metallb.io/loadBalancerIPs: <IP> to Service Share IP across two services Add same metallb.io/allow-shared-ip: "<key>" to both Services Describe MetalLB controller kubectl describe pod -n metallb-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Tool Mode Failover Load Distribution MetalLB L2 ARP/NDP ~10s (leader election) Single node (ingress point) MetalLB BGP BGP routes <1s (with BFD) ECMP across nodes kube-vip ARP/BGP VRRP ~1s Single or ECMP

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does MetalLB L2 mode result in a single ingress node rather than true load balancing, and how does BGP mode solve this?
Answer In L2 mode, MetalLB uses leader election so that exactly one node's speaker answers ARP requests for the VIP. All external traffic therefore enters through that one node, which then uses kube-proxy to forward to pods — the LB layer itself is a single point of ingress. BGP mode solves this by having each speaker on multiple nodes advertise the same /32 host route via BGP; the upstream router installs ECMP routes for the VIP and distributes flows across all announcing nodes, giving true per-node load balancing.
  1. [Scenario question] A LoadBalancer service stays in EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> even after MetalLB pods are running. What two CRDs should you check first?
Answer Check that an `IPAddressPool` exists with a valid address range and that an `L2Advertisement` (or `BGPAdvertisement` for BGP mode) references that pool. Without both CRDs, MetalLB's controller will not allocate an IP or advertise it. Run `kubectl get ipaddresspools,l2advertisements -n metallb-system` to confirm both are present. A missing advertisement CRD is the most common oversight after install.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to find which node is currently announcing a specific VIP in L2 mode?
Answer 
kubectl get events -n metallb-system | grep announcing
Look for event messages of the form `announcing from node worker-X` — the node named in that event is the current elected speaker for the VIP. You can also watch speaker logs with `kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l app.kubernetes.io/component=speaker -f` for real-time announcement events.

docs.title: Lesson 20 — Cloud Provider Load Balancers
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Cloud Provider Prerequisites: Lesson 08 — Cloud Provider Networking, Lesson 13 — Kubernetes Services Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Provision and configure cloud load balancers on AWS, GCP, and Azure, choose between NLB and ALB target types, set externalTrafficPolicy correctly, and diagnose CCM provisioning failures.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. How Cloud LBs Are Provisioned
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    SA["kubectl apply Service type: LoadBalancer"]
    KCM["kube-controller-manager service-controller v1.28"]
    CCM["Cloud Controller Manager aws-cloud-controller-manager or cloud-provider-gcp"]
    CAPI["Cloud Provider API AWS ELBv2 / GCP Compute / Azure ARM"]
    LB["Cloud Load Balancer AWS NLB / GCP Passthrough NLB / Azure Standard LB"]
    SVC["Service.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname or IP EXTERNAL-IP visible via kubectl"]

    SA --> KCM
    KCM --"EnsureLoadBalancer() call"--> CCM
    CCM --"CreateLoadBalancer API call"--> CAPI
    CAPI --"provision + return DNS/IP"--> LB
    LB --"return endpoint"--> CCM
    CCM --"patch Service status"--> SVC

    style LB fill:#cce,stroke:#66c
    style SVC fill:#cec,stroke:#6c6

The CCM provisioning lifecycle:

sequenceDiagram
    participant K as kubectl / API Server
    participant KCM as kube-controller-manager service-controller
    participant CCM as Cloud Controller Manager (aws-cloud-controller-manager)
    participant Cloud as AWS ELBv2 API us-east-1
    participant LB as AWS NLB (internet-facing)

    K->>KCM: Service type=LoadBalancer created app: web
    KCM->>CCM: EnsureLoadBalancer() call with service spec
    CCM->>Cloud: CreateLoadBalancer + CreateTargetGroup + RegisterTargets
    Cloud-->>CCM: NLB provisioned DNS: k8s-web-abc123.elb.amazonaws.com
    CCM->>K: Patch Service.status.loadBalancer.ingress hostname
    K-->>K: EXTERNAL-IP visible via kubectl get svc (30-120 s)
    Note over LB,KCM: Health check probes begin on NodePort :30080 or pod IP :8080
# Track provisioning
kubectl get svc web -w
# EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> → 203.0.113.100

# CCM logs
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=cloud-controller-manager

docs.title: Classic Load Balancer (CLB) — legacy
docs.text: Created by default before the AWS Load Balancer Controller.

docs.title: Network Load Balancer (NLB) — L4
docs.text:
Recommended for TCP/UDP. Very high throughput, static IPs.

service:
  type: LoadBalancer
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "external"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip"   # pod IP targets
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internet-facing"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-protocol: "TCP"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-port: "traffic-port"
    # Cross-zone load balancing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"
    # Preserve client IP
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-target-group-attributes: "preserve_client_ip.enabled=true"

docs.title: Application Load Balancer (ALB) — L7
docs.text:
Created via the AWS Load Balancer Controller (Ingress resource).

# Install AWS LBC
helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts
helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set clusterName=my-cluster \
  --set serviceAccount.create=true \
  --set serviceAccount.annotations."eks\.amazonaws\.com/role-arn"=arn:aws:iam::123:role/alb-role

# ALB Ingress
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip      # pod-level targets
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123:certificate/xxx
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTP": 80}, {"HTTPS": 443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "443"
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /healthz
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: "shared-alb"  # share one ALB across Ingresses

docs.title: AWS NLB Target Types
docs.text: Target Type Traffic Path Use Case instance LB → NodePort → pod Default; simpler, no VPC CNI requirement ip LB → pod IP directly Lower latency; requires AWS VPC CNI; preserves client IP natively

docs.title: Key AWS Annotations
docs.text: Annotation Default Effect When to change aws-load-balancer-type: "external" "" (CLB) Creates an NLB via AWS LBC Use for all new NLB deployments aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip" "instance" Routes directly to pod IPs Preferred for latency-sensitive workloads with VPC CNI aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internet-facing" "internal" Creates internet-accessible LB Public-facing services aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true" "false" Distributes traffic across all AZs Multi-AZ clusters with uneven pod distribution aws-load-balancer-target-group-attributes: "preserve_client_ip.enabled=true" disabled Preserves real client IP in target group Needed for ip target type to pass client IP to pods

docs.title: External Passthrough NLB (default)
docs.text:
# Default LoadBalancer service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer

# Restrict access to specific CIDRs
spec:
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 10.0.0.0/8
    - 203.0.113.0/24

docs.title: Internal L4 (ILB)
docs.text:
metadata:
  annotations:
    networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal"
    # Optional: specify subnet
    networking.gke.io/internal-load-balancer-subnet: "my-subnet"

docs.title: External Global L7 (GCE Ingress)
docs.text:
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "gce"
    kubernetes.io/ingress.global-static-ip-name: "my-static-ip"
    networking.gke.io/managed-certificates: "my-ssl-cert"

# Create a managed SSL certificate
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.gke.io/v1
kind: ManagedCertificate
metadata:
  name: my-ssl-cert
spec:
  domains:
    - web.example.com
EOF

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix EXTERNAL-IP: <pending> indefinitely CCM cannot call cloud API (IAM/RBAC permission missing) kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=cloud-controller-manager | grep -i error Attach the required IAM role/policy to the node instance profile or workload identity LB provisioned but traffic does not reach pods Security Group / Firewall rule not allowing health check probe IPs kubectl describe svc <name> → check Events for health check failures Add ingress rule for cloud health check IPs (AWS: 100.64.0.0/10; GCP: 35.191.0.0/16 + 130.211.0.0/22) ExternalTrafficPolicy: Local — some nodes receive no traffic Cloud LB correctly removes nodes where no ready pods exist; uneven pod distribution kubectl get pods -o wide -l <selector> Distribute pods across all nodes (remove nodeSelector/affinity constraints) or switch to Cluster policy AWS NLB: client IP is the node IP, not the real client target-type: instance mode SNATs traffic at the node Check annotation aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type Switch to ip target type; ensure pods have VPC-routable IPs (AWS VPC CNI) AKS internal LB stuck pending Missing subnet annotation for internal LB kubectl describe svc <name> → look for subnet error Add azure-load-balancer-internal-subnet annotation with correct subnet name GKE: LB health checks fail Backend pod readiness probe path differs from health check path kubectl describe backendconfig <name> Add BackendConfig with correct healthCheck.requestPath matching pod readiness probe Cloud LB account limit reached Cloud provider quota on number of LBs (e.g., AWS default 20 CLBs per region) AWS: aws service-quotas list-service-quotas --service-code elasticloadbalancing Request quota increase or consolidate services behind a single Ingress/ALB using group.name

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• NLB target type set to ip for VPC CNI clusters to avoid double-hop through NodePort
  • externalTrafficPolicy: Local used only when client IP preservation is required AND pods are evenly distributed across nodes
  • Cross-zone load balancing enabled for multi-AZ clusters to prevent traffic imbalance during pod scheduling
  • Cloud LB health check path and port configured to match pod readiness probes (use BackendConfig on GKE)
  • Security Groups / Firewall rules explicitly allow cloud health check probe IP ranges to reach all node ports
  • Internal LB used for services that do not need internet exposure (avoid default internet-facing scheme)
  • IAM permissions for the CCM or AWS LBC service account tested in a staging environment before production deployment

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Create a separate LoadBalancer Service for every microservice Each service creates a new cloud LB — costs multiply quickly; AWS default NLB quota is 50/region Expose multiple services through a single Ingress (ALB/NGINX) using path or host routing; use group.name on AWS ALB Use externalTrafficPolicy: Local without ensuring pods on every node Nodes without pods fail LB health checks and receive zero traffic; app appears down on those nodes Only use Local when pods are deployed as DaemonSets or when node pinning is intentional; otherwise use Cluster Leave the default CLB on AWS EKS (no annotations) CLBs are legacy, more expensive, have no cross-zone load balancing by default, and do not support modern target types Always annotate with aws-load-balancer-type: external to get NLB, and specify nlb-target-type: ip Use instance target type on NLB with many pods per node Traffic is DNAT'd to NodePort then kube-proxy picks a random pod — extra hop, SNAT loses client IP, uneven distribution Use ip target type to route directly to pod IPs and preserve client IP Skip the AKS SKU selection (use Basic LB) Azure Basic LB does not support multiple availability zones or outbound rules for large clusters Always create AKS clusters with --load-balancer-sku standard; Basic LB is deprecated

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserve the real client IP while externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster does not?
Answer With `Cluster` policy, any node can receive the traffic and kube-proxy SNATs the source IP to the node's own IP before forwarding to a pod on a different node — the original client IP is lost at that SNAT step. With `Local` policy, the cloud LB's health check only marks nodes with ready pods as healthy, so traffic is only sent to nodes that already have a pod; kube-proxy does not SNAT because no cross-node hop is needed. The trade-off is that `Local` can cause uneven distribution if pods are not spread across all nodes.
  1. [Scenario question] An AWS NLB is working but pod logs show the source IP as the EC2 node IP, not the original client IP. Which annotation is most likely misconfigured?
Answer The NLB is using `target-type: instance` mode, which routes through NodePort and kube-proxy, causing SNAT. Switch to `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip"` so the NLB routes directly to pod IPs (bypassing NodePort). You may also need `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-target-group-attributes: "preserve_client_ip.enabled=true"` to ensure the NLB passes the client IP through to the pod.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to watch the progression of an EXTERNAL-IP being assigned to a LoadBalancer service?
Answer 
kubectl get svc web -w
Watch for the `EXTERNAL-IP` column to change from `` to an actual IP or DNS hostname; this transition typically takes 30–120 seconds and is driven by the Cloud Controller Manager calling the cloud provider API to provision the load balancer.

docs.title: Lesson 21 — Service Mesh with Istio
docs.text:
Track: Service Mesh | Prerequisites: Lesson 13 — Services, Lesson 16 — Network Policies | Duration: ~3 hours

Goal: Configure Istio sidecar injection, enforce mTLS between services, and control traffic with VirtualService and DestinationRule policies.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.text:
flowchart LR

flowchart LR

docs.title: Sidecar Injection + mTLS Handshake Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as kubectl apply Deployment
    participant API as Kubernetes API Server
    participant MWC as MutatingWebhookConfiguration istiod (istio-sidecar-injector)
    participant POD as Pod (running)
    participant ISTIOD as istiod CA :15012
    participant ENVOY_A as Envoy A sidecar :15001/:15006
    participant ENVOY_B as Envoy B sidecar :15001/:15006

    K->>API: Create pod spec app:frontend sa:frontend
    API->>MWC: Admission webhook POST /inject
    MWC-->>API: Mutated spec + istio-proxy container + istio-init initContainer
    API->>POD: Schedule pod with sidecar
    POD->>ISTIOD: CSR for SPIFFE cert spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/frontend via xDS SDS :15012
    ISTIOD-->>POD: X.509 SVID cert issued valid 24h
    ENVOY_A->>ENVOY_B: TLS ClientHello + SPIFFE cert spiffe://...sa/frontend
    ENVOY_B->>ISTIOD: Verify cert against CA bundle
    ISTIOD-->>ENVOY_B: Valid
    ENVOY_B-->>ENVOY_A: TLS ServerHello + SPIFFE cert spiffe://...sa/backend
    ENVOY_A->>ISTIOD: Verify cert against CA bundle
    ISTIOD-->>ENVOY_A: Valid
    ENVOY_A-->>ENVOY_B: mTLS session established data flows on :8080

docs.title: 2. Installation
docs.text:
# Install Istio using istioctl
curl -L https://istio.io/downloadIstio | sh -
export PATH=$PWD/istio-*/bin:$PATH

# Install with default profile
istioctl install --set profile=default -y

# Verify
istioctl verify-install
kubectl get pods -n istio-system
# expect: istiod Running, istio-ingressgateway Running

# Enable sidecar injection for a namespace
kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled

# Check injection is working
kubectl get namespace default --show-labels
# expect: istio-injection=enabled

# Ambient mode installation
istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y
# No sidecar injection needed — ztunnel handles it per-node
kubectl label namespace default istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient

docs.title: Istio Profile Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change profile default Control plane + ingressgateway Use minimal for custom ingress values.pilot.traceSampling 1.0 % of requests traced Lower in high-traffic prod values.global.proxy.resources.requests.cpu 10m Envoy sidecar CPU request Increase for high-RPS services values.global.proxy.resources.requests.memory 128Mi Envoy sidecar memory Increase for large XDS configs meshConfig.accessLogFile "" (disabled) Envoy access log destination Set /dev/stdout for debugging meshConfig.defaultConfig.concurrency 2 Envoy worker threads Match vCPU count on large nodes

docs.title: 3. mTLS with PeerAuthentication
docs.text:
# Require mTLS for all services in a namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: default
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT     # PERMISSIVE allows plain text too (migration period)

# Verify mTLS is active
istioctl authn tls-check <pod-name>.default
# HOST:PORT                                     STATUS     SERVER     CLIENT
# web.default.svc.cluster.local:80             OK         STRICT     STRICT

# Check certificate used
istioctl proxy-config secret <pod-name>.default
# expect: cert validity, SPIFFE URI in SAN

# See all mTLS CONFLICT states cluster-wide
istioctl authn tls-check --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null | grep CONFLICT
# empty = no conflicts

docs.title: PeerAuthentication Mode Reference
docs.text: Mode Behavior When to use STRICT mTLS only; plain text rejected Full mesh — all sidecars injected PERMISSIVE Accept both mTLS and plain text Migration: external clients still plain DISABLE Plain text only Debug only — never in production

docs.title: 4. AuthorizationPolicy
docs.text:
# Allow only specific services to call the web service
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-allow
  namespace: default
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals:               # service account identity
              - "cluster.local/ns/default/sa/frontend"
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: ["GET", "POST"]
            paths: ["/api/*"]
---
# Default deny everything not explicitly allowed
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: default
spec:
  {}  # empty = deny all

docs.title: VirtualService
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  hosts:
    - web
  http:
    # Canary: route 10% to v2
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: web
            subset: v1
          weight: 90
        - destination:
            host: web
            subset: v2
          weight: 10

    # Fault injection (testing resilience)
    - fault:
        delay:
          percentage:
            value: 10.0
          fixedDelay: 5s
        abort:
          percentage:
            value: 5.0
          httpStatus: 503
      route:
        - destination:
            host: web

    # Retry policy
    - retries:
        attempts: 3
        perTryTimeout: 2s
        retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure
      timeout: 10s
      route:
        - destination:
            host: web

docs.title: DestinationRule
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  host: web
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        h2UpgradePolicy: UPGRADE
        http2MaxRequests: 1000
    outlierDetection:        # circuit breaker
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
  subsets:
    - name: v1
      labels:
        version: v1
    - name: v2
      labels:
        version: v2

docs.title: VirtualService / DestinationRule Key Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change retries.attempts 2 Max retry count Increase for idempotent reads retries.perTryTimeout 25s Timeout per attempt Match upstream SLA outlierDetection.consecutiveGatewayErrors 5 Errors before ejection Lower for fast failover outlierDetection.baseEjectionTime 30s How long host stays ejected Increase for slow recovery connectionPool.tcp.maxConnections 2^32-1 Max TCP connections Set for connection limiting connectionPool.http.http1MaxPendingRequests 2^32-1 Max queued HTTP/1 requests Tune to prevent queue buildup

docs.title: 6. Ingress with Istio Gateway
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: web-gateway
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
    - port:
        number: 443
        name: https
        protocol: HTTPS
      tls:
        mode: SIMPLE
        credentialName: web-tls-cert
      hosts:
        - web.example.com
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: web-vs
spec:
  hosts:
    - web.example.com
  gateways:
    - web-gateway
  http:
    - match:
        - uri:
            prefix: /
      route:
        - destination:
            host: web
            port:
              number: 80

docs.text:
Work through the Theory sections to build a fully configured Istio service mesh:

  1. Install Istio with the default profile (Section 2) and verify istiod + ingressgateway are Running
  2. Label the default namespace for sidecar injection, deploy two services, and confirm sidecars are injected
  3. Apply PeerAuthentication PERMISSIVE, then STRICT (Section 3); use istioctl authn tls-check to confirm
  4. Create an AuthorizationPolicy default-deny + explicit ALLOW (Section 4) and test that blocked paths return 403
  5. Apply a VirtualService with 90/10 weighted routing + a DestinationRule (Section 5) and verify traffic split
  6. Configure the Istio Gateway + VirtualService for HTTPS ingress (Section 6) with a TLS certificate
  7. Deploy observability stack (Section 7) and inspect traffic topology in Kiali

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• PeerAuthentication set to STRICT in all application namespaces (not PERMISSIVE)
  • AuthorizationPolicy default-deny applied per namespace before deploying workloads
  • istioctl analyze runs clean in CI — zero errors or warnings
  • Envoy sidecar CPU/memory requests and limits set to prevent noisy-neighbor starvation
  • Distributed tracing (Jaeger/Zipkin) sampling rate tuned — not 100% in high-RPS production
  • Istio ingress gateway has a PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 1
  • Certificate rotation tested — SVID expiry handled without service interruption

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Apply PeerAuthentication STRICT before all pods have sidecars Non-injected pods cannot complete mTLS handshake — 503 errors Enable PERMISSIVE first, verify all pods have sidecar, then switch to STRICT Use namespace-wide deny-all AuthorizationPolicy without allow rules Blocks health checks and monitoring, causing cascading failures Add explicit ALLOW for health check paths and monitoring principals first Deploy VirtualService subsets before DestinationRule is applied Envoy has no subset configuration — 503 on subset routing Apply DestinationRule before or simultaneously with VirtualService Run Istio control plane (istiod) with a single replica istiod failure causes cert rotation and config push to stop Set replicaCount: 2 or more and add PodAntiAffinity Forget to annotate sidecar resource limits Envoy sidecar consumes unbounded CPU — evicts application containers Always set sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPU and proxyCPULimit annotations

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What is the difference between PeerAuthentication modes PERMISSIVE and STRICT, and when should each be used?
Answer `PERMISSIVE` mode accepts both mTLS-encrypted connections and plain-text connections, which allows non-injected clients (such as external services or pods without sidecars) to still communicate during a migration. `STRICT` mode rejects all plain-text — only connections with valid SPIFFE X.509 certificates are accepted. Use `PERMISSIVE` during the rollout period while injecting sidecars into all workloads, then switch to `STRICT` once every pod in the namespace has an injected Envoy sidecar to guarantee end-to-end mTLS.
  1. [Scenario question] After applying PeerAuthentication with mode: STRICT to a namespace, several services start returning 503 errors. What is the most likely cause?
Answer Some caller pods are missing the Istio sidecar — either their namespace does not have the `istio-injection=enabled` label or they were created before the label was applied. Without a sidecar, those pods send plain-text requests that STRICT mode rejects. Run `istioctl authn tls-check .default` to identify CONFLICT rows and `kubectl describe pod | grep istio-proxy` to confirm whether the sidecar was injected. The fix is to label the namespace and restart affected pods to trigger injection.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to verify that mTLS is active and in STRICT mode between a specific pod and the web service?
Answer 
istioctl authn tls-check <pod-name>.default
Look for the row `web.default.svc.cluster.local:80` and confirm the `STATUS` column shows `OK` with both `SERVER` and `CLIENT` columns showing `STRICT`; a `CONFLICT` status means one side is not enforcing mTLS.

docs.title: 2. Multi-Cluster Services API (MCS)
docs.text:
The Kubernetes Multi-Cluster Services API (SIG-Multicluster KEP-1645) provides a standard for cross-cluster service export/import.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CA as Cluster A kubectl
    participant Ctrl as MCS Controller (mcs-api-controller)
    participant CB as Cluster B
    participant DNS as CoreDNS clusterset.local

    CA->>CA: kubectl apply ServiceExport name:web ns:default
    CA->>Ctrl: Notify: web.default is exported from cluster-a
    Ctrl->>CB: Create ServiceImport name:web ns:default type:ClusterSetIP
    CB->>DNS: Register web.default.svc.clusterset.local -> ClusterSetIP
    CB->>CA: DNS query web.default.svc.clusterset.local
    CA-->>CB: Returns ClusterSetIP (virtual cross-cluster VIP)
    CB->>CA: Traffic via ClusterSetIP TCP :80
# In cluster A — export a service
apiVersion: multicluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ServiceExport
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
---
# In cluster B — import it
apiVersion: multicluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ServiceImport
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
spec:
  type: ClusterSetIP
  ports:
    - port: 80
      protocol: TCP

# DNS name for imported service:
# web.default.svc.clusterset.local
kubectl exec -it pod -- nslookup web.default.svc.clusterset.local
# expect: returns a ClusterSetIP address (virtual IP)

docs.title: MCS API Parameter Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change ServiceImport.spec.type ClusterSetIP Virtual IP for cross-cluster LB Use Headless for direct pod routing ServiceExport annotation multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service auto Maps to derived ClusterIP service Do not modify manually DNS domain clusterset.local Search domain for cross-cluster names Configured in DNS operator

docs.title: 3. Cilium Cluster Mesh
docs.text:
Cilium's Cluster Mesh connects clusters so pods can communicate using their cluster-internal pod IPs and DNS names.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ClusterA["Cluster A (us-east-1)"]
        cilA["Cilium Agent v1.15 eBPF dataplane"]
        etcdA["clustermesh-apiserver :2379 TLS mutual auth"]
        cilA --> etcdA
    end
    subgraph ClusterB["Cluster B (eu-west-1)"]
        cilB["Cilium Agent v1.15 eBPF dataplane"]
        etcdB["clustermesh-apiserver :2379 TLS mutual auth"]
        cilB --> etcdB
    end
    etcdA <--"mTLS :2379 KV sync endpoint sharing"--> etcdB
    cilA --"eBPF policy + WireGuard tunnel (optional)"--> cilB

    style ClusterA fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style ClusterB fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
# Enable Cluster Mesh on cluster A
cilium clustermesh enable \
  --service-type LoadBalancer
cilium clustermesh status --wait
# expect: "Cluster Mesh: OK"

# Connect cluster B to cluster A
# (run with context pointing to cluster A)
cilium clustermesh connect \
  --destination-context cluster-b \
  --source-context cluster-a

# Verify mesh is connected
cilium clustermesh status
# Cluster A ←→ Cluster B  CONNECTED
# expect: "Global services: N" showing shared services count

# Share a service globally (available in all mesh clusters)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    service.cilium.io/global: "true"
    service.cilium.io/shared: "true"   # include this cluster's endpoints
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80

# Global service load balances across all clusters
# Affinity to local cluster:
annotations:
  service.cilium.io/global: "true"
  service.cilium.io/affinity: "local"   # prefer local cluster, fall back cross-cluster

docs.title: Cilium Cluster Mesh Parameter Reference
docs.text: Annotation / Parameter Default Effect When to change service.cilium.io/global "false" Make service visible across all mesh clusters Set "true" for HA global services service.cilium.io/shared "false" Include this cluster's endpoints in global LB Set "true" to contribute backends service.cilium.io/affinity "none" Prefer local ("local") or remote ("remote") endpoints Use "local" to reduce cross-region latency clustermesh.cilium.io/global-service — Alternative annotation form Same as service.cilium.io/global

docs.title: Primary-Remote Model
docs.text:
One cluster has the control plane; remote clusters use it.

# Install Istio on primary cluster
istioctl install --set profile=default \
  --set values.pilot.env.EXTERNAL_ISTIOD=true

# Install remote cluster config
istioctl install --set profile=remote \
  --set values.global.remotePilotAddress=<primary-pilot-ip>

docs.title: Multi-Primary (Recommended for HA)
docs.text:
Each cluster runs its own Istiod.

# Step 1: Create a shared root CA
# (both clusters must trust the same root)

# Step 2: Install Istio on cluster 1
istioctl install -f cluster1.yaml

# Step 3: Install Istio on cluster 2
istioctl install -f cluster2.yaml

# Step 4: Cross-cluster east-west gateway
kubectl apply -n istio-system -f eastwest-gateway.yaml

# Step 5: Expose services for cross-cluster discovery
istioctl x create-remote-secret \
  --context=cluster1 \
  --name=cluster1 | kubectl apply --context=cluster2 -f -

# Services become reachable via their FQDN across clusters
# Verify remote clusters registered:
istioctl remote-clusters
# expect: cluster1 and cluster2 listed as CONNECTED

docs.title: 5. Submariner
docs.text:
Submariner provides direct pod-to-pod connectivity between clusters using encrypted tunnels.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ClusterA["Cluster A (10.244.1.0/24)"]
        podA["Pod A 10.244.1.5 app:frontend"]
        gwA["Gateway Node subctl agent IPsec/WireGuard"]
        podA --> gwA
    end
    subgraph Broker["Broker Cluster"]
        broker["Broker CRD submariner.io endpoint discovery registry"]
    end
    subgraph ClusterB["Cluster B (10.244.2.0/24)"]
        gwB["Gateway Node subctl agent IPsec/WireGuard"]
        podB["Pod B 10.244.2.7 app:backend"]
        gwB --> podB
    end

    gwA --"IPsec ESP or WireGuard UDP :4500 encrypted tunnel"--> gwB
    gwA <--"register endpoints UDP :4800"--> broker
    gwB <--"register endpoints UDP :4800"--> broker

    style ClusterA fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
    style ClusterB fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
    style Broker fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
# Install subctl CLI
curl -Ls https://get.submariner.io | bash

# Deploy broker (coordinates cluster registration)
subctl deploy-broker --kubeconfig broker-cluster.kubeconfig

# Join cluster A
subctl join broker-info.subm --kubeconfig cluster-a.kubeconfig \
  --clusterid cluster-a \
  --natt-discovery-port 4900 \
  --globalnet   # if pod CIDRs overlap

# Join cluster B
subctl join broker-info.subm --kubeconfig cluster-b.kubeconfig \
  --clusterid cluster-b \
  --globalnet

# Verify connectivity
subctl verify --kubeconfig cluster-a.kubeconfig --toconfig cluster-b.kubeconfig
# expect: all connectivity checks PASS

# Export service for cross-cluster access
subctl export service --namespace default web
# Creates ServiceExport → Lighthouse DNS resolves across clusters
# DNS: web.default.svc.clusterset.local

docs.title: 6. AWS Multi-Cluster (EKS)
docs.text:
# Option 1: VPC Peering — flat network, pod IPs routable
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection \
  --vpc-id vpc-cluster-a \
  --peer-vpc-id vpc-cluster-b

# Update route tables in both VPCs
aws ec2 create-route \
  --route-table-id rtb-xxxxxx \
  --destination-cidr-block 10.1.0.0/16 \
  --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-xxxxxx

# Option 2: AWS Transit Gateway — hub-and-spoke for many VPCs
aws ec2 attach-vpc-to-transit-gateway \
  --transit-gateway-id tgw-xxxxx \
  --vpc-id vpc-cluster-a

# Option 3: AWS VPC Lattice (new, service-level)
# Service-to-service connectivity without VPC peering

docs.title: 7. GCP Multi-Cluster (GKE)
docs.text:
# GKE Hub — register clusters to a fleet
gcloud container hub memberships register cluster-a \
  --gke-cluster us-central1/cluster-a

gcloud container hub memberships register cluster-b \
  --gke-cluster us-east1/cluster-b

# Enable Multi-Cluster Services
gcloud container hub multi-cluster-services enable

# Enable Multi-Cluster Ingress
gcloud container hub ingress enable \
  --config-membership=cluster-a

# MultiClusterIngress resource (deployed to config cluster)
apiVersion: networking.gke.io/v1
kind: MultiClusterIngress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      backend:
        serviceName: web
        servicePort: 80

docs.title: 8. Overlapping Pod CIDRs Problem
docs.text:
When clusters have overlapping pod CIDRs (common in independent deployments), you need NAT or Globalnet.

Cluster A: pods 10.244.0.0/16
Cluster B: pods 10.244.0.0/16  ← SAME CIDR

Solution 1: Globalnet (Submariner)
  — Each cluster gets a unique global CIDR
  — Pods are SNATed to the global CIDR for cross-cluster traffic

Solution 2: Service-based communication only
  — Expose services, not pods — services have cluster-unique IPs

Solution 3: Re-IP pods (if possible)
  — Reinitialize clusters with non-overlapping CIDRs

docs.text:
Work through the Theory sections to build a multi-cluster connectivity setup:

  1. Set up two kubeconfig contexts (two separate clusters or two minikube instances) — verify kubectl config get-contexts
  2. Create a ServiceExport on cluster A and verify the MCS controller creates a ServiceImport on cluster B (Section 2)
  3. Enable Cilium Cluster Mesh on both clusters (Section 3): run cilium clustermesh enable and cilium clustermesh connect

  6. Install Submariner (Section 5): deploy broker, join two clusters, run subctl verify to confirm connectivity
  7. Test overlapping CIDR scenario (Section 8): join with --globalnet and verify cross-cluster pod routing works

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Pod CIDRs are non-overlapping across all clusters — or Globalnet is enabled
  • Cross-cluster traffic is encrypted (WireGuard in Cilium, IPsec in Submariner, mTLS in Istio)
  • Cluster identity verification in place — certificates from shared CA or per-cluster identity
  • Global services have service.cilium.io/affinity: local to avoid unnecessary cross-region traffic
  • MCS ServiceExport resources are version-controlled and reviewed before deployment
  • Failover behavior tested: shut down one cluster's endpoints and verify traffic shifts
  • Cross-cluster DNS TTL is low enough for fast failover (≤30s)

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Expose all services as global without affinity Every request potentially crosses regions — high latency and cost Only export services that genuinely need cross-cluster HA; set affinity: local Use overlapping pod CIDRs without Globalnet Pod IP collisions make routing ambiguous — traffic goes to wrong cluster Plan non-overlapping CIDRs at day zero or enable Globalnet in Submariner Share a single root CA between clusters without rotation plan Compromised CA affects all clusters simultaneously Use intermediate CAs per cluster, rotate quarterly Deploy MCS controller without RBAC review ServiceExport allows any namespace to expose services to other clusters Restrict ServiceExport creation to cluster-admins or dedicated operators Rely only on DNS for cross-cluster health detection Stale DNS cache serves dead endpoints during outage Combine DNS failover with health-check-based endpoint removal

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What DNS suffix does the Multi-Cluster Services (MCS) API use for cross-cluster service discovery, and what two objects must exist before the DNS name resolves?
Answer Cross-cluster services resolve under the `clusterset.local` domain — for example, `web.default.svc.clusterset.local`. Two objects must exist: a `ServiceExport` in the source cluster (which signals that the service should be shared) and a corresponding `ServiceImport` in the destination cluster (which the MCS controller creates automatically). Without the ServiceExport in the originating cluster, the MCS controller never notifies other clusters, so the ServiceImport and DNS record are never created.
  1. [Scenario question] A Cilium Cluster Mesh shows DISCONNECTED between cluster-a and cluster-b even though both clusters are running. What port and protocol should you verify is open between nodes?
Answer The Cluster Mesh API server uses TCP port 2379 (etcd) for the clustermesh-apiserver mutual TLS connection between clusters. If a firewall or security group blocks TCP 2379 between the node IPs of the two clusters, the mesh will show DISCONNECTED. Run `kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/clustermesh-apiserver` to see TLS or connection refused errors, and open TCP 2379 bidirectionally between the clusters' node CIDR ranges.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check whether two Cilium Cluster Mesh-connected clusters are CONNECTED and how many global services are shared?
Answer 
cilium clustermesh status
Look for lines showing each connected cluster with status `CONNECTED` and a count of `Global services: N`; a `DISCONNECTED` or `PENDING` state indicates an API server reachability or certificate issue that needs further investigation.

docs.title: Lesson 23 — Network Security Hardening
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud | Prerequisites: Lesson 16 — Network Policies, Lesson 21 — Istio | Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Apply layered network security controls — default-deny policies, metadata API blocks, encrypted transit, and runtime enforcement — that satisfy PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark requirements.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. The Threat Model
docs.text:
flowchart TD

docs.title: 2. Default Deny Network Policies
docs.text:
Start with deny-all and explicitly allow required traffic.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant NS as Namespace (production)
    participant NP as NetworkPolicy engine
    participant Pod as Pod

    Dev->>NS: Apply default-deny-all policy
    NS->>NP: Ingress DENY all, Egress DENY all
    Dev->>NS: Apply allow-dns-egress policy
    NP->>Pod: DNS port 53 egress ALLOWED
    Dev->>NS: Apply allow-healthchecks policy
    NP->>Pod: Ingress from kube-system ALLOWED
    Dev->>NS: Apply app-specific allow rules
    NP->>Pod: Specific ingress/egress ALLOWED
    Note over NP,Pod: Default position: DENY unless explicitly ALLOWED
# Namespace-level default deny
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
---
# Allow only DNS egress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - ports:
        - port: 53
          protocol: UDP
        - port: 53
          protocol: TCP
---
# Allow health check probes from kube-system
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-healthchecks
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system

docs.title: NetworkPolicy Parameter Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change podSelector: {} Selects ALL pods Policy applies namespace-wide Use label selector for per-app granularity policyTypes: [Ingress] Only ingress controlled Egress remains open Always add Egress to policyTypes for full control namespaceSelector Not set (any namespace) Restricts by namespace labels Required for cross-namespace allow rules ipBlock.except Not set Allow all IPs in CIDR Use to carve out cloud metadata API port: 53, protocol: UDP UDP DNS Allow DNS resolution Add TCP 53 for large DNS responses

docs.title: 3. Block Cloud Metadata API
docs.text:
The cloud metadata API (169.254.169.254) exposes credentials and configuration. Block it from pods.

# Block access to cloud metadata service
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-metadata-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except:
              - 169.254.169.254/32   # AWS/GCP/Azure metadata
              - 169.254.170.2/32     # AWS ECS metadata

# Verify block works
kubectl run -it --rm test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
# expect: connection timed out (or refused) — NOT a valid metadata response

# Verify DNS still works after block
kubectl run -it --rm dns-test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
# expect: resolves successfully (DNS egress port 53 is still open)

docs.title: Cilium WireGuard
docs.text:
helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium --reuse-values \
  --set encryption.enabled=true \
  --set encryption.type=wireguard \
  --set encryption.nodeEncryption=true   # encrypt node-to-node too

# Verify encryption
cilium encrypt status
# Encryption: Wireguard
# Keys in use: 1
# expect: all nodes show WireGuard active

docs.title: Calico WireGuard
docs.text:
kubectl patch felixconfiguration default \
  --type='merge' \
  -p '{"spec":{"wireguardEnabled":true}}'

# Verify
kubectl get node <node> -o yaml | grep wireguard
calicoctl node status | grep WireGuard
# expect: "WireGuard: Active" per node

docs.title: Istio mTLS
docs.text:
# Enforce strict mTLS cluster-wide
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: istio-system   # applies to all namespaces
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

docs.title: Encryption Method Comparison
docs.text: Method Layer Scope Key Management Performance Cost WireGuard (Cilium/Calico) L3 Node-to-node Automatic per-node keys ~3-5% CPU overhead IPsec (Cilium/Submariner) L3 Node-to-node Manual or operator-managed ~5-8% CPU overhead Istio mTLS L7 Pod-to-pod istiod CA (SPIFFE) Envoy sidecar overhead TLS (application) L7 Service-to-service App-managed certs Minimal if hardware offloaded

docs.title: 5. Egress Control with FQDN Policies
docs.text:
Cilium allows restricting outbound traffic to specific domain names.

apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-external-apis
  namespace: production
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: worker
  egress:
    - toFQDNs:
        - matchName: "api.github.com"
        - matchPattern: "*.amazonaws.com"
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "443"
              protocol: TCP

# Verify FQDN policy is active
kubectl exec -it -n production worker-pod -- curl -v https://api.github.com
# expect: HTTP 200 — allowed by FQDN policy

kubectl exec -it -n production worker-pod -- curl -v https://evil.example.com
# expect: connection refused or timeout — not in FQDN allowlist

Calico also supports DNS-based policy in Enterprise edition.

docs.title: 6. Pod Security and Network Interaction
docs.text:
Kubernetes PodSecurity Admission enforces security at the pod level, which complements network controls.

# Apply baseline security to a namespace
kubectl label namespace production \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

# Restricted: prevents hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged
kubectl label namespace production \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

Network-relevant pod spec hardening: 

spec:
  hostNetwork: false       # don't share host network namespace
  hostPID: false           # don't share host PID namespace
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
  containers:
    - name: app
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
          add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]  # only if binding ports < 1024

docs.title: PodSecurity Level vs Network Risk
docs.text: Level hostNetwork hostPID Privileged Net Risk privileged Allowed Allowed Allowed Critical — bypasses all pod-level controls baseline Blocked Blocked Blocked Moderate — container escape still possible restricted Blocked Blocked Blocked Low — combined with NetworkPolicy = strong

docs.title: 7. Audit Logging for Network Events
docs.text:
# Cilium flow audit (all denied flows)
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces -o json | \
  jq '{src: .flow.source.pod_name, dst: .flow.destination.pod_name,
       dport: .flow.l4.TCP.destination_port, verdict: .flow.verdict}'
# expect: JSON lines showing blocked flows — use to build allow rules

# Tetragon network audit
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents --event-types PROCESS_ACCEPT,PROCESS_CONNECT -o json
# expect: process-level network events including binary path and args

# kube-apiserver audit log — network policy changes
kubectl get events --all-namespaces | grep NetworkPolicy

docs.title: 8. Network Security Checklist Automation
docs.text:
# 1. Default deny policies in all namespaces
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
  count=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -n $ns 2>/dev/null | grep deny | wc -l)
  echo "$ns: $count deny policies"
done
# expect: each namespace shows ≥1 deny policy

# 2. Pod → metadata API is blocked
kubectl run -it --rm meta-test --image=curlimages/curl -- \
  curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/
# expect: timeout

# 3. Encryption is active
cilium encrypt status   # for Cilium/WireGuard
# expect: "Encryption: Wireguard" and "Keys in use: 1"

# 4. mTLS is enforced (Istio)
istioctl authn tls-check --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null | grep CONFLICT
# expect: empty — no CONFLICT rows

# 5. No hostNetwork pods (except system components)
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces \
  -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostNetwork == true) |
    .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name'
# expect: only kube-system / openshift-* components

# 6. No pods with excessive capabilities
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces \
  -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities.add // empty'
# expect: empty or only NET_BIND_SERVICE

# 7. Egress to internet is controlled
kubectl run -it --rm egress-test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -m 5 https://ifconfig.me
# expect: timeout (if egress blocked) or only expected exit IPs

docs.text: Method Layer Scope Key Management Performance Cost WireGuard (Cilium/Calico) L3 Node-to-node Automatic per-node keys ~3-5% CPU overhead IPsec (Cilium/Submariner) L3 Node-to-node Manual or operator-managed ~5-8% CPU overhead Istio mTLS L7 Pod-to-pod istiod CA (SPIFFE) Envoy sidecar overhead TLS (application) L7 Service-to-service App-managed certs Minimal if hardware offloaded Parameter Default Effect When to change podSelector: {} Selects ALL pods Policy applies namespace-wide Use label selector for per-app granularity policyTypes: [Ingress] Only ingress controlled Egress remains open Always add Egress to policyTypes for full control namespaceSelector Not set (any namespace) Restricts by namespace labels Required for cross-namespace allow rules ipBlock.except Not set Allow all IPs in CIDR Use to carve out cloud metadata API port: 53, protocol: UDP UDP DNS Allow DNS resolution Add TCP 53 for large DNS responses

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Pods can't do DNS after default-deny Missing allow-dns-egress NetworkPolicy kubectl exec pod -- nslookup kubernetes Apply allow-dns-egress policy (port 53 UDP+TCP) Health checks failing after deny-all Kubelet probe traffic blocked from kube-system kubectl describe pod <pod> \| grep Events Add ingress from namespaceSelector: kube-system WireGuard not encrypting between nodes Kernel < 5.6 (no built-in WireGuard) or module missing cilium encrypt status Upgrade kernel or use IPsec fallback Tetragon not capturing events eBPF program not loaded or kernel too old kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/tetragon Check kernel version ≥ 4.19 for eBPF support FQDN egress policy allows wrong IPs DNS cache poisoning or stale entry kubectl exec pod -- nslookup api.github.com and compare to Cilium's cached IPs Add fromEndpoints restriction and flush Cilium DNS cache PodSecurity restricted blocks all pods Pods not compliant (privileged, hostNetwork, etc.) kubectl describe pod <pod> \| grep "violates PodSecurity" Add runAsNonRoot, drop ALL capabilities, remove hostNetwork Hubble shows flows but no drop verdicts PeerAuthentication in PERMISSIVE — policy not enforced kubectl get peerauthentication -A Switch to STRICT after confirming all sidecars injected

See also: Lesson 16 — Network Policies for base NetworkPolicy syntax. Lesson 21 — Istio for mTLS STRICT enforcement.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Default-deny NetworkPolicy applied in every application namespace before workloads deploy
  • Metadata API (169.254.169.254) blocked via ipBlock.except in egress policy
  • Node-to-node encryption enabled (WireGuard in Cilium/Calico or IPsec in Submariner)
  • Istio PeerAuthentication set to STRICT cluster-wide (not per-namespace permissive)
  • pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted on all application namespaces
  • Hubble or Tetragon audit log exported to SIEM for network event retention
  • kube-bench run on all nodes — CIS checks 5.3.1 and 5.3.2 pass

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Apply default-deny without testing first Breaks DNS, monitoring, and health checks immediately Use hubble observe --verdict DROPPED to discover required flows before enforcing Encrypt only pod-to-pod traffic, not node-to-node Host-level processes (kubelet, CNI) still send plain traffic on the wire Enable nodeEncryption: true in Cilium WireGuard config Use PERMISSIVE mTLS permanently No actual encryption guarantee — legacy clients silently bypass mTLS Set a migration deadline; switch to STRICT within sprint Block metadata API only in default namespace Pods in other namespaces still reach metadata API Apply deny-metadata-api NetworkPolicy in every namespace or use Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy Run Tetragon/Hubble but never export to SIEM Audit data only lives in ephemeral pod logs — lost on restart Configure Hubble to export to Kafka/Elasticsearch; Tetragon to Falco/Splunk

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Use Case Command List all NetworkPolicies cluster-wide kubectl get netpol -A Watch denied flows in real time hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces Check WireGuard encryption status cilium encrypt status Enable Calico WireGuard kubectl patch felixconfiguration default --type merge -p '{"spec":{"wireguardEnabled":true}}' Check Istio mTLS conflicts istioctl authn tls-check --all-namespaces \| grep CONFLICT List pods with hostNetwork=true kubectl get pods -A -o json \| jq '.items[]\|select(.spec.hostNetwork==true)\|.metadata.name' Run kube-bench CIS check kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/main/job.yaml Test metadata API block kubectl run -it --rm t --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -m3 http://169.254.169.254/ Check pod capabilities kubectl get pods -A -o json \| jq '.items[].spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities' Trace Cilium policy decision cilium policy trace --src-pod ns/pod-a --dst-pod ns/pod-b --dport 80 Enable Tetragon network event capture kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -- tetra getevents --event-types PROCESS_CONNECT Apply PodSecurity restricted to namespace kubectl label ns <ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Control Tool What It Prevents Default deny NetworkPolicy Lateral movement Metadata block NetworkPolicy (ipBlock except) Credential theft FQDN egress Cilium CiliumNetworkPolicy Exfiltration Encryption WireGuard / mTLS Eavesdropping Pod security PodSecurity Admission hostNetwork bypass Audit Hubble / Tetragon Detecting incidents

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why must you explicitly add a DNS egress policy (allowing port 53 UDP and TCP) when deploying a default-deny NetworkPolicy, and what breaks if you omit it?
Answer A default-deny policy with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` and an empty `podSelector: {}` blocks all outbound traffic including DNS queries to CoreDNS. Without an explicit allow for UDP port 53 (and TCP port 53 for large responses), pods cannot resolve any service names — `nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local` will hang or return SERVFAIL. The allow-dns-egress policy must target `0.0.0.0/0` (or specifically the CoreDNS ClusterIP) on ports 53 UDP and TCP, and must be applied in the same namespace simultaneously with or before the deny-all policy.
  1. [Scenario question] A penetration tester demonstrates that a pod in the production namespace can query the cloud metadata API at 169.254.169.254 and retrieve an IAM role credential. What NetworkPolicy construct blocks this while still allowing all other internet egress?
Answer Use an `ipBlock` with an `except` clause in an egress NetworkPolicy: allow `cidr: 0.0.0.0/0` with `except: [169.254.169.254/32]` (and also `169.254.170.2/32` for AWS ECS metadata). This allows egress to all destinations except the metadata API addresses. Apply this policy with `podSelector: {}` to cover all pods in the namespace, and include it in every application namespace — not just the default namespace.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to see all currently dropped network flows across all namespaces in real time?
Answer 
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces
Each output line shows the source pod, destination pod, destination port, and the drop reason (such as `POLICY_DENIED`); use this to identify which flows are being blocked so you can build the precise allow rules needed before enforcing a default-deny posture.
