docs.title: Lesson 24 — Network Observability and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Track: Network Foundation — Bare Metal & Cloud | Prerequisites: All previous lessons — this is the capstone | Duration: ~3 hours

Goal: Diagnose any Kubernetes network failure — from pod unreachability to DNS timeouts — using a structured L1-to-L7 methodology and tools including Hubble, netshoot, tcpdump, and Prometheus metrics.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. Systematic Troubleshooting Methodology
docs.text:
Work from the bottom of the stack up:

flowchart TD
    L1["L1/L2: Physical / Link — NIC up? veth wired? Interface up?"]
    L3["L3: IP — Route correct? ip_forward on? MTU ok?"]
    L4["L4: TCP/UDP — conntrack full? iptables blocking?"]
    L7["L7: Application — DNS resolving? TLS cert valid? HTTP 200?"]
    K8S["Kubernetes — Service exists? Endpoint healthy? NetworkPolicy denying?"]
    CNI["CNI — Pod IP assigned? veth wired? IPAM exhausted?"]

    L1 --> L3 --> L4 --> L7 --> K8S --> CNI

    style L1 fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
    style L3 fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style L4 fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
    style L7 fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
    style K8S fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#E91E63
    style CNI fill:#e0f2f1,stroke:#009688

The golden rule: confirm each layer before moving up. Don't start at Kubernetes if you haven't confirmed the node NIC is up.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Eng as Engineer
    participant Node as Linux Node (minikube ssh)
    participant CNI as cilium / calicoctl
    participant K8S as kubectl / kube-apiserver
    participant App as netshoot / curl

    Eng->>Node: ip link / ss -tlnp / ping gateway
    Node-->>Eng: L2/L3 OK or FAIL
    Eng->>CNI: cilium status / calicoctl node status
    CNI-->>Eng: CNI healthy or FAIL (BGP/VXLAN down)
    Eng->>K8S: kubectl get ep / netpol / svc
    K8S-->>Eng: Service+Endpoint present or missing
    Eng->>App: nslookup / curl -v http://svc:port
    App-->>Eng: DNS resolved / HTTP status code
    Note over Eng,App: Stop at first layer that fails — fix before proceeding up

docs.title: 2. The Diagnostic Pod
docs.text:
Keep a debug pod manifest ready:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: netshoot
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
    - name: netshoot
      image: nicolaka/netshoot
      command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: "node-to-debug"  # pin to specific node

# Or one-liner:
kubectl run -it --rm netshoot --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
# expect: bash prompt with curl, nslookup, tcpdump, ss, traceroute, iperf3

# In the same network namespace as a running pod:
kubectl debug -it <pod-name> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container-name>
# expect: shares network namespace of target — same IP, same routes

# nsenter trick (from node — sees pod network namespace):
NODE_PID=$(kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
# SSH to node, find PID:
crictl inspect $(crictl ps | grep <pod-name> | awk '{print $1}') | jq '.info.pid'
nsenter -n -t <PID> -- ss -tlnp
# expect: socket table from inside the pod

docs.title: 3. Pod Connectivity Checklist
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: Pod A cannot reach Pod B

# Step 1: Can Pod A reach its own gateway?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -c3 $(ip route | grep default | awk '{print $3}')
# expect: 0% packet loss

# Step 2: Can Pod A reach Pod B's IP directly?
POD_B_IP=$(kubectl get pod pod-b -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -c3 $POD_B_IP
# If fail → routing or NetworkPolicy issue

# Step 3: Is there a NetworkPolicy blocking traffic?
# Check policies selecting pod-a (egress) and pod-b (ingress)
kubectl get networkpolicy -n default -o yaml | grep -A10 "podSelector"
# Use Cilium policy trace:
cilium policy trace --src-pod default/pod-a --dst-pod default/pod-b --dport 80
# expect: "Final verdict: allowed" or "Final verdict: denied — reason: ..."

# Step 4: Is the route present?
NODE=$(kubectl get pod pod-b -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}')
# SSH to node
ssh $NODE
ip route get $POD_B_IP
# expect: a valid route showing the veth or tunnel interface

# Step 5: Cross-node — is VXLAN/BGP working?
# Check CNI status
calicoctl node status   # or: cilium status
# expect: BGP peer state Established, VXLAN/WireGuard active

# Step 6: Packet capture
# On pod-b's node:
tcpdump -i any -n host $POD_B_IP
# expect: ICMP packets arriving from Pod A's IP

docs.title: 4. Service Connectivity Checklist
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: Pod cannot reach Service

# Step 1: Does the service exist?
kubectl get svc web -n default
# expect: ClusterIP shows an IP address (not <none>)

# Step 2: Does it have endpoints?
kubectl get endpoints web -n default
# expect: IP:port entries — if empty: selector doesn't match pods or pods not Ready
kubectl describe endpoints web -n default
# shows notReadyAddresses if pods are failing health checks

# Step 3: Is the DNS name resolving?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup web.default.svc.cluster.local
# expect: returns ClusterIP address
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup web   # short name
# expect: same result via search domain

# Step 4: Is the ClusterIP reachable?
CLUSTER_IP=$(kubectl get svc web -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- curl -v http://$CLUSTER_IP:80
# expect: HTTP response — if fails: iptables DNAT rule missing

# Step 5: Are iptables DNAT rules present?
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep $CLUSTER_IP
# expect: rule with "/* web/default:http cluster IP */"

# Step 6: Is kube-proxy running and healthy?
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy | tail -20
# expect: "Syncing iptables rules" messages without ERROR

docs.title: 5. DNS Troubleshooting
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: DNS lookups failing or slow

# Step 1: Can pod reach CoreDNS?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nc -vzu 10.96.0.10 53
# expect: "open" (UDP) — if fails: NetworkPolicy blocking CoreDNS

# Step 2: Does a simple lookup work?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
# expect: returns 10.96.0.1 (or configured API server ClusterIP)

# Step 3: Enable CoreDNS query logging
kubectl edit cm -n kube-system coredns
# Add: log  (inside the .:53 { block)
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n kube-system coredns

# Watch queries
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -f | grep -v "NOERROR"
# expect: each query logged — look for NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL

# Step 4: Check ndots behavior
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# expect: "ndots:5" — means short names trigger 5 search domain tries before bare lookup
# high ndots:5 → many fallback queries for external names

# Step 5: Check CoreDNS metrics
kubectl port-forward -n kube-system svc/kube-dns 9153:9153 &
curl -s http://localhost:9153/metrics | grep coredns_dns_request_duration
# expect: histogram buckets with 95th percentile < 5ms for healthy DNS

# Step 6: Check for conntrack UDP race condition
# (symptom: 5-second DNS timeouts)
dmesg | grep "nf_conntrack: table full"
# if present: conntrack exhaustion is causing DNS drops
sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count
sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
# expect: count < 80% of max

docs.title: 6. Latency Investigation
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: High latency between pods

# Step 1: Baseline measurement
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- \
  for i in $(seq 10); do curl -w "%{time_total}\n" -o /dev/null -s http://web; done
# expect: p99 < 5ms for in-cluster pod-to-pod on modern hardware

# Step 2: Check for packet loss
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -c100 -f $POD_B_IP
# "%" column shows packet loss
# expect: 0% loss for healthy cluster

# Step 3: MTU mismatch (causes fragmentation → latency)
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -M do -s 1422 $POD_B_IP  # VXLAN
# If "Message too long" → MTU mismatch
# Check effective MTU
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
# expect: 1450 (VXLAN) or 1360 (WireGuard over VXLAN) or 1500 (native)

# Step 4: CPU throttling on pods (affects packet processing)
kubectl top pod pod-a
kubectl describe pod pod-a | grep -A5 "Limits\|Requests"
# expect: CPU usage well below limits — high throttling causes tail latency

# Step 5: conntrack contention
# High conntrack lookup latency on busy nodes:
cat /proc/net/stat/nf_conntrack
# expect: low "searched" vs "found" ratio

# Step 6: Node CPU for network interrupts
# On node:
watch -n1 'cat /proc/interrupts | grep -E "eth0|mlx5"'
# expect: interrupts spread evenly across CPUs (RSS/multi-queue working)

docs.title: 7. Packet Capture Techniques
docs.text:
# Capture on a specific pod's veth (from the host)
# First, find the veth
POD_ID=$(kubectl get pod pod-a -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
# Find matching veth on node:
ip link show | grep -i cali
# Then capture:
tcpdump -i cali1234abcd -n -w /tmp/pod-a.pcap
# expect: raw packets — open in Wireshark to decode

# Capture inside pod
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- tcpdump -i eth0 -n -w /tmp/capture.pcap
# Copy out:
kubectl cp pod-a:/tmp/capture.pcap ./pod-a.pcap
# expect: pcap file on local disk

# ksniff — kubectl plugin for pod packet capture
kubectl sniff pod-a -n default -o ./pod-a.pcap
# expect: live capture piped to Wireshark (requires krew install sniff)

# Capture VXLAN encapsulated traffic (between nodes)
tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 -w /tmp/vxlan.pcap
# expect: UDP frames with inner IP headers visible in Wireshark

# View in Wireshark
# wireshark ./pod-a.pcap
# or analyze with tshark:
tshark -r pod-a.pcap -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e tcp.dstport
# expect: columns showing inner IP flow src/dst/port

docs.title: 8. Hubble — Flow-Level Observability
docs.text:
# Install Hubble CLI
curl -L --fail --remote-name-all \
  https://github.com/cilium/hubble/releases/download/v0.13.0/hubble-linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar xzvf hubble-linux-amd64.tar.gz
mv hubble /usr/local/bin/

# Forward Hubble relay
cilium hubble port-forward &

# Watch all flows
hubble observe
# expect: stream of src → dst flows with verdict (FORWARDED/DROPPED)

# Watch denied flows (policy violations)
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces
# expect: flows that NetworkPolicy or Istio AuthorizationPolicy blocked

# Flow for specific pod
hubble observe --from-pod default/frontend --to-pod default/backend
# expect: flows between those two pods with HTTP method and status

# Count flows per destination
hubble observe --all-namespaces -o json | \
  jq -r '.flow | .destination.namespace + "/" + .destination.pod_name' | \
  sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
# expect: top-N pods by received flow count

# HTTP flows
hubble observe --protocol http --all-namespaces | head -20
# expect: HTTP method, path, response code for each flow

# Service connectivity map (Hubble UI)
cilium hubble ui
# expect: browser opens at localhost:12000 with service topology graph

docs.title: 9. Key Metrics to Monitor
docs.text:
# Kubernetes network metrics (from kube-state-metrics + node-exporter)
# In Prometheus/Grafana:

# Node network throughput
rate(node_network_receive_bytes_total{device="eth0"}[5m])
rate(node_network_transmit_bytes_total{device="eth0"}[5m])
# expect: matches expected app traffic patterns

# Network errors
rate(node_network_receive_errs_total[5m])
rate(node_network_transmit_errs_total[5m])
# expect: near-zero; spikes indicate hardware/driver issues

# conntrack usage
node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit
# expect: < 0.8 (80%) — above this DNS and new connections start dropping

# DNS query rate
rate(coredns_dns_requests_total[5m])
# baseline this per-pod for capacity planning

# DNS error rate
rate(coredns_dns_responses_total{rcode!="NOERROR"}[5m])
# expect: near-zero; NXDOMAIN spike = broken service names

# kube-proxy sync latency
rate(kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])
# expect: < 100ms p99; spikes correlate with iptables rule churn

docs.text:

minikube ssh

conntrack -L 2>/dev/null | head -10  # conntrack table — expect: NAT entries

# Terminal 2 — Mac (kubectl + hubble)

docs.title: Hands-On Lab
docs.text:
# SYMPTOM: Pod A cannot reach Pod B — systematic diagnosis

# Step 1: Can Pod A reach its own gateway?
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -c3 $(ip route | grep default | awk '{print $3}')
# expect: 0% packet loss

# Step 2: Can Pod A reach Pod B's IP directly?
POD_B_IP=$(kubectl get pod pod-b -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -c3 $POD_B_IP

# Step 3: Trace Cilium policy decision
cilium policy trace --src-pod default/pod-a --dst-pod default/pod-b --dport 80
# expect: "Final verdict: allowed" or specific deny reason

# Step 4: Check DNS resolution
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
# expect: returns ClusterIP

# Step 5: Check conntrack table usage (5-second DNS timeout root cause)
dmesg | grep "nf_conntrack: table full"
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count
# expect: count < 80% of nf_conntrack_max

# Step 6: MTU fragmentation check
kubectl exec -it pod-a -- ping -M do -s 1422 $POD_B_IP
# If "Message too long" → MTU mismatch; set CNI MTU to 1450 for VXLAN

# Step 7: Packet capture on veth
# From the node — find pod veth
ip link show | grep -i cali
tcpdump -i cali1234abcd -n -w /tmp/pod-a.pcap
kubectl cp pod-a:/tmp/capture.pcap ./pod-a.pcap

docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Pod can't ping pod NetworkPolicy block or missing route cilium policy trace --src-pod ns/a --dst-pod ns/b --dport 80 Add NetworkPolicy allow rule or fix CNI route Pod can't reach service No endpoints or kube-proxy not synced kubectl get endpoints <svc>; iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n \| grep <clusterIP> Fix pod readiness probe or restart kube-proxy DNS timeout (5s) conntrack UDP race or CoreDNS crash dmesg \| grep conntrack; kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns Increase conntrack table size or scale CoreDNS replicas Intermittent connections conntrack table exhausted cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count vs max sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=524288 High latency MTU fragmentation (VXLAN overhead ignored) ping -M do -s 1422 <pod-ip> Lower pod MTU to 1450 for VXLAN or 1360 for WireGuard LoadBalancer pending CCM not installed or cloud IAM insufficient kubectl describe svc <svc> \| grep Events Install cloud CCM or grant IAM role for LB provisioning BGP not established TCP/179 blocked or ASN mismatch calicoctl node status \| grep BGP; telnet <peer> 179 Open TCP 179 and verify peer ASN config VXLAN drops UDP/4789 blocked on firewall or MTU exceeded tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 4789 Open UDP 4789 and set CNI MTU to 1450

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Hubble or equivalent flow exporter deployed and exporting to centralized log store
  • Prometheus alerts configured for cilium_drop_count_total and node_nf_conntrack_entries
  • netshoot (or equivalent debug image) added to cluster image pull policy allowlist
  • ss -tlnp and conntrack -L available on nodes — conntrack-tools package installed
  • MTU set correctly for CNI overlay (1450 VXLAN, 1360 WireGuard+VXLAN) — not default 1500
  • CoreDNS scaled to minimum 2 replicas with PodAntiAffinity across nodes
  • Network troubleshooting runbook stored in team wiki with this lesson's methodology

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Start troubleshooting at Kubernetes layer (services, policies) Lower layers (MTU, routing, CNI) may be broken — Kubernetes can't fix a missing route Always start at L1/L2 and work up: NIC → route → conntrack → K8s Use kubectl exec curl as the only test Passes through kube-proxy DNAT — hides raw routing issues Also test pod-IP directly and use tcpdump on the node Run tcpdump without specifying interface Captures loopback and all interfaces — overwhelming noise Always specify -i cali1234 (veth) or -i eth0 udp port 4789 Ignore MTU for overlay networks 1500-byte packets are fragmented in VXLAN tunnels — silent performance loss Calculate: physical MTU (1500) − VXLAN header (50) = 1450 max pod MTU Assume DNS failure = CoreDNS issue conntrack table exhaustion or NetworkPolicy blocking DNS are more common Check dmesg \| grep conntrack and netpol before touching CoreDNS config

docs.text:
You have covered the full Kubernetes networking stack:

Lessons 01-04: Linux primitives — namespaces, veth, routing, iptables
Lessons 05-06: Overlay networks and BGP

Lesson  09:    CNI specification

Lessons 12-13: Services and DNS — the discovery layer

Lessons 15-16: Ingress and Gateway API — L7 traffic
Lessons 17-18: Load balancers — bare metal and cloud

You can now trace a packet from a pod's application socket all the way to its destination across any infrastructure — and diagnose where it breaks.

See also: Lesson 23 — Network Security Hardening for Hubble verdict filtering to build security policies. Lesson 21 — Istio for istioctl proxy-config and Envoy access log troubleshooting.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does the L1-to-L7 troubleshooting methodology require confirming each layer before moving up, rather than starting at the Kubernetes service layer where the symptom is visible?
Answer Higher-layer Kubernetes components (Services, NetworkPolicies, kube-proxy) depend on lower-layer correctness — if a route is missing or a veth pair is not wired to the OVS bridge, no amount of Kubernetes-level fixes will restore connectivity. Starting at L1/L2 (interface up, veth connected) and L3 (route present, ip_forward enabled) rules out the most fundamental issues before you spend time debugging iptables rules or Kubernetes endpoints that are actually fine. The golden rule is: confirm each layer is working before moving up, so you stop at the first layer that fails.
  1. [Scenario question] DNS lookups from a pod occasionally time out with exactly a 5-second delay. CoreDNS pods are running and healthy. What two root causes should you check first?
Answer The two most common causes of 5-second DNS timeouts in Kubernetes are: (1) conntrack table exhaustion — when the nf_conntrack table is full, new UDP connections (including DNS queries) are dropped silently and the client waits for the timeout; check with `dmesg | grep "nf_conntrack: table full"` and compare `nf_conntrack_count` to `nf_conntrack_max`. (2) The conntrack UDP race condition with parallel DNS queries on the same socket — the kernel can SNAT both A and AAAA queries to the same 5-tuple and drop one; check CoreDNS logs for `NXDOMAIN` or timeout patterns, and consider setting `ndots:3` or enabling NodeLocal DNSCache.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to watch all denied network flows across the entire cluster in real time?
Answer 
hubble observe --verdict DROPPED --all-namespaces
Each line shows the source and destination pod names, namespace, destination port, and drop reason (such as `POLICY_DENIED` or `UNSUPPORTED_L3_PROTOCOL`); use this output to identify which flows are being blocked and by what policy, then work down the stack with `cilium policy trace` or `tcpdump` if the reason is not a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy.

Track: OpenShift Networking | Prerequisites: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification, Lesson 12 — Services | Duration: ~2.5 hours

docs.title: 2. OpenShift Network Operator (CNO)
docs.text:
OpenShift manages its network configuration through the Cluster Network Operator (CNO). You never edit CNI configs directly — you edit the Network.operator.openshift.io custom resource.

flowchart TD
    Admin["oc edit network.operator.openshift.io/cluster"]
    CNO["Cluster Network Operator (openshift-network-operator)"]
    OVN_DS["ovnkube-node DaemonSet (openshift-ovn-kubernetes)"]
    OVN_Master["ovnkube-master Deployment (NB DB + SB DB + ovn-northd)"]
    OVS["OVS ovs-vswitchd -- br-int bridge per node"]
    OVN_CTRL["ovn-controller (translates logical to physical flows)"]

    Admin --> CNO
    CNO --"manages"--> OVN_DS
    CNO --"manages"--> OVN_Master
    OVN_DS --> OVS
    OVN_DS --> OVN_CTRL
    OVN_Master --"NB to SB sync via OVSDB :6641"--> OVN_CTRL

    style Admin fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
    style CNO fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
    style OVN_DS fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style OVN_Master fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9C27B0
sequenceDiagram
    participant Admin as Cluster Admin
    participant CNO as Cluster Network Operator
    participant OVN_N as ovn-northd (control plane)
    participant OVN_C as ovn-controller (node)
    participant OVS as OVS br-int (node)

    Admin->>CNO: Edit network.operator CR (e.g. change MTU)
    CNO->>OVN_N: Update NorthBound DB logical topology via OVSDB :6641
    OVN_N->>OVN_C: Compile logical flows to SouthBound DB via OVSDB :6642
    OVN_C->>OVS: Program OpenFlow rules on br-int
    OVS-->>Admin: New MTU active on all nodes
    Note over CNO,OVS: Never edit OVS or OVN directly — CNO will overwrite
# View current network configuration
oc get network.operator.openshift.io cluster -o yaml
# Key fields:
# spec.defaultNetwork.type: OVNKubernetes
# spec.clusterNetwork: pod CIDR
# spec.serviceNetwork: service CIDR
# spec.networkType: OVNKubernetes

# View the cluster-level network config (read-only summary)
oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster -o yaml
# status.clusterNetwork:
#   - cidr: 10.128.0.0/14
#     hostPrefix: 23          ← /23 per node = 512 pods max per node
# status.serviceNetwork:
#   - 172.30.0.0/16
# status.networkType: OVNKubernetes
# expect: matches install-config.yaml values set at cluster creation

docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change spec.defaultNetwork.type OVNKubernetes Active CNI plugin Set at install time only — migration requires maintenance window spec.clusterNetwork[].cidr 10.128.0.0/14 Pod IP CIDR Set at install time — cannot change post-install spec.clusterNetwork[].hostPrefix 23 Subnet size per node Smaller = more nodes; larger = more pods per node spec.serviceNetwork 172.30.0.0/16 ClusterIP range Set at install time only spec.defaultNetwork.ovnKubernetesConfig.mtu 1400 (Geneve) Pod network MTU Lower if physical MTU < 1450 (e.g. VPN overhead) spec.defaultNetwork.ovnKubernetesConfig.genevePort 6081 UDP tunnel port Change if 6081 is blocked

docs.title: 3. Default Pod and Service CIDRs
docs.text:
OpenShift uses different default CIDRs from vanilla Kubernetes:

Pod CIDR:      10.128.0.0/14   (4 × /16 blocks)
Service CIDR:  172.30.0.0/16
Node prefix:   /23             (512 IPs per node)

Each node gets a /23 from the pod CIDR: 

Node 1: 10.128.0.0/23   (pods 10.128.0.1 – 10.128.1.254)
Node 2: 10.128.2.0/23
Node 3: 10.128.4.0/23
...


# See per-node pod CIDR allocations
oc get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.podCIDRs}{"\n"}{end}'
# expect: each node shows its /23 subnet

# Verify service CIDR
oc get svc kubernetes -n default -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'
# expect: 172.30.0.1 (or first IP in service CIDR)

docs.title: 4. Namespace Network Isolation
docs.text:
OpenShift enforces namespace isolation by default using NetworkPolicy. When you create a namespace, OpenShift automatically creates policies that: - Allow traffic within the same namespace - Deny traffic from other namespaces - Allow ingress from the router namespace - Allow ingress from the monitoring namespace

# View auto-created NetworkPolicies
oc get networkpolicy -n my-namespace
# NAME                                    POD-SELECTOR   AGE
# allow-from-openshift-ingress            <none>         5m
# allow-from-openshift-monitoring         <none>         5m
# allow-same-namespace                    <none>         5m
# expect: these three policies in every new namespace

# Verify traffic between namespaces is blocked by default
# (without an explicit allow policy)
oc exec -it -n namespace-a pod-a -- curl -m5 http://<pod-b-ip>
# expect: timeout (blocked by auto-created isolation policy)

To allow traffic between namespaces: 

# Allow namespace B to receive from namespace A
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-namespace-a
  namespace: namespace-b
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: namespace-a

docs.title: 5. OpenShift DNS
docs.text:
CoreDNS is used but configured via the DNS operator:

# View DNS operator config
oc get dns.operator.openshift.io default -o yaml
# expect: spec.servers empty (no custom upstream) by default

# Custom upstream DNS servers
oc edit dns.operator.openshift.io default
# spec:
#   servers:
#     - name: corporate-dns
#       zones:
#         - corp.example.com
#       forwardPlugin:
#         upstreams:
#           - 10.100.0.53
# expect: CoreDNS CoreFile updated automatically by DNS operator

# DNS service (runs on each node via NodeLocal DNSCache)
oc get svc -n openshift-dns
# dns-default   ClusterIP   172.30.0.10   53/UDP,53/TCP

# NodeLocal cache address: 10.0.0.10 (or the node's local DNS cache)
# Verify pods use the local cache:
oc exec -it pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# expect: nameserver 172.30.0.10 (or NodeLocal DNSCache IP)

docs.title: 6. OpenShift Monitoring Network
docs.text:
OpenShift's built-in monitoring stack (Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana) lives in openshift-monitoring and needs network access to scrape all pods.

# Check monitoring pods
oc get pods -n openshift-monitoring
# expect: prometheus-k8s, alertmanager-main, grafana pods Running

# NetworkPolicy allows monitoring ingress automatically
oc get networkpolicy -A | grep monitoring
# expect: "allow-from-openshift-monitoring" in every namespace

# Check monitoring scrape targets
oc port-forward -n openshift-monitoring svc/prometheus-k8s 9090
# Browse to localhost:9090 → Status → Targets
# expect: all namespace/pod targets UP

docs.title: 7. OpenShift SDN (Legacy — Deprecated)
docs.text:
Before OVN-Kubernetes, OpenShift used its own SDN plugin with three modes:

Mode Description subnet Flat network, no isolation between namespaces multitenant Per-namespace VXLAN VNI — full isolation networkpolicy NetworkPolicy API — selective isolation 
# Check if a cluster still uses OpenShift SDN (older clusters)
oc get network.operator.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.defaultNetwork.type}'
# OpenShiftSDN  ← legacy
# OVNKubernetes ← current

# expect: OVNKubernetes on any cluster >= 4.12

Migration from OpenShift SDN to OVN-Kubernetes is supported but requires a maintenance window.

docs.title: 8. Key OpenShift Networking CLI Commands
docs.text:
# Overall network status
oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster
# expect: networkType, clusterNetwork, serviceNetwork fields

oc get clusteroperator network
# expect: Available=True, Progressing=False, Degraded=False

# CNO health
oc get pods -n openshift-network-operator
oc logs -n openshift-network-operator deploy/network-operator
# expect: "reconciliation successful" messages; no ERROR lines

# OVN-Kubernetes pods
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes
# expect: ovnkube-node Running on every worker/master node

# Node network status
oc get pods -n openshift-network-diagnostics
# expect: network-check-source and network-check-target pods Running

# Run network connectivity checks
oc get podnetworkconnectivitycheck -n openshift-network-diagnostics | head -20
# expect: "NetworkCheckSuccess" conditions; failures indicate routing problems

# Collect full diagnostic bundle
oc adm must-gather --image=registry.redhat.io/openshift4/ose-must-gather -- \
  /usr/bin/gather_network_logs
# produces /must-gather/network/ with OVN NB/SB DB dumps and flow tables

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• oc get clusteroperator network shows Available=True, Degraded=False after every upgrade
  • PodNetworkConnectivityCheck conditions are all NetworkCheckSuccess on all nodes
  • Custom upstream DNS configured for internal zones via DNS Operator (not CoreDNS ConfigMap directly)
  • EgressIP configured and tested for namespaces that need a stable external IP (compliance)
  • oc adm must-gather procedure documented and tested — ensure network logs are captured
  • Pod/service CIDR capacity reviewed: /14 pod CIDR supports ~1024 nodes at /23 host prefix
  • Namespace-level NetworkPolicy customizations version-controlled — OpenShift auto-policies must not be deleted

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Edit OVN or OVS config files directly on nodes CNO overwrites all changes on next reconcile Always edit network.operator.openshift.io/cluster CR only Delete auto-created NetworkPolicies in namespace Breaks monitoring scraping and router ingress Never delete allow-from-openshift-monitoring or allow-from-openshift-ingress Set pod CIDR to /16 at install and add nodes beyond /23 capacity Pod IP exhaustion on individual nodes — new pods stuck Pending Plan: clusterNetwork size ≥ max_nodes × 2^(32-hostPrefix) Mix OpenShift SDN and OVN-Kubernetes concepts SDN used netnamespace and VNIs; OVN uses OVN logical switches — confusion leads to wrong troubleshooting Know which CNI is active: oc get network.operator cluster -o jsonpath='{.spec.defaultNetwork.type}' Use kubectl for OpenShift-specific resources kubectl lacks oc shorthand for Routes, SCCs, and Projects — silent failures on some resources Always use oc on OpenShift — it is a superset of kubectl

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why does OpenShift manage OVN-Kubernetes through the Cluster Network Operator (CNO) rather than allowing administrators to edit CNI configuration files directly on nodes?
Answer The CNO acts as the single source of truth for network configuration: it continuously reconciles the `network.operator.openshift.io/cluster` custom resource against the actual state of OVN pods, ConfigMaps, and node settings. If you edit OVS or OVN files directly on a node, the CNO's next reconciliation loop will overwrite your changes. This design ensures consistency across all nodes, makes upgrades safe (the CNO knows how to roll out new OVN versions), and prevents configuration drift that would be impossible to audit through GitOps.
  1. [Scenario question] A pod in namespace-a cannot reach a pod in namespace-b even though both pods are running. No custom NetworkPolicies have been created. What three auto-created NetworkPolicies does OpenShift place in every new namespace, and which one is preventing this traffic?
Answer OpenShift automatically creates `allow-same-namespace` (allows traffic within the same namespace), `allow-from-openshift-ingress` (allows the HAProxy router to reach pods), and `allow-from-openshift-monitoring` (allows Prometheus scraping). The policy preventing cross-namespace traffic is the absence of any explicit allow between namespaces — `allow-same-namespace` only permits intra-namespace traffic, and there is no auto-created policy that allows arbitrary cross-namespace traffic. Add a NetworkPolicy in `namespace-b` with a `namespaceSelector` allowing ingress from `namespace-a`.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check the current CNI type, pod CIDR, and service CIDR of an OpenShift cluster?
Answer 
oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster -o yaml
Look for `status.networkType` (should be `OVNKubernetes`), `status.clusterNetwork[].cidr` (default `10.128.0.0/14` with `/23` host prefix), and `status.serviceNetwork` (default `172.30.0.0/16`); these values are set at install time and cannot be changed post-install.

docs.title: Lesson 26 — OVN-Kubernetes: OpenShift's Default CNI
docs.text:
Track: OpenShift Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 25 — OpenShift Networking Overview, Lesson 03 — iptables Duration: ~3 hours

Goal: Inspect the OVN/OVS control and data planes on a live OpenShift cluster, trace a packet from source pod to destination pod, and explain how NetworkPolicy is enforced without iptables.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: Theory
docs.text: See also: Lesson 03 — iptables and Netfilter for why OVN replaces iptables entirely.

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Control["Control Plane (master nodes)"]
        NB["OVN NorthBound DB (nbdb) -- logical switches, routers, ACLs, LBs"]
        NORTHD["ovn-northd (logical to physical compiler)"]
        SB["OVN SouthBound DB (sbdb) -- chassis bindings, flows, BFD"]
    end
    subgraph Node1["Worker Node 1"]
        OC1["ovn-controller (reads SB, programs OVS flows)"]
        OVS1["OVS br-int (kernel OpenFlow table)"]
        POD1["pod-a 10.128.0.5 -- veth to OVS port"]
    end
    subgraph Node2["Worker Node 2"]
        OC2["ovn-controller (reads SB, programs OVS flows)"]
        OVS2["OVS br-int (kernel OpenFlow table)"]
        POD2["pod-b 10.128.2.5 -- veth to OVS port"]
    end
    NB --"OVSDB :6641"--> NORTHD --> SB
    SB --"OVSDB :6642"--> OC1 --> OVS1 --- POD1
    SB --"OVSDB :6642"--> OC2 --> OVS2 --- POD2
    OVS1 --"Geneve UDP :6081"--> OVS2

Components per worker node: - ovn-controller — reads Southbound DB, programs OVS flows - ovs-vswitchd — OVS daemon implementing the dataplane - ovsdb-server — OVS local database

Components on control-plane nodes only: - ovn-northd — translates logical network to physical bindings - nbdb — OVN Northbound database (logical topology) - sbdb — OVN Southbound database (physical topology)

docs.title: 2. OVN-Kubernetes Pods in OpenShift
docs.text:
# View OVN-Kubernetes pods — confirm all Running
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -o wide
# NAME                          NODE           STATUS
# ovnkube-node-aaaaa            worker-1       Running   <- per worker node
# ovnkube-node-bbbbb            worker-2       Running
# ovnkube-master-ccccc          master-1       Running   <- control-plane only

# Check health (any non-Running pods are a problem)
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes | grep -v Running

# Inspect individual containers in ovnkube-node
oc get pod -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $OVNNODE \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'
# ovn-controller ovs-vswitchd ovsdb-server ovnkube-node

docs.title: 3. The OVS Bridge (br-int)
docs.text:
Each node has an OVS integration bridge (br-int) that connects all pods and handles all forwarding:

# From the node debug shell (chroot /host):
ovs-vsctl show
# Bridge "br-int"
#   Port eeb73ac0d1e3789      <- pod veth port (hex = iface ID)
#       Interface eeb73ac0d1e3789
#   Port k8s-worker-1
#       Interface k8s-worker-1  <- node's own port
#   Port patch-br-int-to-breth0_worker-1
#       Interface patch-br-int-to-breth0_worker-1
#           type: patch          <- connects to external bridge

# List ports with their OF port numbers
ovs-vsctl list-ports br-int

# Show OpenFlow tables (actual forwarding rules — 1000s of entries)
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | wc -l       # count
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | head -30    # first few rules

# Show all OVS interfaces with metadata
ovs-vsctl list Interface | grep -E "^name|external_ids|ofport" | head -40

docs.title: 4. Logical Network Topology
docs.text:
OVN creates a virtual topology mirroring Kubernetes objects — changes to pods/services trigger updates here:

# View entire logical network (run against master pod)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl show | head -60
# switch <uuid> (egressip-no-reroute-node-subnets)
# switch <uuid> (node-local-switch)
#     port node-local-switch-to-join ...
# router <uuid> (ovn_cluster_router)
#     port rtoj-ovn_cluster_router ...

# List logical switches (one per node + cluster-wide switches)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl ls-list

# List logical routers
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl lr-list
# <uuid> (ovn_cluster_router)   <- routes between all nodes/pods
# <uuid> (GR_worker-1)          <- gateway router per node

# List load balancers (each Service = one LB entry)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl lb-list | head -20
# <uuid>  None   tcp    10.96.0.1:443 = 192.168.0.5:6443,...

# View Southbound DB — physical chassis bindings
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-sbctl show | head -40

docs.title: 5. Pod Traffic Flow — Same Node
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PA as Pod A<br/>10.128.0.5
    participant OVS as OVS br-int<br/>(flow tables)
    participant PB as Pod B<br/>10.128.0.6

    PA->>OVS: Ethernet frame via veth
    Note over OVS: Table 0: in_port match<br/>Table 8: IP destination<br/>Action: direct output
    OVS->>PB: Frame via pod-b veth
    Note over PA,PB: No tunnel, no routing —<br/>same OVS bridge

docs.title: 6. Pod Traffic Flow — Cross-Node (Geneve Tunnel)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant PA as Pod A<br/>10.128.0.5 (Node1)
    participant OVS1 as OVS Node1<br/>br-int
    participant TUN as Geneve Tunnel<br/>UDP port 6081
    participant OVS2 as OVS Node2<br/>br-int
    participant PB as Pod B<br/>10.128.2.5 (Node2)

    PA->>OVS1: veth frame
    Note over OVS1: Flow: route via ovn_cluster_router<br/>Encapsulate with Geneve header<br/>Outer src: Node1 IP, dst: Node2 IP<br/>Tunnel key (VNI) encodes metadata
    OVS1->>TUN: UDP/Geneve encapsulated
    TUN->>OVS2: Delivered to Node2
    Note over OVS2: Decapsulate<br/>Match inner dst IP<br/>Output to pod-b port
    OVS2->>PB: Frame via veth
# Verify Geneve tunnels exist on a node
ip link show type geneve     # Geneve tunnel interfaces
ovs-vsctl list-ports br-int | grep -i tun

# Confirm Geneve port (6081) is open between nodes
ss -ulnp | grep 6081

# View tunnel endpoints in OVN Southbound DB
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-sbctl list Encap | grep -E "ip|type"

docs.title: 7. NetworkPolicy Implementation — OVN ACLs
docs.text:
OVN implements NetworkPolicy using ACLs in the Northbound DB — not iptables. ovn-northd compiles ACLs → Southbound logical flows → ovn-controller programs OVS.

# Find the logical switch for a namespace
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl ls-list | grep production

# View ACLs on that switch (derived from NetworkPolicy objects)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl acl-list <ls-name> | head -20
# to-lport  1000 (ip4 && ip4.dst == 10.128.1.5 && tcp.dst == 80) allow-related
# to-lport  0    (ip4 && ip4.dst == {10.128.1.5}) drop   <- default deny

# Count total ACLs in the cluster
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl find ACL | grep -c "^_uuid"

# Trace what happens to a specific packet (ovn-trace — no actual traffic)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-trace <ls-name> \
  'inport == "pod-a-port"; ip4; ip4.src=10.128.0.5; ip4.dst=10.128.1.5; tcp; tcp.dst=80'
# output: "Policy drop" or "output to pod-b-port"

ACL to NetworkPolicy mapping: | NetworkPolicy field | OVN ACL field | |---------------------|--------------| | podSelector | ip4.src / ip4.dst match on port | | namespaceSelector | address set for namespace pod IPs | | ports | tcp.dst == X or udp.dst == X | | policyType: Ingress | to-lport direction | | policyType: Egress | from-lport direction |

docs.title: Local Gateway Mode (default OpenShift 4.10+)
docs.text: Egress traffic leaves via each node's own interface. Preserves pod source IPs for external traffic. Recommended.

docs.title: Shared Gateway Mode (legacy)
docs.text:
All external traffic routes through master nodes. Single bottleneck. Not recommended for production.

# Check current gateway mode
oc get network.operator.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.defaultNetwork.ovnKubernetesConfig.gatewayConfig}'
# {"routingViaHost": true}   <- local gateway (recommended)
# {"routingViaHost": false}  <- shared gateway (legacy)

# Change to local gateway (rolling restart of ovnkube-node pods)
oc patch network.operator.openshift.io cluster \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"defaultNetwork":{"ovnKubernetesConfig":{"gatewayConfig":{"routingViaHost":true}}}}}'

docs.title: 9. IPsec Encryption
docs.text:
OVN-Kubernetes supports transparent IPsec encryption for all Geneve tunnel traffic between nodes. No application changes required.

# Enable IPsec (takes 10-15 min — rolls out per node)
oc patch network.operator.openshift.io cluster \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"defaultNetwork":{"ovnKubernetesConfig":{"ipsecConfig":{"mode":"Full"}}}}}'

# Check IPsec pod status
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes | grep ipsec

# Verify IPsec is active on a node
oc debug node/<node> -- chroot /host \
  ip xfrm state | head -20
# src 192.168.0.1 dst 192.168.0.2
#     proto esp ... <- IPsec ESP state

# Check OVS certificate used for IPsec
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes ovnkube-node-xxxxx -- \
  ovs-vsctl get Open_vSwitch . other_config:certificate

docs.title: 10. Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change gatewayConfig.routingViaHost false (shared) Routes egress via node NIC vs master Set true for local gateway in production ipsecConfig.mode Disabled Encrypts Geneve tunnels with IPsec ESP Enable for compliance (PCI, HIPAA) mtu auto-detected Overlay MTU (subtract Geneve overhead ~50B) Lower if jumbo frames unavailable hybridOverlayConfig.enabled false Allows Windows nodes using VXLAN hybrid Enable for mixed Linux/Windows clusters v4InternalSubnet 100.64.0.0/16 Transit subnet for OVN join switch Change only if 100.64.x conflicts egressIPConfig.reachabilityTotalTimeoutSeconds 1 Time to detect EgressIP node failure Lower for faster HA failover

docs.title: Hands-On Lab
docs.text:
# Step 1 — inspect the OVS bridge on a node
# (from oc debug node → chroot /host)
ovs-vsctl show
# expect: Bridge "br-int" with pod veth ports and tunnel ports

# Step 2 — list logical switches and routers
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl ls-list
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- ovn-nbctl lr-list
# expect: ovn_cluster_router and per-node GR_worker-N routers

# Step 3 — inspect NetworkPolicy ACLs
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl acl-list <ls-name> | head -20
# expect: allow-related and drop ACLs corresponding to NetworkPolicy objects

# Step 4 — simulate a packet (no actual traffic)
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-trace <ls-name> \
  'inport=="pod-a-port"; ip4; ip4.src=10.128.0.5; ip4.dst=10.128.1.5; tcp; tcp.dst=8080'
# expect: "output to pod-b-port" (allow) or "Policy drop" (deny)

# Step 5 — verify Geneve tunnel is active
ip link show type geneve     # Geneve tunnel interfaces
ss -ulnp | grep 6081         # UDP :6081 listening

# Step 6 — OVS packet trace (live dataplane)
oc debug node/<node> -- chroot /host \
  ovs-appctl ofproto/trace br-int \
  "in_port=1,ip,ip_src=10.128.0.5,ip_dst=10.128.1.5,tcp,tcp_dst=8080"

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• All ovnkube-node pods Running on every worker node — zero CrashLoopBackOff
  • All ovnkube-master pods Running on control-plane nodes with no restarts in 24 h
  • Geneve UDP port 6081 allowed between all node security groups / firewall rules
  • Gateway mode set to routingViaHost: true (local gateway) for production traffic
  • IPsec enabled if workloads are subject to data-in-transit compliance requirements
  • podnetworkconnectivitycheck resources all show no failures
  • OVN NBDB and SBDB Raft quorum healthy — at least 3 control-plane nodes

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Edit OVS flows directly with ovs-ofctl mod-flows ovn-controller overwrites manual flows on next reconcile All changes go through OVN NB via operator (network.operator.openshift.io) Delete OVN pods to "restart networking" NBDB or SBDB pod restart triggers full re-sync — brief outage on all nodes Restart only the specific container (ovn-controller) when needed Mix shared and local gateway mode expectations Shared gateway NATs egress through masters; local gateway does not — source IPs differ Pick one mode at cluster install time; migration requires rolling restart Allow only TCP 6081 for Geneve Geneve uses UDP — TCP 6081 does nothing Allow UDP 6081 between all node IPs Expect iptables -L to show NetworkPolicy rules OVN uses ACLs + OVS flows, not iptables — iptables is empty Use ovn-nbctl acl-list and ovs-ofctl dump-flows

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail Data plane Open vSwitch (OVS) flow tables — kernel module Control plane OVN: Northbound DB → ovn-northd → Southbound DB → ovn-controller Encapsulation Geneve tunnels between nodes (UDP port 6081) NetworkPolicy Compiled to OVN ACLs — no iptables involved Services OVN Logical Load Balancers (DNAT in flow tables) Encryption IPsec transparent mode over Geneve tunnels Configuration Via Cluster Network Operator — never edit OVS/OVN directly Packet tracing ovn-trace for logical simulation; ovs-appctl ofproto/trace for dataplane

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] How does OVN-Kubernetes enforce NetworkPolicy without using iptables, and what is the control-plane path from a NetworkPolicy object to an enforced flow rule?
Answer OVN-Kubernetes compiles NetworkPolicy objects into OVN ACLs stored in the Northbound database. `ovn-northd` reads those ACLs and translates them into logical flows in the Southbound database. Each node's `ovn-controller` reads the Southbound DB and programs OpenFlow rules into the OVS `br-int` bridge. The result is that packet filtering happens in the OVS kernel dataplane flow tables — `iptables -L` shows no NetworkPolicy rules because they are enforced entirely within OVS, not netfilter.
  1. [Scenario question] Cross-node pod-to-pod traffic fails but pods on the same node can communicate. What port and protocol must be open between all nodes, and how would you verify it is the issue?
Answer OVN-Kubernetes uses Geneve tunnels on **UDP port 6081** for cross-node encapsulation. If a firewall or security group blocks UDP 6081 between nodes, intra-node traffic (which stays on the OVS bridge without tunneling) works fine while cross-node traffic silently drops. Verify by running `ss -ulnp | grep 6081` on a node to confirm the port is listening, and use `tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp port 6081` on both nodes to check whether tunnel packets are arriving. The fix is to open UDP 6081 bidirectionally between all node IPs.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to simulate a packet from pod-a to pod-b on port 8080 without sending real traffic, to see whether OVN ACLs would allow or drop it?
Answer 
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-trace <ls-name> \
  'inport=="pod-a-port"; ip4; ip4.src=10.128.0.5; ip4.dst=10.128.1.5; tcp; tcp.dst=8080'
The output shows each logical flow table that the simulated packet passes through; look for `output to pod-b-port` for an allow result or `Policy drop` / `drop` for a deny result, which tells you which ACL matched.

docs.title: Lesson 27 — OpenShift Routes and HAProxy Router
docs.text:
Track: OpenShift Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers, Lesson 25 — OpenShift Overview Duration: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Create edge, passthrough, and reencrypt Routes on OpenShift, configure a custom IngressController for router sharding, and read HAProxy backend stats to diagnose a 503 error.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: Theory
docs.text: See also: Lesson 17 — Ingress Controllers for Kubernetes Ingress API comparison. See also: Lesson 28 — OpenShift Egress for controlling outbound traffic from the same namespace.

docs.title: 1. Route vs Kubernetes Ingress
docs.text: Feature OpenShift Route Kubernetes Ingress API group route.openshift.io/v1 networking.k8s.io/v1 Controller HAProxy Router Any Ingress Controller TLS passthrough Native Requires SNI-based annotation TLS reencrypt Native Not standard A/B weight splitting Native (alternateBackends) Controller-specific annotation Wildcard host Native Via annotation Admission status Per-route .status.ingress LB IP in .status.loadBalancer Path-based routing Yes Yes

docs.title: 2. Route Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Client
        BR["Browser / Client"]
    end
    subgraph DNS
        WDNS["*.apps.cluster.example.com to router EXTERNAL-IP"]
    end
    subgraph OpenShift
        SVC_LB["LoadBalancer Service router-default (NLB / MetalLB) :443/:80"]
        subgraph IC["openshift-ingress namespace"]
            RP1["router-default-pod-1 HAProxy :80/:443"]
            RP2["router-default-pod-2 HAProxy :80/:443"]
        end
        subgraph App["application namespace"]
            SVC["Service (ClusterIP)"]
            POD1["Pod"]
            POD2["Pod"]
        end
        ROUTE["Route CR -- host, TLS mode, weight"]
    end

    BR --"HTTPS :443"-->DNS
    DNS -->SVC_LB -->RP1
    SVC_LB -->RP2
    RP1 --"watches / reconciles"-->ROUTE
    RP2 --"watches / reconciles"-->ROUTE
    RP1 --"HTTP backend :8080"-->SVC -->POD1
    RP1 -->SVC -->POD2

docs.title: 3. The IngressController Operator
docs.text:
OpenShift manages routers via the IngressController CRD — never edit router pods directly.

# View the default IngressController
oc get ingresscontroller default -n openshift-ingress-operator -o yaml
# spec.domain: apps.cluster.example.com   <- wildcard DNS base
# spec.replicas: 2
# spec.endpointPublishingStrategy.type: LoadBalancerService
# status.conditions: Available True

# View router pods created by the operator
oc get pods -n openshift-ingress -o wide
# router-default-xxxxx-yyyyy   (one per replica, spread across infra nodes)

# View the LoadBalancer service (holds EXTERNAL-IP)
oc get svc -n openshift-ingress router-default

# Create a custom IngressController for internal traffic
oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: operator.openshift.io/v1
kind: IngressController
metadata:
  name: internal
  namespace: openshift-ingress-operator
spec:
  domain: internal.cluster.example.com
  replicas: 2
  endpointPublishingStrategy:
    type: LoadBalancerService
    loadBalancer:
      scope: Internal     # Internal LB (AWS: internal NLB)
  nodePlacement:
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        node-role.kubernetes.io/infra: ""
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      router: internal    # only routes in namespaces with this label
EOF

docs.title: 4. IngressController Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change spec.replicas 2 Number of HAProxy router pods Increase for high throughput spec.domain cluster install value Wildcard DNS base for auto-generated hostnames Set at install; changing disrupts all routes endpointPublishingStrategy.type LoadBalancerService How the router is exposed (LB, NodePort, HostNetwork) Use HostNetwork on bare metal tuningOptions.maxConnections 50000 HAProxy global maxconn Increase for high-connection workloads tuningOptions.threadCount auto HAProxy worker threads Set to vCPU count of infra nodes httpHeaders.forwardedHeaderPolicy Append Handling of X-Forwarded-For Set Replace if upstream proxy already sets it logging.access.destination.type Container Access log destination Use Syslog for centralized logging routeAdmission.wildcardPolicy WildcardsDisallowed Whether *.example.com routes are accepted Set WildcardsAllowed for multi-tenant platforms routeAdmission.namespaceOwnership InterNamespaceAllowed Whether routes can claim hostnames across namespaces Set Strict for tenant isolation

docs.title: Edge — TLS terminates at the router
docs.text:
apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: web-edge
  namespace: default
spec:
  host: web.apps.cluster.example.com
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: web
    weight: 100
  port:
    targetPort: 8080
  tls:
    termination: edge
    insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy: Redirect   # HTTP → HTTPS 301
    # Optional: provide custom certificate
    # certificate: |-
    #   -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
    # key: |-
    #   -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
    # caCertificate: |-   (chain if needed)

docs.title: Passthrough — TLS goes all the way to the pod
docs.text:
spec:
  tls:
    termination: passthrough
  # Router does NOT decrypt — routes by SNI hostname only
  # Cannot use path-based routing in passthrough mode
  # Pod must present a valid certificate

docs.title: Reencrypt — terminate at router, then re-establish TLS to pod
docs.text:
spec:
  tls:
    termination: reencrypt
    destinationCACertificate: |-   # CA cert to verify the pod's server cert
      -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
      ...
    # Optional: custom cert for the client-facing side

docs.title: 6. Route Lifecycle — Admission Sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User / CI
    participant API as API Server
    participant RO as Route Operator
    participant RP as Router Pod (HAProxy)

    U->>API: oc apply -f route.yaml
    API->>RO: Route created event
    RO->>RO: Validate hostname ownership<br/>Check routeAdmission policy
    RO->>API: Update route.status.ingress<br/>Admitted: True / False
    RP->>API: Watch Route objects (every 10s)
    RP->>RP: Regenerate haproxy.config<br/>Reload HAProxy (soft reload)
    Note over RP: HAProxy reload is zero-downtime:<br/>old process drains, new one takes over
# Check if a route was admitted
oc describe route web-edge | grep -A 15 "Status:"
# Ingress:
#   Host:  web.apps.cluster.example.com
#   Conditions:
#     Type: Admitted  Status: True
#     RouterName: default

# Check route admission across all routes
oc get routes -A -o custom-columns=\
'NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,HOST:.spec.host,ADMITTED:.status.ingress[0].conditions[0].status'

docs.title: 7. Route Management Commands
docs.text:
# Expose a service as a route (auto-generates hostname from service name + domain)
oc expose svc web
# → web.apps.cluster.example.com

# Expose with explicit hostname
oc expose svc web --hostname=web.apps.cluster.example.com

# Create a TLS edge route with custom certificates
oc create route edge web-tls \
  --service=web \
  --hostname=web.apps.cluster.example.com \
  --cert=tls.crt \
  --key=tls.key

# View all routes across all namespaces
oc get routes -A

# Delete
oc delete route web-edge -n default

docs.title: 8. Weighted Routes — A/B Traffic Splitting
docs.text:
OpenShift Routes support native A/B splits — no service mesh required.

apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: web-ab
spec:
  host: web.apps.cluster.example.com
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: web-v1
    weight: 80          # 80% to v1
  alternateBackends:
    - kind: Service
      name: web-v2
      weight: 20        # 20% to v2
  port:
    targetPort: 8080
  tls:
    termination: edge

# Verify weights are reflected in HAProxy
oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- \
  grep -A5 "web.apps.cluster.example.com" /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config \
  | grep "weight"
# server pod-v1-xxx 10.128.0.5:8080 weight 256  <- 80% → 256
# server pod-v2-xxx 10.128.0.6:8080 weight 64   <- 20% → 64

docs.title: 9. HAProxy Annotations
docs.text:
metadata:
  annotations:
    # Connection timeouts
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/timeout: 60s
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/connect-timeout: 5s

    # Load balancing algorithm
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/balance: "leastconn"   # roundrobin, source, leastconn

    # Sticky sessions (source IP based)
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/balance: "source"

    # Rate limiting
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/rate-limit-connections: "true"
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/rate-limit-connections.rate-http: "100"

    # IP allowlist (space-separated CIDRs)
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/ip_whitelist: "192.168.1.0/24 10.0.0.1"

    # HTTP Strict Transport Security
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/hsts_header: "max-age=31536000;includeSubDomains;preload"

    # CORS
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/cors-allow-origin: "https://example.com"

    # Rewrite incoming request path
    haproxy.router.openshift.io/rewrite-target: /

docs.title: 10. IngressController Tuning
docs.text:
apiVersion: operator.openshift.io/v1
kind: IngressController
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: openshift-ingress-operator
spec:
  replicas: 3
  tuningOptions:
    headerBufferBytes: 32768
    headerBufferMaxRewriteBytes: 8192
    maxConnections: 50000
    threadCount: 4
  logging:
    access:
      destination:
        type: Container    # stdout — scrape with Fluentd/Vector
      httpLogFormat: >-
        %ci:%cp [%t] %ft %b/%s %B %tsc %ac/%fc/%bc/%sc/%rc %{+Q}r
  httpHeaders:
    forwardedHeaderPolicy: Append

docs.title: 11. Router Sharding
docs.text:
Deploy multiple IngressControllers on different node groups, each serving different namespaces:

# Label namespace so the internal IngressController picks it up
oc label namespace my-app router=internal

# Confirm the internal router has admitted the route
oc describe route my-route -n my-app | grep RouterName
# RouterName: internal

docs.title: 12. Wildcard Routes
docs.text:
# Allow wildcard routes on the IngressController
oc patch ingresscontroller default \
  -n openshift-ingress-operator \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"routeAdmission":{"wildcardPolicy":"WildcardsAllowed"}}}'

# Create a wildcard route
oc apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: wildcard-route
spec:
  host: "*.apps.cluster.example.com"
  wildcardPolicy: Subdomain
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: web
  tls:
    termination: edge
EOF

docs.title: 13. Standard Kubernetes Ingress on OpenShift
docs.text:
OpenShift accepts standard Ingress resources — the router automatically converts them to Routes:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
  annotations:
    route.openshift.io/termination: edge   # OpenShift TLS annotation
spec:
  ingressClassName: openshift-default
  rules:
    - host: web.apps.cluster.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — verify router is running and has an external IP
oc get pods -n openshift-ingress
oc get svc -n openshift-ingress router-default
# EXTERNAL-IP should be populated (NLB address or IP)

# Terminal 2 — inspect IngressController
oc get ingresscontroller default -n openshift-ingress-operator -o yaml \
  | grep -E "domain|replicas|endpointPublishing|conditions" | head -20

# Terminal 3 — peek at live HAProxy config inside the router
ROUTER=$(oc get pods -n openshift-ingress -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
echo "Router pod: $ROUTER"
oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- \
  cat /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config | head -60

docs.title: Hands-On Lab
docs.text:
# Step 1 — expose a service and verify Route is admitted
oc expose svc web --hostname=web.apps.cluster.example.com
oc describe route web | grep -A 15 "Status:"
# expect: Admitted: True

# Step 2 — check HAProxy backend health via UNIX socket
oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- \
  bash -c 'echo "show stat" | socat - /var/lib/haproxy/run/haproxy.sock | \
  cut -d, -f1,2,18,19 | grep -v "^#"'
# expect: be_<namespace>_<service>_<port>,pod-name,UP — UP = healthy backend

# Step 3 — test route internally (bypass DNS)
oc run -it --rm test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -Hv "Host: web.apps.cluster.example.com" \
  http://router-default.openshift-ingress.svc
# expect: HTTP 200 response from the backend pod

# Step 4 — verify weighted A/B split in HAProxy config
oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- \
  grep -A5 "web.apps.cluster.example.com" /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config \
  | grep "weight"
# expect: weight 256 (80%) and weight 64 (20%) for alternateBackends split

# Step 5 — check router logs for 5xx errors
oc logs -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER | grep " 5[0-9][0-9] " | tail -20

# Step 6 — check all route admission status
oc get routes -A -o json \
  | jq '.items[] | select(.status.ingress[0].conditions[0].status != "True") | .metadata.name'

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix Route not admitted Hostname claimed by another route / admission policy oc describe route <name> \| grep Conditions Check routeAdmission.namespaceOwnership; delete conflicting route 503 Service Unavailable No healthy pod endpoints behind service echo "show stat" \| socat - /var/lib/haproxy/run/haproxy.sock \| cut -d, -f1,2,18 Check pod readiness probes; check service selector Certificate error (browser) Custom cert doesn't match hostname oc get route <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls.certificate}' \| openssl x509 -noout -subject Re-create route with correct cert No EXTERNAL-IP on router service Cloud LB not provisioned / MetalLB missing oc get svc -n openshift-ingress router-default Check IngressController endpointPublishingStrategy; install MetalLB on bare metal Route admitted but traffic returns 404 Wrong targetPort or missing path in backend oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- curl -s http://<svc-ip>:<port>/path Verify service port and pod HTTP server path HAProxy 502 Bad Gateway Pod starts but not yet ready oc get endpoints <service> — check address count Add/tune readiness probe; check haproxy.router.openshift.io/connect-timeout 
# Check HAProxy backend health via UNIX socket
oc exec -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER -- \
  bash -c 'echo "show stat" | socat - /var/lib/haproxy/run/haproxy.sock | \
  cut -d, -f1,2,18,19 | grep -v "^#"'
# be_<namespace>_<service>_<port>,pod-name,UP,0  <- UP = healthy
# be_<namespace>_<service>_<port>,pod-name,DOWN,-- <- DOWN = no connection

# Check router log for 5xx errors
oc logs -n openshift-ingress $ROUTER | grep " 5[0-9][0-9] " | tail -20

# Test route from inside cluster (bypass DNS)
oc run -it --rm test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  curl -Hv "Host: web.apps.cluster.example.com" \
  http://router-default.openshift-ingress.svc

# Check all route status at once
oc get routes -A -o json \
  | jq '.items[] | select(.status.ingress[0].conditions[0].status != "True") | .metadata.name'

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• At least 2 router replicas spread across infra nodes (spec.replicas >= 2)
  • maxConnections tuned to expected peak concurrent connections per router pod
  • All production routes use TLS (edge minimum; passthrough/reencrypt for mTLS)
  • Custom certificates loaded for non-wildcard hostnames; wildcard cert for *.apps.*
  • routeAdmission.namespaceOwnership: Strict for multi-tenant environments
  • HAProxy access logs enabled and forwarded to centralized log aggregation
  • IngressController podDisruptionBudget reviewed — router upgrades must not cause full outage

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use passthrough TLS for a path-based route HAProxy cannot inspect SNI beyond hostname — no path routing Use reencrypt if path routing + TLS to pod is needed Set insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy: Allow on public routes Allows plain HTTP to production services — credentials in transit Use Redirect or None on all production routes Create routes directly instead of via IngressController Router sharding and admission policies are bypassed Always use oc expose or YAML; let the operator manage routing Expect X-Forwarded-For to show real client IP without cloud LB proxy protocol Cloud NLB replaces source IP unless proxy protocol or PROXY header is configured Enable PROXY protocol on the NLB and set httpHeaders.forwardedHeaderPolicy: Replace Ignore the Admitted condition A route can exist but be silently unserved if the router rejects it Monitor oc get routes -A and alert on Admitted != True

docs.text: Concept Detail Route CRD route.openshift.io/v1 — OpenShift's first-class Ingress equivalent TLS modes edge (terminate at router), passthrough (pod handles TLS), reencrypt (router re-encrypts to pod) A/B routing Native weight-based splitting via alternateBackends IngressController Operator-managed HAProxy deployment — openshift-ingress-operator Wildcard DNS *.apps.cluster.example.com — base domain set in IngressController spec.domain Router sharding Multiple IngressControllers with namespaceSelector / routeSelector for multi-tenant isolation Standard Ingress Also supported — auto-converted to Routes by the router

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] What are the three TLS termination modes for OpenShift Routes, and in which mode is path-based routing impossible?
Answer The three modes are: **edge** (TLS terminates at the HAProxy router; plain HTTP is forwarded to the backend pod), **reencrypt** (TLS terminates at the router, and HAProxy opens a new TLS connection to the pod using a destination CA certificate), and **passthrough** (the encrypted stream is forwarded unchanged to the pod based solely on SNI hostname). Path-based routing is impossible in **passthrough** mode because HAProxy never decrypts the connection and therefore cannot inspect the HTTP path — it can only route by the hostname in the TLS SNI field.
  1. [Scenario question] A Route shows Admitted: True but users receive 503 Service Unavailable. How would you check whether the backend pods are healthy from the HAProxy router's perspective?
Answer Connect to the HAProxy stats socket inside the router pod using `echo "show stat" | socat - /var/lib/haproxy/run/haproxy.sock | cut -d, -f1,2,18,19` — the output shows each backend server entry with `UP` or `DOWN` status. A `DOWN` entry means HAProxy cannot reach the pod (readiness probe failing, wrong targetPort, or pod not yet ready). Also check `oc get endpoints ` to verify that at least one pod IP is in the `Addresses` list rather than `NotReadyAddresses`.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run to check whether a specific Route was admitted by the HAProxy router?
Answer 
oc describe route web-edge | grep -A 15 "Status:"
Look for the `Admitted: True` condition under the `Ingress` section and confirm the `RouterName` field shows which IngressController accepted it; `Admitted: False` means the router rejected the route due to a hostname conflict or admission policy violation, and the `Message` field will explain why.

docs.title: Lesson 28 — OpenShift EgressIP and EgressFirewall
docs.text:
Track: OpenShift Networking Prerequisites: Lesson 16 — Network Policies, Lesson 25 — OpenShift Overview Duration: ~2 hours

Goal: Assign a stable egress IP to a namespace so external firewall rules remain valid across pod rescheduling, and restrict outbound destinations per namespace using EgressFirewall with CIDR and DNS-based rules.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: Theory
docs.text: See also: Lesson 26 — OVN-Kubernetes for how OVN ACLs underpin both EgressIP and EgressFirewall. See also: Lesson 16 — Network Policies for controlling ingress traffic.

docs.title: 1. The Egress Problem
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Without["Without EgressIP"]
        P1A["billing-pod (on worker-1) src: 192.168.1.10"]
        P1B["billing-pod (on worker-2) src: 192.168.1.11"]
        FW["External DB Firewall whitelist: ???"]
    end
    P1A --"SNAT to node IP 192.168.1.10"--> FW
    P1B --"SNAT to node IP 192.168.1.11"--> FW
    note1["Pod reschedules -- source IP changes -- firewall rules break"]
flowchart LR
    subgraph With["With EgressIP"]
        P2A["billing-pod (on any node)"]
        EIP["EgressIP 192.168.1.100 assigned to worker-1 (moves on node failure)"]
        FW2["External DB Firewall whitelist: 192.168.1.100 OK"]
    end
    P2A --"SNAT to EgressIP 192.168.1.100 always"--> EIP --"fixed src IP"--> FW2

Core principle: EgressIP decouples outbound source IP from the node the pod runs on. The IP floats between eligible nodes using OVN SNAT rules.

docs.title: 2. EgressIP Configuration
docs.text:
# Step 1 — mark worker nodes as EgressIP candidates
oc label node worker-1 k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable=""
oc label node worker-2 k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable=""

# Step 2 — verify nodes appear as assignable
oc get nodes -l k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable

# Step 3 — create the EgressIP resource
apiVersion: k8s.ovn.org/v1
kind: EgressIP
metadata:
  name: billing-egress
spec:
  egressIPs:
    - 192.168.1.100     # must be in the same subnet as the egress node
    - 192.168.1.101     # second IP → HA: each IP lands on a different node
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      egress: billing   # namespaces with this label use these IPs
  podSelector:          # optional: restrict to specific pods within the namespace
    matchLabels:
      app: billing-processor

# Step 4 — label the target namespace
oc label namespace billing egress=billing

# Step 5 — apply and verify
oc apply -f egress-ip.yaml
oc get egressip billing-egress -o yaml
# status:
#   items:
#     - egressIP: 192.168.1.100
#       node: worker-1          <- which node holds this IP now
#     - egressIP: 192.168.1.101
#       node: worker-2          <- second IP on a different node

# Step 6 — confirm source IP from inside the pod
oc exec -n billing billing-pod -- curl -s ifconfig.me
# 192.168.1.100   <- EgressIP, not the node IP

docs.title: 3. EgressIP Assignment Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API
    participant OVN as OVN-Kubernetes Controller
    participant NB as OVN Northbound DB (OVSDB :6641)
    participant Node as Worker Node (ovn-controller)

    K8s->>OVN: EgressIP created event
    OVN->>OVN: Select eligible nodes (egress-assignable label)
    OVN->>Node: Add secondary IP to node NIC (e.g. 192.168.1.100 on eth0)
    OVN->>NB: Add SNAT rule -- pods in namespace to 192.168.1.100
    NB->>Node: ovn-controller programs OVS SNAT flow
    Note over Node: All egress from billing namespace now SNATs to 192.168.1.100

docs.title: 4. EgressIP High Availability
docs.text:
EgressIP is automatically HA when multiple nodes are assignable and multiple IPs are configured. Failover uses BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) for sub-second node failure detection.

# View current IP-to-node assignment
oc get egressip -o wide
# NAME             EGRESSIPS                     ASSIGNED NODE    ASSIGNED EGRESSIPS
# billing-egress   192.168.1.100,192.168.1.101   worker-1         192.168.1.100
#                                                worker-2         192.168.1.101

# Simulate node failure — cordon worker-1 to trigger reassignment
oc adm cordon worker-1
# OVN detects node failure via BFD (~1 second)
# 192.168.1.100 moves to another egress-assignable node

# Confirm reassignment
oc get egressip billing-egress -o jsonpath='{.status.items}' | jq .

# Verify continuous egress (from a pod, while cordon is active)
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  oc exec -n billing billing-pod -- curl -s --connect-timeout 2 ifconfig.me
  sleep 0.5
done
# Should return 192.168.1.100 on all requests (brief gap < 2s during failover)

# Restore
oc adm uncordon worker-1

docs.title: 5. EgressFirewall
docs.text:
EgressFirewall restricts which external destinations a namespace's pods can reach. It is enforced via OVN ACLs — no iptables involved.

apiVersion: k8s.ovn.org/v1
kind: EgressFirewall
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: production
spec:
  egress:
    # Rule order matters — first match wins
    - type: Allow
      to:
        cidrSelector: 10.100.0.0/16    # corporate internal network

    - type: Allow
      to:
        dnsName: api.example.com       # DNS-based rule (wildcard supported)
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443

    # Always allow DNS resolution — without this, DNS lookups fail
    - type: Allow
      to:
        cidrSelector: 0.0.0.0/0
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53

    # Implicit deny-all for everything else
    - type: Deny
      to:
        cidrSelector: 0.0.0.0/0

# Apply and verify
oc apply -f egress-firewall.yaml
oc get egressfirewall -n production
# NAME      EGRESSFIREWALL STATUS
# default   EgressFirewall Rules applied

# Test: allowed traffic
oc exec -n production app-pod -- curl -m5 https://api.example.com    # allowed
oc exec -n production app-pod -- curl -m5 https://10.100.0.5         # allowed

# Test: blocked traffic (times out — Deny rule drops silently)
oc exec -n production app-pod -- curl -m5 https://google.com
# curl: (28) Connection timed out after 5001 milliseconds

# View OVN ACLs generated from EgressFirewall
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl find ACL external_ids:egressFirewall=production | head -30

docs.title: 6. EgressFirewall Configuration Reference
docs.text: Parameter Values Effect When to change spec.egress[].type Allow / Deny Permit or block matching traffic First match wins — order rules carefully spec.egress[].to.cidrSelector CIDR string Match by destination IP range Use for RFC1918 or known IP blocks spec.egress[].to.dnsName FQDN or *.example.com Match by DNS name (OVN resolves it) Use for SaaS APIs with dynamic IPs spec.egress[].ports[].protocol TCP / UDP / SCTP Protocol filter per rule Omit to match all protocols spec.egress[].ports[].port 1–65535 Port filter per rule Combine with CIDR for precise control

docs.title: 7. DNS-Based EgressFirewall Rules
docs.text:
DNS-based rules are resolved by the OVN-Kubernetes DNS interceptor — it polls DNS and updates ACLs when IPs change:

egress:
  - type: Allow
    to:
      dnsName: "*.amazonaws.com"   # wildcard DNS names supported
    ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 443

# Check how OVN resolves DNS names for the firewall
oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -c northd | grep -i dns | tail -20

# Check DNS cache TTL used by OVN
oc exec -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -- \
  ovn-nbctl find DNS | grep -E "records|external_ids"

# Important: DNS rules are eventually consistent (up to TTL seconds)
# For highly dynamic IPs, use CIDR rules instead

docs.title: 8. EgressFirewall on Legacy OpenShift SDN
docs.text:
On older clusters using OpenShift SDN, EgressFirewall is a different resource:

# Check which network type you have
oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.networkType}'
# OVNKubernetes → use EgressFirewall (k8s.ovn.org/v1)
# OpenShiftSDN  → use EgressNetworkPolicy (network.openshift.io/v1)

# Legacy — OpenShift SDN only
apiVersion: network.openshift.io/v1
kind: EgressNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: production
spec:
  egress:
    - type: Allow
      to:
        cidrSelector: 10.100.0.0/16
    - type: Deny
      to:
        cidrSelector: 0.0.0.0/0

docs.title: 9. EgressRouter (Legacy — Redirect Mode)
docs.text:
EgressRouter is an older mechanism that deploys a dedicated pod acting as a fixed-destination traffic redirector. Largely superseded by EgressIP + EgressFirewall.

# Check if any EgressRouter resources exist
oc get egressrouter -A 2>/dev/null

# EgressRouter use case: redirect all traffic from a namespace to a fixed IP
# Rarely needed in OVN-Kubernetes deployments
# Prefer EgressIP for stable source IP + EgressFirewall for destination control

docs.title: Industry Applications
docs.text: Company / Project Context Technology from this lesson Outcome Telcos (billing systems) Regulatory compliance — fixed source IP for call data record APIs EgressIP per namespace for billing-processor pods Stable 192.168.x.x source regardless of pod rescheduling; firewall whitelist never changes SAP BTP Restrict pod egress to approved API endpoints only EgressFirewall with CIDR + DNS-based allow rules Only approved SaaS endpoints reachable from tenant namespaces; all other egress blocked Financial institutions (PCI) Payment gateway fixed-IP whitelisting EgressIP + EgressFirewall on payment-processor namespace PCI DSS requirement for fixed source IP to acquirer gateway met without static pods Healthcare (HIPAA) PHI workload egress to on-prem EHR system EgressIP (stable src) + EgressFirewall (CIDR allow for EHR subnet) HIPAA audit: every PHI egress flow from known fixed IPs to whitelisted CIDR only

docs.text:

oc get egressip -o wide 2>/dev/null

'NAME:.metadata.name,EGRESS:.metadata.labels.k8s\.ovn\.org/egress-assignable'

docs.text:
# Step 1 — label worker nodes as EgressIP candidates
oc label node worker-1 k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable=""
oc label node worker-2 k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable=""

Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix EgressIP not assigned to any node No nodes labeled k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable oc get nodes -l k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable Label at least 2 worker nodes with the egress-assignable label EgressIP assigned but pod still uses node IP Namespace not labeled / label mismatch oc get ns <ns> --show-labels Match namespace label to egressIPs.spec.namespaceSelector.matchLabels EgressIP not in node subnet IP not routable on node's NIC — OVN can't add it oc get egressip <name> -o yaml \| grep conditions Use an IP from the same subnet as the egress node EgressFirewall blocking DNS Missing UDP/TCP port 53 Allow rule at top oc exec -n <ns> pod -- nslookup google.com — SERVFAIL Add explicit Allow rule for 0.0.0.0/0 port 53 before the Deny-all DNS-based rule not matching dynamic IP OVN DNS cache hasn't refreshed yet oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes $MASTER -c northd \| grep dns Wait for TTL expiry; for critical rules use CIDR instead of DNS name EgressFirewall not found Running OpenShift SDN not OVN-Kubernetes oc get network.config.openshift.io cluster -o jsonpath='{.status.networkType}' Use EgressNetworkPolicy for OpenShift SDN EgressIP failover not working Only one egress-assignable node configured oc get egressip -o wide — only one node listed Label a second node; configure a second EgressIP address

# 1. Verify EgressIP assignment

# 2. Verify namespace selector matches

# 3. Test actual source IP from pod

# 4. Check OVN SNAT rules

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• At least 2 nodes labeled k8s.ovn.org/egress-assignable for EgressIP HA
  • EgressIPs are within the subnet CIDR of their assigned nodes and not used by other hosts
  • Each critical namespace has an EgressFirewall with explicit Deny-all as the final rule
  • All EgressFirewall rules include an explicit Allow for DNS (UDP/TCP port 53) before the Deny-all
  • EgressIP failover tested by cordoning the primary egress node and verifying the IP moves
  • DNS-based EgressFirewall rules reviewed — high-TTL domains only; use CIDR for dynamic IPs
  • oc get egressip and oc get egressfirewall -A included in cluster health monitoring

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use a single egress-assignable node No HA — node failure removes the EgressIP entirely Label at least 2 nodes; configure 2 EgressIPs (one per node) Put EgressIP in a different subnet than the node OVN cannot attach the IP as a secondary NIC address Coordinate with network team — EgressIP must be from the node's subnet Write DNS-based EgressFirewall rules for fast-TTL hostnames ACL misses traffic until OVN's DNS cache refreshes Use CIDR-based rules for rapidly changing IP sets; DNS rules for stable SaaS endpoints Forget the DNS Allow rule before the Deny-all All DNS lookups fail — application breaks on first name resolution Always put UDP/TCP port 53 Allow to 0.0.0.0/0 before any broad Deny Use EgressRouter for new deployments EgressRouter is a legacy single-pod redirect — no HA, no policy Use EgressIP (stable source) + EgressFirewall (destination policy) together
