docs.title: Lesson 33 — ArgoCD and GitOps for Network Configuration
docs.text:
Track: GitOps & Delivery Prerequisites: Lesson 22 — Multi-Cluster Networking, Lesson 16 — Network Policies Duration: ~2 hours

Goal: Use ArgoCD to manage NetworkPolicies, CoreDNS configs, and Ingress rules as code — with sync waves for ordered delivery, ApplicationSets for multi-cluster rollout, and drift auto-remediation.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. ArgoCD Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Git["Git Repository"]
        NP["network-policies/"]
        IC["ingress/"]
        CNI["cni-configs/"]
    end
    subgraph ArgoCD["ArgoCD (argocd namespace)"]
        RS["repo-server clones repo renders Helm/Kustomize"] --> Redis[("Redis cache")]
        AC["application-controller watches Application CRDs compares live vs desired"]
        SRV["argocd-server REST API + Web UI + CLI"]
        DEX["Dex OIDC/SSO (optional)"]
    end
    subgraph Clusters["Target Clusters"]
        K1["Cluster 1 NetworkPolicy Ingress"]
        K2["Cluster 2 NetworkPolicy Ingress"]
    end
    Git --"pull every 3 min or webhook push TCP :443"--> RS
    RS --> AC
    AC --"kubectl apply HTTPS :443"--> K1
    AC --"kubectl apply HTTPS :443"--> K2
    SRV --> AC
# Install ArgoCD
kubectl create namespace argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Wait for all pods
kubectl wait --for=condition=available deployment -l app.kubernetes.io/name=argocd-server -n argocd --timeout=120s

# Get initial admin password
argocd admin initial-password -n argocd

# Port-forward the UI (or expose via Ingress/LoadBalancer)
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443

docs.title: 2. GitOps Sync Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Network Engineer
    participant Git as Git Repository
    participant Webhook as GitHub Webhook
    participant ArgoCD as ArgoCD application-controller
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API

    Dev->>Git: git push (new NetworkPolicy or Ingress change)
    Git->>Webhook: POST /api/webhook (if webhook configured)
    Webhook->>ArgoCD: trigger immediate sync
    ArgoCD->>Git: clone / fetch latest revision
    ArgoCD->>K8s: GET live manifests (compare)
    Note over ArgoCD,K8s: Diff: live != desired (OutOfSync)
    ArgoCD->>K8s: kubectl apply (sync waves order)
    K8s-->>ArgoCD: resource events (applied/failed)
    ArgoCD->>ArgoCD: health check (Healthy / Degraded)
    Note over Dev,ArgoCD: selfHeal=true: reverts manual changes automatically
    Dev->>ArgoCD: argocd app get (verify Synced + Healthy)

docs.title: Application — single cluster, single source
docs.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: network-policies
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/your-org/k8s-network-config
    targetRevision: main
    path: network-policies/production
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: default
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true        # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true     # re-apply if someone edits by hand
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

# CLI equivalent
argocd app create network-policies \
  --repo https://github.com/your-org/k8s-network-config \
  --path network-policies/production \
  --dest-server https://kubernetes.default.svc \
  --dest-namespace default \
  --sync-policy automated \
  --auto-prune \
  --self-heal

# Check sync status
argocd app get network-policies
argocd app diff network-policies   # show what would change
argocd app sync network-policies   # force immediate sync

docs.title: Deploying CoreDNS config from Git
docs.text:
# In Git: coredns/configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: coredns
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  Corefile: |
    .:53 {
        errors
        health
        kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
          pods insecure
          fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
        }
        hosts /etc/coredns/NodeHosts {
          ttl 60
          fallthrough
        }
        prometheus :9153
        forward . /etc/resolv.conf
        cache 30
        loop
        reload
        loadbalance
    }
    # Custom stub zone for internal services
    internal.corp:53 {
        forward . 10.100.0.53
    }

ArgoCD will detect drift the moment someone edits this ConfigMap manually.

docs.title: 4. Sync Waves for Network-Dependent Resources
docs.text:
Network resources must deploy in a specific order. A NetworkPolicy that blocks traffic must exist before the app starts, not after.

Sync Wave Order:

Wave -1: CRDs (Gateway API CRDs, Calico CRDs, cert-manager CRDs)
           │
Wave  0: CNI configuration (IPPool, BGPConfiguration, Cilium ConfigMap)
           │
Wave  1: NetworkPolicy (default-deny + allow rules)
           │
Wave  2: Application workloads (Deployments, StatefulSets)
           │
Wave  3: Ingress / Route / HTTPRoute (external access last)
           │
Wave  4: Monitoring (ServiceMonitor — after service exists)

# Wave -1: CRDs first
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"

---
# Wave 0: CNI IP pool
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: IPPool
metadata:
  name: production-pool
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
spec:
  cidr: 10.244.0.0/16
  ipipMode: Never
  natOutgoing: true

---
# Wave 1: NetworkPolicy before the app
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: frontend

---
# Wave 2: Application
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: backend
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "2"

---
# Wave 3: Ingress (only after pods are ready)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: backend-ingress
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "3"

# Watch sync waves progress in real time
argocd app get network-stack --watch

# See which wave each resource is in
argocd app resources network-stack

docs.title: 5. Multi-Cluster Deployment with ApplicationSet
docs.text:
Deploy the same NetworkPolicy baseline to every cluster from a single Application definition.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: network-baseline
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - clusters:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            environment: production   # only prod clusters
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "network-baseline-{{name}}"   # name = cluster name
    spec:
      project: network-team
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/your-org/k8s-network-config
        targetRevision: main
        path: network-baseline/
        helm:
          values: |
            clusterName: "{{name}}"
            clusterCIDR: "{{metadata.annotations.podCIDR}}"
      destination:
        server: "{{server}}"   # cluster API server URL
        namespace: kube-system
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          selfHeal: true

# Register clusters with ArgoCD
argocd cluster add production-eu-west-1 --name eu-west-1
argocd cluster add production-us-east-1 --name us-east-1
argocd cluster add production-ap-southeast-1 --name ap-southeast-1

# Label clusters to match the ApplicationSet generator
kubectl label secret -n argocd eu-west-1 environment=production
kubectl label secret -n argocd us-east-1 environment=production

# ApplicationSet creates one Application per cluster automatically
kubectl get applications -n argocd | grep network-baseline

# Check sync status across all clusters
argocd app list | grep network-baseline

docs.title: 6. Health Checks for Network Resources
docs.text:
ArgoCD has built-in health checks for core Kubernetes resources. Network resources vary:

Resource ArgoCD Health Behavior Service (ClusterIP) Healthy immediately Service (LoadBalancer) Healthy when .status.loadBalancer.ingress is populated Ingress Healthy when .status.loadBalancer.ingress is populated NetworkPolicy Always Healthy — ArgoCD cannot verify enforcement Gateway (Gateway API) Healthy when .status.conditions[Ready]=True HTTPRoute Healthy when parent Gateway accepts it Certificate (cert-manager) Healthy when .status.conditions[Ready]=True

NetworkPolicy is a critical gap — ArgoCD marks it healthy the moment it's applied, but cannot know if the CNI is actually enforcing it.

docs.title: Custom Lua health check for NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
-- In argocd-cm ConfigMap, resource.customizations section:
-- resource.customizations.health.networking.k8s.io_NetworkPolicy: |
hs = {}
if obj.metadata.creationTimestamp == nil then
  hs.status = "Progressing"
  hs.message = "NetworkPolicy not yet created"
  return hs
end
-- Check for a custom annotation set by a policy verification job
if obj.metadata.annotations ~= nil then
  if obj.metadata.annotations["network-policy/verified"] == "true" then
    hs.status = "Healthy"
    hs.message = "Policy applied and verified"
    return hs
  end
end
hs.status = "Degraded"
hs.message = "Policy applied but not verified — run policy conformance test"
return hs

# In argocd-cm ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  resource.customizations.health.networking.k8s.io_NetworkPolicy: |
    hs = {}
    hs.status = "Healthy"
    hs.message = "Applied (enforcement depends on CNI)"
    return hs

docs.title: 7. Detecting Network Policy Drift
docs.text:
selfHeal: true means ArgoCD detects and reverses any out-of-band change within seconds.

# Scenario: network engineer manually tightens a firewall rule
kubectl patch networkpolicy allow-frontend-to-backend -n production \
  --type='json' -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/ingress/0/ports"}]'

# ArgoCD detects the diff within ~3 minutes (or immediately via webhook)
argocd app get network-policies
# STATUS: OutOfSync
# MESSAGE: NetworkPolicy production/allow-frontend-to-backend
#          spec.ingress[0].ports: missing (live) vs [{port:8080}] (desired)

# With selfHeal=true: ArgoCD automatically reverts it
# Without selfHeal: notify and wait for manual sync

# To allow intentional overrides, use ignoreDifferences:
spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: networking.k8s.io
      kind: NetworkPolicy
      jsonPointers:
        - /metadata/annotations/kubectl.kubernetes.io~1last-applied-configuration

# Webhook setup (GitHub): push-triggered sync instead of poll
argocd app set network-policies --sync-policy automated
# Configure webhook in GitHub repo settings:
# URL: https://argocd.your-domain.com/api/webhook
# Secret: $(kubectl get secret argocd-secret -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.data.webhook\.github\.secret}' | base64 -d)

docs.title: 8. Argo Rollouts: Progressive Delivery with Network Integration
docs.text:
Argo Rollouts enables canary and blue-green deployments with network-layer traffic splitting.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: backend
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: backend-canary   # separate Service for canary pods
      stableService: backend-stable   # Service for stable pods
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService:
            name: backend-vsvc
            routes:
              - primary
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10    # 10% traffic to canary
        - pause: {duration: 5m}
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: success-rate
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 5m}
        - setWeight: 100

The VirtualService is updated automatically by the Rollout controller:

# ArgoCD syncs this; Rollouts controller modifies weights during deployment
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: backend-vsvc
spec:
  http:
    - name: primary
      route:
        - destination:
            host: backend-stable
          weight: 90      # Rollout controller updates this
        - destination:
            host: backend-canary
          weight: 10

See also: Lesson 31 — AWS Load Balancer Controller for weighted ALB target groups as an alternative to Istio for canary traffic splitting.

docs.title: 9. Practical: Zero-Trust Network Stack via GitOps
Git repository structure
docs.text:
k8s-network-config/
├── network-baseline/
│   ├── default-deny.yaml         # wave 0: deny-all NetworkPolicy

docs.title: Default-deny as wave 0 (foundation of zero-trust)
docs.text:
# network-baseline/default-deny.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
---
# Always allow DNS (without this, pods can't resolve service names)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - ports:
        - port: 53
          protocol: UDP
        - port: 53
          protocol: TCP

docs.title: ApplicationSet deploying the full stack
docs.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: zero-trust-stack
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - cluster: production-eu
            url: https://eks-eu.example.com
          - cluster: production-us
            url: https://eks-us.example.com
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "zero-trust-{{cluster}}"
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/your-org/k8s-network-config
        path: .
        targetRevision: main
      destination:
        server: "{{url}}"
        namespace: production
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
        syncOptions:
          - RespectIgnoreDifferences=true
          - ServerSideApply=true

docs.title: Hands-On Lab
docs.text:
# 1. Check ArgoCD application health and sync status
argocd app list
# EXPECTED: NAME=network-policies, STATUS=Synced, HEALTH=Healthy

# 2. See current diff between Git and live cluster
argocd app diff network-policies
# EXPECTED: no output (synced) or +/- lines showing drift

# 3. Simulate drift — manually edit a NetworkPolicy
kubectl patch networkpolicy allow-frontend-to-backend -n production \
  --type='json' -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/ingress/0/ports/0","value":{"port":9999}}]'

# 4. Observe ArgoCD detects OutOfSync within 3 min (or faster with webhook)
argocd app get network-policies
# EXPECTED: STATUS=OutOfSync, details show the spurious port 9999

# 5. Force a dry-run sync to preview changes
argocd app sync network-policies --dry-run
# EXPECTED: shows kubectl apply operations that would run

# 6. Trigger real sync to revert the drift
argocd app sync network-policies
# EXPECTED: Synced, NetworkPolicy restored to Git state

# 7. Watch waves progress in an ApplicationSet sync
argocd app sync zero-trust-production-eu
argocd app get zero-trust-production-eu --watch
# EXPECTED: resources sync in wave order -1, 0, 1, 2, 3

# 8. Verify ArgoCD can manage NetworkPolicies (RBAC check)
kubectl auth can-i create networkpolicies \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-application-controller -n production
# EXPECTED: yes

See also: Lesson 16 — Network Policies for NetworkPolicy syntax and default-deny patterns used in wave 0.

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• ArgoCD namespace has wave -1 NetworkPolicy allowing egress to all cluster API servers
  • selfHeal: true enabled on all NetworkPolicy and security-critical Applications
  • prune: true enabled — ghost resources from deleted Git entries are removed
  • AppProject RBAC configured — teams can only sync to their own namespace
  • Webhook configured for sub-minute drift detection (not relying on 3-minute poll)
  • timeout.reconciliation tuned or webhooks used for security-sensitive applications
  • All cluster secrets in ArgoCD are labeled correctly for ApplicationSet generators

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Deploy default-deny without wave -1 ArgoCD allow policy ArgoCD loses access to its own cluster mid-sync Always put ArgoCD self-allow NetworkPolicy at wave -1 selfHeal: false on NetworkPolicies Manual edits (even accidental kubectl apply) persist undetected Enable selfHeal: true for all security-enforcing resources No sync waves — all resources at wave 0 Ingress created before Deployment, NetworkPolicy after app traffic starts Annotate with sync-wave: CRDs first, policies before apps, Ingress last One Application per namespace with no AppProject No team isolation — any ArgoCD user can deploy to any cluster Create AppProject per team with destinations and sourceRepos restricted Managing coredns ConfigMap manually alongside ArgoCD ArgoCD reverts manual DNS changes immediately with selfHeal Commit all CoreDNS changes to Git; use kubectl edit only in ArgoCD-managed PRs

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] Why must network CRDs (such as Gateway or NetworkPolicy CRDs) be deployed in an earlier sync wave than the resources that use them, and what wave number is typically assigned to CRDs?
Answer ArgoCD applies resources in wave order and waits for each wave's resources to become healthy before proceeding to the next wave. If a `Gateway` CRD is deployed in wave 0 at the same time as a `Gateway` object, Kubernetes will reject the `Gateway` object with "no matches for kind" because the CRD hasn't been registered yet. CRDs are typically assigned wave `-1` using the annotation `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"` so they are created and established first. CNI plugins go in wave 0, and higher-level network resources (NetworkPolicy, Gateways, Routes) go in wave 1 or higher.
  1. [Scenario question] An ArgoCD Application syncs a default-deny NetworkPolicy into the argocd namespace in wave 0. Mid-sync, the ArgoCD application controller pod can no longer reach the managed cluster's API server and the sync stalls permanently. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?
Answer The default-deny NetworkPolicy was applied before the ArgoCD allow-ingress policy that permits the application controller to reach the cluster API. As a result, ArgoCD blocked its own control-plane connectivity mid-sync. The fix is to place the ArgoCD allow-ingress NetworkPolicy in wave `-1` or the same wave as the default-deny, so both are applied atomically before ArgoCD's connectivity window closes. Alternatively, place any NetworkPolicy that affects the `argocd` namespace in a separate Application that runs before the main security-hardening Application.
  1. [Practical question] What ArgoCD CLI command would you run to preview the diff between what ArgoCD has cached as the live state and what the Git repository currently contains for a specific Application, without triggering a sync?
Answer 
argocd app diff network-policies
The output shows a standard diff (minus for live, plus for desired) for every resource in the Application. Use this before syncing to confirm that only intended changes will be applied, and to catch accidental drift between what Git says and what is currently running in the cluster.

docs.title: Lesson 34 — AI Platform Networking on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Track: AI Platform Operations Prerequisites: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification, Lesson 07 — Bare Metal Network Infrastructure, Lesson 10 — eBPF and XDP Duration: ~3 hours

Goal: Design and operate the network stack for GPU-intensive AI training clusters — including SR-IOV, RDMA via Multus, rail-optimized topology, NCCL tuning, and lossless RoCE configuration with PFC and ECN.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. Why Standard Kubernetes Networking Fails for AI
docs.text:
A training job for a large model uses NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) to perform all-reduce across all GPUs. All-reduce is a collective: every GPU must send and receive simultaneously.

AllReduce collective (ring algorithm):

GPU0 → GPU1 → GPU2 → GPU3 → GPU4 → GPU5 → GPU6 → GPU7 → (back to GPU0)

Each GPU sends ~(model_size / N) bytes per step.
GPT-3 (175B params, fp16): 350 GB / 8 GPUs = 43 GB per step per GPU
At 100 Gbps NIC:   43 GB / 12.5 GB/s = 3.4 seconds per step    ← too slow
At 400 Gbps NIC:   43 GB / 50 GB/s   = 0.86 seconds per step
Via NVLink (H100): 43 GB / 450 GB/s  = 0.1 seconds per step    ← need NVLink scale-out

Multi-node all-reduce bottleneck: the network between servers is the bottleneck.
H100 NVLink bandwidth within a node: 900 GB/s bidirectional
H100 required inter-node bandwidth: 400 Gbps × 8 NICs = 3.2 Tbps per server

Standard pod networking adds kernel overhead (copy to/from sk_buff, through iptables) that adds microseconds of latency and reduces throughput. RDMA eliminates this.

docs.title: Rail-Optimized Topology
docs.text:
The standard design for GPU clusters. Each GPU in a server has its own NIC connected to a dedicated ToR switch ("rail"). Within a server, GPUs communicate via NVLink; between servers, all-reduce traffic flows over the rails.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Spine["Spine Switches (400 GbE uplinks)"]
        S1["Spine-1 (400 GbE)"]
        S2["Spine-2 (400 GbE)"]
        S3["Spine-3 (400 GbE)"]
        S4["Spine-4 (400 GbE)"]
    end
    subgraph Rails["Leaf / ToR Switches — one per GPU rail"]
        R0["Rail-0 ToR-0 (400 GbE PFC+ECN)"]
        R1["Rail-1 ToR-1 (400 GbE PFC+ECN)"]
        R2["Rail-2 ToR-2 (400 GbE PFC+ECN)"]
        R3["Rail-3 ToR-3 (400 GbE PFC+ECN)"]
    end
    subgraph ServerA["GPU Server A (DGX H100 SXM5)"]
        subgraph NVSwitchFabric["NVSwitch Fabric (3x NVSwitch)"]
            NVS["NVSwitch (900 GB/s all-to-all)"]
        end
        G0["GPU0 H100 80GB + ConnectX-7 NIC0 RoCE v2 UDP :4791"]
        G1["GPU1 H100 80GB + ConnectX-7 NIC1 RoCE v2 UDP :4791"]
        G2["GPU2 H100 80GB + ConnectX-7 NIC2 RoCE v2 UDP :4791"]
        G3["GPU3 H100 80GB + ConnectX-7 NIC3 RoCE v2 UDP :4791"]
        G0 --"NVLink 900 GB/s"--> NVS
        G1 --"NVLink 900 GB/s"--> NVS
        G2 --"NVLink 900 GB/s"--> NVS
        G3 --"NVLink 900 GB/s"--> NVS
    end
    S1 --"400 GbE uplink"--> R0
    S2 --"400 GbE uplink"--> R1
    S3 --"400 GbE uplink"--> R2
    S4 --"400 GbE uplink"--> R3
    R0 --"400 GbE RoCE v2"--> G0
    R1 --"400 GbE RoCE v2"--> G1
    R2 --"400 GbE RoCE v2"--> G2
    R3 --"400 GbE RoCE v2"--> G3

Each NIC connects to a different ToR switch (rail). AllReduce between servers: each GPU uses its own NIC, so no congestion on a single switch. Bisection bandwidth = 8 × 400 Gbps = 3.2 Tbps per server (non-blocking).

docs.title: Fat-Tree (Classic HPC)
docs.text:
Three-tier Clos topology. Standard for InfiniBand clusters. Provides non-blocking bandwidth for any traffic pattern when all switches are equal capacity.

k=4 Fat-Tree: 16 servers, 32 Gbps links

Core switches (k/2)² = 4:   [C1] [C2] [C3] [C4]
Aggregation (k pods × k/2): [A1][A2]  [A3][A4]  [A5][A6]  [A7][A8]
Edge switches (k pods × k/2): [E1..E8]
Servers:                       16 servers, 2 per edge switch

docs.title: 3. InfiniBand vs RoCE vs TCP
docs.text:
Property InfiniBand RoCE v2 TCP/IP Latency ~1 μs ~2–5 μs ~50–100 μs Bandwidth (single link) 200 Gbps (HDR) / 400 Gbps (NDR) 400 Gbps (400GbE) 400 Gbps CPU overhead Near zero (RDMA bypasses CPU) Near zero (RDMA) ~20% CPU per 100 Gbps Requires PFC/ECN No (IB has own flow control) Yes — without it, drops destroy RDMA perf No Cost High (dedicated IB switch fabric) Medium (standard Ethernet ASICs) Low Kubernetes support Via Multus + SR-IOV + RDMA plugin Via Multus + SR-IOV + RoCE config Standard pod networking Cloud availability Azure NDv5, rare AWS EFA (custom), Azure NDv5 Universal

RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) — the key technology behind both IB and RoCE: 

Traditional TCP send:
  App buffer → kernel copy → socket buffer → NIC → wire → NIC → socket buffer → kernel copy → App buffer
  CPU involved at every step, 2 memory copies

RDMA:
  App buffer ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────► App buffer (remote)
  NIC reads/writes directly from app memory via DMA
  Zero CPU cycles on data path, zero copies
  Requires pinned (non-swappable) memory pages (hugepages)

docs.title: 5. NCCL AllReduce Training Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Volcano Scheduler (gang scheduling)
    participant P0 as Pod-0 GPU0 Node-A
    participant P1 as Pod-1 GPU1 Node-B
    participant NCCL as NCCL library (libncclso)

    S->>P0: schedule (all 8 pods start together)
    S->>P1: schedule (gang scheduling)
    P0->>NCCL: init (NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0)
    P1->>NCCL: init
    Note over P0,P1: Rendezvous via management eth0
    NCCL->>NCCL: topology discovery (NVLink > IB > RoCE > TCP)
    NCCL->>P0: assign ring roles
    NCCL->>P1: assign ring roles
    loop Every training step
    P0->>P1: send gradient shard via net1 SR-IOV VF GPUDirect RDMA RoCE v2 UDP :4791
    P1->>P0: send gradient shard via net1 SR-IOV VF GPUDirect RDMA RoCE v2 UDP :4791
        Note over P0,P1: AllReduce completes when all shards aggregated
    end
    P0->>P0: update model weights
    P1->>P1: update model weights

docs.title: 6. SR-IOV: Giving Pods Direct NIC Access
docs.text:
SR-IOV (Single Root I/O Virtualization) partitions one physical NIC into multiple Virtual Functions (VFs). Each pod gets a VF — a hardware NIC slice — bypassing the kernel entirely.

Physical NIC (ConnectX-7, 400 GbE):
  PF (Physical Function) — managed by host
  ├── VF0 ──► Pod A (training job, GPU0)   direct hardware access
  ├── VF1 ──► Pod B (training job, GPU1)   no kernel, no iptables
  ├── VF2 ──► Pod C (training job, GPU2)
  └── VF3 ──► reserved

Performance: ~95% of bare metal NIC performance from inside a pod
Latency:     microsecond-level (vs millisecond for TCP through kernel)

# Install SR-IOV Network Operator
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/k8snetworkplumbingwg/sriov-network-operator/releases/download/v1.3.0/deploy.yaml

# Check physical functions and VF capacity
kubectl get sriovnetworknodestates -n sriov-network-operator -o yaml

# Example SriovNetworkNodePolicy — create 8 VFs on each node's mlx5_0 NIC
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: sriovnetwork.openshift.io/v1
kind: SriovNetworkNodePolicy
metadata:
  name: rdma-mlx5-policy
  namespace: sriov-network-operator
spec:
  resourceName: mlx5_rdma           # kubectl resource name
  nodeSelector:
    feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-15b3.present: "true"   # Mellanox NIC present
  numVfs: 8
  nicSelector:
    pfNames: ["ens4f0"]             # physical function name
  deviceType: netdevice             # or vfio-pci for DPDK
  isRdma: true                      # enable RDMA on VFs
EOF

# Create SriovNetwork (NetworkAttachmentDefinition) for pods to use
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: sriovnetwork.openshift.io/v1
kind: SriovNetwork
metadata:
  name: rdma-net
  namespace: sriov-network-operator
spec:
  resourceName: mlx5_rdma
  networkNamespace: default
  ipam: |
    {
      "type": "whereabouts",
      "range": "192.168.100.0/24"
    }
EOF

docs.title: 7. Multus: Dual NIC Pods (Management + RDMA)
docs.text:
AI training pods need two networks: - eth0 (standard CNI): kubelet health probes, DNS, kubectl exec - net1 (SR-IOV RDMA): high-speed inter-GPU traffic, invisible to kube-proxy

                        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │  Training Pod (GPU0)                      │
                        │                                          │
                        │  eth0: 10.244.0.5/24   (Calico/Cilium)  │◄─── management
                        │  net1: 192.168.100.5/24 (SR-IOV RDMA)   │◄─── NCCL all-reduce
                        │                                          │
                        │  nvidia.com/gpu: 1                       │
                        │  rdma/rdma: 1                            │
                        └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

# Pod using Multus to attach SR-IOV RDMA interface
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: gpu-training-0
  annotations:
    k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: rdma-net   # second NIC from SriovNetwork above
spec:
  containers:
  - name: trainer
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.08-py3
    resources:
      limits:
        nvidia.com/gpu: 1          # one GPU
        rdma/rdma: 1               # one RDMA VF
        hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi         # required for RDMA memory registration
        memory: 32Gi
        cpu: "16"
    volumeMounts:
    - name: hugepages
      mountPath: /dev/hugepages
  volumes:
  - name: hugepages
    emptyDir:
      medium: HugePages
  runtimeClassName: nvidia          # use NVIDIA container runtime
  nodeSelector:
    nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3

# Verify dual NIC inside the pod
kubectl exec -it gpu-training-0 -- ip addr show
# 2: eth0: ...  inet 10.244.0.5/24     ← standard pod network
# 3: net1: ...  inet 192.168.100.5/24  ← RDMA NIC

# Verify RDMA device is accessible
kubectl exec -it gpu-training-0 -- ls /dev/infiniband/
# uverbs0  rdma_cm

# Test RDMA bandwidth (run ibv_rc_pingpong between two pods)
kubectl exec -it gpu-training-0 -- ibv_rc_pingpong -d mlx5_0 -g 0

helm install gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator \
  --namespace gpu-operator \
  --create-namespace \
  --set driver.enabled=true \
  --set mig.strategy=single         # or mixed for per-GPU MIG config

# Install Network Operator
helm install network-operator mellanox/network-operator \
  --namespace network-operator \
  --create-namespace \
  --set deployCR=true               # deploys NicClusterPolicy

# Check GPU allocation across nodes
kubectl get node -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name + " GPUs: " + .status.allocatable["nvidia.com/gpu"]'

# Check RDMA resources
kubectl get node -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name + " RDMA: " + .status.allocatable["rdma/rdma"]'

docs.title: 9. MIG — Multi-Instance GPU Partitioning
docs.text:
NVIDIA H100/A100 support MIG (Multi-Instance GPU): hardware partitioning of one GPU into up to 7 isolated slices. Network engineers need to understand MIG for resource planning.

H100 80GB MIG configurations:

Full GPU:         1×  80GB memory, 100% compute, 1 instance
1g.10gb:          7×  10GB memory, 1/7 compute  (7 instances)
2g.20gb:          3×  20GB memory, 2/7 compute  + leftover
3g.40gb:          2×  40GB memory, 3/7 compute
4g.40gb + 3g.40gb: mixed (1×4g + 1×3g)
7g.80gb:          1×  80GB (full MIG profile = same as no MIG)

# Enable MIG on a node
kubectl label node gpu-node-1 nvidia.com/mig.config=all-1g.10gb

# After operator applies config, see 7 MIG instances:
kubectl get node gpu-node-1 -o json | jq '.status.allocatable | with_entries(select(.key | startswith("nvidia")))'
# "nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb": "7"

# Pod requesting a MIG slice:
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1   # gets 10GB GPU slice, isolated from others

docs.title: 10. NCCL and All-Reduce Tuning
docs.text:
NCCL is the communication library that PyTorch and TensorFlow use for distributed training. It auto-selects the best transport: NVLink > InfiniBand > RoCE > TCP.

# NCCL environment variables (set in Pod env or ConfigMap):
env:
- name: NCCL_DEBUG
  value: "INFO"                    # verbose NCCL logging
- name: NCCL_IB_DISABLE
  value: "0"                       # 0 = use InfiniBand/RoCE, 1 = force TCP
- name: NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL
  value: "5"                       # GPUDirect RDMA: GPU→NIC without CPU
- name: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME
  value: "eth0"                    # management interface (not RDMA) for discovery
- name: NCCL_IB_HCA
  value: "mlx5_0,mlx5_1"          # which RDMA NICs to use
- name: NCCL_TOPO_FILE
  value: "/etc/nccl/topology.xml"  # cluster topology hint for NCCL

# GPUDirect RDMA: data path GPU memory → NIC → wire, bypassing CPU and system RAM
# Requires: nvidia-peermem kernel module + RDMA-capable NIC + CUDA >= 10.1

docs.title: 11. AWS EFA — Elastic Fabric Adapter
docs.text:
AWS's custom RDMA-capable interconnect for P4d/P5 instances running LLM training.

AWS EFA Architecture:

  P4d.24xlarge (8× A100 GPU, 4× EFA)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GPU0  GPU1  GPU2  GPU3  GPU4  GPU5  GPU6  GPU7                │
  │   ↕ NVLink (600 GB/s peer-to-peer within instance)            │
  │  EFA0  EFA1  EFA2  EFA3   (100 Gbps each = 400 Gbps total)    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────-─┘
         ↓ Placement Group (Cluster)
  P4d instance 2  P4d instance 3  ... (all in same AZ, low-latency fabric)

EFA is not Ethernet/IP at the app level — uses libfabric + aws-ofi-nccl plugin

# EKS Pod with EFA (AWS-specific resource)
resources:
  limits:
    hugepages-2Mi: 5120Mi
    vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 4       # request 4 EFA interfaces
    nvidia.com/gpu: 8
    memory: 320Gi
    cpu: "96"
  requests:
    hugepages-2Mi: 5120Mi
    vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 4

# Node selector for P4d instances
nodeSelector:
  node.kubernetes.io/instance-type: p4d.24xlarge

# Install EFA device plugin on EKS
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/amazon-eks-node-problem-detector/main/config/efa-device-plugin.yaml

# Verify EFA allocatable
kubectl get node -l node.kubernetes.io/instance-type=p4d.24xlarge \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.allocatable.vpc\.amazonaws\.com/efa}'
# 4

docs.title: PyTorchJob (Kubeflow)
docs.text:
apiVersion: "kubeflow.org/v1"
kind: PyTorchJob
metadata:
  name: llm-finetune
spec:
  pytorchReplicaSpecs:
    Master:
      replicas: 1
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: pytorch
            image: nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.08-py3
            resources:
              limits:
                nvidia.com/gpu: 8
                rdma/rdma: 8
            env:
            - name: NCCL_IB_DISABLE
              value: "0"
    Worker:
      replicas: 7                  # 8 total nodes × 8 GPUs = 64 GPUs
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: pytorch
            image: nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.08-py3
            resources:
              limits:
                nvidia.com/gpu: 8
                rdma/rdma: 8
  # Volcano gang scheduling: all 8 replicas start together or not at all
  schedulingPolicy:
    minAvailable: 8

docs.title: Ray Cluster
docs.text:
apiVersion: ray.io/v1
kind: RayCluster
metadata:
  name: llm-cluster
spec:
  headGroupSpec:
    serviceType: ClusterIP
    rayStartParams:
      num-cpus: "0"              # head node: no compute, only scheduling
  workerGroupSpecs:
  - groupName: gpu-workers
    replicas: 16
    rayStartParams:
      num-gpus: "8"
      resources: '{"RDMA": 8}'
    template:
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: ray-worker
          image: rayproject/ray-ml:2.9.0-gpu
          resources:
            limits:
              nvidia.com/gpu: 8
              rdma/rdma: 8

docs.title: 13. Network Policy Considerations for AI Clusters
docs.text:
AI training pods have different network requirements than web services:

# Allow all-to-all within the training job (NCCL needs direct pod-to-pod)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-training-job
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      training-job: llm-finetune
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          training-job: llm-finetune   # allow within job
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          training-job: llm-finetune
  - to:                               # allow DNS
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP

Important: RDMA traffic on the secondary network (net1) is NOT subject to Kubernetes NetworkPolicy — NetworkPolicy only applies to the primary pod interface (eth0). To restrict RDMA-plane traffic, use SR-IOV VF admission control or InfiniBand subnet manager partitions (PKeys).

docs.title: 14. Observability for AI Networks
docs.text:
# DCGM metrics (GPU Operator deploys dcgm-exporter automatically)
# Key network-relevant metrics:
#   DCGM_FI_DEV_NVLINK_BANDWIDTH_TOTAL  — NVLink utilization
#   DCGM_FI_DEV_PCIE_TX_BYTES           — PCIe bandwidth (CPU↔GPU)

# View GPU metrics
kubectl port-forward -n gpu-operator svc/dcgm-exporter 9400:9400 &
curl -s localhost:9400/metrics | grep NVLINK

# Network congestion on IB fabric:
kubectl exec -n network-operator ds/mofed-ubuntu22.04 -- \
  perfquery -x 0 1  # port counters: check PortRcvErrors, PortXmitDiscards

# NCCL bandwidth test between two pods
kubectl exec -it gpu-training-0 -- \
  /opt/nccl-tests/build/all_reduce_perf -b 1G -e 16G -f 2 -g 1
# Out-of-band reference: H100×8 DGX on IB NDR should see ~350 GB/s all-reduce

docs.title: 15. Topology-Aware Scheduling
docs.text:
The scheduler must place training pods to minimize network hops. Use topology hints and affinity rules.

# Volcano TopologyPolicy — place pods on same rack if possible
apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1
kind: Queue
metadata:
  name: ai-training
spec:
  weight: 10
  capability:
    nvidia.com/gpu: "64"
---
# Gang scheduling: all pods start simultaneously (critical for NCCL init)
# In PyTorchJob: schedulingPolicy.minAvailable = total replicas

# Node labels for topology:
#   topology.kubernetes.io/zone: us-east-1a
#   topology.kubernetes.io/hostname: gpu-node-07
#   network.topology/rack: rack-03
#   network.topology/rail-switch: tor-07

# Pod affinity: prefer same rack (1 hop) over cross-rack (2 hops)
affinity:
  podAffinity:
    preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    - weight: 100
      podAffinityTerm:
        topologyKey: network.topology/rack
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            training-job: llm-finetune

docs.title: 16. PFC and ECN for RoCE Stability
docs.text:
RoCE requires lossless Ethernet. Without Priority Flow Control (PFC), a single dropped packet can stall RDMA for hundreds of milliseconds.

RoCE Traffic Flow:

Sender NIC → ToR switch buffer fills → 
  WITHOUT PFC: drop packet → RDMA retry (200ms+) → training stall
  WITH PFC:    switch sends PAUSE frame → sender pauses → no drop

Switch configuration (vendor-specific, e.g. Arista EOS):
  interface Ethernet1
    priority-flow-control mode on
    priority-flow-control priority 3 no-drop    # CoS 3 = RDMA/RoCE traffic

ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) + DCQCN:
  Congested switch marks packets with ECN CE bit (instead of dropping)
  Receiver's NIC sends CNP (Congestion Notification Packet) to sender
  Sender's NIC rate-reduces → backpressure without drops

Both PFC and ECN must be configured end-to-end: ToR + spine + server NIC

# On ConnectX NIC (Mellanox): set trust DSCP for RoCE traffic class
mlnx_qos -i ens4f0 --trust dscp
# Set PFC on priority 3
mlnx_qos -i ens4f0 -f 0,0,0,1,0,0,0,0   # enable PFC on priority 3 only

# Verify ECN config
ethtool -A ens4f0   # check pause frames
cat /sys/class/net/ens4f0/ecn_enable   # 1 = ECN enabled

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 — check GPU and RDMA resources on minikube node
minikube ssh
ls /dev/infiniband/ 2>/dev/null || echo "No IB devices (expected in minikube)"
lspci | grep -i "mellanox\|infiniband\|ConnectX" 2>/dev/null || echo "No RDMA NICs"

# Terminal 2 — Mac (kubectl)
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[].status.allocatable | with_entries(select(.key | test("nvidia|rdma|hugepages")))'
kubectl get pods -n nvidia-operator 2>/dev/null || echo "NVIDIA Operator not installed"

Note: Most labs in this lesson require real GPU/RDMA hardware. Use the commands to understand the patterns; the architecture diagrams are the core learning objective here.

docs.title: Hands-On Lab
docs.text:
# 1. Check allocatable GPU and RDMA resources per node
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '
  .items[] |
  .metadata.name as $name |
  .status.allocatable |
  "\($name): GPU=\(.["nvidia.com/gpu"] // "0") RDMA=\(.["rdma/rdma"] // "0") hugepages=\(.["hugepages-2Mi"] // "0")"'

# 2. Verify SR-IOV VFs are created on the node
kubectl get sriovnetworknodestates -n sriov-network-operator -o json | \
  jq '.items[].status.interfaces[] | {name:.name, numVfs:.numVfs, totalvfs:.totalvfs}'

# 3. Confirm Multus is active (secondary networks available)
kubectl get network-attachment-definitions -A
# EXPECTED: rdma-net in the namespace where training pods run

# 4. Launch a test pod with dual NIC and verify interfaces
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: rdma-test
  annotations:
    k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: rdma-net
spec:
  containers:
  - name: test
    image: nicolaka/netshoot
    command: ["sleep","infinity"]
    resources:
      limits:
        rdma/rdma: 1
        hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi
        memory: 4Gi
EOF

kubectl exec rdma-test -- ip addr show
# EXPECTED: eth0 (CNI address) + net1 (SR-IOV RDMA address)

kubectl exec rdma-test -- ls /dev/infiniband/
# EXPECTED: uverbs0 (if RDMA NIC present on node)

# 5. Run NCCL bandwidth test (requires GPU nodes)
kubectl exec -it gpu-training-0 -- \
  /opt/nccl-tests/build/all_reduce_perf -b 128M -e 4G -f 2 -g 1
# EXPECTED: >200 GB/s on H100 with IB NDR fabric

# 6. Check DCGM NVLink metrics (GPU Operator required)
kubectl port-forward -n gpu-operator svc/dcgm-exporter 9400:9400 &
curl -s localhost:9400/metrics | grep -E "NVLINK|PCIE" | head -20

# 7. Verify PFC is active on the RDMA NIC
kubectl debug node/<gpu-node> -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  ethtool -a ens4f0
# EXPECTED: PFC enabled on priority 3

See also: Lesson 07 — Bare Metal Network Infrastructure for ToR switch configuration and ECMP fabric design that underpins rail-optimized GPU clusters.

docs.title: SR-IOV and RDMA Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect When to change numVfs in SriovNetworkNodePolicy 0 Number of VFs to create on the PF Set to 1 per GPU (8 for 8-GPU servers) deviceType netdevice vfio-pci for DPDK/userspace; netdevice for kernel + RDMA Use netdevice for RDMA; vfio-pci for DPDK only isRdma false Expose RDMA resource alongside VF Always true for AI training workloads hugepages-2Mi limit (none) Pre-allocates huge pages for RDMA pinned memory Required for RDMA; set to 2–8 Gi per pod NCCL_IB_DISABLE env (auto) 0 forces IB/RoCE; 1 forces TCP Force 0 to prevent NCCL falling back to slow TCP NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL 0 5 enables GPUDirect RDMA (GPU mem directly to NIC) Set 5 on nodes with nvidia-peermem loaded NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME (auto) Interface for NCCL rendezvous (use management eth0, not RDMA) Always set explicitly on dual-NIC pods

docs.title: PFC/ECN Switch Configuration
docs.text: Parameter Recommended Value Effect Risk if wrong PFC priority 3 (CoS 3 = RDMA) Marks RDMA traffic class as no-drop Wrong priority = PFC not protecting RDMA flows ECN threshold 150–200 KB Buffer fill level that triggers ECN marking Too low = excessive CNPs; too high = too many drops DCQCN alpha 0.0625 Rate reduction factor per congestion event Too high = oscillation; too low = slow convergence MTU (jumbo frames) 9000 bytes Reduces header overhead for large RDMA messages Must match end-to-end: NIC, switch, and remote NIC

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Diagnostic Command Fix NCCL falls back to TCP, training very slow RDMA NIC not visible inside pod or NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1 kubectl exec <pod> -- env \| grep NCCL and ls /dev/infiniband/ Set NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0, verify SR-IOV VF and RDMA resource allocated Pod stuck in Pending with rdma/rdma: 0 available SR-IOV device plugin not running or VFs not created kubectl get pods -n sriov-network-operator Check SriovNetworkNodePolicy and node labels; verify VF count with ip link show on node RDMA bandwidth test shows ~10% of expected PFC not enabled — packet drops causing RDMA retries kubectl exec <pod> -- ibv_devinfo -v \| grep port_state and ethtool -S <nic> \| grep discard Enable PFC on switch and NIC for RDMA traffic class (CoS 3) Training job hangs at NCCL init Gang scheduling failure — not all pods started together kubectl get pods -l training-job=<name> Use Volcano with minAvailable=total_replicas for gang scheduling GPU Operator pods CrashLooping Kernel version incompatible with NVIDIA driver kubectl logs -n gpu-operator <driver-pod> Use GPU Operator with driver.version matching node kernel; use pre-installed driver mode hugepages-2Mi allocation fails Hugepages not pre-allocated on node kubectl describe node <node> \| grep hugepages Add --max-pods=110 --reserved-memory or configure hugepages via NodeFeatureDiscovery NCCL topology file error Pods cannot find topology XML kubectl exec <pod> -- cat $NCCL_TOPO_FILE Mount topology file via ConfigMap or bake into training image

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Rail-optimized topology: each GPU's NIC is on a separate ToR switch (no two GPUs per server share a ToR)
  • PFC enabled on priority 3 end-to-end: server NIC, ToR switch, and spine switch
  • ECN + DCQCN configured on all switches; jumbo frames (MTU 9000) enabled end-to-end
  • SR-IOV VFs created equal to max GPUs per node (1 VF per GPU); isRdma: true
  • NVIDIA GPU Operator and Network Operator both healthy; DCGM exporter shipping metrics
  • Volcano scheduler deployed; all training jobs use schedulingPolicy.minAvailable=total_replicas
  • NCCL env vars set explicitly: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0, NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0, NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5

docs.title: Common Anti-Patterns
docs.text: What people do Why it breaks Correct approach Use standard pod networking (eth0 only) for training Kernel overhead and 10 Gbps limits reduce AllReduce bandwidth by 10-40x Add SR-IOV secondary interface via Multus for RDMA traffic Apply NetworkPolicy to RDMA interface (net1) NetworkPolicy only applies to eth0 — net1 is unmanaged by Kubernetes CNI Use SR-IOV VF ACLs or InfiniBand PKeys for RDMA-plane access control Place multiple GPUs from same server on same ToR AllReduce between servers all competes for one switch uplink Rail-optimized topology: one ToR per GPU rail, never share a ToR within a server No gang scheduling for multi-node jobs Pods start at different times; first pods idle-wait, wasting GPU compute budget Use Volcano gang scheduling with minAvailable = total replicas Disable jumbo frames to avoid MTU mismatches RDMA SEND/RECV efficiency drops 30-50% at 1500 MTU Set MTU 9000 end-to-end: NIC, switch ports, and pod network interface

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Detail Rail-optimized topology Each GPU's NIC on a separate ToR switch — no congestion SR-IOV Hardware NIC partitioning into VFs — pod gets direct NIC access RDMA Zero-copy, zero-CPU data path between GPU memory across nodes InfiniBand Purpose-built RDMA fabric, 200–400 Gbps, used in HPC/AI RoCE v2 RDMA over standard Ethernet, needs PFC+ECN, cheaper than IB Multus Pod gets eth0 (management) + net1 (RDMA) simultaneously NVIDIA GPU Operator Manages GPU drivers, device plugin, MIG, DCGM metrics NVIDIA Network Operator Manages OFED drivers, SR-IOV, RDMA device plugin NCCL AllReduce library — auto-selects NVLink > IB > RoCE > TCP EFA (AWS) AWS-custom RDMA for P4d/P5 instances, 400 Gbps per node NetworkPolicy + RDMA NP only applies to eth0 — RDMA plane needs separate controls PFC + ECN Required for lossless RoCE — configure on every switch and NIC

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. [Concept question] How does RDMA eliminate CPU overhead for GPU-to-GPU communication, and why does this matter for distributed training workloads?
Answer RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) allows the NIC to read from and write directly into application memory (registered GPU or host buffers) using DMA, completely bypassing the CPU and OS kernel. In contrast, conventional TCP communication requires the CPU to copy data into a kernel socket buffer, process TCP/IP headers, and copy again into the application buffer — multiple CPU cycles and memory copies per message. For AllReduce operations in NCCL during distributed training, each rank exchanges gigabytes of gradient data per step; RDMA reduces that exchange latency from microseconds (TCP) to sub-microsecond, and frees GPU-local CPUs to stay focused on the training computation rather than network I/O.
  1. [Scenario question] An NCCL AllReduce operation falls back to TCP/IP instead of RDMA, dramatically slowing a multi-node GPU training job. What two things would you check first to diagnose whether RDMA is unavailable in the pod?
Answer First, check the `NCCL_IB_DISABLE` environment variable inside the pod: if it is set to `1`, NCCL explicitly skips InfiniBand/RDMA. Set it to `0` or remove it. Second, check whether the InfiniBand device is present in the pod by running `ls /dev/infiniband/` — if no devices appear (such as `uverbs0` or `rdma_cm`), the SR-IOV virtual function or RDMA device was not passed through to the pod. Verify that the pod's resource request includes the RDMA resource (e.g. `rdma/hca_shared_devices_a: 1`) and that the RDMA device plugin DaemonSet is running.
  1. [Practical question] What command would you run inside a GPU training pod to verify that InfiniBand RDMA devices are available and accessible to the workload?
Answer 
kubectl exec -it gpu-training-0 -- ls /dev/infiniband/
You should see character devices such as `uverbs0`, `rdma_cm`, and `issm0`. If the directory is empty or does not exist, the RDMA device was not allocated to the pod. Also run `kubectl exec -it gpu-training-0 -- ibv_devinfo` (if `libibverbs` is installed) to list all RDMA devices with their ports and GIDs — a device in `PORT_ACTIVE` state with a valid GID confirms end-to-end RDMA capability.

docs.title: Lesson 35 — Tetragon: eBPF Runtime Security
docs.text:
Track: Security & Compliance · Prereqs: Lesson 10 — eBPF and XDP, Lesson 12 — Cilium CNI and eBPF Dataplane, Lesson 23 — Network Security Hardening · Time: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Deploy Tetragon, write TracingPolicy to enforce syscall and network access controls at the kernel level, correlate runtime security events with Hubble network flows, and produce audit-trail output suitable for HIPAA/PCI-DSS/banking compliance review.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. Why NetworkPolicy Is Not Enough
docs.text:
NetworkPolicy enforces at the network layer: it can allow or deny connections between pods. It cannot answer questions like:

  • Did a process inside this pod call execve("/bin/sh")?
  • Did a container open /etc/shadow?
  • Did a pod establish a TCP connection to an unexpected external IP from a specific binary?
  • Did a privileged process attempt to load a kernel module?

These are runtime security questions. They require observability and enforcement inside the kernel, below the network layer.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Kernel["Linux Kernel"]
        SC["System Call Interface\n(execve, open, connect, write)"]
        NET["Network Stack\n(tcp_connect, sendmsg)"]
        FS["Filesystem Layer\n(vfs_open, vfs_write)"]
    end
    subgraph Tools["What enforces what"]
        NP["NetworkPolicy / iptables\nenforces: IP:port allow/deny\nblind to: which process, which file"]
        TG["Tetragon TracingPolicy\nenforces: syscall-level allow/deny\nsees: process, binary, args, fd, IP"]
    end
    SC --> TG
    NET --> NP
    NET --> TG
    FS --> TG

    style NP fill:#c0392b,color:#fff
    style TG fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff

Tetragon fills this gap. It hooks into the Linux kernel using eBPF kprobes and tracepoints, intercepting syscalls and kernel functions at the source — before they execute — and can enforce policy with a Sigkill or Override action without modifying any application code.

docs.title: 2. Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Node["Kubernetes Node"]
        subgraph Kernel["Linux Kernel"]
            KP["kprobe/kretprobe\n(kernel function hooks)"]
            TP["tracepoint\n(stable kernel ABI hooks)"]
            BM[("BPF Maps\n(ring buffer, hash maps)")]
        end
        subgraph TG["tetragon DaemonSet Pod"]
            AG["tetragon-agent\n(reads BPF ring buffer)"]
            GS["gRPC server\n(:54321)"]
        end
        subgraph App["Application Pod"]
            PR["process (nginx, python, java)"]
        end
    end
    subgraph CP["Control Plane"]
        OP["tetragon-operator\n(reconciles TracingPolicy CRDs)"]
        API["kube-apiserver"]
    end
    subgraph Consumers["Event Consumers"]
        CLI["tetra CLI\n(hubble-style flow viewer)"]
        HUB["Hubble Relay\n(correlated net + process events)"]
        SIEM["SIEM / Splunk / Elastic\n(JSON log export)"]
    end

    PR -->|"syscall: execve/connect/open"| KP
    KP -->|"eBPF program runs: allow/kill/log"| BM
    BM -->|"perf ring buffer"| AG
    AG --> GS
    API -->|"TracingPolicy watch"| OP
    OP -->|"loads eBPF programs onto node"| KP
    GS --> CLI
    GS --> HUB
    AG -->|"JSON to stdout"| SIEM

    style TG fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style Kernel fill:#2d2d2d,color:#fff

Key components:

Component Role tetragon DaemonSet Runs on every node; loads eBPF programs; exports events via gRPC and stdout JSON tetragon-operator Reconciles TracingPolicy and PodInfo CRDs with the API server TracingPolicy CRD Declares which kernel functions to hook, what to match, and what action to take tetra CLI Like hubble observe but for process/syscall events; supports filtering by namespace/pod/binary BPF ring buffer Kernel-to-userspace event delivery — zero-copy, low overhead

docs.title: 3. The TracingPolicy CRD
docs.text:
A TracingPolicy hooks one or more kernel functions or tracepoints and applies match rules. When a match fires, an action runs: Post (log it), Sigkill (terminate the process), or Override (return an error to the syscall).

flowchart LR
    TP["TracingPolicy YAML"]
    subgraph Spec["spec.kprobes[]"]
        KF["call: 'tcp_connect'\n(kernel function name)"]
        subgraph Match["matchArgs[]"]
            M1["arg index: 0\noperator: 'NotEqual'\nvalues: ['10.0.0.0/8']"]
        end
        subgraph Action["matchActions[]"]
            A1["action: Sigkill\n(terminate violating process)"]
        end
    end
    TP --> Spec
    KF --> Match
    Match --> Action

The three action types:

Action Effect Use case Post Log the event, allow execution Audit / detection mode Sigkill Send SIGKILL to the process Enforcement — block and terminate Override Return error code to syscall Enforcement — deny without kill (e.g., return EPERM)

docs.title: Banking / Financial Services (PCI-DSS, MaRisk, FINMA)
docs.text:
PCI-DSS Requirement 10 mandates audit trails of all access to cardholder data. Tetragon provides kernel-level evidence:

  • Which binary accessed which file (vfs_read/vfs_write on PCI-scoped paths)
  • Which process established network connections to payment processors
  • Any shell spawn inside a container (execve with argv[0] = /bin/sh)

docs.title: Medtech / Healthcare (HIPAA)
docs.text: HIPAA Security Rule §164.312(b) requires audit controls. Tetragon satisfies this at the process level — no application-level logging needed.

docs.title: SRE / Platform Engineering (all sectors)
docs.text: Tetragon events correlate with Hubble network flows: you can see "this specific nginx process (PID 12345, in pod frontend-6d7b8) opened a connection to 10.0.1.5:5432 at 14:03:22.001" — microsecond-resolution, process-attributed, kernel-verified.

docs.title: 5. Event Schema
docs.text:
Every Tetragon event is a JSON object with a consistent envelope:

{
  "process_exec": {
    "process": {
      "exec_id": "node-1:1234567890:12345",
      "pid": 12345,
      "uid": 0,
      "binary": "/bin/bash",
      "arguments": "-c whoami",
      "flags": "execve",
      "start_time": "2026-11-25T14:03:22.001Z",
      "auid": 4294967295,
      "pod": {
        "namespace": "production",
        "name": "frontend-6d7b8-xk9p2",
        "container": {
          "id": "containerd://abc123",
          "name": "nginx",
          "image": { "name": "nginx:1.25" }
        }
      },
      "host_name": "node-1"
    },
    "parent": { "pid": 1, "binary": "/usr/sbin/nginx" }
  },
  "time": "2026-11-25T14:03:22.001Z",
  "node_name": "node-1"
}

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
# Terminal 2 (Mac) — Cilium must be installed (Lesson 12)
cilium status
# Ensure cilium-operator and agents are Running

# Install Tetragon via Helm
helm repo add cilium https://helm.cilium.io
helm repo update

helm install tetragon cilium/tetragon \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set tetragon.enableProcessCred=true \
  --set tetragon.enableProcessNs=true

# Verify DaemonSet is running
kubectl get ds -n kube-system tetragon
kubectl rollout status ds/tetragon -n kube-system

docs.title: Lab 1 — Observe process execution (audit mode)
docs.text:
# Terminal 2: Install tetra CLI
GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 curl -L \
  https://github.com/cilium/tetragon/releases/latest/download/tetra-linux-amd64.tar.gz \
  | tar xz -C /usr/local/bin

# Stream all process exec events across the cluster
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact --pods frontend

# Terminal 1 (minikube ssh): trigger an exec event
kubectl exec -it deploy/frontend -- /bin/sh -c "id && whoami"

# You will see in Terminal 2:
# 🚀 process production/frontend-xxx /bin/sh -c "id && whoami"
# 📬 process production/frontend-xxx /usr/bin/id
# 📬 process production/frontend-xxx /usr/bin/whoami
# 💥 exit    production/frontend-xxx /bin/sh -c "id && whoami" 0

docs.title: Lab 2 — Detect and kill shell spawns (enforcement mode)
docs.text:
This TracingPolicy blocks any shell binary executed inside pods with label app=payment-processor — a common banking hardening requirement.

# manifests/35/no-shell-exec.yaml
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata:
  name: no-shell-exec
spec:
  kprobes:
  - call: "security_bprm_check"
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "linux_binprm"
    selectors:
    - matchArgs:
      - index: 0
        operator: "Equal"
        values:
        - "/bin/sh"
        - "/bin/bash"
        - "/usr/bin/sh"
        - "/usr/bin/bash"
        - "/bin/dash"
      matchNamespaces:
      - operator: In
        values:
        - "production"
      matchCapabilities:
      - type: Effective
        operator: NotIn
        values:
        - "CAP_SYS_ADMIN"
      matchActions:
      - action: Sigkill

kubectl apply -f manifests/35/no-shell-exec.yaml

# Verify policy loaded
kubectl get tracingpolicy no-shell-exec

# Try to exec a shell in a production pod — it will be killed
kubectl exec -n production deploy/payment-processor -- /bin/sh
# Output: command terminated with exit code 137 (SIGKILL)

# Tetragon event shows the kill:
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact --namespaces production
# 🚀 process production/payment-xxx /bin/sh
# 🔴 Sigkill  production/payment-xxx /bin/sh (security_bprm_check)

docs.title: Lab 3 — Network egress enforcement by binary identity
docs.text:
This policy kills any process other than nginx that attempts outbound TCP connections on port 443. Useful in medtech to prevent data exfiltration from compromised containers.

# manifests/35/egress-by-binary.yaml
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress-by-binary
spec:
  kprobes:
  - call: "tcp_connect"
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "sock"
    selectors:
    - matchArgs:
      - index: 0
        operator: "DPort"
        values:
        - "443"
      matchBinaries:
      - operator: NotIn
        values:
        - "/usr/sbin/nginx"
        - "/usr/bin/curl"      # allow curl for health checks
      matchNamespaces:
      - operator: In
        values:
        - "production"
      matchActions:
      - action: Sigkill

kubectl apply -f manifests/35/egress-by-binary.yaml

# This will be ALLOWED (nginx making upstream request)
kubectl exec -n production deploy/frontend -- \
  curl -sk https://upstream-api/health

# This will be KILLED (python script attempting unexpected egress)
kubectl exec -n production deploy/frontend -- \
  python3 -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('https://evil.example')"
# terminated with exit code 137

docs.title: Lab 4 — File access audit (HIPAA / PCI-DSS)
docs.text:
Track all reads of sensitive files — no enforcement, audit-only (Post action).

# manifests/35/file-access-audit.yaml
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata:
  name: sensitive-file-audit
spec:
  kprobes:
  - call: "security_file_open"
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "file"
    selectors:
    - matchArgs:
      - index: 0
        operator: "Prefix"
        values:
        - "/etc/ssl/"
        - "/var/run/secrets/"
        - "/proc/1/"
      matchActions:
      - action: Post
        rateLimit: "1m"    # deduplicate: at most 1 event per path per minute

kubectl apply -f manifests/35/file-access-audit.yaml

# Trigger a secret read
kubectl exec -n production deploy/frontend -- \
  cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token

# See the audit event
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents --event-types PROCESS_KPR -o json \
  | jq 'select(.process_kprobe.function_name == "security_file_open")'

docs.title: Lab 5 — Hubble + Tetragon correlation
docs.text:
# Terminal 2: watch Hubble flows for a pod
hubble observe --pod production/frontend-xxx --follow &

# Terminal 2: watch Tetragon events for the same pod
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents --pods frontend-xxx --follow &

# Terminal 1: trigger a database connection
kubectl exec -n production deploy/frontend -- \
  python3 -c "import psycopg2; psycopg2.connect(host='postgres', port=5432)"

# Hubble shows: network flow frontend → postgres:5432 (policy: forwarded)
# Tetragon shows: tcp_connect from python3 PID 9876 to 10.0.1.5:5432
# Combined: you now know WHICH PROCESS made WHICH network call

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix TracingPolicy applied but no events Tetragon agent not running on that node kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=tetragon Pods being killed unexpectedly Overly broad Sigkill policy Switch to Post mode first to audit before enforcing tetra getevents returns nothing Wrong namespace/pod filter Omit filters first: tetra getevents -o compact High CPU on tetragon-agent Too many kprobe hooks Add matchNamespaces or matchCapabilities selectors to narrow scope kprobe: 'xyz' not found Kernel function name varies by kernel version Use tracepoints (tracepoints: key) for stable ABI; check /proc/kallsyms for exact name TracingPolicy stuck in NotReady Incompatible Tetragon/kernel version Check kubectl describe tracingpolicy <name> for error message

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Deploy Tetragon as DaemonSet on all nodes (including control plane if relevant)
  • Start in Post (audit) mode — never enforce before you understand your baseline
  • Add rateLimit to high-frequency kprobes to avoid event flood
  • Export events to SIEM (Splunk/Elastic) via stdout JSON — Tetragon events are structured
  • Write a default policy detecting shell spawns in production namespaces (audit only initially)
  • Correlate Tetragon process events with Hubble network flows for incident investigation
  • Review and tune TracingPolicies after 2 weeks of audit data
  • For PCI-DSS: retain Tetragon events for 12 months (Requirement 10.7)
  • For HIPAA: document Tetragon as your "audit control" in the Security Rule §164.312(b) implementation
  • Pin Tetragon version — kernel hook compatibility must be tested before upgrades

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
# Install Tetragon
helm install tetragon cilium/tetragon -n kube-system

# Stream all events (compact)
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- tetra getevents -o compact

# Filter by namespace
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact --namespaces production

# Filter by pod
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents -o compact --pods frontend-xxx

# Filter by event type (exec only)
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents --event-types PROCESS_EXEC -o compact

# List TracingPolicies
kubectl get tracingpolicy

# Describe a policy (see load status)
kubectl describe tracingpolicy no-shell-exec

# Delete a policy
kubectl delete tracingpolicy no-shell-exec

# Check Tetragon agent logs
kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon --tail=50

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a kprobe and a tracepoint in a TracingPolicy, and when would you prefer each?

  2. A pod in namespace payment is killed with exit code 137 and you find it correlates with a Sigkill action in a TracingPolicy. How do you identify which exact TracingPolicy and which kernel function triggered the kill?

  3. You need to meet HIPAA §164.312(b) audit control requirements using Tetragon. Write the TracingPolicy skeleton that would audit all opens of files under /var/run/secrets/ without killing any processes. What rateLimit would you set and why?

  4. Explain how Tetragon's matchBinaries selector provides a stronger security guarantee than a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy for restricting which processes can make outbound network connections.

  5. A security audit asks: "Can you prove no shell was executed inside pod X between 09:00 and 10:00 on 2026-11-20?" What Tetragon configuration and log retention strategy enables you to answer this question?

docs.title: Lesson 36 — KubeEdge and Industrial Edge Networking
docs.text:
Track: Manufacturing / IoT / Industry 4.0 · Prereqs: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification, Lesson 04 — Network Namespaces Deep Dive, Lesson 16 — Network Policies · Time: ~3 hours

Goal: Deploy KubeEdge, run workloads on edge nodes that survive cloud disconnection, understand how edge networking differs from datacenter networking, and apply IEC 62443–aware network segmentation to an OT/IT boundary.

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. Why Standard Kubernetes Networking Fails at the Edge
docs.text:
A standard Kubernetes node assumes: - Persistent, low-latency connectivity to the API server - Full list-watch capability for all resources - kube-proxy or Cilium can reach cluster DNS

In industrial environments (factory floors, medical devices, wind turbines, logistics warehouses), the network looks different:

Standard DC:              Industrial Edge:

API server ←─ 1ms ─→ node    API server ←─ 200ms ─→ 4G router ←─ intermittent ─→ edge device
Uptime: 99.99%               Uptime: 95% (maintenance windows, RF interference, power events)
Bandwidth: 10 Gbps           Bandwidth: 10–100 Mbps (shared LTE, single fiber)
Topology: flat               Topology: hierarchical (cloud → regional hub → factory → machine)

When an edge node loses connectivity to the API server, standard K8s behavior: - kube-proxy stops getting Service/Endpoint updates - CoreDNS may become unreachable - kubelet cannot list pods → cannot restart crashed pods - DaemonSets cannot reconcile - Workloads stop functioning within minutes

KubeEdge solves this with edge autonomy: the edge node continues operating using a local metadata store, even with no cloud connectivity.

docs.title: 2. KubeEdge Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Cloud["Cloud / Datacenter"]
        API["kube-apiserver"]
        subgraph CE["CloudEdge components"]
            EC["EdgeController\n(sync resources cloud ↔ edge)"]
            DC["DeviceController\n(sync device state/twin)"]
            CS["CloudStream\n(exec/logs tunnel)"]
        end
        API <--> EC
        API <--> DC
    end
    subgraph Edge["Edge Node (factory / hospital / vehicle)"]
        subgraph EE["EdgeCore components"]
            MM["MetaManager\n(SQLite cache of all K8s resources)"]
            EM["EdgeMesh\n(service discovery without cloud DNS)"]
            ES["EdgeStream\n(kubectl exec/logs proxy)"]
            ET["EventBus\n(MQTT broker for IoT devices)"]
            DT["DeviceTwin\n(device state sync, offline buffer)"]
            ED["EdgeHub\n(WebSocket/QUIC to CloudHub)"]
        end
        KL["kubelet\n(reads from MetaManager, not API server)"]
        subgraph Pods["Edge Pods"]
            WL["Workload containers\n(PLC driver, ML inference, sensor aggregator)"]
        end
        subgraph Devices["Physical Devices"]
            PLC["PLC / SCADA sensor"]
            CAM["Camera / Vision AI"]
            ACT["Actuator"]
        end
    end
    subgraph Protocol["Connectivity"]
        WS["WebSocket (primary)\nor QUIC (low-bandwidth)"]
    end

    EC <-->|"resource sync"| WS
    WS <-->|"compressed, resumable"| ED
    ED <--> MM
    MM <--> KL
    KL <--> Pods
    ET <-->|"MQTT"| PLC
    ET <-->|"MQTT"| CAM
    DT <-->|"desired/reported state"| ET
    DC <-->|"device twin sync"| DT
    CS <-->|"tunnel"| ES

    style Cloud fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style Edge fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
    style Devices fill:#5a2d27,color:#fff

docs.title: Key components explained
docs.text: Component Location Role EdgeHub Edge Single WebSocket/QUIC connection to cloud. All sync goes through here. MetaManager Edge SQLite database storing all K8s objects (pods, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Services) for the node. kubelet reads from here, not from API server. EdgeMesh Edge Distributed service proxy. Handles DNS and load balancing for Services, locally, without cloud CoreDNS. EventBus Edge MQTT broker. Bridges IoT device messages into K8s DeviceTwin events. DeviceTwin Edge Maintains desired and reported state for physical devices. Buffers state changes during disconnection. EdgeController Cloud Watches API server; pushes resource changes to edge nodes via CloudHub. DeviceController Cloud Syncs device twin state between cloud and edge. CloudStream Cloud Tunnels kubectl exec and kubectl logs through the WebSocket connection.

docs.title: 3. Disconnected Operation — The Core Value
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Cloud as API Server (cloud)
    participant EH as EdgeHub
    participant MM as MetaManager (SQLite)
    participant KL as kubelet
    participant Pod as Edge Pod

    Note over Cloud,Pod: Normal operation
    Cloud->>EH: Pod spec updated (new image)
    EH->>MM: Write pod spec to SQLite
    MM->>KL: Pod spec available
    KL->>Pod: Pull image, start container

    Note over Cloud,Pod: Network disconnection (factory maintenance)
    Cloud--xEH: Connection lost
    Note over EH: EdgeHub enters offline mode
    Pod->>KL: Container crashes (OOM)
    KL->>MM: Read pod spec from SQLite (no cloud needed)
    MM->>KL: Return cached pod spec
    KL->>Pod: Restart container from local spec

    Note over Cloud,Pod: Reconnection
    EH->>Cloud: Reconnect + sync delta (device twin state, events)
    Cloud->>EH: Push any pending resource updates

During disconnection: - Existing pods restart normally using cached specs from MetaManager SQLite - DeviceTwin buffers device state changes and syncs them when reconnected - New pods cannot be scheduled (scheduler runs in cloud) - kubectl exec and kubectl logs will fail (CloudStream is down)

docs.title: 4. Edge Networking Topology
docs.text:
Industrial edge networks follow a purdue model or ISA-95 hierarchy, with strict layer separation between OT (operational technology) and IT networks.

flowchart TD
    subgraph L4["Level 4 — Enterprise IT (cloud/datacenter)"]
        K8S["Kubernetes control plane\nkube-apiserver, CoreDNS, registry"]
    end
    subgraph L35["Level 3.5 — DMZ (firewall zone)"]
        FW["Firewall / NAT\nOnly port 10000 (CloudHub WebSocket) outbound\nNo inbound connections to OT"]
        PROXY["Optional: forward proxy\nfor image pulls, telemetry"]
    end
    subgraph L3["Level 3 — Site Operations (edge node)"]
        EN["KubeEdge edge node\nEdgeCore, EdgeMesh, containers"]
    end
    subgraph L2["Level 2 — Control Zone (OT network)"]
        HMI["HMI / SCADA server"]
        PLC2["PLC supervisory layer"]
    end
    subgraph L1["Level 1 — Field Devices"]
        PLC1["PLCs, sensors, actuators"]
        CAM["Machine vision cameras"]
    end
    subgraph L0["Level 0 — Process"]
        MACH["Physical machines, conveyors, robots"]
    end

    K8S <-->|"WebSocket :10000\n(only cloud-initiated is edge→cloud)"| FW
    FW <--> EN
    EN <-->|"MQTT :1883 (EventBus)\nor OPC-UA :4840"| HMI
    EN <-->|"MQTT"| PLC2
    PLC2 <--> PLC1
    PLC1 <--> MACH
    CAM <-->|"RTSP / GigE Vision"| EN

    style L4 fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style L35 fill:#5a4a1a,color:#fff
    style L3 fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
    style L2 fill:#5a2d27,color:#fff
    style L1 fill:#4a3060,color:#fff

Critical networking rules for industrial edge:

  1. OT network is never directly reachable from IT. The edge node is dual-homed: one NIC on the IT network (for K8s control plane), one NIC on the OT network (for MQTT/OPC-UA to PLCs).
  2. Only outbound connections from edge to cloud. Cloud-to-edge communication piggybacks on the edge-initiated WebSocket. No inbound ports are opened on the edge firewall.
  3. Edge node must function without NAT hairpin. KubeEdge uses a WebSocket tunnel specifically to avoid this.
  4. Pod-to-PLC communication uses MQTT EventBus, not standard K8s Services — PLC devices are not Kubernetes endpoints.

docs.title: 5. EdgeMesh — Service Discovery Without Cloud CoreDNS
docs.text:
Standard Kubernetes service discovery: pod queries CoreDNS → CoreDNS queries kube-apiserver → returns ClusterIP → kube-proxy routes packet.

This chain breaks when the cloud is unreachable. EdgeMesh replaces it:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Edge["Edge Node"]
        P1["Pod A\n(requests svc-b.ns.svc.cluster.local)"]
        EM["EdgeMesh\n(local DNS proxy + service proxy)"]
        P2["Pod B\n(svc-b target)"]
        MM[("MetaManager\n(cached Service/Endpoint objects)")]
    end

    P1 -->|"DNS query"| EM
    EM -->|"lookup"| MM
    MM -->|"Service: svc-b → 10.96.0.50"| EM
    EM -->|"proxy TCP"| P2
    Note1["No cloud DNS needed\nNo kube-proxy needed\nWorks during disconnection"]

    style EM fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff
    style MM fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff

EdgeMesh intercepts DNS queries via iptables rules, resolves from the local MetaManager cache, and proxies traffic — entirely within the edge node, with zero cloud dependency.

docs.title: 6. IEC 62443 and Kubernetes Networking
docs.text:
IEC 62443 (ISA/IEC 62443) is the international standard for industrial automation and control system (IACS) cybersecurity. It defines zones and conduits:

  • Zone: a grouping of assets with the same security level (Security Level 1–4)
  • Conduit: a controlled communication path between zones

Mapping to Kubernetes:

IEC 62443 concept Kubernetes equivalent Zone Namespace + NetworkPolicy Conduit NetworkPolicy egress/ingress rules between namespaces Security Level (SL) Combination of NetworkPolicy + mTLS + Tetragon enforcement DMZ A dedicated namespace with strict ingress/egress policies Zone boundary enforcement Cilium L7 policy or NetworkPolicy + CNI

See also: Lesson 37 — Compliance Networking for explicit IEC 62443 → NetworkPolicy YAML mappings.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
# Terminal 2 (Mac): Install KubeEdge tooling
# Option A: Use a VM as edge node (recommended for local dev)
# minikube start --driver=virtualbox --nodes=1 --profile=cloud
# OR use an existing K8s cluster as cloud

# Install keadm (KubeEdge admin CLI)
KEADM_VERSION=v1.17.0
