docs.title: Lab 1 — Initialize the cloud side (CloudCore)
docs.text:
# Terminal 2 (Mac): Initialize CloudCore on the K8s cluster
# This installs the KubeEdge CRDs and CloudCore deployment
keadm init --advertise-address=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[0].address}') \
  --set cloudCore.service.type=NodePort \
  --kubeedge-version=1.17.0

# Verify CloudCore is running
kubectl get pods -n kubeedge
# NAME                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# cloudcore-7d9b8f6c5d-xk2p9   1/1     Running   0          2m

# Get the join token for edge nodes
keadm gettoken
# Returns a token like: <hash>.<cert-fingerprint>
# Save this token for Lab 2
TOKEN=$(keadm gettoken)
echo $TOKEN

docs.title: Lab 2 — Join an edge node
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 (minikube ssh OR a separate VM acting as edge node):

# Install EdgeCore on the edge node
# Replace CLOUD_IP and TOKEN with values from Lab 1
CLOUD_IP="<your-cloud-node-ip>"
TOKEN="<token-from-Lab1>"

keadm join \
  --cloudcore-ipport=${CLOUD_IP}:10000 \
  --token=${TOKEN} \
  --kubeedge-version=1.17.0 \
  --cgroupdriver=systemd

# Verify EdgeCore is running on the edge node
systemctl status edgecore

# Terminal 2 (Mac): Verify edge node appears in kubectl
kubectl get nodes
# NAME         STATUS   ROLES        AGE   VERSION
# cloud-node   Ready    control-plane  5m   v1.29.0
# edge-node    Ready    agent,edge     1m   v1.29.0+kubeedge

docs.title: Lab 3 — Deploy a workload to the edge node
docs.text:
# manifests/36/edge-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: sensor-aggregator
  namespace: iot
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: sensor-aggregator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: sensor-aggregator
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        node-role.kubernetes.io/edge: ""    # schedule only on edge nodes
      tolerations:
      - key: "node-role.kubernetes.io/edge"
        operator: "Exists"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
      containers:
      - name: aggregator
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
        args:
        - |
          while true; do
            echo "$(date): sensor reading: $((RANDOM % 100))°C"
            sleep 5
          done
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "16Mi"
            cpu: "10m"
          limits:
            memory: "32Mi"
            cpu: "50m"

kubectl create namespace iot
kubectl label nodes edge-node node-role.kubernetes.io/edge=""
kubectl apply -f manifests/36/edge-deployment.yaml

# Verify pod runs on edge node
kubectl get pods -n iot -o wide
# NAME                                READY   STATUS    NODE
# sensor-aggregator-xxx               1/1     Running   edge-node

# Check logs (routed through CloudStream tunnel)
kubectl logs -n iot deploy/sensor-aggregator

docs.title: Lab 4 — Simulate disconnection and verify autonomy
docs.text:
# Terminal 1 (edge node): block the WebSocket port to simulate disconnection
sudo iptables -I OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 10000 -j DROP

# Wait 30 seconds, then crash the pod manually
kubectl delete pod -n iot -l app=sensor-aggregator --grace-period=0

# Terminal 2 (Mac): kubectl will appear to hang (can't reach edge node)
# But on the edge node itself:

# Terminal 1: check EdgeCore logs — should show reconnect attempts
journalctl -u edgecore -f | grep -E "connect|reconnect|offline"

# Check MetaManager SQLite cache
sqlite3 /var/lib/kubeedge/edgecore.db ".tables"
# Should show: meta, metaV2 tables with cached pod specs

# After ~60 seconds, check if pod restarted
# Terminal 1: list containers directly via containerd
crictl pods
# You should see sensor-aggregator has restarted LOCALLY without cloud

# Restore connectivity
sudo iptables -D OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 10000 -j DROP

# Terminal 2: kubectl recovers
kubectl get pods -n iot

docs.title: Lab 5 — IoT device twin (simulated sensor)
docs.text:
# manifests/36/device-model.yaml
apiVersion: devices.kubeedge.io/v1beta1
kind: DeviceModel
metadata:
  name: temperature-sensor
  namespace: iot
spec:
  properties:
  - name: temperature
    description: "Current temperature reading"
    type:
      int:
        accessMode: ReadOnly
        defaultValue: 25
        unit: "°C"
  - name: status
    description: "Sensor operational status"
    type:
      string:
        accessMode: ReadOnly
        defaultValue: "online"
---
# manifests/36/device-instance.yaml
apiVersion: devices.kubeedge.io/v1beta1
kind: Device
metadata:
  name: factory-temp-sensor-01
  namespace: iot
  labels:
    zone: "assembly-line-1"
spec:
  deviceModelRef:
    name: temperature-sensor
  nodeName: edge-node
  protocol:
    mqtt:
      topic: "factory/sensors/temp/01"
  propertyVisitors:
  - propertyName: temperature
    mqtt:
      topic: "factory/sensors/temp/01/data"

kubectl apply -f manifests/36/device-model.yaml
kubectl apply -f manifests/36/device-instance.yaml

# Verify device created
kubectl get devices -n iot
# NAME                      AGE
# factory-temp-sensor-01    10s

# Simulate device reporting state via MQTT (from edge node)
# Terminal 1 (edge node):
mosquitto_pub -h localhost -t "factory/sensors/temp/01/data" \
  -m '{"temperature": 73}'

# Terminal 2 (Mac): read device twin state
kubectl get device factory-temp-sensor-01 -n iot -o jsonpath='{.status.twins}'

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix Edge node shows NotReady after join CloudCore not reachable on port 10000 Check firewall: telnet <cloud-ip> 10000 from edge node kubectl logs hangs CloudStream not configured or edge offline Check kubectl get pods -n kubeedge — ensure cloudcore is running Pod not scheduled on edge node Missing nodeSelector or taint not tolerated Add nodeSelector: node-role.kubernetes.io/edge: "" and toleration Pod crashes on edge, doesn't restart MetaManager SQLite corrupted Check /var/lib/kubeedge/edgecore.db; restart edgecore: systemctl restart edgecore EdgeMesh DNS not resolving EdgeMesh not installed or iptables rules missing helm install edgemesh edgemesh/edgemesh -n kubeedge; check iptables -t nat -L Device twin not syncing EventBus MQTT topic mismatch Verify spec.protocol.mqtt.topic matches what the device publishes to High latency on edge pod comms Using cluster ClusterIP service (routes via cloud) Use EdgeMesh for edge-local services; label service with service.edgemesh.kubeedge.io/loadbalancer-mode: random

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Edge nodes use dedicated hardware (industrial PC, fanless x86) — not shared with OT control systems
  • Edge node has two NICs: one for IT (K8s control plane), one for OT (PLCs/sensors)
  • Firewall allows only outbound port 10000 (CloudHub WebSocket) from edge to cloud — no inbound
  • MetaManager SQLite on persistent storage (not tmpfs) — survives node reboot
  • EdgeMesh installed for in-cluster service discovery without cloud dependency
  • Container images pre-pulled or mirrored locally — do not pull from cloud registries during operation
  • NetworkPolicy applied to isolate iot namespace from other namespaces
  • DeviceTwin state includes sensor health / last-seen timestamp for dead-sensor detection
  • Tetragon deployed on edge nodes for runtime security (see Lesson 35)
  • Alerting on edgecore service failure (systemd watchdog + cloud-side device availability metrics)
  • Test disconnection scenario: unplug WAN cable, verify workloads keep running for >1 hour
  • Document zone/conduit mapping (IEC 62443) — which namespaces correspond to which security level

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
# Install keadm
curl -LO https://github.com/kubeedge/kubeedge/releases/download/v1.17.0/keadm-v1.17.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz

# Initialize cloud side
keadm init --advertise-address=<IP>

# Get join token
keadm gettoken

# Join edge node
keadm join --cloudcore-ipport=<IP>:10000 --token=<TOKEN>

# Check edge node status
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/edge

# View EdgeCore logs on edge node
journalctl -u edgecore -f

# Check MetaManager SQLite cache
sqlite3 /var/lib/kubeedge/edgecore.db "select * from meta limit 10;"

# Reset edge node
keadm reset

# Install EdgeMesh
helm repo add edgemesh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubeedge/edgemesh/main/build/helm/edgemesh
helm install edgemesh edgemesh/edgemesh -n kubeedge

# List devices
kubectl get devices -A

# Watch device twin state
kubectl get device <name> -n iot -o jsonpath='{.status.twins}' -w

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. A factory edge node loses connectivity to the cloud API server for 4 hours due to a fiber cut. A pod on that node crashes. What happens, step by step? Which component is responsible for restarting it, and where does it get the pod spec from?

  2. Explain the role of the WebSocket connection in KubeEdge. Why is it initiated from the edge to the cloud rather than the other way around? What industrial networking constraint does this satisfy?

  3. You are designing a network for an edge node that processes camera feeds from an assembly line. The node needs to: (a) receive new pod deployments from the cloud Kubernetes cluster, (b) pull OPC-UA data from PLCs on the OT network, (c) never allow OT devices to initiate connections to the IT network. How many NICs do you need, and what firewall rules do you apply?

  4. Map the following IEC 62443 requirements to specific KubeEdge/Kubernetes constructs: (a) Zone isolation between cloud and edge, (b) Conduit with controlled data flow between OT and IT, (c) Availability during partial network failure.

  5. EdgeMesh provides service discovery without cloud CoreDNS. What does it use instead, and what is the operational implication for pod-to-pod communication during a 24-hour cloud disconnection?

Next: Lesson 37 — Compliance Networking See also: Lesson 34 — AI Platform Networking for Multus CNI multi-interface patterns that also apply to industrial edge

docs.title: Lesson 37 — Compliance Networking
docs.text:
Track: Security & Compliance · Prereqs: Lesson 16 — Network Policies, Lesson 12 — Cilium CNI and eBPF Dataplane, Lesson 23 — Network Security Hardening, Lesson 35 — Tetragon Runtime Security · Time: ~3 hours

Goal: Map specific Kubernetes network controls to audit requirements in HIPAA, PCI-DSS, IEC 62443, and GDPR. Produce the exact YAML, CLI commands, and evidence artifacts that satisfy each control — ready to show an auditor.

Jump to: Theory · HIPAA · PCI-DSS · IEC-62443 · GDPR · Practice · Production Checklist · Quick Reference

docs.title: 1. The Compliance Gap No Course Covers
docs.text:
Every K8s security course teaches NetworkPolicy syntax. No course explains which policy satisfies which audit requirement. The result: platform engineers pass CKS but can't answer an auditor's question.

This lesson closes that gap. For each framework, we provide: 1. The exact regulatory text (control number and wording) 2. The K8s network control that implements it 3. The YAML that proves it 4. The evidence artifact an auditor accepts

flowchart LR
    subgraph Frameworks["Regulatory Framework"]
        H["HIPAA\nHealthcare (USA)"]
        P["PCI-DSS v4.0\nPayment cards (global)"]
        I["IEC 62443\nIndustrial OT (DE/CH/global)"]
        G["GDPR Art. 25/32\nData protection (EU/CH)"]
    end
    subgraph Controls["K8s Network Controls"]
        NP["NetworkPolicy\n(L3/L4 segmentation)"]
        CP["CiliumNetworkPolicy\n(L7, FQDN, identity)"]
        WG["WireGuard\n(node-level encryption)"]
        MT["mTLS\n(pod-level encryption)"]
        TG["Tetragon TracingPolicy\n(runtime audit trail)"]
        AE["Audit + Events\n(API audit log + Hubble)"]
    end

    H --> NP
    H --> TG
    H --> AE
    P --> NP
    P --> CP
    P --> WG
    P --> TG
    I --> NP
    I --> CP
    G --> NP
    G --> WG
    G --> MT

docs.title: 2. The CNI Enforcement Prerequisite
docs.text:
Before any compliance claim can be made, verify your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy.

# Test: apply a default-deny policy and verify it works
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: compliance-prereq-test
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
EOF

# From another pod, try to reach a pod in default namespace
# If the connection succeeds → your CNI does NOT enforce NetworkPolicy → STOP
# If the connection is refused → CNI enforces policy → proceed

kubectl delete networkpolicy compliance-prereq-test -n default

CNI plugins that enforce NetworkPolicy: Cilium, Calico, Antrea, WeaveNet CNI plugins that do NOT: Flannel, kubenet (policies are silently ignored)

docs.title: Applicable rules
docs.text:
HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR Part 164) covers three safeguard categories. The network controls in this lesson address:

Rule reference Title Network control §164.312(a)(1) Access Control NetworkPolicy (least-privilege pod access) §164.312(b) Audit Controls Tetragon TracingPolicy (process + network audit trail) §164.312(e)(1) Transmission Security WireGuard / mTLS (encryption in transit) §164.312(a)(2)(iv) Encryption/Decryption WireGuard node encryption

docs.title: HIPAA §164.312(a)(1) — Access Control
docs.text:
Requirement: Implement technical policies that allow only authorized persons or software to access ePHI.

K8s control: Default-deny NetworkPolicy + explicit allow rules scoped to pods that handle ePHI.

# manifests/37/hipaa-default-deny.yaml
# Step 1: Deny all ingress and egress in the ePHI namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: hipaa-default-deny
  namespace: phi-workloads          # namespace containing ePHI-handling pods
  annotations:
    compliance.hipaa/control: "164.312(a)(1)"
    compliance.hipaa/description: "Default-deny: only explicitly authorized pods access ePHI"
spec:
  podSelector: {}                   # applies to ALL pods in namespace
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
---
# Step 2: Allow only the EHR application pod to reach the ePHI database
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: hipaa-allow-ehr-to-db
  namespace: phi-workloads
  annotations:
    compliance.hipaa/control: "164.312(a)(1)"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: phi-database             # the ePHI datastore
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: ehr-application      # only the authorized EHR app
          compliance/phi-access: "approved"
    ports:
    - port: 5432
      protocol: TCP
---
# Step 3: Allow ePHI pods to reach DNS and nothing else by default
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: hipaa-allow-dns
  namespace: phi-workloads
  annotations:
    compliance.hipaa/control: "164.312(a)(1)"
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
    - port: 53
      protocol: TCP

Auditor evidence: kubectl get networkpolicy -n phi-workloads -o yaml — show the policies are present, then demonstrate with a denied connection test.

docs.title: HIPAA §164.312(b) — Audit Controls
docs.text:
Requirement: Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems containing ePHI.

K8s control: Tetragon TracingPolicy logging all file access and process execution in the ePHI namespace.

# manifests/37/hipaa-audit-tracingpolicy.yaml
apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata:
  name: hipaa-phi-audit
  annotations:
    compliance.hipaa/control: "164.312(b)"
spec:
  kprobes:
  - call: "security_file_open"
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "file"
    selectors:
    - matchNamespaces:
      - operator: In
        values:
        - "phi-workloads"
      matchActions:
      - action: Post
        rateLimit: "5m"
  - call: "security_bprm_check"
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "linux_binprm"
    selectors:
    - matchNamespaces:
      - operator: In
        values:
        - "phi-workloads"
      matchActions:
      - action: Post

# Export Tetragon events to a file for audit retention (90-day minimum per HIPAA)
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents --namespaces phi-workloads -o json \
  >> /var/log/hipaa-audit/$(date +%Y%m%d).jsonl

# Verify the audit log contains required fields
# HIPAA requires: date/time, user/process ID, type of access, description of data
cat /var/log/hipaa-audit/$(date +%Y%m%d).jsonl | \
  jq '{time: .time, pid: .process_exec.process.pid, binary: .process_exec.process.binary, pod: .process_exec.process.pod.name}'

Auditor evidence: Show the TracingPolicy is running, then show 30 days of JSON log files with timestamps, process identities, and accessed resources.

docs.title: HIPAA §164.312(e)(1) — Transmission Security
docs.text:
Requirement: Implement technical security measures to guard against unauthorized access to ePHI transmitted over electronic communications networks.

K8s control: WireGuard transparent encryption between all nodes in the ePHI cluster.

# Enable WireGuard encryption in Cilium (encrypts all inter-node pod traffic)
# Requires: Cilium 1.14+, Linux kernel 5.6+
cilium encrypt status    # check current status

helm upgrade cilium cilium/cilium \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set encryption.enabled=true \
  --set encryption.type=wireguard \
  --set encryption.nodeEncryption=true   # encrypt node-to-node traffic too

# Verify encryption is active
cilium encrypt status
# Encryption: Wireguard
# Keys in use: 1
# Max Seq. Number: 0x0/never
# Errors: 0

# Verify on a specific node
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -c cilium-agent -- \
  cilium encrypt status

Auditor evidence: cilium encrypt status output on each node. Optionally: packet capture showing ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) protocol between nodes.

docs.title: Applicable requirements (v4.0)
docs.text:
Req Title Network control 1.3.1 Inbound traffic to CDE restricted NetworkPolicy default-deny + allow rules 1.3.2 Outbound traffic from CDE restricted NetworkPolicy egress rules 1.4.1 NSC between trusted and untrusted networks Namespace isolation + CiliumNetworkPolicy 2.2.1 No unnecessary services/ports NetworkPolicy limiting allowed ports 4.2.1 Strong cryptography for PAN in transit WireGuard / mTLS 7.2.1 Access control based on need-to-know NetworkPolicy + RBAC 10.2.1 Audit log all access to CDE Tetragon + Hubble

The Cardholder Data Environment (CDE) = the namespace(s) containing payment data.

docs.title: PCI-DSS Req 1.3 — CDE Network Segmentation
docs.text:
# manifests/37/pci-cde-segmentation.yaml
# Namespace label: kubernetes.io/metadata.name=payment-cde

# Deny all by default in CDE
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: pci-default-deny
  namespace: payment-cde
  annotations:
    compliance.pci-dss/requirement: "1.3.1, 1.3.2"
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
# Allow only the payment API (from DMZ namespace) to reach card processor
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: pci-allow-payment-api
  namespace: payment-cde
  annotations:
    compliance.pci-dss/requirement: "1.3.1"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: card-processor
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          zone: dmz
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: payment-api
    ports:
    - port: 8443
      protocol: TCP
---
# Allow CDE to reach external payment network (Visa/Mastercard) only via FQDN
# Requires Cilium CiliumNetworkPolicy (standard NetworkPolicy cannot filter by FQDN)
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: pci-cde-egress-fqdn
  namespace: payment-cde
  annotations:
    compliance.pci-dss/requirement: "1.3.2"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: card-processor
  egress:
  - toFQDNs:
    - matchPattern: "*.visa.net"
    - matchPattern: "*.mastercard.com"
    - matchName: "api.stripe.com"
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "443"
        protocol: TCP
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
        k8s-app: kube-dns
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "53"
        protocol: UDP

docs.title: PCI-DSS Req 4.2.1 — Encryption of PAN in Transit
docs.text:
# Option A: WireGuard node-level encryption (encrypts all pod-to-pod traffic transparently)
# (same as HIPAA §164.312(e)(1) above — same cilium encrypt command)

# Option B: mTLS at pod level using Cilium (requires Cilium 1.18+ + ACNS on AKS)
# This provides per-connection cryptographic identity proof
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: pci-require-mtls
  namespace: payment-cde
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: card-processor
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: payment-api
    authentication:
      mode: required      # reject connections without valid mTLS certificate
EOF

# Verify mTLS is active between pods
kubectl exec -n payment-cde deploy/payment-api -- \
  cilium monitor --type policy-verdict | grep "card-processor"

docs.title: PCI-DSS Req 10.2 — Audit Log Access to CDE
docs.text:
# manifests/37/pci-audit-tracingpolicy.yaml
# PCI-DSS Req 10.2.1.1–10.2.1.7 requires logging:
# - All access by individuals with root/admin privileges
# - All access to audit logs
# - Invalid logical access attempts
# - Use of and changes to identification/auth mechanisms
# - Initialization/stopping/pausing of audit logs
# - Creation/deletion of system-level objects

apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1
kind: TracingPolicy
metadata:
  name: pci-cde-audit
  annotations:
    compliance.pci-dss/requirement: "10.2.1"
spec:
  kprobes:
  # Log all privileged process execution (Req 10.2.1.1)
  - call: "security_bprm_check"
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "linux_binprm"
    selectors:
    - matchCapabilities:
      - type: Effective
        operator: In
        values:
        - "CAP_SYS_ADMIN"
        - "CAP_NET_ADMIN"
        - "CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE"
      matchNamespaces:
      - operator: In
        values:
        - "payment-cde"
      matchActions:
      - action: Post
  # Log all network connections from CDE pods (Req 10.2.1.3 — invalid access attempts)
  - call: "tcp_connect"
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: "sock"
    selectors:
    - matchNamespaces:
      - operator: In
        values:
        - "payment-cde"
      matchActions:
      - action: Post
        rateLimit: "1m"

# Verify audit log retention: PCI-DSS Req 10.5.1 requires 12 months (3 months immediately available)
# Configure log rotation:
kubectl create configmap audit-retention -n kube-system \
  --from-literal=retention-days=365 \
  --from-literal=min-available-days=90

Auditor evidence: TracingPolicy spec + 12 months of JSON log files + demonstration that a denied connection attempt appears in logs within 60 seconds.

docs.title: Standard structure relevant to K8s networking
docs.text: Part Title K8s relevance IEC 62443-2-1 Security management system Namespace policies as security zones IEC 62443-3-3 System security requirements Zone/conduit model, SL 1–4 IEC 62443-4-2 Component security requirements Pod-level security (NetworkPolicy, Tetragon)

docs.title: Zone and Conduit Model
docs.text:
IEC 62443-3-3 SR 5.1 (Network Segmentation): "Segment the control system from other systems using boundaries."

flowchart TD
    subgraph Zone4["Zone 4 — SL1 (Enterprise IT)"]
        ERP["ERP / MES systems"]
    end
    subgraph Zone3["Zone 3 — SL2 (Operations)"]
        SCADA["SCADA / Historian"]
        EDGE["KubeEdge node\n(sensor aggregator)"]
    end
    subgraph Zone2["Zone 2 — SL3 (Control)"]
        PLC["PLC supervisory layer"]
    end
    subgraph Zone1["Zone 1 — SL4 (Field)"]
        SENSOR["Sensors / Actuators"]
    end
    C1["Conduit 1\nNetworkPolicy: Zone4→Zone3\nonly port 443/TCP to historian API"]
    C2["Conduit 2\nNetworkPolicy: Zone3→Zone2\nonly MQTT :1883 to EventBus"]

    Zone4 -->|"C1"| Zone3
    Zone3 -->|"C2"| Zone2
    Zone2 --> Zone1
# manifests/37/iec62443-zones.yaml
# Zone = Namespace, Conduit = NetworkPolicy

# Zone 3 → Zone 4 conduit: only historian query (read-only, port 8443)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: iec62443-conduit-z4-to-z3
  namespace: zone-operations           # Zone 3
  annotations:
    compliance.iec62443/requirement: "SR 5.1"
    compliance.iec62443/conduit: "C1"
    compliance.iec62443/security-level: "SL2"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: scada-historian
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          iec62443/zone: "enterprise"  # Zone 4 namespace
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: erp-reporting
    ports:
    - port: 8443
      protocol: TCP
---
# Zone 3 egress to Zone 2: only MQTT to KubeEdge EventBus
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: iec62443-conduit-z3-to-z2
  namespace: zone-operations
  annotations:
    compliance.iec62443/requirement: "SR 5.1"
    compliance.iec62443/conduit: "C2"
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: edge-aggregator
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          iec62443/zone: "control"     # Zone 2 namespace
    ports:
    - port: 1883
      protocol: TCP                    # MQTT to PLC supervisory layer

# Label namespaces with zone metadata for auditing
kubectl label namespace zone-enterprise iec62443/zone=enterprise iec62443/sl=1
kubectl label namespace zone-operations iec62443/zone=operations iec62443/sl=2
kubectl label namespace zone-control    iec62443/zone=control    iec62443/sl=3
kubectl label namespace zone-field      iec62443/zone=field       iec62443/sl=4

docs.title: IEC 62443-4-2 CR 2.1 — Authorization Enforcement
docs.text:
Require authentication before allowing communication between zones:

# manifests/37/iec62443-mtls-conduit.yaml
# Use Cilium mTLS to require cryptographic identity for conduit C1
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: iec62443-conduit-c1-mtls
  namespace: zone-operations
  annotations:
    compliance.iec62443/requirement: "CR 2.1"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: scada-historian
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: zone-enterprise
        app: erp-reporting
    authentication:
      mode: required
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8443"
        protocol: TCP

docs.title: Applicable articles
docs.text: Article Title Network control Art. 25 Data Protection by Design and by Default Default-deny NetworkPolicy Art. 32(1)(a) Encryption of personal data WireGuard / mTLS Art. 32(1)(b) Ongoing confidentiality/integrity Network segmentation + Tetragon Art. 44–49 Transfers to third countries FQDN-based egress control (block non-EU endpoints)

docs.title: GDPR Art. 25 — Data Protection by Design
docs.text:
# manifests/37/gdpr-privacy-by-design.yaml
# Default-deny for any namespace processing personal data
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: gdpr-default-deny
  namespace: user-data
  annotations:
    compliance.gdpr/article: "25"
    compliance.gdpr/description: "Privacy by design: deny all, allow only necessary flows"
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]

docs.title: GDPR Art. 44 — Cross-Border Data Transfer Restriction
docs.text:
Personal data must not leave the EU/EEA unless specific conditions are met. Use Cilium FQDN egress policy to enforce this:

# manifests/37/gdpr-data-residency.yaml
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: gdpr-eu-only-egress
  namespace: user-data
  annotations:
    compliance.gdpr/article: "44"
    compliance.gdpr/description: "Block egress to non-EU endpoints for personal data pods"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      gdpr/personal-data: "true"
  egress:
  # Allow only EU-hosted services (by FQDN)
  - toFQDNs:
    - matchPattern: "*.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com"    # AWS Frankfurt
    - matchPattern: "*.europe-west3.gcp.com"           # GCP Frankfurt
    - matchPattern: "*.northeurope.azure.com"           # Azure Northern Europe
    - matchPattern: "*.westeurope.azure.com"            # Azure Western Europe
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "443"
        protocol: TCP
  # Block everything else implicitly (no other egress rules = deny)
  # Allow DNS
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
        k8s-app: kube-dns
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "53"
        protocol: UDP

# Verify FQDN policy is enforced
kubectl exec -n user-data deploy/user-service -- \
  curl -sk https://api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/  # should be DENIED
# curl: (28) Connection timed out

kubectl exec -n user-data deploy/user-service -- \
  curl -sk https://api.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/health  # should be ALLOWED

docs.title: Lab — Full compliance audit run
docs.text:
# 1. Verify CNI enforces NetworkPolicy
kubectl apply -f manifests/37/hipaa-default-deny.yaml
kubectl run test-pod --image=busybox --rm -it --restart=Never \
  -n phi-workloads -- wget -qO- http://phi-database:5432
# Expected: wget: download timed out (policy enforced)

# 2. Verify WireGuard encryption is active
cilium encrypt status | grep -E "Encryption|Keys"

# 3. Verify Tetragon audit is capturing events
kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/tetragon -c tetragon -- \
  tetra getevents --namespaces phi-workloads -o compact | head -20

# 4. Generate a compliance evidence report
kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | \
  jq '.items[] | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, annotation: .metadata.annotations}' \
  > compliance-evidence/networkpolicies-$(date +%Y%m%d).json

kubectl get ciliumnetworkpolicy -A -o json | \
  jq '.items[] | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}' \
  >> compliance-evidence/networkpolicies-$(date +%Y%m%d).json

# 5. Test data residency (GDPR)
kubectl apply -f manifests/37/gdpr-data-residency.yaml
kubectl exec -n user-data deploy/user-service -- \
  curl -sk --max-time 5 https://api.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/ || echo "BLOCKED (expected)"

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• CNI enforces NetworkPolicy — verify with a deny test, not just kubectl get networkpolicy
  • Default-deny NetworkPolicy in every namespace containing regulated data
  • Namespace labels include compliance annotations (framework, control number)
  • WireGuard encryption enabled for all inter-node traffic (HIPAA §164.312(e)(1), PCI-DSS Req 4.2.1)
  • Tetragon TracingPolicies deployed with Post action — audit before enforcing
  • Log retention: 90 days immediately accessible, 12 months total (PCI-DSS Req 10.5.1)
  • FQDN egress policies deployed for GDPR data residency requirements
  • IEC 62443 zone/conduit model documented and namespace labels match
  • Quarterly audit: run kubectl get networkpolicy -A and validate against control matrix
  • Change management: NetworkPolicy changes require compliance review annotation

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. A PCI-DSS auditor asks: "Show me evidence that cardholder data cannot leave the CDE namespace and reach a non-approved external endpoint." Walk through the exact commands and output you would show them.

  2. You are deploying a medtech application in Germany that must comply with both GDPR and IEC 62443. The application processes patient vital signs from hospital bedside monitors over MQTT. Design the namespace structure and write the two most critical NetworkPolicy objects.

  3. Flannel is the CNI plugin in your cluster. A NetworkPolicy default-deny object exists in the payment-cde namespace. Is PCI-DSS Requirement 1.3 satisfied? Explain your reasoning and what action you must take.

  4. Your HIPAA audit requires proof of "access control" for ePHI. You have NetworkPolicy limiting which pods can reach the ePHI database. The auditor also asks: "What prevents a compromised container inside an allowed pod from exfiltrating data to an external IP?" What additional control do you add, and which YAML in this lesson implements it?

  5. A GDPR data subject requests deletion of their data. During the deletion process, a pod in user-data namespace attempts to call https://backup.us-east-2.amazonaws.com to remove a backup copy. The GDPR egress policy blocks this call. How do you temporarily allow this specific egress while maintaining the data residency posture for all other traffic?

docs.title: Lesson 38 — Multus CNI and Multi-Homed Pods
docs.text:
Track: Track J — Security & Compliance · Prereqs: Lesson 09 — CNI Specification, Lesson 12 — Cilium CNI and eBPF Dataplane · Time: ~2.5 hours

Goal: Deploy Multus CNI, attach secondary network interfaces to pods using NetworkAttachmentDefinitions, and apply multi-homed networking to AI/GPU training workloads, industrial edge nodes, and telco CNFs — covering CKNE Domain 1 (Core Infrastructure & CNI, 15%).

Jump to: Theory · Practice · Troubleshooting · Production Checklist · Quick Reference · Check Your Understanding

docs.title: 1. Why Standard Kubernetes Single-NIC Pods Are Not Enough
docs.text:
Every standard Kubernetes pod gets exactly one network interface (eth0) managed by the primary CNI plugin. This is sufficient for most web services. It fails for:

Use case Why single NIC fails What Multus enables AI/GPU training (NCCL/RDMA) RDMA requires a dedicated NIC on a separate network; mixing RDMA and control-plane traffic on eth0 causes head-of-line blocking Separate eth0 (K8s control) + net1 (RDMA/RoCE on 400 GbE) Industrial edge (OT/IT separation) OT network (MQTT/OPC-UA to PLCs) must be isolated from IT network (K8s API server) eth0 (K8s control, IT network) + net1 (OT network, isolated VLAN) Telco CNFs (5G UPF, vRouter) User-plane and control-plane traffic must be separated; DPDK requires dedicated NIC eth0 (management) + net1 (N3/N6 user-plane) + net2 (N4 control) Network appliances (firewall, IDS) Need multiple interfaces to sit inline between network segments Arbitrary number of interfaces with different subnets

docs.title: 2. Multus Architecture
docs.text:
Multus is a meta-CNI plugin — it does not implement networking itself. Instead, it calls other CNI plugins (delegates) in sequence, attaching one interface per plugin call.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Kubelet["kubelet (node)"]
        CNI["CNI invocation\n(ADD command)"]
    end
    subgraph Multus["Multus CNI (meta-plugin)"]
        M1["1. Read pod annotation\nk8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks"]
        M2["2. Call primary CNI\n(Cilium/Calico/Flannel)\n→ creates eth0"]
        M3["3. For each NetworkAttachmentDefinition\ncall delegate CNI\n→ creates net1, net2, ..."]
    end
    subgraph Delegates["Delegate CNI plugins"]
        D1["macvlan\n(layer 2 secondary NIC)"]
        D2["ipvlan\n(shared MAC, separate IP)"]
        D3["SR-IOV\n(virtual function, hardware NIC)"]
        D4["host-device\n(move physical NIC into pod ns)"]
        D5["bridge\n(Linux bridge attachment)"]
    end
    subgraph Pod["Pod network namespace"]
        E0["eth0\n(primary CNI — K8s cluster network)"]
        N1["net1\n(delegate 1 — RDMA/VLAN/SR-IOV)"]
        N2["net2\n(delegate 2 — optional third interface)"]
    end

    CNI --> M1
    M1 --> M2
    M2 --> M3
    M3 --> D1
    M3 --> D2
    M3 --> D3
    M2 --> E0
    D1 --> N1
    D3 --> N1
    D2 --> N2

    style Multus fill:#1a3a5c,color:#fff
    style Delegates fill:#2d5a27,color:#fff

docs.title: The NetworkAttachmentDefinition CRD
docs.text:
NetworkAttachmentDefinition (NAD) is a Kubernetes CRD from the CNCF Network Plumbing Working Group. It describes one secondary network interface — which CNI plugin to use and its configuration.

flowchart LR
    POD["Pod\nannotation:\nk8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: rdma-net"]
    NAD["NetworkAttachmentDefinition\nname: rdma-net\nspec.config: macvlan config JSON"]
    CNI["macvlan CNI plugin\n(called by Multus)"]
    NIC["net1 interface\n(inside pod)"]

    POD -->|"references by name"| NAD
    NAD -->|"Multus reads config, calls"| CNI
    CNI -->|"creates"| NIC

docs.title: 3. Delegate CNI Plugin Comparison
docs.text: Plugin MAC address Performance Use case macvlan Each pod gets unique MAC Near-wire speed RDMA, storage traffic, secondary VLAN ipvlan L2 Shared parent MAC Near-wire speed DPDK, environments where multiple MACs are blocked ipvlan L3 Shared parent MAC, L3 routing Near-wire speed Multi-subnet pod routing without ARP sr-iov Hardware VF MAC Wire speed, RDMA-capable AI/GPU training, telco, latency-critical host-device Moves physical NIC into pod Wire speed Single-tenant pods needing full NIC access bridge Connects to Linux bridge Moderate Dev/test, internal VLAN switching

docs.title: 4. Use Case: AI/GPU Training (NCCL/RDMA)
docs.text:
NCCL all-reduce across GPU nodes requires all-to-all bandwidth at 400 Gbps. Pod eth0 on the K8s overlay adds latency and bandwidth overhead. The pattern:

eth0 (Cilium/Calico overlay) → used for K8s API, DNS, management
net1 (SR-IOV VF on 400 GbE RDMA NIC) → used exclusively for NCCL all-reduce

Training pods select net1 for NCCL via environment variables: 

NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=net1
NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5_0        # Mellanox HCA on net1

docs.title: 5. Use Case: Industrial Edge (OT/IT Separation)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph EdgePod["Edge Pod (sensor aggregator)"]
        E0b["eth0 — IT network\n10.0.0.5/24\n(K8s API, cloud connectivity)"]
        N1b["net1 — OT network\n192.168.100.5/24\n(MQTT to PLCs, isolated VLAN)"]
    end
    subgraph ITNet["IT Network (K8s overlay)"]
        API["kube-apiserver\nGorouter / Kyma"]
    end
    subgraph OTNet["OT Network (IEC 62443 Zone 2)"]
        PLC["PLC / SCADA\n192.168.100.10"]
    end

    E0b <-->|"K8s control, pod scheduling"| ITNet
    N1b <-->|"MQTT :1883, OPC-UA :4840"| OTNet
    ITNet -.->|"firewall: blocked"| OTNet

This isolates OT traffic completely from the K8s overlay — no CNI policy or iptables rule can accidentally bridge them, because they are on physically separate network paths.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
# Terminal 2 (Mac): Install Multus
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/k8snetworkplumbingwg/multus-cni/master/deployments/multus-daemonset.yml

# Verify Multus DaemonSet is running
kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-multus-ds
kubectl rollout status ds/kube-multus-ds -n kube-system

# Verify NetworkAttachmentDefinition CRD installed
kubectl get crd network-attachment-definitions.k8s.cni.cncf.io

docs.title: Lab 1 — macvlan secondary interface
docs.text:
# manifests/38/macvlan-nad.yaml
apiVersion: k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1
kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition
metadata:
  name: macvlan-conf
  namespace: default
spec:
  config: |
    {
      "cniVersion": "0.3.1",
      "type": "macvlan",
      "master": "eth0",
      "mode": "bridge",
      "ipam": {
        "type": "host-local",
        "subnet": "192.168.1.0/24",
        "rangeStart": "192.168.1.200",
        "rangeEnd": "192.168.1.250",
        "gateway": "192.168.1.1"
      }
    }

kubectl apply -f manifests/38/macvlan-nad.yaml

# Deploy a pod requesting the secondary interface
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: multus-test
  annotations:
    k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: macvlan-conf   # attach net1
spec:
  containers:
  - name: test
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: [sleep, "3600"]
EOF

# Verify pod has two interfaces
kubectl exec multus-test -- ip addr
# Should show: eth0 (K8s overlay) + net1 (macvlan, 192.168.1.x)

# Check Multus annotation status
kubectl get pod multus-test -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.k8s\.v1\.cni\.cncf\.io/network-status}' | python3 -m json.tool

docs.title: Lab 2 — Multiple secondary interfaces
docs.text:
# manifests/38/multi-nad.yaml
apiVersion: k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1
kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition
metadata:
  name: vlan100
  namespace: default
spec:
  config: |
    {
      "cniVersion": "0.3.1",
      "type": "macvlan",
      "master": "eth0",
      "mode": "bridge",
      "ipam": {
        "type": "host-local",
        "subnet": "10.100.0.0/24"
      }
    }
---
apiVersion: k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1
kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition
metadata:
  name: vlan200
  namespace: default
spec:
  config: |
    {
      "cniVersion": "0.3.1",
      "type": "macvlan",
      "master": "eth0",
      "mode": "bridge",
      "ipam": {
        "type": "host-local",
        "subnet": "10.200.0.0/24"
      }
    }

kubectl apply -f manifests/38/multi-nad.yaml

# Pod with 3 interfaces: eth0 + net1 (vlan100) + net2 (vlan200)
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: triple-homed
  annotations:
    k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: vlan100,vlan200
spec:
  containers:
  - name: test
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: [sleep, "3600"]
EOF

kubectl exec triple-homed -- ip addr
# eth0: K8s overlay
# net1: 10.100.0.x
# net2: 10.200.0.x

docs.title: Lab 3 — Interface naming and static IP assignment
docs.text:
# manifests/38/static-ip-nad.yaml
# Assign a specific interface name and static IP via annotation
apiVersion: k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1
kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition
metadata:
  name: rdma-static
  namespace: gpu-workloads
spec:
  config: |
    {
      "cniVersion": "0.3.1",
      "type": "macvlan",
      "master": "eth1",
      "mode": "bridge",
      "ipam": {
        "type": "static"
      }
    }

# Use annotation to specify interface name and static IP
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: gpu-worker-0
  namespace: gpu-workloads
  annotations:
    # name the interface "rdma0", assign static IP
    k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: '[
      {
        "name": "rdma-static",
        "interface": "rdma0",
        "ips": ["192.168.100.10/24"],
        "gateway": ["192.168.100.1"]
      }
    ]'
spec:
  containers:
  - name: trainer
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: [sleep, "3600"]
    env:
    - name: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME
      value: rdma0
EOF

kubectl exec -n gpu-workloads gpu-worker-0 -- ip addr show rdma0
# inet 192.168.100.10/24

docs.title: Lab 4 — Verify network-status annotation
docs.text:
# After pod is running, Multus writes results back to annotation
kubectl get pod multus-test \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.k8s\.v1\.cni\.cncf\.io/network-status}' \
  | python3 -m json.tool

# Output shows each interface with name, mac, IPs:
# [
#   {"name": "", "interface": "eth0", "ips": ["10.244.0.5"], "mac": "...", "default": true},
#   {"name": "default/macvlan-conf", "interface": "net1", "ips": ["192.168.1.200"], "mac": "..."}
# ]

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix Pod stuck in ContainerCreating NAD not found in pod's namespace NADs are namespace-scoped — create NAD in same namespace as pod net1 interface missing Multus DaemonSet not running on that node kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-multus-ds — check node readiness master: eth0 not found in macvlan config The parent interface name differs on the node ip link show on the node — find actual interface name (may be ens3, enp2s0) IP not assigned on net1 IPAM range exhausted Check host-local IPAM state: ls /var/lib/cni/networks/<net-name>/ on the node NCCL not using net1 NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME not set or wrong Set NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=net1 (or the custom interface name) in pod env network-status annotation missing Pod came up before Multus was ready Delete and recreate pod; Multus writes the annotation after successful attachment SR-IOV VFs not available SR-IOV not enabled in BIOS or VF count not set echo 8 > /sys/class/net/ens2f0/device/sriov_numvfs on node; check BIOS SR-IOV setting

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text:
• Multus DaemonSet deployed on all nodes that run multi-homed pods
  • NetworkAttachmentDefinitions are namespace-scoped — create them in every namespace that needs them
  • Parent interface name (master) in NAD config matches actual node interface name
  • SR-IOV VF count configured via node feature discovery or operator — not manually
  • IPAM ranges per NAD do not overlap between nodes (use whereabouts for cluster-wide IPAM instead of host-local)
  • GPU training pods set NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to the RDMA interface name
  • OT/IT isolation: OT interface NAD uses a master that is physically on the OT VLAN — not the K8s overlay NIC
  • NetworkPolicy on eth0 still applies — Multus secondary interfaces are NOT controlled by K8s NetworkPolicy
  • Monitor Multus logs on node: journalctl -u kubelet | grep multus

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
# Install Multus
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/k8snetworkplumbingwg/multus-cni/master/deployments/multus-daemonset.yml

# List NetworkAttachmentDefinitions in a namespace
kubectl get network-attachment-definitions -n <namespace>

# Describe a NAD
kubectl describe network-attachment-definition <name> -n <namespace>

# Check pod interface attachment status
kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.k8s\.v1\.cni\.cncf\.io/network-status}' | python3 -m json.tool

# Check interfaces inside pod
kubectl exec <pod> -- ip addr
kubectl exec <pod> -- ip route

# Check Multus logs on a node
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=multus --tail=50

# List SR-IOV VFs on a node (run via bosh ssh or node shell)
ls /sys/class/net/ens2f0/device/virtfn*

# Set SR-IOV VF count
echo 8 | sudo tee /sys/class/net/ens2f0/device/sriov_numvfs

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
1. A pod annotated with k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: rdma-net is stuck in ContainerCreating. The NAD rdma-net exists in namespace default but the pod is in namespace gpu-workloads. What is the problem and how do you fix it?

  2. You are deploying an edge pod that must communicate with PLCs on a 192.168.100.0/24 OT VLAN (via eth1 on the node) and also receive K8s scheduling from the cloud control plane (via eth0). Write the NAD and pod annotation you would use.

  3. Explain why K8s NetworkPolicy does NOT apply to traffic on Multus secondary interfaces (net1, net2). What can you use instead to control traffic on those interfaces?

  4. A GPU training job uses NCCL for all-reduce across 8 nodes. Despite Multus attaching an SR-IOV VF as net1, NCCL is still routing traffic over eth0. What environment variable is missing from the pod spec, and what value should it have?

  5. You are using host-local IPAM for a macvlan NAD across 20 nodes. After 2 weeks, some pods cannot get an IP on net1. What is the likely cause, and what IPAM plugin should you migrate to?

Previous: Lesson 37 — Compliance Networking See also: Lesson 34 — AI Platform Networking for SR-IOV and RDMA context, Lesson 36 — KubeEdge and Industrial Edge Networking for OT/IT separation patterns

docs.title: Should I Migrate This App Now?
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A([Start: Evaluate App]) --> B{12-factor app?}
    B -- No --> LOW[Score: Low]
    B -- Yes --> C{Stateless or\nexternal state?}
    C -- No --> LOW
    C -- Yes --> D{Runs on Linux cell\nnot Windows?}
    D -- No --> LOW
    D -- Yes --> E{No route service\ndependency?}
    E -- No --> MED[Score: Medium]
    E -- Yes --> F{No isolation\nsegment required?}
    F -- No --> MED
    F -- Yes --> HIGH[Score: High]

    HIGH --> REC1[Migrate Now]
    MED  --> REC2[Migrate Later — address blockers first]
    LOW  --> REC3[Keep on CF or re-architect]

    style REC1 fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style REC2 fill:#e9c46a,color:#000
    style REC3 fill:#c1121f,color:#fff

docs.title: Migration Readiness Checklist
docs.text:
• App follows 12-factor principles (config via env vars, no local state)
  • App is stateless or stores state in an external service (DB, cache)
  • App runs on a Linux Diego cell (not Windows)
  • App does not depend on a route service (inline proxy broker)
  • App does not require an isolation segment; or NodeSelector/Taint equivalent is planned
  • All CF service bindings (CredHub) have a K8s Secret + envFrom.secretRef equivalent mapped
  • C2C network policies are translated to K8s NetworkPolicy podSelector ingress/egress rules
  • ASG egress rules are translated to NetworkPolicy egress ipBlock.cidr entries
  • CF routes are translated to Ingress or Gateway API HTTPRoute/TCPRoute resources
  • Internal routes (apps.internal) are translated to ClusterIP Service + svc.cluster.local DNS
  • Blue-green or canary strategy is defined (Gateway API HTTPRoute backendRefs[].weight)
  • Coexistence period is planned: CF callable from K8s via external route; K8s callable from CF via ASG egress + DNS

docs.title: Quick Scoring Table
docs.text: Criterion Points App is 12-factor 20 Stateless or external state store 20 Runs on Linux cell 15 No route service dependency 15 No isolation segment required 10 All service bindings mapped to K8s Secrets 10 C2C policies translated to NetworkPolicy 5 ASG rules translated to NetworkPolicy egress 5 Total possible 100 Score Recommendation 80 – 100 Migrate Now — all prerequisites met 50 – 79 Migrate Later — resolve blockers (route service, Windows cell, isolation segment) 0 – 49 Keep on CF — re-architect required before migration is viable

docs.title: Lessons in This Migration Track
docs.text:
• mig-01 — Migration Strategy: Strangler Fig Pattern
  • mig-02 — Translation Cookbook: CF Constructs to K8s
  • mig-03 — Coexistence and Cutover

docs.title: Migration Strategy: Strangler Fig Pattern for CF→K8s
Quick Read
docs.text:
Goal: Move workloads from Cloud Foundry to Kubernetes incrementally, one service at a time, using weighted traffic splitting rather than a big-bang cutover.

Core idea — Strangler Fig: - A routing facade sits in front of both CF and K8s backends simultaneously - Traffic weight shifts from CF (100%) toward K8s (100%) per service - CF handles traffic until each function is proven stable in K8s - Rollback at any point = patch the weight back to 100% CF

Key mapping at a glance:

CF construct K8s equivalent cf map-route app domain --hostname h Ingress / HTTPRoute hostnames: cf map-route app apps.internal ClusterIP Service cf add-network-policy src --destination-app dst NetworkPolicy podSelector ASG CIDR/port allow NetworkPolicy egress ipBlock.cidr cf map-route v2 --weight 20 HTTPRoute backendRefs[].weight cf create-route tcp.domain --port 1234 Gateway API TCPRoute Org / Space Namespace Isolation segment NodeSelector + Taint apps.internal DNS svc.cluster.local 0.svc.apps.internal pod-0.svc.ns.svc.cluster.local (StatefulSet) CredHub secret K8s Secret + envFrom.secretRef Route service Istio EnvoyFilter / HTTPRoute filter CF blue-green (cf map-route + weight) Argo Rollouts / HTTPRoute weights Gorouter health check readinessProbe CF environment (BTP) Kyma environment (BTP) — same XSUAA

Canary traffic schedule: - Day 0: 5% K8s — monitor for 10 min, check error rate and p99 latency - Day 1: 20% K8s — if healthy - Day 2: 50% K8s — if healthy - Day 3: 100% K8s — if healthy; CF app stopped (not deleted) for 30-day rollback window

Rule: Never delete the CF app or unmap its route until the rollback window expires.

flowchart LR
    Client --> Facade["Gateway API HTTPRoute\n(weight split)"]
    Facade -->|"95%"| CF["CF App\n(Gorouter)"]
    Facade -->|"5%"| K8s["K8s Pod\n(canary)"]
    CF --> Monitor
    K8s --> Monitor["Prometheus\nerror rate / p99"]

docs.title: Practice Setup
docs.text:
Terminal 1 — minikube (Linux kernel commands): 

minikube start --driver=docker --cpus=4 --memory=8192 \
  --kubernetes-version=v1.30.0
minikube ssh

Terminal 2 — Mac / local (kubectl, cf CLI, gateway API): 

# Install Gateway API CRDs
kubectl apply -f \
  https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.1.0/standard-install.yaml

# Install Istio with Gateway API support
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled

# CF CLI — point at SAP BTP CF environment
cf api https://api.cf.<region>.hana.ondemand.com
cf login --sso

# Verify both platforms are reachable
cf apps
kubectl get nodes

Namespaces used in this lesson: 

kubectl create namespace migration-demo
kubectl create namespace orders
kubectl create namespace inventory

Simulate CF-side and K8s-side backends for local practice: 

# Simulate legacy CF workload (served locally to represent Gorouter backend)
kubectl create namespace cf-side
kubectl create deployment cf-app --image=hashicorp/http-echo:latest \
  --namespace=cf-side -- /http-echo -listen=:5678 -text="hello from CF-side"
kubectl expose deployment cf-app --port=5678 --namespace=cf-side

# Deploy K8s migration target
kubectl create namespace k8s-side
kubectl create deployment k8s-app --image=hashicorp/http-echo:latest \
  --namespace=k8s-side -- /http-echo -listen=:5678 -text="hello from K8s-side"
kubectl expose deployment k8s-app --port=5678 --namespace=k8s-side

docs.title: 1. Strangler Fig Pattern
docs.text:
The Strangler Fig pattern (Martin Fowler, 2004) replaces a legacy system incrementally. A thin routing facade sits in front of both old and new backends. Traffic shifts gradually from the legacy system to the new one — service by service — until the legacy handles zero requests and can be decommissioned.

Applied to CF→K8s: - Facade = Gateway API HTTPRoute (or Istio VirtualService) - Legacy = CF application behind Gorouter - New system = K8s Deployment behind Istio Gateway

The CF Gorouter is modelled as an ExternalName Service in K8s so both backends appear as backend refs in the same HTTPRoute.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Client
    participant GW as Gateway API HTTPRoute
    participant CF as CF Gorouter → CF App
    participant K8s as K8s Service → Pod
    participant Prom as Prometheus

    Client->>GW: HTTPS GET /orders (day 0)
    Note over GW: weight CF=100, K8s=0
    GW->>CF: 100% of traffic
    CF-->>Client: 200 OK

    Note over GW: Migration starts — canary at 5%

    Client->>GW: HTTPS GET /orders (day 1)
    Note over GW: weight CF=95, K8s=5
    GW->>CF: 95% of traffic
    GW->>K8s: 5% of traffic
    CF-->>Client: 200 OK (95% requests)
    K8s-->>Client: 200 OK (5% requests)
    GW-->>Prom: expose per-backend error rate

    Prom-->>GW: K8s error rate < 0.5% — healthy

    Note over GW: Increment to 20% K8s

    Client->>GW: HTTPS GET /orders (day 2)
    Note over GW: weight CF=80, K8s=20

    Note over GW: Full cutover — 100% K8s

    Client->>GW: HTTPS GET /orders (day 3+)
    Note over GW: weight CF=0, K8s=100
    GW->>K8s: 100% of traffic
    K8s-->>Client: 200 OK

    Note over CF: cf stop orders — CF app idle; route retained for rollback

docs.title: HTTPRoute implementing the weighted split
docs.text:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: orders-route
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: main-gateway
  hostnames:
    - "orders.example.com"
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /orders
      backendRefs:
        - name: orders-cf-external   # ExternalName → CF Gorouter
          namespace: cf-side
          port: 443
          weight: 95
        - name: orders-k8s-svc       # K8s Service in orders namespace
          namespace: orders
          port: 8080
          weight: 5

docs.title: CF Gorouter modelled as ExternalName Service
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-cf-external
  namespace: cf-side
spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: orders.cfapps.example.com   # CF public route hostname
  ports:
    - port: 443

docs.title: Incrementing the canary weight without full replacement
docs.text:
# Bump K8s to 20%, CF to 80%
kubectl patch httproute orders-route -n istio-system \
  --type=json \
  -p='[
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/backendRefs/0/weight","value":80},
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/backendRefs/1/weight","value":20}
  ]'

# Full cutover — 100% K8s
kubectl patch httproute orders-route -n istio-system \
  --type=json \
  -p='[
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/backendRefs/0/weight","value":0},
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/backendRefs/1/weight","value":100}
  ]'

docs.title: Coexistence networking
docs.text:
During the migration window both platforms handle live traffic. Cross-platform calls must work in both directions.

CF Cell overlay CIDR:  10.255.0.0/16  (Diego/Silk)
K8s Pod CIDR:          10.244.0.0/16  (minikube/Flannel)
K8s Node CIDR:         192.168.49.0/24

K8s → CF: Create an Istio ServiceEntry so K8s pods can resolve and call the CF Gorouter hostname:

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: cf-gorouter
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  hosts:
    - "*.cfapps.example.com"
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  ports:
    - number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
  resolution: DNS

CF → K8s: CF ASGs must permit egress to K8s node CIDRs:

[{
  "protocol": "tcp",
  "destination": "192.168.49.0/24",
  "ports": "443",
  "description": "K8s cluster ingress"
}]

cf update-security-group k8s-egress asg-k8s.json
cf bind-running-security-group k8s-egress

K8s NetworkPolicy — allow ingress from CF cell overlay:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-cf-cell-ingress
  namespace: orders
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  ingress:
    - from:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 10.255.0.0/16   # CF Silk/Diego cell overlay
      ports:
        - port: 8080

docs.title: 2. Assessment Phase
docs.text: Run the full checklist for every CF application before scheduling its migration slot. Classify each app as: Green (migrate as-is), Amber (requires refactor), or Red (block — deep dependency or unsupported feature).

docs.title: 12-Factor App Checklist
docs.text: Factor CF behavior K8s migration action Status I. Codebase Single repo per app Same — no change auto-pass II. Dependencies buildpack-managed Dockerfile / CNB image verify III. Config cf set-env / VCAP_APPLICATION ConfigMap / Secret envFrom migrate IV. Backing services cf bind-service / VCAP_SERVICES ServiceBinding CRD or Secret migrate V. Build/release/run cf push pipeline CI → OCI image → Helm migrate VI. Processes Stateless Diego instances Pod replicas, no local state assess VII. Port binding PORT env var, 8080 default containerPort + ClusterIP Service migrate VIII. Concurrency cf scale -i kubectl scale / HPA migrate IX. Disposability Fast start / graceful stop preStop hook + terminationGracePeriodSeconds assess X. Dev/prod parity CF Spaces map to environments Namespaces per environment migrate XI. Logs stdout → Loggregator firehose stdout → Fluentd / Loki migrate XII. Admin processes cf run-task one-off kubectl create job / CronJob migrate

docs.title: Stateless Check
docs.text:
A CF app that writes to local disk or uses session affinity cannot run with replicas > 1 in K8s without refactoring.

# Check CF manifest for disk dependencies
grep -E 'disk_quota|services' manifest.yml

# Check whether the CF route has session affinity (sticky sessions)
cf curl "/v3/apps/$(cf app myapp --guid)/routes" | jq '.[].options.session_affinity'
# true → app stores session locally → not K8s-ready without Redis/HANA Cloud

# Check for local filesystem writes in CF app source
grep -rE 'File\.open|open\(.*w\)|fs\.writeFile|ioutil\.WriteFile' src/ | head -20

If stateful: externalise state to Redis or HANA Cloud, then use a K8s StatefulSet with PVC for any truly persistent processes.

docs.title: Linux-Only Check
docs.text:
CF Diego cells run Linux only. Confirm no Windows artefacts in source:

grep -rE '\\\\|\.exe|\.dll|CRLF|windows' src/ && echo "FAIL: Windows artefacts found" \
  || echo "PASS: no Windows artefacts"

docs.title: No Route Services Check
docs.text:
CF route services inject an inline HTTP proxy before the app receives the request. There is no native K8s equivalent — the nearest mapping is an Istio EnvoyFilter or an HTTPRoute request filter.

# Identify apps with route service bindings
cf curl /v3/service_route_bindings | \
  jq '.resources[] | {app: .relationships.app.data.guid, route: .relationships.route.data.guid}'

If route services are present, design an Istio EnvoyFilter or external auth/rate-limit sidecar before migration. Classify app as Amber.

docs.title: No TCP Router Check
docs.text:
CF TCP Router exposes arbitrary TCP ports via route mapping. K8s uses Gateway API TCPRoute or a LoadBalancer Service with a static NodePort.

# List TCP routes in CF org
cf curl "/v2/shared_domains" | jq '.resources[] | select(.entity.router_group_type=="tcp") | .entity.name'

# List apps using TCP routes
cf routes | grep tcp

If TCP routes exist: verify the target gateway controller (Istio, Contour, Cilium) supports TCPRoute before migration. Classify app as Amber unless gateway support is confirmed.

TCP route translation: 

# cf create-route tcp.example.com --port 1234
# →
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: TCPRoute
metadata:
  name: legacy-tcp-1234
  namespace: orders
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: main-gateway
      sectionName: tcp-1234
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: legacy-tcp-svc
          port: 1234

docs.title: 3. SAP BTP — CF Environment → Kyma
docs.text: SAP BTP offers both a Cloud Foundry environment and a Kyma environment under the same global account and subaccount. XSUAA (SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service) is the shared identity layer — JWT tokens issued by XSUAA are valid in both environments.

docs.title: Environment comparison
docs.text: Concept SAP BTP CF Environment SAP BTP Kyma Environment Runtime Diego cells (Garden containers) Kubernetes (Gardener-managed) Auth XSUAA — VCAP_SERVICES.xsuaa XSUAA — K8s Secret via BTP Operator Service binding cf bind-service → VCAP_SERVICES JSON ServiceBinding CRD → K8s Secret Networking Gorouter + C2C overlay Istio + NetworkPolicy DNS *.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com Kyma cluster domain Org / Space Org / Space model Namespace model

docs.title: XSUAA token validation — identical in both environments
docs.text:
In CF the app reads credentials from VCAP_SERVICES: 

# CF: inspect XSUAA binding
echo $VCAP_SERVICES | jq '.xsuaa[0].credentials | {url, clientid, verificationkey}'

The app validates: token.iss == credentials.url and token.aud contains the app's xsappname. This logic does not change in Kyma — only the credential source changes.

docs.title: Kyma XSUAA binding via BTP Operator
docs.text:
# ServiceInstance — provision the XSUAA service
apiVersion: services.cloud.sap.com/v1
kind: ServiceInstance
metadata:
  name: orders-xsuaa-instance
  namespace: orders
spec:
  serviceOfferingName: xsuaa
  servicePlanName: application
  parameters:
    xsappname: orders-app
    tenant-mode: dedicated
---
# ServiceBinding — creates a K8s Secret with the same credentials as VCAP_SERVICES
apiVersion: services.cloud.sap.com/v1
kind: ServiceBinding
metadata:
  name: orders-xsuaa-binding
  namespace: orders
spec:
  serviceInstanceName: orders-xsuaa-instance
  secretName: orders-xsuaa-secret
---
# Deployment reads from the secret instead of VCAP_SERVICES
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: orders
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders
          image: registry.example.com/orders:v2
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: orders-xsuaa-secret
          # App reads: clientid, clientsecret, url, xsappname
          # Token validation logic is unchanged from CF version

Verify the binding reconciled: 

kubectl get servicebinding orders-xsuaa-binding -n orders
# STATUS: Ready
kubectl get secret orders-xsuaa-secret -n orders -o jsonpath='{.data}' | \
  jq 'keys'   # clientid, clientsecret, url, xsappname, ...

docs.title: BTP service migration reference
docs.text:
BTP Service CF binding Kyma binding XSUAA cf bind-service app xsuaa-inst ServiceBinding → xsuaa-secret HANA Cloud cf bind-service app hana-inst ServiceBinding → hana-secret Destination Service cf bind-service app dest-inst ServiceBinding → destination-secret Object Store cf bind-service app os-inst ServiceBinding → objectstore-secret

During coexistence, the same XSUAA service instance can be bound in both environments simultaneously. JWT tokens issued by UAA are valid in both CF and Kyma — clients do not need to re-authenticate during the migration window.

docs.title: CredHub → K8s Secret
docs.text:
# CF: retrieve a CredHub secret value (requires cf CLI + credhub CLI)
credhub get -n /cf/$(cf org myorg --guid)/$(cf space myspace --guid)/$(cf app myapp --guid)/DB_PASSWORD

# K8s: store in a Secret
kubectl create secret generic myapp-credentials \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD="<value-from-credhub>" \
  --from-literal=API_KEY="<value-from-credhub>" \
  -n migration-demo

# Reference in Deployment
# envFrom:
#   - secretRef:
#       name: myapp-credentials

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
timeline
    title CF to K8s Migration — 20-Week Timeline
    section Assess
        Week 1  : Route and policy inventory
                : Org/Space → Namespace mapping
        Week 2  : 12-factor checklist per app
                : Classify Green / Amber / Red
                : Publish migration backlog
    section Lift-Shift
        Week 3  : Containerise first batch (Green apps)
                : Namespaces, Secrets, ConfigMaps
        Week 4  : Deploy to K8s at 0% traffic — smoke tests
        Week 5  : Canary at 5% — monitor error rate
        Week 6  : Ramp to 20%, then 50%
        Week 7  : 100% K8s for first batch
                : Amber apps containerised
        Week 8  : All apps at 100% K8s traffic
    section Optimise
        Week 9  : HPA, readinessProbe, livenessProbe
                : Argo Rollouts installed
        Week 10 : Istio mTLS between services
                : NetworkPolicy deny-all baseline
        Week 12 : CredHub → K8s Secrets complete
                : apps.internal → svc.cluster.local
        Week 14 : StatefulSets for formerly stateful apps
                : Load test at 2x peak traffic
        Week 16 : Observability: Loki pipeline, Prometheus metrics
    section Decommission
        Week 17 : CF apps stopped (routes retained for rollback)
        Week 19 : Application owner sign-off
        Week 20 : CF routes unmapped, apps deleted, Space/Org teardown

docs.title: Phase 1 — Assess (weeks 1–2)
docs.text:
• Export all CF routes, network policies, service bindings, and CredHub references.
  • Map each CF Org/Space to a K8s Namespace.
  • Map each isolation segment to a NodeSelector + Taint pair.
  • Run the 12-factor checklist and route services / TCP router checks.
  • Classify every app: Green / Amber / Red.
# Export CF routes for an org
cf curl "/v3/routes?organization_guids=$(cf org myorg --guid)" | \
  jq '.resources[] | {host: .host, path: .path, app: .destinations[].app.guid}'

# Export CF network policies
cf network-policies --output json

# Export ASGs bound to a space
cf security-groups | grep myspace

Deliverable: migration inventory spreadsheet; prioritised backlog.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Lift-and-Shift (weeks 3–8)
docs.text:
Migrate apps with minimal code changes. Goal is functional parity, not optimisation.

Steps per service: 1. Containerise using Cloud Native Buildpacks (pack build). 2. Push image to registry accessible from the K8s cluster. 3. Create namespace mirroring the CF Space. 4. Translate cf set-env variables to ConfigMap and Secret. 5. Translate cf bind-service to ServiceBinding CRD (BTP) or manual Secret. 6. Translate cf add-network-policy to NetworkPolicy (see below). 7. Translate cf map-route to HTTPRoute or Ingress. 8. Deploy with HTTPRoute weight 0% K8s — run smoke tests directly against the K8s Service. 9. Ramp traffic: 5% → 20% → 50% → 100%.

# Step 1: containerise
pack build orders-image \
  --builder paketobuildpacks/builder-jammy-base \
  --path ./orders-src
docker push registry.example.com/orders-image:v1

# Step 3: create namespace
kubectl create namespace orders
kubectl label namespace orders env=production istio-injection=enabled

# Step 6: translate C2C policy to NetworkPolicy
# cf add-network-policy orders --destination-app inventory --protocol tcp --port 8080
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-to-inventory
  namespace: inventory
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inventory
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: orders
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orders
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
EOF

ASG egress translation (CIDR/port allow → NetworkPolicy egress ipBlock): 

# CF ASG: { "protocol":"tcp","destination":"10.10.0.5/32","ports":"5432" }
# →
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-egress-db
  namespace: orders
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 10.10.0.5/32
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 5432

Internal DNS translation: - orders.apps.internal → orders.orders.svc.cluster.local - 0.orders.apps.internal (first CF instance) → orders-0.orders.orders.svc.cluster.local (StatefulSet pod)

docs.title: Phase 3 — Optimise (weeks 9–16)
docs.text:
After functional parity, improve K8s-native characteristics:

# HPA — replaces cf scale -i
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: orders-hpa
  namespace: orders
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: orders
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70

# readinessProbe — replaces Gorouter health check
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
# livenessProbe for crash detection
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 15
  periodSeconds: 20
  failureThreshold: 3

Argo Rollouts blue-green — replaces cf map-route v2 --weight 20:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: orders
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: orders-canary
      stableService: orders-stable
      trafficRouting:
        plugins:
          argoproj-labs/gatewayAPI:
            httpRoute: orders-httproute
            namespace: orders
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
        - setWeight: 20
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
        - setWeight: 100
      analysis:
        templates:
          - templateName: success-rate
        startingStep: 1

docs.title: Phase 4 — Decommission (weeks 17–20)
docs.text:
Only after all services in a CF Space have been: - Running in K8s at 100% traffic for at least 2 weeks with zero P1/P2 incidents - Validated under peak-equivalent load tests - Signed off by the application owner

# Stop CF apps; keep routes mapped for rollback window
cf stop orders
cf stop inventory

# After 30-day rollback window with no incidents:
cf unmap-route orders cfapps.example.com --hostname orders
cf delete orders -f
cf delete inventory -f
cf delete-space production -f -o myorg

docs.title: 5. Rollback Strategy
docs.text: The rollback strategy has three tiers depending on how far decommissioning has progressed. The cheapest rollback is always a weight patch.

docs.title: Tier 1 — Canary phase (weight < 100% K8s)
docs.text:
Rollback is instantaneous while CF still handles any share of traffic:

# Revert immediately to 100% CF
kubectl patch httproute orders-route -n istio-system \
  --type=json \
  -p='[
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/backendRefs/0/weight","value":100},
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/backendRefs/1/weight","value":0}
  ]'

# Confirm CF app is still alive
cf app orders   # expected state: started
curl -s https://orders.cfapps.example.com/health | jq .status

docs.title: Tier 2 — Full cutover (100% K8s, CF app stopped, route still mapped)
docs.text:
# Restart CF app
cf start orders

# Wait for running state
cf app orders

# Traffic still flows to K8s via HTTPRoute; switch weight back to CF
kubectl patch httproute orders-route -n istio-system \
  --type=json \
  -p='[
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/backendRefs/0/weight","value":100},
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/backendRefs/1/weight","value":0}
  ]'

docs.title: Tier 3 — Post-delete rollback (CF app deleted — slow path)
docs.text:
If the CF app has been deleted, rollback requires a full re-push from source:

cf push orders -f manifest.yml
cf bind-service orders orders-db
cf bind-service orders orders-xsuaa
cf restage orders

This is the highest-risk scenario and should require an explicit approval gate. Never reach this tier during active business hours.

docs.title: Automated rollback triggers
docs.text:
Define alert thresholds in your CI/CD pipeline. If any trigger fires during a canary increment, auto-revert to the previous weight step:

Metric Threshold Action HTTP 5xx error rate > 1% over 5 min Revert weight to previous step p99 latency > 2× CF baseline over 5 min Revert weight to previous step Pod CrashLoopBackOff > 2 restarts Revert weight to 0% K8s Readiness probe failures > 30% pods not ready Revert weight to 0% K8s

Argo Rollouts built-in abort: 

# Abort and revert to stable
kubectl argo rollouts abort orders -n orders
kubectl argo rollouts undo orders -n orders

docs.title: Rollback window policy
docs.text: Phase Rollback window Gate to shorten 100% K8s, CF app stopped (not deleted) 30 days Zero P1/P2 in 14 consecutive days 30-day window elapsed CF app deleted Application owner sign-off CF Space decommissioned Permanent (K8s only) —

docs.title: Production Checklist
docs.text: Complete every item before shifting the first production traffic to K8s.

docs.title: Container image
docs.text:
• Image built from pinned base image — no latest tag in FROM
  • Image pushed to private registry with pull secret configured in the namespace
  • Image scan (Trivy / Grype) passes with no critical or high CVEs
  • Container runs as non-root (USER 1000 in Dockerfile)
  • No secrets baked into the image layer

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
• readinessProbe and livenessProbe configured and passing for all pods
  • resources.requests and resources.limits set (CPU + memory)
  • terminationGracePeriodSeconds >= app shutdown time + drain buffer
  • PodDisruptionBudget created (minAvailable: 1 minimum)
  • At least 2 replicas spread across 2 nodes (topologySpreadConstraints)
  • preStop hook delays pod termination to drain in-flight requests

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
• HTTPRoute hostname matches the CF public route hostname exactly
  • TLS certificate covers the hostname (cert-manager or pre-existing Secret)
  • NetworkPolicy: deny-all default (policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]) applied to namespace
  • NetworkPolicy: explicit ingress from gateway pods
  • NetworkPolicy: explicit egress to each backing service (by ipBlock or podSelector)
  • CF ASGs updated to allow egress to K8s node CIDRs (coexistence period)
  • K8s NetworkPolicy allows ingress from CF cell overlay CIDR (coexistence period)
  • Istio ServiceEntry created for each CF Gorouter hostname callable from K8s
  • TCP routes translated to Gateway API TCPRoute with matching port (if applicable)
  • Route services translated to Istio EnvoyFilter (if applicable)

docs.title: Secrets and config
docs.text:
• All cf set-env variables migrated to ConfigMap or Secret
  • All cf bind-service bindings migrated to ServiceBinding CRD (BTP) or manual Secret
  • CredHub references migrated to K8s Secrets with envFrom.secretRef
  • XSUAA binding verified — app starts, reads credentials, validates a JWT end-to-end
  • apps.internal DNS references updated to svc.cluster.local
  • 0.svc.apps.internal references updated to pod-0.svc.ns.svc.cluster.local (StatefulSet)

docs.title: SAP BTP specific
docs.text:
• ServiceBinding for XSUAA reconciles cleanly (kubectl get servicebinding)
  • Kyma cluster domain registered in XSUAA redirect URIs if the app serves OAuth flows
  • CF environment still active in BTP subaccount during the entire coexistence period
  • BTP Operator version is compatible with the Kyma cluster version

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Structured logs flowing to centralised store (Loki / Splunk)
  • Prometheus scrape configured on all pods (annotation or ServiceMonitor)
  • Grafana dashboard: request rate, p50/p99 latency, 5xx rate, pod restarts
  • Alert rules active: error rate > 1% → PagerDuty / Slack
  • Distributed tracing spans correlated between CF and K8s during coexistence

docs.title: Canary gate criteria
docs.text:
• 5% traffic: error rate < 0.5% for 10 minutes
  • 20% traffic: p99 latency within 10% of CF baseline for 10 minutes
  • 50% traffic: no crash loops, readiness > 99% for 10 minutes
  • 100% traffic: stable for 2 hours before stopping CF app

docs.title: Sign-off
docs.text:
• Application owner approved production traffic switch
  • Security review completed (NetworkPolicy least-privilege verified)
  • Rollback runbook tested in staging with a simulated failure
  • On-call engineer briefed; rollback commands pre-written and tested
